papers.abstract: Modern visual generative models operate on tokens, and every visual asset they receive, whether an identity, a scribble, a depth map, or a motion video, is tokenized and appended to the input token sequence. Consequently, conditioning quickly dominates the computation cost. Yet most of these tokens carry redundant spatiotemporal information. Our key insight is that identifying what is genuinely new is exactly the problem that classical video codecs have long solved. Thus, we first introduce a codec-based token pruning method that discards redundant tokens. Then, we propose an on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) strategy to train a DiT adapter capable of learning the codec pruning pattern well without quality degradation. Together, they form On-Policy Codec Distillation (CodecOPSD). We scale CodecOPSD to 16 condition modalities on our own video diffusion model, where it prunes 66% of the condition tokens on average with almost no quality drop. Therefore, denoising becomes 2x faster, and the cache memory shrinks by up to 73% in KV cache mode. CodecOPSD also extends to other state-of-the-art pretrained image and video generative models, where its benefit grows further with more conditions, longer frames, and higher resolution.
authors: Boyang Wang, Kevin Blackburn-Matzen, Oindrila Saha, Matheus Gadelha, Zezhou Cheng
bullets: Condition tokens from modalities such as identity, scribbles, depth, and motion videos create substantial computation and memory costs.
A codec-based pruning method removes redundant spatiotemporal conditioning tokens.
On-policy self-distillation trains a DiT adapter to reproduce the codec’s pruning pattern without degrading quality.
Scaled to 16 conditioning modalities, it prunes 66% of condition tokens on average, makes denoising 2× faster, and reduces KV-cache memory by up to 73%.
Benefits extend to pretrained image and video generators and increase with more conditions, longer videos, and higher resolution.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Pipeline of CodecOPSD. Left: Codec pruning runs in parallel with the VAE encoder and drops condition tokens at a dynamic rate per condition, and the kept tokens concatenate with the noisy latent as the DiT input. It optionally drops the vision tokens of a VLM, which enter the DiT by cross-attention or joint attention depending on the model. Right: On-Policy Codec Distillation provides the tokens removed by codec pruning to the frozen teacher as privileged information and compares the student’s prediction with the teacher’s.

Top: MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA with more reference videos, higher resolution, and more frames; the speedup keeps growing without a clear quality drop relative to the dense teacher. For both speedup and quality, MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA runs the 8-step FastH3-Omni of FastVideo [79]. Bottom: MiniMax-H3-Image with more reference images and higher resolution, which has the same trend. At 20482 pixels, with every module (DiT, VLM, and VAE) loaded on the GPU and no offloading, ours still fits 16 images, while the dense model runs out of memory from 12 images on. Quality averages the five scores of Tab. 4 and the three judge scores of Tab. 5, relative to the dense model.

Figure 5. Per-condition drop rates. We drop the tokens of a single condition at different rates in the order of Eq. 3 and measure quality relative to the teacher in each target metric, for (a) dense conditions and (b) sparse conditions. The grey band is the teacher’s seed noise (±2σ). The green region marks the free drop, where quality stays within this band, and the orange region marks the lossy drop. (c) provides the free drop value of each condition.

Figure 4. Denoising time and memory change. Test cases run at 512×896 with 121 frames, 8 sampling steps [76], and one H200. Ours is faster both without the KV cache (left) and with the KV cache (right top). The KV cache requires extra memory cost, and ours needs much less of it (right bottom).

Figure 2. From codec signals to kept tokens. (a) An I-frame predicts each block from its coded neighbours. (b) A P-frame finds the best match of each block in a previous frame and stores its motion vector. (c) The residual is the difference between the block and its best match. (d) Each token receives a motion score and a residual score from the blocks it covers, and threshold-based or priority-based pruning then selects the kept tokens.

Our CodecOPSD shows better numerical performance on most metrics and stays close to the teacher. Prep. is the token selection time in seconds per case, and ours runs on 6 CPU cores of an Intel Xeon Platinum 8275CL. The best results in each group are highlighted, and the second best are underlined.

Table 4. MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA on OmniVBench [37]. Ours drops 71.6% of condition tokens in the DiT and 36.2% in the VLM. It denoises 1.87× faster, and no overall score drops more than 0.6 points. Subscripts are changes from the dense model.

Table 3. Teacher–student gap ablation. We control the gap by the drop rate, dropping 90% of student tokens for the larger gap and some teacher tokens for the smaller gap. Both are worse than ours on at least 8 of the 9 metrics. The best results are highlighted.

papers.selection_reason: Codec-based token pruning and on-policy distillation for efficient video diffusion, relevant to efficient AI and video generation.
papers.title: On-Policy Codec Distillation for Efficient All-in-One Video Generation
papers.tldr: CodecOPSD uses video-codec redundancy detection and on-policy self-distillation to prune conditioning tokens, accelerating all-in-one video generation with minimal quality loss.

papers.abstract: A generalist manipulation policy should perform new tasks, operate in unfamiliar scenes, and transfer skills across robot embodiments. We present Wrist Video Policy (WVP), a closed-loop manipulation framework that learns how manipulation unfolds through video prediction and recovers executable motion through geometric estimation. Our key idea is to represent robot motion through wrist-camera trajectories, which determine the corresponding end-effector poses through a fixed hand-eye transformation. We pair a video generator that predicts future wrist views with a pose estimator adapted from a pretrained 3D model to recover the corresponding camera trajectories. Model stitching maps the generator's predicted latents directly into the estimator's intermediate feature space, bypassing RGB decoding. This decomposition allows task knowledge to expand through broad human and robot video data while reusing geometric motion estimation across tasks and embodiments. The resulting pose estimator transfers across Franka Panda, PiPER-X, and Galaxea R1 Pro without further fine-tuning. Across tabletop and laundry-room settings, WVP generalizes to tasks ranging from precise grasping and inserting to handling deformable objects, achieving a success rate of over 50% in zero-shot out-of-distribution evaluations. Our project page is at https://wrist-video-policy.github.io.
authors: Jingyuan Liu, Yongwei Chen, Yishan Yang, Zexin He, Xingang Pan, Zhi Hou
bullets: Targets manipulation policies that generalize to new tasks, unfamiliar scenes, and different robot embodiments.
Predicts future wrist-camera views with a video generator, then estimates camera trajectories and converts them to end-effector motion via a fixed hand-eye transform.
Uses model stitching to connect predicted video latents directly to a pretrained 3D pose estimator without RGB decoding.
Transfers across Franka Panda, PiPER-X, and Galaxea R1 Pro without fine-tuning.
Achieves over 50% success in zero-shot out-of-distribution evaluations across tabletop and laundry-room tasks, including deformable-object handling.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that visual diffusion models can learn to predict the next best move (NBM) in tasks requiring sequential reasoning and lookahead, without explicitly exploring future steps or exhaustive searching at inference. Previous work demonstrated that these models can generate complete solutions to geometric and reasoning problems. Here, we show that simple fine-tuning on visual state--NBM pairs enables a pretrained model to select actions whose value depends on consequences several steps ahead. Each move is predicted directly in image space from the current state, without an explicit symbolic representation or search procedure. Repeated NBM predictions then construct a solution one decision at a time. We demonstrate this capability on chess puzzles and tile-based pathfinding, and show that it extends to Connect Four, Go and billiards. In chess, the model predicts legal moves and finds the best move far more often than by recalling similar training positions, including piece sacrifices whose benefit emerges only through later tactical continuations. In pathfinding, it constructs shortest paths on uniform-cost maps and cost-optimal routes across terrain tiles with different traversal costs, choosing longer routes when they are cheaper overall. These costs are learned implicitly from examples, without numerical cost supervision. These results show that direct visual move prediction can support globally informed decisions and successful sequential problem solving.
authors: Amir Razlighi, Ali Mahdavi Amiri, Yiorgos Chrysanthou, Andrey Voynov, Daniel Cohen-Or
bullets: Fine-tuning on visual state–next-best-move pairs teaches a pretrained model to account for consequences several steps ahead.
The model predicts each action directly in image space, and repeated predictions build a complete solution.
Demonstrated on chess and tile-based pathfinding, with extensions to Connect Four, Go, and billiards.
It handles chess tactics such as strategically useful sacrifices and learns cost-aware paths without numerical cost supervision.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that visual diffusion models can learn to predict the next best move for sequential reasoning tasks, bridging the gap between video generation and decision-making/world modeling.
papers.title: Learning the Next Best Move with Visual Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: Visual diffusion models can learn to predict globally informed next moves directly from images, enabling sequential problem solving without explicit search or symbolic planning.

papers.abstract: Video-to-audio generation synthesizes sound that matches a video in content and timing, with applications ranging from film post-production to live streaming, games and interactive world models. Interactive applications receive video continuously and need the sound to follow it in real time, yet most existing video-to-audio models are bidirectional and must observe an entire clip before producing any sound. We propose LiveAudio, a streaming video-to-audio framework that generates high-quality and synchronized audio in real time while the video is playing. In contrast to prior streaming models trained from scratch, LiveAudio converts a bidirectional model into a streaming generator so as to build on its audio quality and synchronization. LiveAudio generates audio block by block, and each block depends only on the video that has already been played. The streaming generator is obtained from the bidirectional model through progressive causal fine-tuning and distillation, so that each block needs only a few sampling steps. Experiments on VGGSound show that LiveAudio outperforms existing streaming models in audio quality and synchronization, and surpasses the bidirectional model it starts from in synchronization. On a single A100 GPU, it runs in real time with a real-time factor of 0.79 and a time to first frame of 143 ms. Audio samples are available at https://streamaudio.github.io.
authors: Yuxuan Jiang, Zehua Chen, Yusheng Dai, Andong Wang, Weibei Dou, Jun Zhu
bullets: Targets real-time video-to-audio generation for interactive applications, unlike models requiring the full video first.
Generates audio block by block using only video already observed, preserving causality during streaming.
Uses progressive causal fine-tuning and distillation to retain the source model’s quality while reducing sampling steps.
On VGGSound, it outperforms existing streaming models in audio quality and synchronization and improves synchronization over its bidirectional source model.
Runs in real time on a single A100 GPU, with a reported real-time factor of 0.79 and 143 ms time to first frame.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LiveAudio. papers.title: LiveAudio: From Bidirectional to Autoregressive Diffusion for Real-Time Streaming Video-to-Audio Generation

papers.abstract: Conditional generation under constraints that can only be checked on a finished sample, such as a molecular property filter, remains challenging for diffusion models: most guidance methods require differentiable measurement operators, paired conditional data, or rollouts of the base model at every step. We present a framework grounded in the Doob $h$-transform that reduces conditional generation to learning a single function, the probability that a noisy sample denoises into the constraint set. We learn this function from binary clean-sample evaluations alone, by squared-error regression on forward-noised labels; the base model is frozen, one lightweight head is trained per constraint, and noisy-state classifier guidance arises as a special case. The exact guidance step fades where the constraint signal provably vanishes and carries a factor of the inverse probability across samples, which normalized guidance discards: with the schedule and mean step size held fixed, equalizing the step costs 17.0 to 18.5 points of constraint satisfaction on CIFAR-10 at comparable FID, across independently trained estimators. Guidance is more than 50$\times$ cheaper per satisfying sample than rejection sampling at a 1.7% base rate, raises a Lipinski-type property filter on QM9 from 54.3% to 96.8%, and lifts satisfaction on Stable Diffusion 1.5 from 7.2% to 60.0% at one sixteenth of the cost of derivative-free selection, which reaches 9.0%. These results demonstrate that binary evaluations of clean samples are sufficient supervision for constrained generation across pixel, latent, and molecular diffusion.
bullets: Addresses constrained generation when constraints are only evaluable on completed samples and lack differentiable guidance or paired conditional data.
Learns one probability function per constraint by regressing forward-noised binary labels, while keeping the base diffusion model frozen.
Derives guidance whose strength vanishes when the constraint signal does and preserves inverse-probability weighting that normalized guidance loses.
Improves constraint satisfaction on CIFAR-10, QM9, and Stable Diffusion 1.5, while reducing cost relative to rejection or derivative-free selection.
Scope: requires binary clean-sample evaluations and separately trained lightweight guidance heads for each constraint.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a framework for constrained diffusion generation using Doob h-transforms, enabling guidance from binary evaluations without differentiable operators.
papers.title: Constrained Diffusion from Binary Evaluations via Learned Doob h-Functions
papers.tldr: A Doob $h$-transform-based method enables diffusion models to satisfy nondifferentiable constraints using only binary evaluations of clean samples, with strong gains across image and molecular generation.

papers.abstract: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) enables fast video generation by distilling a multi-step teacher into a few-step student. However, DMD-based methods often suffer from unnatural motion and costly training. We trace these limitations to the DMD gradient, which jointly optimizes appearance, layout, and motion without distinguishing their learning dynamics. Its static component, which carries appearance and layout, has a much higher signal-to-noise ratio than its motion component. As a result, per-frame quality converges within a few hundred iterations, whereas motion lags far behind. Beyond being noisy, the gradient also lacks two signals. (1) Video VAEs encode several frames into one latent frame (four in Wan2.1), and the gradient provides little guidance for spreading motion over these frames, causing periodic stutter. (2) DMD does not constrain the final sampling step to preserve the layout set by earlier steps, so objects merge and drift once the video moves. We propose HorizonFlow, which decouples the correction of motion from that of layout. It keeps the DMD loss and only shifts its regression target, with one training-only correction in the motion component and one in the orthogonal layout component. Chunk Evenness addresses (1) by spreading the motion of each latent chunk evenly over its frames, and Semantic Commitment addresses (2) by anchoring the coarse layout to the teacher's completion of the student's last step. In only 600 iterations, HorizonFlow distills Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B into a 4-step model using 8.4k training samples, 4.6-304$\times$ fewer than prior work. On VBench, HorizonFlow outperforms all released few-step Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B models. The same recipe transfers to Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B, where our student outperforms NVIDIA's distilled model. Code: https://github.com/XIANGLONGGUO/HorizonFlow-repo
authors: Xianglong Guo, Haobo Xu, Zanyi Wang, Zhen Lei, Chang Yu
bullets: DMD distillation often produces unnatural motion because appearance/layout signals dominate noisier motion signals.
Chunk Evenness spreads motion evenly across latent frames to reduce periodic stutter.
Semantic Commitment anchors the final sampling step to the teacher’s layout, limiting object merging and drift.
The method distills Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B using 8.4k samples and transfers to Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B.
It outperforms released Wan2.1 few-step models on VBench and NVIDIA’s distilled Cosmos model.‌

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative comparison with released few-step models on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B. Every method gets the same VBench prompt and seed; columns are frames 1, 17, 33, 49, 65 and 81 of 81. Red boxes mark failures; insets enlarge them. rCM fuses the giraffe’s head with a zebra, loses the bird from its nest and smears the train. FastWan barely moves the giraffe, opens the bird clip with a blurred double exposure and melts the train into the rails. Self-Forcing cuts to a new shot halfway through the bird clip and pushes the bird out of the frame. HorizonFlow carries out each prompt: the giraffe bends down and drinks, the bird settles on its nest, and the train crosses the bridge toward the camera, with every subject intact from the first frame to the last. CoDMD and more prompts are in the supplementary material.

Figure 3. One student update of HorizonFlow. The student rolls out k ∈ {1, . . . , 4} steps from noise; gradients flow only through the last step, which maps (xin, tin) to xG. DMD (blue) re-noises xG and compares the critic with the guided teacher, giving the DMD gradient g. Chunk Evenness (orange) decodes a random window of xG with the frozen VAE, measures how evenly its motion is spread over the four frame phases of each latent chunk, and, where it is less even than the training clips, takes a few normalized steps that keep motion and detail, giving ∆CE. Semantic Commitment (green) lets the teacher complete the student’s last step from the same input and keeps only the block- and time-averaged difference, gated by tin and capped, as ∆SC. Both corrections only move the DMD target, x̃ = sg(xG − g + ∆CE − ∆SC), each in its own component of the update (CE: motion; SC: layout); the critic update, the sampler, and inference are those of a plain 4-step student.

Figure 2. Video DMD learns appearance before motion, and correcting the motion disturbs the layout. (a) After 4100 iterations of conventional DMD training, the glove’s fingers lose their shape from frame to frame; HorizonFlow keeps them intact after 600. (b) Plain DMD: imaging and aesthetic quality reach their final level by 300 iterations, while the dynamic degree is still 18. (c) Top: signal-to-noise ratio over noise draws of the static and motion components of the plain DMD gradient (dashed: signal = noise). Bottom: push of the update toward evenly spread motion, divided by its noise; the DMD gradient stays below the noise (dashed), while our update (DMD + CE + SC, same samples) exceeds it at every noise level. (d) Motion per frame transition in one clip, divided by its mean: plain DMD (300 iterations) moves mostly at the transitions between latent chunks (shaded); the teacher moves evenly. (e) The stutter amplitude A4, the period-4 component of these changes, peaks at 4.6 times the teacher’s level at 200 iterations. (f) Chunk Evenness alone (600 iterations) removes the stutter and raises the dynamic degree from 76 to 97, but the dog fuses with the horse, the bear with the zebra, and the drummer’s head leaves the frame. Details are in Secs. D and E.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) models can now generate visually plausible short clips, but multi-shot generation requires a different set of skills: composing multiple shots with intended cut timing, transition style, camera language, and cross-shot continuity. How far this multi-shot output can be controlled from text remains unmeasured: existing benchmarks either evaluate single shots or, when they provide shot-level scripts, typically check whether the requested shots appear but not when they change or how they are joined. We introduce MSBench, a benchmark for controllable text-driven multi-shot video generation built around structured Scene-Entity-Shot mini-scripts that specify each shot's time span, camera state, content, and outgoing transition. MSBench defines a four-dimensional hybrid evaluation framework spanning Visual Quality, Dynamic Quality, Semantic Alignment, and Cross-Shot Consistency with 11 sub-metrics. Experiments on 14 commercial and open-source systems show that visual quality does little to separate the systems, whereas multi-shot control does: many models cut mainly on scene changes and render requested gradual transitions as hard cuts. Human evaluations further validate MSBench, with its system ranking reaching a Spearman correlation of 0.87 with human preferences. The project page is available at https://totalhuang.github.io/MSBench-page/.
authors: Tao Huang, ZiHao Liang, Junhao Liu, Junzhe Li, Yuancheng Wei, Sifan Zuo, Beiming Yu, Taojin Liu, Zhuoyang Li, Bing Cao

Many systems favor hard cuts at scene changes and struggle to produce requested gradual transitions.

papers.abstract: Physical counterfactual video editing turns a source video and a language-specified physical edit at a given execution frame into a counterfactual video that shows how the scene would evolve after the edit. Existing evaluations with counterfactual target videos mainly cover object removal or specific rigid-body motions, although real scenes also involve elastic deformation, fluid flow, and interactions among rigid bodies, elastic solids, and fluids. We introduce PhyCoVE, a benchmark of 533 cases on 110 source videos that covers rigid, elastic, and fluid dynamics in five interaction patterns, with edits that remove an object, change a physical quantity, or insert a new object. For the simulated cases, a language model proposes scene designs, coding agents build them with solvers suited to each material and physically based rendering and then simulate each edit from the source scene state, and humans check every stage. For the real cases, we record continuously from one camera position before and after each edit. We also propose counterfactual fidelity, a metric that applies across materials and their interactions and measures how much of the physical change from the source video to the target video a generated video reproduces. We evaluate seven open-source and commercial video editing models and find that counterfactual fidelity ranks them nearly as human preference does, but even the best model reproduces only about one seventh of the physical change. The models change how a scene looks but rarely how it evolves, whereas a physical edit requires understanding the dynamics that it changes. Physical counterfactual video editing thus remains far from solved, and PhyCoVE provides a foundation for developing and evaluating methods for it.
authors: Conghan Yue, Yuanjie Chen, Yunyan Xiao, Zeyu Peng, Xingsong Ye, Ya Gao, Yanglin Huang, WeiYao Zhang, Yue Han, Zhineng Chen, Yu-Gang Jiang
bullets: Introduces 533 benchmark cases from 110 videos spanning rigid, elastic, and fluid materials across five interaction patterns.
Covers object removal, physical-quantity changes, and object insertion in simulated and real-world videos.
Proposes counterfactual fidelity, a cross-material metric that measures how much of the physical change is reproduced.
Evaluates seven open-source and commercial models; the metric closely matches human preferences.
Even the best model reproduces only about one seventh of the physical change, showing that the task remains largely unsolved.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces PhyCoVE, a benchmark for physical counterfactual video editing, which is relevant to understanding dynamics and interactive world models.
papers.title: PhyCoVE: Benchmarking Physical Counterfactual Video Editing across Diverse Material Dynamics

papers.abstract: Generative priors are state-of-the-art for modeling medical images in image reconstruction tasks, but reconstruction with video priors takes tens of seconds to minutes per frame. Latent priors inherit the errors of their autoencoder, the memory of pixel-space whole-frame priors grows with the frame size, and pixel-space patch priors are slow for two reasons. First, their deep networks process every frame at full resolution at every sampling step, even though early steps resolve only low frequencies. Second, their samplers spend many network evaluations per sampling step on overlapping windows, multiple re-noising rounds, or backpropagation through the prior. We introduce TesseraFlow, a complex-valued pixel-space flow prior that reduces the first cost. A global encoder reads a low-resolution view of every frame once per sampling step. A single shallow decoder operates on this view during early steps and on full-resolution space-time tiles during later steps, so no network processes a whole frame at full resolution. Our sampler, ReTile, addresses the second reason. We use randomized grid shifting at every sampling step along with re-noising, which acts as a stochastic gradient instead of computing overlapping tiles, so a single network pass per sampling step suffices. On its own, ReTile speeds up an existing global-context patch prior by 6-9x, and our prior adds a further 3-5x speedup. TesseraFlow reconstructs about one 256x256 frame per second, 20-367x faster than patch and latent video priors, and can match or exceed the best generative baseline on cardiac, brain, and abdominal MRI and lung CT, at a fraction of its GPU time.
authors: Atakan Topcu, Mohammadhossein Momeni, Alfredo De Goyeneche, Michael Lustig
bullets: Addresses the high latency and memory costs of video priors for medical image reconstruction.
Uses a complex-valued pixel-space flow prior with a global low-resolution encoder and a shallow decoder that shifts from low-resolution views to full-resolution space-time tiles.
Introduces ReTile, which uses randomized grid shifting and re-noising to replace overlapping tile evaluations with one network pass per sampling step.
Achieves about one 256×256 frame per second and reports 20–367× speedups over patch and latent video priors.
Matches or exceeds the best generative baseline across cardiac, brain, and abdominal MRI and lung CT while using less GPU time.

Figure 2. TesseraFlow and ReTile. One sampling step: a coarse step (t < ts, top, purple) or a fine step (t ≥ ts, middle, teal), and the schedule of steps (bottom). In a coarse step, the shallow decoder Lθ predicts the velocity of this low-resolution video from all encoder features Gt. In a fine step, it predicts the velocity of each space-time tile from the tile and the features at its location, and the tile predictions are placed side by side. papers.selection_reason: Scalable pixel-space video diffusion prior with a novel tiling sampler for medical imaging inverse problems.
papers.title: TesseraFlow: Scalable Video Diffusion for Dynamic Medical Imaging Inverse Problems

papers.abstract: We present XShot, a framework for cross-shot video object insertion, which adds objects to a shot by watching another shot of the same scene. Video productions show a scene through many shots, and objects added to one shot must appear consistently in the others. Most video editors take the appearance of new objects from reference images and their location from a text prompt, a mask or an edited keyframe, leaving this consistency to the user. XShot reads both from a reference video of another shot, which need not be aligned with the target, and needs no mask, box or camera pose. We build on a video Diffusion Transformer and formulate the task as in-context generation over the reference video, a few images of the objects and the target video. A geometry-aware cross-shot attention estimates the epipolar geometry between the two shots from the model's own correspondences and uses it to guide where the target reads the reference and the exemplars. We train XShot with an erase-and-restore data engine: objects are erased from one shot of a film or a multi-camera recording and restored from another shot of the scene. Experiments show that XShot places objects more accurately and renders them more faithfully than open-source and commercial video editors, while leaving the rest of the shot intact.
bullets: Addresses cross-shot object consistency, reducing manual placement and appearance specification by editors.
Uses in-context generation with a video Diffusion Transformer, reference video, object images, and target video.
Geometry-aware cross-shot attention estimates epipolar relationships from learned correspondences to guide reference information.
Trains via an erase-and-restore pipeline using shots from films or multi-camera recordings.
Experiments report more accurate placement, more faithful rendering, and preservation of the unchanged scene compared with open-source and commercial editors.

(b) Positions of the reference and exemplar tokens. (c) Epipolar geometry estimated from the model’s own matching points guides the attention to the reference and the exemplars.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow-based models have achieved remarkable success in generation, yet their samples often remain suboptimal in fidelity and text alignment. Two lines of inference-time methods address this: extrapolation guidance, such as classifier-free guidance (CFG) and its variants, and reward guidance, which aligns samples with reward models of human preference. Extrapolation guidance needs only forward passes, but it builds its reference by heuristic rules unrelated to the reward and therefore cannot steer sampling toward a given reward. Gradient-based reward guidance steers sampling directly toward a higher reward, but backpropagates through the entire generator at every step. This trade-off raises the question of whether extrapolation guidance can steer sampling toward a higher reward without a full backward pass. To answer this, we introduce Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance (RadAG), which constructs the reference by perturbing the attention logits of a single block against their reward gradient and extrapolates away from it. We prove that this update increases the reward of the clean estimate to first order, while its backward pass stops at the perturbed block instead of traversing the entire generator. On FLUX.2-klein-4B and 9B with PickScore and aesthetic rewards, RadAG achieves the highest target reward in every setting with 30-65% less time than gradient-based and candidate-based baselines.
bullets: Targets suboptimal sample fidelity and text alignment in diffusion and flow-based models.
Perturbs attention logits in a single block against the reward gradient, then extrapolates away from the perturbed reference.
Theoretically shown to increase the clean estimate’s reward to first order.
Achieves the highest target reward across reported FLUX.2-klein settings with 30–65% less time than gradient- and candidate-based baselines.

papers.title: RadAG: Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment of Diffusion Models

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models can render convincing frames while failing to produce the requested action. Increasing classifier-free guidance (CFG) can strengthen motion, but also saturates and shifts colors. Scalar CFG assigns the same coefficient to the averaged and frame-varying components of its prediction difference, limiting independent control of temporal variation. THAW, Temporal Harmonic Amplification during Warm-up, retains stock CFG and adds a separately weighted residual during an initial denoising window. Its dose specifies the added norm relative to the current CFG difference, giving the extra guidance a consistent relative budget across sampling steps. THAW is training-free and reuses CFG's two model predictions with an unchanged network evaluation count. It improves cost-matched motion over scalar and scheduled CFG on five video models, with positive point estimates against existing guidance methods on three of them. On VBench, THAW raises dynamic degree by about 14 to 15 points over stock CFG while increasing total scores on a different set of three models.
authors: Xuanhua Yin, Boyu Wei, Chengkun Yue, Shunqi Mao, Chuanzhi Xu, Wei Guo, Weidong Cai
bullets: Scalar CFG can strengthen motion but may saturate and shift colors because it controls averaged and frame-varying components together.
THAW adds a separately weighted residual during an initial denoising window while retaining standard CFG.
Its dose is normalized to the current CFG difference, providing a consistent relative guidance budget across sampling steps.
The training-free method improves cost-matched motion across five video models and shows positive point estimates against existing guidance methods on three.
On VBench, THAW increases dynamic degree by about 14–15 points over stock CFG, while total-score gains occur on a different set of three models.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free temporal guidance improves motion in video diffusion models.
papers.title: Frozen by the Mean: Early Temporal Guidance Unfreezes Motion in Video Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: THAW improves motion in video diffusion models by adding separately controlled temporal guidance early in denoising without extra model evaluations or retraining.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models have enabled the synthesis of high-fidelity, visually compelling videos. However, despite being trained on internet-scale video data, understanding underlying physical laws and generating physically plausible dynamics remain challenging. To mitigate this, conditioning video generators on explicit physical reasoning has emerged as a promising direction. Nevertheless, existing conditioning approaches often fail to incorporate detailed physical guidance into generation, resulting in physically implausible motion or visual artifacts. We propose PSC-Gen, a training-free framework that employs an agentic approach to synthesize visual conditions and inject their core dynamics via low-frequency filtering. By iteratively planning physical states and verifying generated keyframes, our Physics Agent constructs visually and physically consistent keyframe sequences. We then interpolate these keyframes into a continuous physical sequence and inject only its low-frequency components, steering the video model to preserve physical dynamics while synthesizing fine visual details. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations across physics-informed and robotic manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that PSC-Gen faithfully follows instructions and generates physically plausible videos.
authors: Wonsik Shin, Jinju Jang, Junhoo Lee, Yeonjin Chang, Jimyeong Kim, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses physically implausible motion and artifacts in video diffusion models despite large-scale video training.
Uses a training-free Physics Agent to iteratively plan physical states and verify generated keyframes.
Interpolates verified keyframes into continuous physical sequences and injects their low-frequency components into the video generator.
Evaluations on physics-informed and robotic manipulation benchmarks show improved instruction following and physically plausible videos.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method Overview. PSC-Gen generates physically plausible videos through (a) Agentic Visual Planning and (b) Physical Sequence Conditioning. A vision-language model (VLM) acts as a Physics Agent to plan physical states and iteratively generate and verify keyframes. These keyframes are interpolated into a physical sequence, which guides diffusion sampling through low-frequency velocity injection. This design effectively transfers physical dynamics while allowing the diffusion model to synthesize fine visual details.

papers.tldr: PSC-Gen improves physical plausibility in video generation by planning, verifying, and injecting physically consistent visual sequences without training the generator.

papers.abstract: Event cameras capture brightness changes with high temporal resolution and dynamic range, but converting event streams into videos remains fundamentally ill-posed due to the lack of absolute intensity information. Resolving this ambiguity calls for a brightness reference that complements the intensity changes recorded by events. Inspired by the complementary spatial and temporal processing of the parvocellular and magnocellular pathways in human vision, we propose EvDualDiff, a dual-stream framework that combines a brightness reference from temporal-mapping events with motion-event cues for video reconstruction. Conditioned on both streams, our video diffusion model autoregressively reconstructs long sequences from a single temporal map. Photometric constraints and finetuning on self-generated rollouts reduce accumulated drift. At the hardware level, our approach requires only a minimal light-modulation mechanism on the lens of an event camera. We build this setup and collect a dataset comprising temporal-mapping events, motion events and synchronised ground-truth RGB frames. Experiments on a public benchmark and on our collected EvDual dataset demonstrate that EvDualDiff outperforms existing event-to-video reconstruction methods in fidelity, perceptual quality and video-level realism. The code and dataset will be released.
authors: Lei Sun, Zhendong Li, Chenxin Shao, Weilun Li, Ruibo Ming, Kaiwei Wang, Jinjin Gu, Danda Pani Paudel, Luc Van Gool
bullets: Addresses the ill-posed nature of event-to-video reconstruction caused by missing absolute intensity information.
Uses temporal-mapping events as a brightness reference alongside motion events, inspired by complementary visual pathways.
Autoregressively reconstructs long sequences with photometric constraints and rollout finetuning to reduce drift.
Requires only a minimal lens-based light-modulation mechanism and introduces the EvDual dataset with synchronized RGB frames.
Outperforms existing methods on a public benchmark and EvDual in fidelity, perceptual quality, and video-level realism.

(c) Etb is trained to map frames degraded by D to the latent of the clean frame. The brightness stream is drawn in orange and the motion stream in blue.

papers.tldr: EvDualDiff reconstructs long RGB videos from event streams by combining brightness-reference and motion-event cues in a dual-stream diffusion framework.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion streams a video chunk by chunk, but large AR models are too slow for real-time use. We ask where in an AR rollout a large model is actually needed. Pairing Krea-Realtime-14B with Self-Forcing-1.3B, which share their latent space and denoising schedule, we find that the order of the two models matters: when the 14B model generates only the first chunk and the 1.3B model continues, the rollout keeps 95\% of the 14B model's semantic advantage, whereas the reverse allocation keeps 16\% at about ten times the cost. The large model decides what the video shows; the small model only has to carry it forward. We turn this into BigSmall, a training-free planner--renderer sampler. The 14B model plans the opening chunk and sketches the chunks in which content changes, which preserves motion, and the 1.3B model renders the rest; a faster variant, BigSmall, plans only the opening chunk. A cross-model KV cache that is approximate, windowed and lazy lets the planner leave and re-enter the rollout at low cost. On VBench, BigSmall is $3.02\times$ faster than the 14B model at an unchanged semantic score and motion, and $1.55\times$ faster than SDVG, which lets the small model draft first; BigSmall reaches $3.77\times$ at the same semantic score, trading away 10\% of the motion. On minute-long videos (LoCoT2V-Bench), where the 14B model degrades when it reads its own long history, BigSmall is $3.14\times$ faster than the 14B model and scores higher ($+1.78$).`
bullets: Large-model computation is most valuable at the rollout’s beginning and when video content changes; reversing the model order largely loses the semantic benefit.
BigSmall is a training-free planner–renderer sampler: the 14B model plans the opening and selected transition chunks, while the 1.3B model renders the rest.
An approximate, windowed, lazy cross-model KV cache enables the large planner to leave and re-enter generation efficiently.
On VBench, BigSmall is 3.02× faster than the 14B model with unchanged semantic score and motion; a faster variant reaches 3.77× speedup with a 10% motion trade-off.
On minute-long videos, BigSmall is 3.14× faster and scores 1.78 points higher than the 14B model.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of BIGSMALL on a real rollout (“a teddy bear and a frisbee”). Top: a zero-cost change score decides, chunk by chunk, whether the 14B planner is called. The planner generates the plan chunk c0 with all four denoising steps and only the first step t1 of each sketch chunk; the 1.3B renderer takes all other steps (squares: denoising steps t1–t4; orange: 14B, blue: 1.3B). Bottom: each model reads its own KV cache; dashed arrows write a finished chunk into a cache, solid arrows read from it. The renderer’s cache is exact: every chunk is written. The planner’s cache is windowed: a planner call reads only the sink c0 and the previous chunk. It is lazy: that previous chunk is written only when the planner needs it (c1 when c2 is sketched, c4 when c5 is sketched), and other chunks are never written. It is approximate: a chunk is re-encoded sparsely, only its moving tokens, while the others copy K/V from the previous frame with re-rotated RoPE; it is re-encoded densely if the chunk before it was never written, as for c4. Right: inside sketch chunk c5, the planner’s first step from noise already fixes the layout (x̂(1) 0 ); it is re-noised to σ2, keeping 6% of the signal, and the renderer completes the chunk from its own cache.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison with large–small cooperation and acceleration baselines (VBench, seed 0, same noise for all methods; frames at t = 0, 2.5 and 5 s). BIGSMALL produces videos of the same quality as SDVG, Speculative Forcing and SRDiffusion (two 14B steps per chunk) while running at 10.0 instead of 4.6–6.5 FPS. Prompts drawn at random from the evaluation set and selected for diverse content and motion.

Figure 1. Semantic score versus throughput on VBench (946 prompts, 5 seeds). BIGSMALL is 3.02× faster than KreaRealtime-14B at the same semantic score, and BIGSMALL-Fast, which calls the 14B model only for the first chunk, is 3.77× faster, also at the same semantic score. Fewer 14B steps lose semantics quickly; single-model accelerators and large–small cooperation stay at or below 6.5 FPS. ∆Semantic: paired difference to the 14B model; FPS: DiT throughput for 81-frame videos on one GPU (Tab. 1).

Figure 2. Who begins decides. Noise fixed; only the model allocation changes. Each row is an allocation (peach: 14B, blue: 1.3B). (a) Within one chunk, over denoising steps t1–t4: LPIPS to the 14B video (24 prompts). (b) Along the video, over chunks c0–c6 (a split c0: 14B on its first one or three steps): semantic gap recovered on VBench; cost = share of the 14B model’s additional computation.

papers.selection_reason: Semantic-aware computation allocation between large and small autoregressive video models with a cross-model KV cache; relevant to video generation and inference efficiency.
papers.title: Plan Big, Paint Small: Semantic-Aware Computation Allocation for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.tldr: BigSmall accelerates autoregressive video generation by using a large model to plan key content and a small model to render the remaining chunks, preserving semantics and motion at substantially lower cost.

papers.abstract: Instruction-based image editors are trained on millions of edit pairs and follow instructions far more reliably than current video editors. We show that this ability can be transferred to video editing without any training. Our key observation is that a growing number of image editors and video generators share the same latent space. Their velocity fields can therefore be combined at sampling time: the difference between the editor's velocity under the instruction and under a neutral prompt, which we call the \emph{edit velocity}, can be added to the sampler of a video model. Added naively, however, it blurs the video, alters the background and flickers. An analysis of the edit velocity explains why. It is small and reliable only at coarse scales and high noise levels, not concentrated on the edited object, and uncorrelated across frames. From these properties, we derive a simple guidance operator that amplifies the edit velocity and restricts it in noise level, space, and time. The video model then turns the incoherent per-frame signal into a temporally coherent edit. Our method, TOGO, combines Qwen-Image-Edit with the Wan2.1 video model without training or fine-tuning. On FiVE-Bench, it raises the edit success rate from 47.0\% (the same video model without the editor) to 65.6\%, above the best published method (59.2\%). At the same time, it maintains the background PSNR and obtains the best LPIPS and SSIM of all methods. Because the video editor is assembled at inference time, it can be upgraded to any newer image editor that shares the latent space with no cost.
authors: Yixuan Luo, Jose Caballero, Yanjing Li
bullets: Addresses unreliable instruction following and artifacts in current video editors.
Combines image-editor and video-model velocity fields through an edit-velocity guidance operator.
Restricts guidance by noise level, spatial region, and time to reduce blur, background changes, and flicker.
Combines Qwen-Image-Edit with Wan2.1 without training or fine-tuning.
On FiVE-Bench, improves edit success from 47.0% to 65.6% while maintaining background PSNR and achieving the best reported LPIPS and SSIM.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of TOGO. Two frozen models that share a latent space are combined at sampling time. At every step, the video model provides the FlowEdit velocity ∆σ , and the image editor provides, for each latent frame k, the edit velocity ∆vk between the instruction and a neutral prompt. The raw ∆v is weak, unlocalized and incoherent across frames; G amplifies, windows, smooths and gates it, and the video model turns G(∆v) into a coherent edit that keeps the motion and background of the source.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison between TOGO and other baselines on FiVE-Bench. Each example shows frames 0 and 39 of a source video edited with the instruction above it. Wan-Edit, which uses the same video model and sampler as TOGO but no edit velocity, makes weak or no change. Other baselines apply the edit only partially or alter the background over time. TOGO applies the edit in both fra es while keeping the background and motion of the source.

Figure 3. What the edit velocity ∆v contains (8 local edits from DAVIS-2017 [28], two noise seeds). Top: for “make the rhino shiny gold” (latent frame 0), the residual D of the editor’s full edit concentrates on the object M⋆, whereas ∆v spreads over the whole frame. (a) ∆v is a small fraction of the full velocity. (b) Its alignment with the ideal direction −D (latent frame 0) grows with noise level and spatial pooling (mean ± s.e. over videos). (c) Its energy fraction outside the object (mean over videos) matches that of a spatially uniform signal. (d) Cross-frame cosine similarity at σ = 0.7 (latent frames 0–20, sampled): D is shared across frames; ∆v is not.

Figure 5. Edit success vs. background preservation TOGO for λ ∈ {0, . . . , 16} (λ = 0: video model alone; default λ = 8 circled), the editor’s guidance alone, copying the source, and the baselines on the same pairs. FF: first frame edited with the same editor, then propagated.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free transfer of instruction-based image editing to video editing by combining diffusion velocity fields; directly relevant to video diffusion synthesis and editing.
papers.title: TOGO: Take One Image Editor, Get One Video Editor for Free
papers.tldr: TOGO transfers instruction-following ability from an image editor to a video model at inference time, enabling training-free, temporally coherent video edits.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers (vDiTs) have become the main backbone for video generation. The quadratic cost of self-attention limits their efficiency at high resolutions and long durations. Existing sparse attention methods often rely on preserving high attention weights. However, these criteria do not fully capture the fidelity of the final value-weighted output, whose error depends jointly on changes to the attention numerator and the softmax denominator. We propose NOVA, a coarse-to-fine sparse attention framework that first approximates the full normalized output using size-weighted key/value centroids. Building on this estimate, we construct a residual proxy that accounts for coupled numerator-denominator errors by centering value contributions around the estimated output. This proxy guides the selection of query-key blocks for refinement under a predefined block budget for each query cluster. Selected blocks are evaluated through exact token-level computation, while the remaining blocks contribute through their centroids under a shared softmax normalization. On five vDiTs, NOVA achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among sparse attention methods, improving PSNR by up to 1.55\,dB over the strongest baseline, while delivering up to 1.82$\times$ end-to-end speedup on an H100 GPU.
authors: Wenxuan Miao, Haosong Liu, Aiyue Chen, Yiwu Yao, Zihan Liu, Anbang Wu, Yiming Gan, Jingwen Leng, Minyi Guo, Yu Feng
bullets: Targets the quadratic self-attention cost of high-resolution and long-duration video generation.
Uses size-weighted key/value centroids to estimate full normalized attention outputs coarsely.
Builds a residual proxy that captures coupled softmax numerator and denominator errors.
Refines selected query-key blocks exactly while approximating the rest with centroids under shared normalization.
Across five vDiTs, reports the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among compared sparse-attention methods, with up to 1.55 dB PSNR improvement.

papers.title: NOVA: Normalization-Aware Output-Guided Attention Acceleration for Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: NOVA accelerates video diffusion transformer attention by selecting blocks based on their estimated impact on the normalized output, achieving higher fidelity and up to 1.82× end-to-end speedup.

papers.abstract: Two centuries ago, an early cinema-like theater called the Diorama could already control its scenes at will. Today's video generation models produce videos of near-cinematic quality, yet they still lack this controllability. This limitation stems from the inherent semantic gap between text and pixels, since a prompt can describe a video only coarsely and leaves its details and relations beyond control. We bring this ability to video generation with Causal Dioramas, modules that decompose a video into a concept graph of variables that can be intervened on individually. Each instruction is translated into an intervention on the concept graph, modifying the specified concepts and their dependents. A connector then conveys this intervention to the video generator, which reuses the original noise to produce a counterfactual video while preserving all other content. Building on Causal Dioramas, we develop a unified framework for controllable generation, counterfactual revision of generated videos and editing of real videos. We outperform both open-source and commercial models in controllability on T2V-CompBench, CoVEBench and OpenVE-Bench.
authors: Yifan Shen, Xinyi Yang, Peiyuan Zhu, Yichang Jian, Jinyuan Hu, Xilin He, Fengming Zhu, Guangyi Chen, Kun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited detail and relational control of text-to-video prompts caused by the semantic gap between text and pixels.
Decomposes videos into concept graphs whose variables can be individually intervened on, including their dependents.
Translates instructions into graph interventions and uses a connector to guide the video generator with reused noise for counterfactual outputs.
Supports unified text-to-video generation, revision of generated videos, and editing of real videos.
Reports better controllability than open-source and commercial models on T2V-CompBench, CoVEBench, and OpenVE-Bench.

papers.abstract: Current leading video generation models can synthesize highly realistic videos, while still frequently violating physical and logical constraints in multi-step reasoning and planning, even after training with large-scale reasoning data or existing diffusion RL methods. We attribute these failures to the conventional video training paradigm, which treats a solution as a fixed-length clip rather than a chain of decisions. We present ViDecide, a decision-centric framework that trains video diffusion models to predict state transitions causally and decide when to stop, with a decision-focused training schedule. We further propose Corrective Fine-tuning (CFT), which corrects failed decisions by mapping their noise to the model's own successful continuations, achieving stable improvement without policy-gradient optimization. Across abstract games, planning tasks, and a new benchmark of multi-step robot planning, ViDecide achieves an average strict success rate of 83.8%, far above 23.3% for standard fine-tuning and 67.8% for the strongest prior method, and generalizes to larger puzzles and unseen layouts. Our framework therefore unlocks greater potential for video generation models as reliable reasoners and planners in the visual world. Project page: https://kevin-thu.github.io/ViDecide.
bullets: Targets physical and logical failures in multi-step video reasoning and planning.
Models solutions as causal state transitions with an explicit stopping decision.
Uses decision-focused training and Corrective Fine-tuning to repair failed decisions without policy-gradient optimization.
Reports an 83.8% average strict success rate across games, planning tasks, and robot-planning benchmarks, with generalization to larger puzzles and unseen layouts.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. (a) Instead of jointly generating a fixed-length clip, the model generates state transitions causally and ends with a visual EOS frame. (b) The decision-focused schedule moves training to high noise levels, where the next state is hidden and must be inferred from the rules and the history. (c) From the state hd before a failed decision, CFT resamples a successful continuation and trains the noise ϵ−d that produced the failed decision to generate the successful decision X+ d , shifting the decision distribution toward solvable moves.

papers.abstract: Cardiovascular imaging offers several ways to measure blood flow, but each provides an incomplete, resolution-limited, or noisy view of the underlying dynamics. Reconstructing the missing information is inherently ambiguous because several flow fields may be compatible with the same observation. Here, we investigate generative diffusion models as tools for cardiovascular-flow generation and reconstruction using a fully controlled state-of-the-art dataset from a digital twin of a healthy human left heart. First, we show how unconditional samples reproduce the changing anatomy and the highly fluctuating statistical properties of the flow throughout the cardiac cycle. Second, we test the conditional inference of our generative model by reconstructing an entire 2D planar section of geometry and flow configurations from a limited portion. Repeated reconstructions allow us to represent a range of plausible completions, going beyond a single deterministic estimate, while their mean retains the principal features of the reference flow. Comparison with a Gaussian process regression baseline on the same reduced domain highlights the main advantage of diffusion models: their reconstructed ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations, better encompassing ground-truth features that the baseline distributions can miss. Our results provide a quantitative proof of concept for probabilistic reconstruction of incomplete cardiovascular-flow measurements and demonstrate the potential for groundbreaking applications to the augmentation of in-vivo cardiovascular imaging data.
authors: Fabio Guglietta, Tianyi Li, Francesco Viola, Luca Biferale
bullets: Cardiovascular imaging provides noisy, incomplete, and resolution-limited observations, making flow reconstruction inherently ambiguous.
Using a controlled digital twin of a healthy human left heart, the study evaluates unconditional generation and conditional reconstruction.
Repeated conditional samples produce plausible completions rather than a single deterministic estimate; their mean preserves key reference-flow features.
Compared with Gaussian process regression, diffusion-model ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations and better encompass ground-truth features.
The work is a quantitative proof of concept, with scope demonstrated on simulated healthy-heart data and potential application to in-vivo imaging augmentation.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based probabilistic reconstruction of temporally structured flow; transferable to video and world-model generation.
papers.title: Augmentation of cardiovascular flow measurements with generative diffusion models
papers.tldr: Generative diffusion models can probabilistically reconstruct incomplete cardiovascular flow measurements while capturing diverse, physically plausible flow patterns.

papers.abstract: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.
authors: Luca Glawion, Julius Polz, Harald Kunstmann, Benjamin Fersch, Patrick Ludwig, Antonio S\'anchez-Ben\'itez, Christian Chwala
bullets: Targets the gap between snapshot-based skill evaluation and temporal coherence needed for sub-daily climate-impact applications.

Trains a diffusion U-Net with a noised previous high-resolution state, enabling continuous interpolation between autoregressive and per-timestep-independent sampling through one inference-time noise parameter.
On hourly European precipitation and 2-meter temperature downscaling, autoregressive rollouts remain stable for up to six months, with only slight early ensemble-spread contraction.
Autoregressive precipitation better preserves daily maxima, while independent generation underestimates them by up to 2×; temperature differences are negligible.
Noise-free conditioning diverges, indicating that the noise-conditioned scheme is important for stable long rollouts.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed temporal-noise-conditioned diffusion framework. (a) Training: The conditional diffusion model learns to emulate high-resolution RCM fields from coarse GCM input. The previous-hour RCM state is additionally provided as temporal condition input, corrupted with randomly sampled noise. (b) Inference: The conditioning noise level is controlled by the parameter τ . At its maximum value (τ = 999), the temporal condition consists of pure noise, resulting in per-timestep independent (PTI) samples (dashed lines). This regime also serves to initialize the autoregressive rollout. At a lower noise level (e.g. τ = 50), the previous timestep’s prediction is perturbed with noise and used as the temporal conditioning input. This provides informative temporal context, resulting in temporally consistent autoregressive (AR) sampling (solid lines).

papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based temporal sequence generation with controllable consistency; relevant to video and world-model generation.
papers.title: Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
papers.tldr: A noise-conditioned diffusion downscaling model provides a tunable trade-off between temporally coherent autoregressive rollouts and independent per-timestep generation without progressive degradation.

papers.abstract: Gameplay videos are a rich source of experience for learning virtual-world dynamics, yet their frames contain heads-up displays (HUDs) that follow interface rules rather than scene dynamics. Removing HUDs would make this footage directly usable for learning world dynamics. However, training a removal model requires paired clips with and without HUDs, whereas real recordings contain only HUD-overlaid footage. Existing work synthesizes pairs by compositing HUD graphics onto HUD-free footage, requiring a separately curated clean corpus and producing HUDs that only approximate real ones. Models trained on such pairs leave 40 to 50% of real HUD elements untouched. We instead recover pseudo-clean targets directly from real recordings by inpainting HUD regions with a pretrained video diffusion model. Preventing HUD traces from leaking into recovered targets is challenging because latent video autoencoders mix information across mask boundaries. Our training-free recovery pipeline, GameScrub-Data, pre-fills HUD regions with flow-guided background estimates before encoding, excludes HUDs from scene conditioning, and confines restoration to masked regions through pixel-space compositing. The resulting pairs train GameScrub, a video diffusion removal model that handles diverse HUDs without inference-time masks or clean reference images. On the in-the-wild Game2World benchmark, GameScrub achieves an artifact-adjusted removal score of 71.95, compared with 57.86 for the strongest reference-free GameCleaner configuration, and removes 90.06% of annotated HUD elements versus 59.07%. These results demonstrate that real recordings with recovered targets can support effective HUD removal, advancing HUD-free gameplay data for world models and controllable video generation.
authors: Mohammad Areeb Qazi, Yiyan Hu, Yanan Wang, Xuezhi Liang, Xin Li, Fan Yang, Xin Gao, Guangyi Liu
bullets: Real gameplay is valuable for world-model learning, but HUD overlays obscure scene dynamics and lack clean paired training data.
GameScrub-Data recovers HUD-free targets using flow-guided pre-filling, HUD-excluded conditioning, and masked pixel-space compositing.
The resulting video diffusion model removes HUDs without inference-time masks or clean reference images.
On the Game2World benchmark, it scores 71.95 artifact-adjusted removal versus 57.86 for GameCleaner and removes 90.06% of annotated HUD elements versus 59.07%.
The approach is scoped to improving HUD-free gameplay data for world modeling and controllable video generation.

papers.selection_reason: Video diffusion model for HUD removal from real gameplay; fits video editing and world-model data preparation.
papers.title: GameScrub: Learning HUD Removal from Real Gameplay with Recovered Targets
papers.tldr: GameScrub learns to remove diverse HUDs from real gameplay videos by creating pseudo-clean training targets with a leakage-resistant video inpainting pipeline.

papers.abstract: Visual perspective taking, the ability to infer what another person sees from their position, is fundamental to human collaboration. However, prior works reduced perspective taking to state estimation, geometric reconstruction, or discrete question answering, whereas existing cross-view video generation methods either inferred the target view from the input video alone or required an external camera that observes the target person. We introduce generative visual perspective taking: Given an ego person's egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and a collaborator's camera trajectory, the task is to generate the continuous egocentric video from the collaborator's perspective. This task is challenging given extreme viewpoint shifts, dynamic occlusions, and sparse visual overlap. We address these challenges with Ego2Ego -- a set of backbone-agnostic geometric modules that provide a pretrained video diffusion model with the 3D scene geometry shared by both interactants. Ego2Ego renders dense, temporally consistent scene coordinate maps into every view as a shared spatial reference, aligns cross-view tokens in 3D ray space through relative geometric attention, and recovers regions outside the ego person's current view from the ego person's visual memory. Experiments on the CoMind dataset across three video diffusion backbones show that Ego2Ego consistently improves visual quality, Level-2 scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion, outperforming state-of-the-art cross-view video generation baselines on every backbone. By generating the collaborator's egocentric video more accurately, Ego2Ego brings visual perspective taking to human-robot collaboration, where it can help infer what a human collaborator sees and does, and can turn single-person recordings into synchronised multi-perspective videos for robot learning.
authors: Chuhan Jiao, John Gideon, Anshul Gupta, Guy Rosman, Andreas Bulling
bullets: Addresses visual perspective taking beyond state estimation, reconstruction, and discrete question answering.
Uses backbone-agnostic geometric modules with scene coordinate maps, 3D ray-space token alignment, and visual-memory-based view completion.
Handles extreme viewpoint changes, dynamic occlusions, and sparse overlap between collaborators’ views.
Across three video diffusion backbones on CoMind, improves visual quality, scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion over prior cross-view generation methods.
Enables applications in human–robot collaboration and synchronized multi-perspective video generation for robot learning.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Ego2Ego. Given the ego person’s egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and both camera trajectories, Ego2Ego generates the collaborator’s egocentric video with a pretrained video diffusion transformer equipped with three geometry-grounded modules. All conditions are encoded by the frozen VAE and form a single token sequence with the noisy collaborator latent. (1) Since the same surface appears entirely different from the two viewpoints and hands occlude the scene, dense geometric rendering rasterises the point cloud into every view, colouring each pixel by its 3D coordinate in a shared frame, so that the same scene point carries the same colour across views and provides a shared spatial reference. (2) To relate tokens across substantially different viewpoints, relative geometric attention aligns the geometric components of keys and values to each query token’s ray-aligned frame. (3) To recover regions the ego person does not currently observe, the ego person’s visual memory supplies past ego-person frames together with their renderings.
Figure 3. Qualitative comparison. Two test examples, each at two time steps. For each baseline, we show the version with the higher PSNR in Tab. 1.

papers.title: Ego2Ego: Generative Visual Perspective Taking Across Collaborators
papers.tldr: Ego2Ego generates a collaborator’s continuous egocentric video from another person’s video, shared scene geometry, and the collaborator’s camera trajectory.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become an important component in the post-training of diffusion models. In practice, however, standard RL often improves the target reward without reliably preserving holistic generation quality, leading to unstable reward-quality trade-offs that we view as a form of reward hacking. Since Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is known to improve visual clarity, prompt alignment, and perceptual quality in generation, we investigate whether its underlying structure can serve as a useful prior during RL. We present a unified geometric view that interprets both CFG and RL as correction vectors in a common prediction space, and identify the projection of the RL-induced correction onto the pretrained CFG correction as a useful diagnostic of quality-related structural preservation. Geometric analysis and rotation intervention further show that the pretrained CFG direction carries information useful for generation quality that reward-driven RL updates do not necessarily preserve. Based on this insight, we propose Conditional Contrast Regularization (CCR), which uses the frozen reference model's conditional contrast as a local structural prior during RL. Experiments across multiple reward settings and backbones show that CCR more consistently preserves generation quality while maintaining competitive reward, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than standard RL and generic regularization methods.
authors: Yunfei Zheng, Xiaolong Wang, Dandan Zheng, Xianjun Deng, Shenghao Liu, Wei Xiang, Yuqian Li, Laurence Tianruo Yang
bullets: Standard RL can increase target reward while degrading holistic generation quality, causing reward hacking.
The paper views CFG and RL updates as correction vectors and uses their alignment to diagnose structural preservation.
Geometric analysis suggests pretrained CFG directions encode quality-relevant information that RL may discard.
CCR applies the frozen reference model’s conditional contrast as a local structural prior during RL.
Across multiple rewards and backbones, CCR maintains competitive reward while more consistently preserving quality than standard RL and generic regularization.

papers.title: Preserving Pretrained CFG Structure in RL for Diffusion Models with Conditional Contrast Regularization
papers.tldr: Conditional Contrast Regularization preserves pretrained CFG structure during diffusion-model RL, improving the balance between reward optimization and generation quality.

papers.abstract: A streamed video generator releases each chunk the moment that it is produced, so a safety decision that waits for the finished clip arrives after the harm has been seen. We measure a guardrail by exposure, the harmful frames a viewer is shown, and ask where a fixed moderation budget should be spent. The accurate detector reads decoded frames with a video language model and is too expensive for every chunk, so our guard reads hidden states the generator has computed already and spends a cheap score on deciding when to call it. On 599 streams from a distilled causal generator the undefended model shows 46.25 harmful frames of 81. The video model on every chunk leaves 0.91 frames at 80.1 scored per benign stream, and the same model triggered by our guard leaves 2.35 at 5.3. Spending that budget at random leaves 37.20 frames, so the gain is in the ordering, and a frame detector in the same role gives up almost six, so the judging stage must read the chunk as a clip. The ordering is worth more as the stream lengthens, and the guard carries to a second system. An independent guardrail model agrees with our oracle at $\kappa=0.74$, and a blinded audit by 50 participants puts its precision at 96.1% and recall at 82.8%. Warning. This paper contains examples of generated content that some readers may find disturbing or offensive in nature.
authors: Yuxin Cao, Ziqi Ding, Jiayu Zhang, Xianglin Yang, Wei Song, Jin Song Dong
bullets: Streaming generators can expose harmful frames before a completed-clip safety check finishes.
The guard uses generator hidden states to decide when to invoke an expensive video-language-model detector on decoded chunks.
On 599 streams, guard-triggered checking reduced exposure to 2.35 harmful frames using 5.3 scored chunks per benign stream, versus 37.20 with random allocation and 0.91 with checking every chunk.
Clip-level judging was substantially more effective than using a frame detector, and the ordering benefit increased with stream length and transferred to a second system.
An independent guard agreed moderately with the oracle (κ=0.74); a 50-person blinded audit measured 96.1% precision and 82.8% recall.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a guardrail strategy for streaming video generation that optimizes safety verification by reading hidden states to minimize exposure to harmful content.
papers.title: Budgeted Safety Verification for Streaming Video Generation
papers.tldr: A cheap hidden-state guard can prioritize video chunks for expensive clip-level safety checks, greatly reducing harmful exposure under a fixed moderation budget.

papers.abstract: Few-step diffusion distillation reduces sampling cost but often weakens adjustable classifier-free guidance (CFG) and runtime negative prompting. We introduce PP-CFG, an architecture that keeps positive and negative text conditions separate and combines their attention responses with opposite signs within a shared visual backbone. Its Scale-Time Polarity Mixer refines each condition using the guidance scale and denoising timestep, allowing prompt influence to vary throughout generation. The student retains a continuous scale input and selectable negative prompts with one visual backbone pass per step. We evaluate PP-CFG on Wan2.1 for video generation with distribution matching distillation (DMD), and on Qwen-Image with both latent consistency model (LCM) distillation and DMD. PP-CFG achieves 81.46 VBench in four steps and lower video teacher-student distances across guidance scales than step-distilled DMD. On NegElement-1K, our benchmark of 1,000 matched image and video prompt cases, it achieves higher target-removal rates than the corresponding teachers. These experiments support the method's generality across attention architectures, generation modalities, and distillation objectives while retaining competitive generation quality.
authors: Junyi He, Xu Peng, Chengming Xu, Sixiao Zheng, Donghao Luo, Chao Wen, Peng Tang, Xijie Huang, Chengjie Wang, Yanwei Fu
bullets: Addresses weakened classifier-free guidance and negative prompting after diffusion distillation.
Separates positive and negative text conditions and combines their attention responses with opposite signs in one visual backbone.
Uses a Scale-Time Polarity Mixer to adapt prompt influence based on guidance scale and denoising timestep.
Achieves 81.46 VBench in four-step video generation and higher target-removal rates than corresponding teachers on NegElement-1K.
Evaluated across Wan2.1 and Qwen-Image using DMD and LCM distillation, supporting broad applicability.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables real-time streaming generation, with each generated chunk serving as historical context for subsequent generation. To avoid the memory explosion of backpropagation through time, previous self-rollout methods typically truncate cross-chunk gradients or detach historical latents. As a result, earlier denoising computations receive no downstream feedback through the generated history on how to synthesize frames that facilitate subsequent generation, leading to visual drift and structural collapse as rollouts extend. To address this limitation, we propose Hindsight Forcing, which allows historical chunks to learn directly from future outcomes by decoupling forward generation from backward credit assignment via a latent straight-through bridge. In the forward pass, each chunk completes a full multi-step rollout to update the KV cache. In the backward pass, the bridge routes gradients from future losses back to a single selected denoising step per historical chunk, training both the context writer and historical denoiser on shared parameters without retaining the full trajectory graph. Remarkably, Hindsight Forcing requires no additional model parameters, architecture modifications, or separate trajectory replay. Extensive experiments on VBench demonstrate that Hindsight Forcing outperforms existing baselines in overall visual quality and dynamic motion, while ablation studies validate the benefit of supervising historical denoising. Code is available at https://github.com/haonanAN309/Hindsight-Forcing.
authors: Haonan An, Yihang Tao, Yu Guo, Renlong Chen, Jiasheng Zhang, Yuguang Fang
bullets: Addresses visual drift and structural collapse caused by detached or truncated gradients across generated video chunks.
Uses a latent straight-through bridge to separate full forward rollout from efficient backward credit assignment.

Requires no extra parameters, architectural changes, or separate trajectory replay.
Experiments on VBench report better overall visual quality and dynamic motion than existing baselines; ablations support historical-denoising supervision.
