papers.abstract: Video fusion integrates complementary information in multiple source video streams into a single sequence for complete scene perception. Existing methods perform frame-wise fusion and lack unified spatio-temporal modeling across sequences, damaging temporal coherence across sequences. When dealing with degradations, they also ignore temporal dynamics and overload a single network with diverse degradations, leading to limited and imbalanced degradation suppression. To address these issues, we propose V2VFusion, the first unified video-to-video fusion framework that directly generates temporally coherent, high-quality fused videos from degraded multi-source inputs. By reformulating video fusion as a video-to-video conditional generation problem in latent diffusion space, our approach holistically models spatio-temporal dependencies across entire sequences and intrinsically ensures sequence-level consistency. On this basis, a text-guided degradation-conditioned ControlNet bridges high-level textual degradation descriptions with low-level visual priors, enabling interpretable and controllable guidance for structure-preserving fusion beyond purely data-driven conditioning. To handle heterogeneous and compound degradations, a state-modulated degradation-aware hierarchical mixture-of-experts module decouples expert selection into diffusion-state-aware filtering and degradation-aware routing. It prevents unreliable routing and fosters expert specialization to mitigate representation conflicts among diverse degradations. Experiments on infrared-visible, multi-exposure, and multi-focus video fusion tasks and complex degradations validate that V2VFusion surpasses existing methods in fusion quality and temporal stability. The code is available at https://github.com/ChenDoubleJ/V2VFusion.
authors: Jiajun Chen, Han Xu, Yunfei Huang, Zhuoya Zhang, Guangcan Liu, Jiayi Ma
bullets: Targets frame-wise fusion methods that fail to model sequence-level spatio-temporal dependencies and diverse degradations effectively.
Reformulates video fusion as conditional video-to-video generation in latent diffusion space for improved temporal consistency.

Introduces a diffusion-state-aware, degradation-aware mixture-of-experts module for heterogeneous and compound degradations.
Experiments across infrared-visible, multi-exposure, and multi-focus fusion report improved fusion quality and temporal stability over existing methods.

papers.abstract: Existing game super-resolution methods typically operate at moderate upscaling factors, struggling to recover fine visual details from extremely low-resolution inputs (e.g., 120p). At such resolutions, super-resolution shifts from reconstructing existing information toward synthesizing missing visual details. While video diffusion models offer powerful generative priors for this challenging task, their dependence on future frames limits their applicability to interactive games. We present CIDER, a causal diffusion framework for extreme game super-resolution that synthesizes high-frequency details from current and past low-resolution frames, guided by G-buffers (depth and motion vectors) to preserve scene structure and temporal consistency. We collect data from two AAA games (Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong). To reduce inference load, we develop a lightweight latent projection encoder tailored to ultra-low-resolution inputs, fine-tune a decoder (TAE) on our high-resolution outputs, and distill the diffusion model to reach interactive frame rates. Our experiments demonstrate high-fidelity 8$\times$ upscaling from 120p to 960p at around 13 FPS, outperforming state-of-the-art game upscalers in visual quality and showing potential for 16$\times$ magnification.
authors: Christina Zhang, Jenna Kang, Colin Groth, Akshay Jindal, Stavros Diolatzis, Qi Sun
bullets: Targets extreme upscaling, where ultra-low-resolution inputs lack recoverable visual detail.

Evaluated on Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong, achieving about 13 FPS for 8× upscaling and showing potential for 16× magnification.
Scope: designed for interactive games and relies on temporal context and G-buffer guidance.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) diffusion models have made remarkable progress in generating high-fidelity visuals, yet their outputs still often exhibit physically implausible phenomena, including discontinuous dynamics and implausible event interactions. Existing representation alignment methods mainly transfer generic video features or short-range motion cues, treating physical plausibility as a single-level representation problem. To address this issue, we propose MiMaAlign, a hierarchical micro-macro alignment framework that transfers complementary dynamics-oriented and event-oriented knowledge into different abstraction depths of a pretrained video diffusion model. Specifically, micro-level continuous dynamics alignment imposes constraints by aligning diffusion features with a continuous-time motion representation learned by a Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE), while macro-level event-commonsense alignment provides representations of object interactions and event semantics through an instruction-prompted vision-language model (VLM). With training-only auxiliary objectives, we align the complementary supervision from the two teachers with shallower and deeper generator features, respectively, enabling the generator to internalize the corresponding physical priors. Empirical evaluations show that, on CogVideoX-2B, MiMaAlign achieves a relative improvement of up to 21.0% in the Physical Commonsense (PC) score on the VideoPhy benchmark over the baseline, and also delivers substantial gains on the highly challenging VideoPhy2 benchmark, while maintaining general video quality on VBench and being supported by blind user comparisons.
bullets: Addresses discontinuous dynamics and implausible object-event interactions in T2V video generation.

papers.abstract: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.
authors: Hidir Yesiltepe, Julius Berner, Arash Vahdat, Pinar Yanardag
bullets: Addresses reverse-KL distillation’s mode-seeking bias and resulting loss of sample diversity.
Uses exponentially reweighted student samples to match teacher posterior means at shifted noisy inputs.

On SDXL and FLUX.2 4B, PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods while remaining competitive on alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 4. PMD Training Framework. A noisy state zt is obtained through the student’s on-policy sampling process. The frozen teacher is evaluated at the shifted input zt + ρtλ, yielding the tilted posterior mean Tλ = Dt(zt + ρtλ, t). Conditioned on the same zt, the stochastic student generates multiple clean-image predictions using independent random inputs. These predictions are combined into an exponentially weighted mean, which is compared with the teacher target Tλ. PMD minimizes the resulting posterior-matching discrepancy through the loss LPMD, encouraging the student to recover the teacher’s conditional posterior distribution.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.
authors: Tuna Han Salih Meral, Kaan Oktay, Alec Helbling, Atakan Kara, Duen Horng Chau, Pinar Yanardag
bullets: RL improves visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy in diffusion transformers.
The study adds fixed steering vectors to frozen model block outputs, independent of prompts, tokens, and sampling seeds.
These vectors use 65× fewer parameters than an RL-tuned LoRA on SD3.5-M.
They recover 90.0–96.3% of reward gains across six image models and 89.8% and 111.9% across two video models.
Online RL with only steering vectors surpasses weight-based RL on OCR and PickScore for SD3.5-M.

figures.caption: Figure 5 Steering vectors recover most of the gain of each RL-tuned imagemodel. Each prompt’s images share one starting noise.

Figure 2 The steering vectors add the same vector to every token of every prompt. Block ℓ on two text-rendering prompts, with a linear layer W, token inputs zi and zj , and block outputs hi and hj . Base + s adds the same s (black) to every token of both prompts; s changes only with the block, guidance pass, step bin and stream. In the RL-tuned model, the weight change gives each input its own shift, ∆Wzi ̸= ∆Wzj (gray). papers.selection_reason: Shows RL post-training in diffusion transformers can be captured by fixed steering vectors, relevant to efficient video diffusion adaptation.
papers.title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering

papers.abstract: Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher's trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.
authors: Nathaniel Cohen, Nicolas Dufour, Am\'elie Royer, Alasdair Newson, Patrick P\'erez
bullets: Addresses the latency and multi-second audio look-ahead requirements of existing audio-driven video diffusion models.
Generates video chunk by chunk using only the current audio chunk and a rolling KV cache.
Uses two-stage distillation: causal teacher-trajectory matching followed by Distribution Matching Distillation with backward simulation.
AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time at 20.7 fps on one GPU; AURA 5B streams 720p at 9.7 fps.
Released resources include both model weights, 30K synthetic videos, and precomputed teacher trajectories.

papers.tldr: AURA enables low-latency, causal streaming avatar video generation by distilling diffusion models into chunk-wise generators with rolling KV caches.

papers.abstract: Low-dose and thin-slice computed tomography (CT) images suffer from elevated noise that obscures anatomical detail, while clean references for supervised denoising are often unavailable. Although Noise2Noise permits self-supervised training from noisy pairs, direct regression tends to oversmooth fine structure. Averaging multiple independently generated samples mitigates this blur, though repeating multi-step diffusion sampling is costly. We introduce Noise2Noise with Improved Mean Flow (N2N-iMF) to accelerate this process via few-step sampling. N2N-iMF learns to generate one noisy image conditioned on its paired counterpart; at inference, independent outputs are sampled and averaged to suppress noise. We evaluated image quality and sampling efficiency on simulated thin-slice brain and low-dose abdominal CT across four sampling methods and averaging counts from 1 to 20, and validated the approach on real-world photon-counting CT (PCCT) brain scans. With ten samples per conditioning input and three network evaluations per sample, N2N-iMF achieved a mean absolute error of 2.60 HU on brain CT and 14.02 HU on abdominal CT, outperforming 50-evaluation denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM) sampling (2.91 and 14.53 HU). On the same GPU, per-output generation time dropped from 7.29 to 0.43 s. Across eight PCCT cases, N2N-iMF reached a mean gray-white matter contrast-to-noise ratio of 1.341, versus 0.916 for Noise2Noise and 1.176 for DDIM. N2N-iMF accelerates self-supervised generative CT denoising without distillation while keeping the number of averaged outputs adjustable at inference.
authors: Xingyi Yao, Zhengtao Ma, Zhennong Chen
bullets: Addresses noisy low-dose and thin-slice CT when clean reference images are unavailable.
Trains on paired noisy images and uses Improved Mean Flow to generate denoised candidates with only a few network evaluations.
Averages independently sampled outputs to suppress noise and preserve fine anatomical structure.
Using 10 samples and 3 evaluations per sample, it improved MAE over 50-evaluation DDIM and reduced generation time from 7.29 to 0.43 seconds per output.
On eight real PCCT brain cases, it achieved higher gray-white matter contrast-to-noise ratio than Noise2Noise and DDIM.

papers.title: Fast Self-Supervised Generative CT Denoising via Few-Step Sampling
papers.tldr: N2N-iMF enables fast self-supervised generative CT denoising by averaging independently generated outputs from few-step sampling, improving image quality while greatly reducing inference time.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers reuse key--value (KV) caches across denoising steps, which quickly becomes a bottleneck for long video generation. We find that quantizing temporally distant cache vectors leads to a large range and high quantization error, but that nearby video tokens in the KV-cache share a persistent pattern per channel. These patterns also vary across videos, motivating rotations that are adapted to each video's unique cache. We propose Temporal Rotation Quantization (TRQ), a method that rotates frames in the cache that are adjacent in time before quantization. For each block of temporally adjacent cache vectors, TRQ fits an orthogonal transform that maps the block's per-channel means to a vector that is close to a constant across channels. To keep the quantization format lightweight, we parameterize this rotation as a tree of $2 \times 2$ planar rotations, each stored with only two bits, followed by a fixed Hadamard transform shared across all blocks. The rotations are fit without gradients or changes to model weights, and we prove that a simple greedy fit is globally optimal for our 'mean-flattening' objective. The transforms are fit online for each new video, and we release fused Triton kernels to make this process efficient at inference. At 2-bit precision and matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over the state-of-the-art method QVG from 90.38 to 92.02 on LongCat-Video-13B and from 86.33 to 87.61 on HY-WorldPlay-8B, as well as improving other metrics.
authors: Ryan Lucas, Petros Prastakos, Rahul Mazumder
bullets: Temporal KV-cache reuse creates memory bottlenecks, while distant-token quantization suffers from large ranges and errors.
TRQ rotates temporally adjacent cache vectors to flatten per-channel means before quantization.
It uses gradient-free, online-fitted trees of 2-bit planar rotations followed by a shared Hadamard transform.
A greedy fitting procedure is proven globally optimal for the mean-flattening objective, with efficient fused Triton inference kernels.
At matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over QVG on LongCat-Video-13B and HY-WorldPlay-8B, while also improving other metrics.

We observe that (i) Within a video, nearby frames share persistent spatial patterns and (ii) the final two panels show that these patterns differ across videos, even at the same frame index and channel. Together, these observations motivate fitting rotations online to each video’s cache and sharing them within local temporal blocks. For other channels, see Section 7 of the appendix.

papers.abstract: Real-time streaming video generation has gained rapid momentum in live content creation and interactive media. Deploying such systems in practice requires flexible scaling factors to accommodate diverse source resolutions, target displays, and computational budgets. However, extending fixed-scale generative video super-resolution (VSR) to varying target scales poses two challenges: downsampling from a larger fixed scale incurs redundant cost, while re-optimizing the diffusion transformer (DiT) is costly and alters the shared generative prior. To address both, we propose FlexVSR, a decoupled framework for continuous-scale streaming generative VSR with supervision at only a few scales. Our key insight is that naively resampling fixed-scale latents onto a new target grid induces scale-dependent input mismatch, which can be effectively addressed through parameter-efficient, scale-aware adaptation of the latent interface without updating the DiT. To this end, FlexVSR introduces ReLSA (Refined Latent Scale Adaptation), a lightweight latent adapter that constructs and refines target-grid latents before they enter the DiT, enabling a shared frozen VSR prior to generalize across continuous scales with only 0.274M trainable parameters and an adaptation cost of 7.3 H100 GPU-hours, while introducing no additional temporal dependencies and preserving the native causal streaming protocol. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive or superior reconstruction and temporal quality, lower latency than most native-scale streaming baselines and offline methods, and effective generalization to unseen continuous scales, filling the continuous-scale gap in real-time streaming generative VSR.
authors: Ji Wang, Haonan An, Jiasheng Zhang, Renlong Chen
bullets: Addresses the cost and inefficiency of extending fixed-scale streaming VSR to diverse target resolutions.
Introduces ReLSA, a lightweight scale-aware latent adapter that refines target-grid latents before the diffusion transformer.
Uses supervision at only a few scales while generalizing to unseen continuous scales.
Preserves causal streaming and adds no temporal dependencies, with 0.274M trainable parameters and 7.3 H100 GPU-hours of adaptation.
Reports competitive or better reconstruction and temporal quality with lower latency than most compared streaming and offline methods.

papers.abstract: Exocentric-to-egocentric (Exo2Ego) video generation transforms third-person recordings into first-person viewpoints, unlocking immersive AR/VR experiences and scalable demonstration synthesis for embodied robotics. Extending it to a streaming setting is expected to further enable live applications. However, existing methods suffer from degraded manipulation regions, overfitting and confinement to fixed-length clips with prohibitive latency. To address these limitations, we present StreamEgo, a real-time framework for unbounded, generalizable Exo2Ego video generation. To resolve intricate manipulation dynamics while supporting the streaming pipeline, a streaming dual-branch prior provides pixel-aligned guidance for translating appearance and skeletal kinematics. We also introduce a region-aware loss curriculum to improve generalization and stabilize multi-objective diffusion training. Furthermore, we distill the model into a chunk-wise autoregressive model, augmented with a region-aware corruption mechanism and a first-chunk curriculum, enabling high-quality, generalizable real-time streaming Exo2Ego generation at 24.3 FPS on a single H100 GPU.
authors: Tianyi Xu, Boyang Lyu, Yunkai Tang, Kairan Ding, Jiahang Li, Weiyu Guo, Yandong Guo, Shuchen Weng, Boxin Shi
bullets: Targets live AR/VR and embodied-robotics applications by converting third-person video into first-person views.
Uses a streaming dual-branch prior to provide pixel-aligned appearance and skeletal-kinematic guidance.
Introduces a region-aware loss curriculum to stabilize diffusion training and improve generalization.
Distills the system into a chunk-wise autoregressive model with region-aware corruption and first-chunk training.
Generates streaming video at 24.3 FPS on a single H100 GPU.

papers.abstract: Personalized video generation faces a significant scalability challenge: as the number of custom subjects increases, existing methods suffer from severe identity leakage and semantic entanglement, resulting in videos with blended attributes and incoherent narratives. We identify that this stems from a lack of explicit binding between textual entity phrases and their corresponding visual patterns prior to fusion in diffusion models. To address this, we propose MultiBinder, a novel framework built on a ``bind-then-narrate'' paradigm. Our approach introduces a two-stage conditioning process before video diffusion. First, Cross-modal Entity Binding devises an entity-aware Q-Former to extract identity-centric features from each subject's reference image and tightly align them with its unique entity phrase, yielding disentangled ``identity tokens.'' Second, a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) acts as a ``narrative director'' in the Narrative-Aware Subject Arrangement stage, capturing the action of each subject from the text prompt and synthesizes contextualized subject features that encapsulate ``who is doing what'' and preserve role-specific distinctions. These features are then injected into a video diffusion model via dedicated conditioning pathways, ensuring precise attribute allocation. Extensive experiments on both general and newly curated multi-subject benchmarks show that MultiBinder significantly outperforms existing methods in multi-subject identity fidelity.
authors: Wei Li, Yiheng Zhang, Zhaofan Qiu, Ting Yao, Xiaoyan Sun, Tao Mei
bullets: Addresses identity leakage, blended attributes, and incoherent narratives as the number of custom subjects grows.
Uses an entity-aware Q-Former to align each reference image with its corresponding entity phrase, producing disentangled identity tokens.
Employs an MLLM to determine each subject’s role and action, creating context-aware features that preserve subject distinctions.
Injects these features through dedicated conditioning pathways into a video diffusion model.
Experiments on general and newly curated multi-subject benchmarks report significantly better identity fidelity than existing methods.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video generation has made remarkable progress with diffusion models and transformer-based video architectures, yet generating coherent long videos from evolving textual descriptions remains challenging. Training long-video models from scratch requires substantial computation and large-scale multi-event data, while training-free multi-prompt generation must activate new prompt semantics without breaking temporal continuity. We identify a frequency-agnostic boundary coupling problem in existing transition strategies: weak coupling causes abrupt changes, flicker, and background jumps, whereas overly strong or coarse coupling may over-preserve source semantics and produce ghosting or duplicated subjects around prompt boundaries. To address this problem, we propose FreqSync, a training-free framework that formulates prompt transitions as frequency-selective boundary coupling. FreqSync combines Frequency-Synchronized Source-Conditioned Attention (FS-SCA) with Residual-Clipped Spectral Stitching (RCSS), enabling adjacent segments to share stable low- and mid-frequency structure and motion cues while keeping high-frequency prompt-specific details target-dominant under explicit residual constraints. Extensive experiments show that FreqSync achieves state-of-the-art transition smoothness and prompt alignment while maintaining strong perceptual video quality, demonstrating its effectiveness for coherent multi-prompt long video generation.
authors: Yipan Xu, Shuyong Gao, Jiyuan Fu, Keliang Yin, Jiayu Chen, Qianyu Guo, Yang Liu, Wenqiang Zhang
bullets: Addresses abrupt transitions, flicker, background jumps, ghosting, and duplicated subjects in multi-prompt long-video generation.
Combines Frequency-Synchronized Source-Conditioned Attention with Residual-Clipped Spectral Stitching.
Shares low- and mid-frequency structure and motion across adjacent segments while preserving target-prompt high-frequency details.
Experiments report state-of-the-art transition smoothness and prompt alignment with strong perceptual video quality.
Scope: training-free generation; effectiveness depends on frequency-selective boundary coupling and explicit residual constraints.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of FREQSYNC. Given a prompt sequence, FREQSYNC first encodes frozen text conditions and initializes overlapped latent segments with noise reuse. During iterative denoising, FS-SCA performs frequency-synchronized source-conditioned attention inside selected attention layers, while RCSS applies residual-clipped spectral stitching to denoised overlap predictions before the sampler update. After denoising, overlapped regions are removed and the clean latent segments are concatenated for VAE decoding, producing the final long video.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison. On a three-prompt driving sequence, baselines suffer from viewpoint drift, weak prompt transition, ghosting, or duplicated traces. FREQSYNC preserves vehicle identity and motion while producing smoother semantic transitions.

Figure 6: Visual ablation of FREQSYNC. Isolated generation produces a hard cut. RCSS alone smooths the overlap region but lacks attention-level semantic handover. FS-SCA alone preserves the global layout but changes the chapel structure. Full FREQSYNC combines both modules for smooth transitions and stable identity.

Figure 2: Diagnostic observation. Strong frequency-agnostic coupling may over-preserve sourceside evidence and cause duplicated subjects. FREQSYNC transfers mainly low- and mid-frequency continuity cues while keeping target details controlled.
Figure 1: Teaser of FREQSYNC. Given a prompt sequence, FREQSYNC generates coherent long videos with smooth transitions, stable motion, and prompt-specific details.

Figure 9: Additional three-prompt generated examples. We show three representative three-prompt sequences, where each example spans two rows to cover a longer temporal range and two consecutive prompt boundaries. FREQSYNC maintains coherent temporal evolution across multiple semantic changes, such as scene, illumination, and action transitions. The results suggest that the proposed boundary coupling is not limited to a single transition, but can also support longer prompt sequences with successive target-prompt activations.

Figure 11: Additional qualitative comparison on a skateboarder sequence. The base prompt describes a young skateboarder gliding forward through an open public square, while the segment prompts transition from an empty dawn plaza to a festival plaza and then to a rain-washed night plaza. Kling2.6 [1] produces visually stable frames but shows limited scene progression. MEVG [33] and VideoInfinity [42] suffer from identity, viewpoint, or motion inconsistency. DiTCtrl [7] improves crosssegment continuity but introduces ghosting and blurred boundary artifacts. In contrast, FREQSYNC preserves the skateboarder’s motion trajectory while progressively changing the plaza environment and illumination.

Figure 12: Additional qualitative comparison on a hot-air-balloon sequence. The base prompt describes a hot air balloon, and the segment prompts change the lighting condition from early sunrise glow to bright daylight and then to violet dusk light. Kling-2.6 [1] preserves the balloon appearance but shows limited temporal and illumination transition. MEVG [33] and Video-Infinity [42] produce noticeable subject or scene inconsistencies, including multiple balloons, unstable scale, or abrupt viewpoint changes. DiTCtrl [7] maintains partial continuity but shows over-preserved source-side evidence and boundary-local artifacts. FREQSYNC better preserves the balloon identity and desert layout while producing a smoother lighting transition across the prompt sequence.

Figure 5: Temporal self-similarity around prompt boundaries. FREQSYNC preserves local diagonal continuity while reducing excessive cross-boundary similarity, supporting frequency-selective boundary coupling.

Figure 8: Additional two-prompt generated examples. We show eight representative two-prompt sequences. Each row corresponds to one generated video and visualizes key frames across a single prompt boundary. Across diverse transition types, FREQSYNC preserves the main subject, scene layout, and motion trajectory while allowing the target-prompt condition to emerge progressively. These examples further illustrate that the frequency-synchronized boundary coupling used by FS-SCA and RCSS can reduce abrupt visual changes without suppressing prompt-specific details.

Figure 10: Single-prompt long-video generation with FREQSYNC. We apply FREQSYNC to singleprompt long-video generation by assigning the same prompt to all segments. The four examples show a sunlit courtyard fountain, warm paper lanterns, a drifting maple leaf, and a Mars rover driving across a red crater plain. Even without semantic prompt changes, long-video generation still requires stable cross-segment continuation. FREQSYNC produces smooth motion and coherent visual content over extended durations, suggesting that its boundary-coupling mechanism can also benefit single-prompt video extension.

Figure 7: Boundary temporal-frequency analysis. FREQSYNC shows stronger low-frequency continuation and lower high-frequency variation around prompt boundaries. This supports our frequencysynchronized boundary coupling design, where low-frequency components preserve structural continuity and high-frequency instability is suppressed near transitions.

papers.abstract: Controllable streaming video generation offers a promising route toward interactive game simulation, yet existing methods remain far from practical gameplay. They often fail to jointly achieve high visual fidelity, high frame rates, and low interaction latency, resulting in poor responsiveness and degraded user experience. We present Streaming-AAA, a new paradigm for controllable infinite generation of AAA-quality game videos. Our system generates 1080p gameplay videos at 43 FPS with 198 ms end-to-end latency interaction on merely NVIDIA A800 GPUs, while supporting long-horizon play without severe temporal degradation or collapse. Streaming-AAA is built upon three key designs. First, we redesign the VAE architecture for efficient high-resolution decoding, enabling real-time synthesis at 1080p. Second, we pretrain the diffusion model using diffusion forcing and significantly extend the temporal training horizon, allowing the model to capture long-term dependencies and maintain persistent memory. Third, we perform post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while retaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Experiments show that Streaming-AAA substantially improves visual fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation approaches, enabling a significantly more playable experience for interactive AAA game video generation.
authors: Zhihao Hu, Jianqi Ma, Jun Zhang, Jiayang Bai, Haifeng Shi, Yanxiang Zhuang, Zhongqian Sun, Weidong Zhang, Wei Yang
bullets: Targets the challenge of jointly achieving high visual fidelity, frame rate, responsiveness, and long-term stability in interactive game video generation.
Redesigns the VAE for efficient 1080p decoding and real-time synthesis.
Uses diffusion forcing with an extended temporal training horizon to capture long-term dependencies and persistent memory.
Applies post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while preserving visual and temporal quality.
Experiments report improved fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the inference pipeline. During inference, the 3D UNet-based Diffusion Model takes noise as input, injects control signals via cross-attention, and propagates historical frame information through temporal attention. After multiple denoising steps, the reconstructed latents are decoded by the VAE decoder to produce the generated video frames.

Figure 2: Overview of the ADCS. Designed to capture rich features of AAA games—including diverse landscapes, dynamic interactions (e.g., climbing, swimming), and photorealistic lighting—the system achieves a daily throughput of >10M frames and densely covers KM2s of virtual terrain within several days.
Figure 6: Qualitative results of our method on Genshin Impact. The top eleven rows show rollouts from in-domain frames, while the bottom two rows show rollouts from out-of-domain frames.

Figure 7: Qualitative comparison with state-of-the-art approaches on Genshin Impact. We show our method and the competing approaches on four different cases over a one-minute rollout; rows are methods and columns are timestamps.
Figure 4: Overview of the Hybrid KV-Cache Memory. First row shows the Vanilla KV-cache array, second row shows the proposed Hybrid KV-Cache array.

Figure 8: The results of playing continuously for one hour using our model.
Table 1: Statistics of the Collected AAA Game Dataset. Our dataset provides high-resolution video paired with rich metadata.

papers.abstract: Few-step diffusion models are widely deployed for their efficiency. However, reinforcing them with black-box rewards, as is routine for multi-step models, faces two structural challenges. First, a few-step generator is a sampler rather than a score model, so its velocity is not the forward velocity of the generated distribution. Second, it must be anchored to the undistilled teacher, which shares no transitions with it. Existing few-step RL methods handle the latter with a marginal KL to the teacher, but each pays for the former in its reward credit. We propose Shadow Posterior Matching (SPM), which renoises generated samples into shadow inputs and obtains the credit from their shadow posterior. From the KL-regularized reward objective, we derive a regression loss that turns reward values into a reward direction while anchoring the generator's outputs to the teacher and aligning the shadow inputs with the deployed inputs. Applied to 4-step generators, SPM achieves higher rewards with less reward hacking than prior few-step RL methods.
bullets: Few-step diffusion generators are samplers, making standard reward-credit assignment unsuitable because their velocity differs from the generated distribution’s forward velocity.
They also require anchoring to an undistilled teacher despite sharing no transitions with it.
SPM renoises generated samples into shadow inputs and uses their shadow posterior to obtain reward credit.
A regression loss derived from a KL-regularized reward objective converts reward values into a reward direction while aligning deployed and shadow inputs and anchoring outputs to the teacher.
On 4-step generators, SPM achieves higher rewards with less reward hacking than prior few-step reinforcement-learning methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Shadow Posterior Matching. (a) The deployed few-step sampler generates final samples without gradients, and their black-box rewards yield group-relative advantages. (b) Renoising with fresh noise pairs each shadow input ys with a posterior sample x and the velocity u. (c) Colored arrows show three velocity differences: u − F (ys, s) for shadow credit, and vT − F̂s and F − F̂s at (ŷ, τ) for teacher anchor and endpoint matching. A regression loss pulls the generator’s velocity vθ(ys, s) along their weighted sum Gs.
Figure 3. Qualitative comparison. Samples are generated from GenEval (left), OCR (center), and PickScore (right) test prompts.

Figure 1. Reward curves with a single black-box reward. The reward is GenEval (top) or OCR (bottom). Left: training reward on test prompts. Right: ImageReward on DrawBench prompts. SPM achieves higher task rewards with better image quality.

Figure 4. Ablation results on visual text rendering. Left: OCR reward on test prompts. Right: ImageReward on DrawBench prompts. EM and AW denote endpoint matching and adaptive weighting, respectively. α is the tilting temperature, with a default value of 0.1.

Table 2. Quantitative results. We report training rewards on test prompts, and image-quality metrics and preference scores on DrawBench prompts. Higher is better for all metrics. The best 4-NFE results within each task are shown in bold and second-best results are underlined.

Table 1. Few-step RL paradigms, distinguished by their reward credit. Reward value: the credit is computed from measured reward values, without the reward’s gradient or a learned proxy. Final call: the deterministic final call receives credit from a black-box reward (◦ means only through a learned proxy, and – means not applicable, since the paradigm needs the reward’s gradient). Sharp sample: no reference in the update is built from the generator’s own velocity, so the samples receive no shift toward the posterior mean and stay sharp. Reward direction: the reward provides an update direction independent of the anchor’s force instead of only reweighting the anchor. Teacher KL: the generator is anchored to the teacher by a KL between their marginal distributions.

papers.selection_reason: Reward fine-tuning method for few-step diffusion generators; technically transferable to video diffusion models.
papers.title: Reinforcing Few-Step Diffusion Models via Shadow Posterior Matching
papers.tldr: Shadow Posterior Matching enables more effective and less reward-hacking reinforcement of few-step diffusion generators by deriving reward guidance from renoised shadow samples.

papers.abstract: Flow matching enables high-quality image and video generation, but its iterative sampling process requires repeated evaluations of large neural networks. Existing few-step methods can distort the output and reduce its agreement with a many-step reference. We propose TrajCal, a training-free calibration framework for few-step sampling. Based on scatter search, a well-established metaheuristic for difficult optimization problems, TrajCal starts with diverse seed schedules, deforms and combines these candidates, and selects one fixed schedule by final output fidelity for reuse on new inputs. For both image and video generation, TrajCal achieves higher reference fidelity than all compared baselines at low evaluation budgets while maintaining competitive visual quality. The search is effective even with randomly generated seeds, while trajectory-based seeds further improve fidelity. For cross-style generalization, photography-calibrated schedules also improve fidelity on unseen image styles.
authors: Junchi Zhang, Zihan Gu, Jiangcan Jia, Lulu Zhao, Wenbo Su, Hua Zhang
bullets: Addresses quality degradation and reference mismatch caused by few-step flow sampling.
Uses scatter search to generate, deform, combine, and select candidate time schedules based on final-output fidelity.
Calibrated schedules can be reused across new inputs without retraining.
Improves reference fidelity for image and video generation at low evaluation budgets while retaining competitive visual quality.
Schedules transfer across styles, and trajectory-based seeds improve fidelity beyond random seeds.

papers.abstract: Interactive game world models separate executable world evolution from visual generation, using video models to render engine-provided scene representations into detailed observations. During sustained gameplay, however, existing generative renderers struggle to follow changing conditions while preserving visual continuity across diverse proxies and target styles. We therefore introduce ContextRenderer, an autoregressive video diffusion framework designed for both dynamic conditioning and cross-proxy generalization. It couples Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) for chunk-level interaction supervision with Recurrent History Compression (RHC) to follow condition updates while preserving visual continuity within a bounded token budget. Across proxy representations, Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects proxy reconstruction with appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction. WorldPrism, our interaction-centric dataset constructed from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos, supplies the corresponding renderings and chunk-level annotations for these learning tasks. Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench show improved reconstruction and visual quality, while qualitative results demonstrate minute-long interactive rendering under changing prompts and subject references. Project page: https://rainzor.github.io/contextrenderer/
authors: Runze Wang, Fei Zha, Bing He, Ke Xu, Zhongyuan Wu, Yuxuan Xie, Wenzheng Wu, Zhongyuan Liu, Youcheng Cai, Ligang Liu
bullets: Targets generative renderers that lose continuity and fail to follow evolving gameplay conditions.
Uses Dynamic-Context Learning for chunk-level interaction supervision and Recurrent History Compression to maintain continuity within a bounded token budget.
Introduces Cross-Representation Flow Alignment to support generalization across diverse scene proxies and target appearances.
Provides WorldPrism, a dataset of agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos with renderings and chunk-level annotations.
Improves reconstruction and visual quality on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench; qualitative results show sustained interactive rendering under changing prompts and references.

figures.caption: Figure 3. ContextRenderer overview. (a) Refreshed text, subject references, and proxy chunks condition next-chunk generation alongside visual history. (c) Cross-Representation Flow Alignment jointly trains direct rendering, shared reconstruction, and reconstruction-to-target variation; inference uses the direct path. Scene images and token counts are schematic.

(b) Conditional synthesis and VLM filtering produce corresponding proxies and target variants. (c) Each trajectory’s m proxies and n target variants form m×n training pairs with synchronized chunks, interaction prompts, and subject references.

papers.abstract: When a storm can head north or south, a forecast down the middle may score better under squared error than either plausible path. The same paradox appears when video generators are tested as world models: fewer denoising steps can raise physics scores even as videos blur or stop moving early. Why? Physics-IQ compares each generated video with one recording, although a scene can have multiple valid futures. An exact decomposition shows its scores can reward reduced variation among generated futures, even when their distribution becomes less accurate. We introduce Kernel Physics-IQ to remove this incentive in expectation, needing only two independent samples per condition. Two-step sampling lowers Kernel Physics-IQ in all five image-to-video models. For CogVideoX, the official score rises by 0.055 while ours falls by 0.131. Changing the sampling schedule reveals further differences official scores miss. In controlled physical systems with known outcome probabilities, our metric favors the true distribution over collapsed predictions. In short, a world model should be judged not only by how closely one video matches what happened, but by how faithfully its predictions represent what could have happened.
bullets: Single-reference squared-error evaluation may favor blurred or prematurely stopped videos that reduce prediction variance.
The authors formally decompose this bias and show that Physics-IQ can improve as generated futures collapse, even when their distribution worsens.
Kernel Physics-IQ removes the incentive in expectation using two independent samples per condition.
Across five image-to-video models, two-step sampling lowered Kernel Physics-IQ; for CogVideoX, the official score rose by 0.055 while the proposed score fell by 0.131.
Controlled physical-system tests show the new metric prefers the true outcome distribution over collapsed predictions.

figures.caption: Figure 6. Tied official scores hide different futures. (a) Predictors in a pendulum world that swings left or right with equal probability: each card shows what the predictor draws (line weight: probability; dashed: never drawn), and the pixel mean blends both swings into one video (diamond: mean position). (b) Exact scores, averaged with a ball dropped onto a peg: the raw official composite ties the first four, whereas Kernel Physics-IQ ranks the true distribution first, as it does among all 34 predictors. (c) Mask distance: staying still wins below the thresholds of Prop. 2.

Figure 3. What one sample cannot see. A sample is scored by its distance to the recording (blue), which on average is the kernel score plus half the self-dispersion (green). Two-step samples disperse less: the dispersion premium they collect (dashed) outweighs their kernel loss, so single-sample scoring prefers them. A second sample measures the self-dispersion, which Kernel Physics-IQ subtracts. Frames: paper-smoke 2 s after the switch frame (Wan2.2, two seeds). Brackets (root-mean-square) and bars: Wan2.2 ST IoU distances on whole clips, mean over 66 scenes.

Figure 4. Fewer steps align seeds far more than they match truth. (a) Recording (x̄) vs. seed overlap (ȳ) with Eq. (6) contours and the 0.695 no-overlap line. (b) Dispersion-premium and kernelpart bars behind net diamonds for the official split. (c) Spatial masks behind x and y: Wan2.2 seeds 43 and 44 on rolling-reflection (Fig. 2b) against take 1 (teal). (d) ST IoU splits by scene motion.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes evaluation of video generators as world models and denoising-step effects; relevant to world models and video diffusion.
papers.title: What One Sample Cannot See: Why Fewer Denoising Steps Can Score Higher on Physics Benchmarks
papers.tldr: Physics-IQ can reward video world models for producing less varied, less realistic futures; Kernel Physics-IQ corrects this using two independent samples per condition.

papers.abstract: Human-object motion synthesis requires coordinated human participation as objects move toward specified goals. However, reaching object targets does not ensure that contact is established and maintained, while adjustments that improve contact may interfere with task completion. We introduce CoRelate, a diffusion framework that coordinates full-body human-object motion through explicit interaction relations and task feedback for rigid and articulated objects. We represent intended participation through hand-part relations that specify the participating hand, its part-relative reference position, and participation interval. These relations serve both as generation conditions and as references for measuring interaction realization. At each denoising step, a temporal refiner trained jointly with the generator combines relation deviations, task residuals, and motion features from the current prediction to jointly update human and object motion across the sequence. After generation, temporal motion correction addresses remaining contact failures by optimizing local motion segments while preserving object trajectories and protected human motion. Experiments demonstrate improved object-goal satisfaction, contact F1, and complete interaction success over the evaluated baselines. Ablation studies support the benefits of relation conditioning and the complementary roles of task and relation feedback.
authors: Zhiwen Qiu, Daisy Lin, Diyu Zhou, Jialin Wu, Rosita Ji, Saleh Kalantari
bullets: Targets the challenge of achieving both object-goal completion and sustained human–object contact.
Conditions generation on participating hand, part-relative reference position, and interaction interval.
Uses a temporal refiner to jointly update human and object motion from relation deviations, task residuals, and current motion features.
Applies local temporal correction after generation to fix contact failures while preserving object trajectories and protected human motion.
Experiments report improved object-goal satisfaction, contact F1, and complete interaction success; ablations support relation conditioning and combined feedback.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video editors possess rich removal and completion priors, yet may retain targets or alter unrelated content. We present H3Remover, which reinforces MiniMax-H3 Base Ref2VA for video object removal without paired object-free training targets. To discourage superficial edits such as recoloring, a target-removal reward favors calibrated depth changes consistent with revealing farther content. To limit unintended scene changes, a background-geometry reward encourages preservation of relative depth ordering. To preserve background appearance without retaining unwanted shadows or reflections, an appearance reward constrains RGB changes in source-derived protected regions while exempting targets and estimated effects. Frozen HPSv3 complements these constraints with perceptual-quality feedback for synthesized content. Evaluation regions remain fixed across candidates, and DiffusionART optimizes LoRA adapters with the backbone frozen. Experiments show substantial reconstruction gains over original H3, with qualitative comparisons demonstrating more effective object removal and better preservation of surrounding scene content.

Adds frozen HPSv3 perceptual feedback for synthesized content.
Optimizes LoRA adapters with the backbone frozen and keeps evaluation regions fixed across candidates.
Achieves substantial reconstruction gains over the original H3, with better removal and background preservation qualitatively.

papers.abstract: Self-attention over long token sequences dominates the inference cost of video diffusion transformers. Clustering-based sparse attention clusters both queries and keys and lets all queries in a cluster share one selection of key clusters. We show that this sharing limits accuracy: with key clusters and density fixed, attention grows more accurate as the query clusters are refined, and is most accurate when each query selects on its own, which needs no query clustering at all. We therefore propose Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention (PQRS), a training-free method that clusters only keys, lets each query select its own key clusters, and compensates for the unselected ones with their centroids. Per-query selections leave no query tile with a shared key list, so PQRS traverses key clusters instead of queries, buckets queries with identical selections into dense tasks, and merges their partial results in one pass under a fixed softmax offset carried from the previous denoising step. On four text-to-video and image-to-video models from the Wan and HunyuanVideo families, PQRS is the fastest of all the sparse attention methods we evaluate and the closest to the dense output, reaching $28.9$ dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and $35.4$ dB on HunyuanVideo at $1.66$--$2.10\times$ end-to-end speedup.
authors: Zhen Huang, Shuwei Li, Ruizhe Yao, Xinrui Chen, Danyi Liu, Haoyuan Liang, Zhiyu Ye, Qiuyan Sun, Bingwei Chen, Yiyuan Li, Xu Zhou, Haohuan Fu
bullets: Clustering queries and keys together limits sparse-attention accuracy because queries in a cluster share key selections.
PQRS clusters only keys, performs per-query key-cluster selection, and approximates unselected keys with cluster centroids.
It efficiently executes per-query routing by grouping queries with identical selections and merging results with a carried softmax offset.
Evaluated on four Wan and HunyuanVideo text-to-video and image-to-video models, it achieves 1.66–2.10× end-to-end speedup.
It reports 28.9 dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and 35.4 dB on HunyuanVideo, while remaining closest to dense attention among evaluated sparse methods.

papers.abstract: Long video sequences make attention a substantial cost in video diffusion models. Block sparse attention (BSA) reduces this cost by computing selected blocks exactly while compressing the remaining blocks. However, fixed token grouping can place tokens with dissimilar attention preferences in the same group, while uniform key averaging can underestimate the attention mass of compressed blocks. We introduce Spark-Attn, a training-free BSA method comprising Spark-Reblock and Spark-Reweight. Spark-Reblock recursively groups tokens by attention preference while preserving regular block shapes for efficient GPU execution. Spark-Reweight uses the global mean query as an anchor to construct attention-weighted key-value representations and logit biases for the compressed blocks, calibrating their attention mass. We instantiate Spark-Attn in MiniMax-H3 as Spark-H3. At 10% exact-block density, Spark-H3 delivers a 2.49$\times$ DiT speedup and reaches 24.81 dB PSNR against the corresponding dense outputs on MiniMax-H3 (20 denoising steps, 345 frames, 1344$\times$768). Increasing the density to 20% further improves PSNR to 26.76 dB while still achieving a 2.26$\times$ DiT speedup. These results demonstrate that Spark-H3 achieves a state-of-the-art quality-efficiency trade-off for training-free BSA on video diffusion models.
authors: Zecheng Tang, Jiaye Fu, Youtian Lin, Xinyao Rao, Liuxuan Sun, Jian Zhang, Yao Yao, Wei Li
bullets: Targets the high attention cost of long video sequences in diffusion models.
Spark-Reblock recursively groups tokens with similar attention preferences while retaining GPU-friendly regular blocks.
Spark-Reweight uses a global-mean-query anchor to build weighted key-value summaries and calibrate compressed-block attention mass.
At 10% exact-block density, it achieves a 2.49× DiT speedup and 24.81 dB PSNR versus dense outputs.
At 20% density, PSNR rises to 26.76 dB with a 2.26× speedup; the method is training-free and instantiated in MiniMax-H3.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Spark-Attn overview. (1) Block routing: Spark-Reblock groups query and key–value (KV) tokens into preference-aware, uniformly sized tiles; tile means guide selection of a fraction ρ of KV tiles per query tile. (2) Two-branch attention: Selected blocks are computed exactly, while the rest are approximated using Spark-Reweight’s weighted KV representatives and logit biases. Both branches share one softmax normalization, with compressed entries for selected blocks masked to avoid double counting. N , M , and ρ denote the number of video tokens, the number of KV tiles, and the exact-block density, respectively.

Figure 1. MiniMax-H3 and Spark-H3. (a,b) Qualitative comparisons on 14.4s, 1344× 768 videos generated using 20 denoising steps. Spark-H3 uses exact-block density ρ = 0.2 in these examples. papers.abstract: Filming a scene from an additional angle after production usually requires a costly reshoot. We present One Shot Any View, a system that takes a recorded clip and generates a reshot video of the same performance along a user-specified camera trajectory. As in recent geometry-grounded methods, the system conditions generation on the source video and an explicit 3D prior, namely a point video rendered along the requested trajectory from a feed-forward reconstruction of the source video. We target human-centric cinematic videos, which are often shot with long lenses, shallow depth of field, and low-key lighting, all of which degrade feed-forward reconstruction. Existing geometry-grounded methods tend to inherit the degraded point video, and their output quality drops visibly. Two designs make such point videos usable. First, in addition to rendered videos of 3D assets, we train on real-world multi-camera videos, whose point videos are produced by the same reconstruction pipeline as at inference. This training-inference consistency enables the generator to take only the composition of people and scene elements from the point video, and their appearance from the source video. Second, a geometry-anchored RoPE offset keeps the generated video temporally synchronized with the source while largely preventing the output from copying the degraded appearance of the point video. Meanwhile, since the generator is a pretrained reference-to-video (R2V) model, the system also accepts optional character and scene reference images, which supply the appearance of regions that the source never shows. In both objective and human evaluations, One Shot Any View outperforms existing reshooting methods.

Supports optional character and scene reference images, and outperforms existing reshooting methods in objective and human evaluations.

papers.abstract: E-commerce visual effects (EVF) are dynamic, product-centered visual presentations in e-commerce videos, often accompanied by promotional text. They play an important role in attracting viewer attention and conveying product information. However, general measures of visual quality and text relevance alone do not establish whether generated videos preserve product appearance, maintain readable text, and produce coherent, contextually appropriate effects. To address this issue, we introduce EVF-Bench, a dedicated benchmark spanning six evaluation dimensions: visual quality and text relevance as general dimensions, and motion, product consistency, text stability, and creative rationality as EVF-specific dimensions. To complement the benchmark and support task-aligned research and model adaptation, we further construct EVF-32K, a dataset of over 32000 curated image-text-video triples tailored to e-commerce scenarios. Using this suite, we systematically evaluate representative video generation models and their domain-adapted variants. The results reveal complementary strengths, with no evaluated configuration leading all six dimensions. Together, EVF-Bench and EVF-32K provide a task-oriented evaluation framework and a supporting data resource for e-commerce video generation.

Provides a task-oriented benchmark and data resource for evaluating and adapting e-commerce video generation models.

papers.abstract: Simulating how physical systems respond to changing conditions is central to control, design, and scenario studies. To our knowledge, prior PDE foundation models have not been trained or evaluated on changes within trajectories. Our counterfactual test measures how far predictions move toward a changed solver branch from the same state. Models trained on fixed conditions follow changes only partly. A PDE foundation model given a condition input after pretraining barely responds. PhysDial adapts a pretrained video diffusion transformer to eight two-dimensional PDE families. Coefficients enter with the noise level, condition fields as reference frames, and equation text as a prompt. In Kolmogorov flow, switches within trajectories account for about 5% of the training samples. At matched compute, they halve the error after a change in forcing wavenumber or amplitude. A few trajectories at new amplitudes more than halve extrapolation error. Without physics pretraining, PhysDial matches or exceeds PDE foundation models under training conditions on two turbulent flows. At step 64 on the Kolmogorov test split, PhysDial has 1.07 times the solver's small-scale energy and Walrus 7.1 times. Our experiments suggest that a learned simulator uses a condition only as far as its training data make that condition necessary for prediction. Learning from trajectories that diverge under intervention can help scientific simulators predict what would happen if a system's forcing or parameters changed.
authors: Yilong Dai, Yiming Sun, Shengyu Chen, Jiaqi Gong, Xiaowei Jia, Runlong Yu
bullets: Fixed-condition PDE models only partially follow within-trajectory changes, while simply adding condition inputs after pretraining has little effect.
PhysDial combines coefficients, condition fields, and equation text as conditioning for a pretrained video diffusion transformer across eight 2D PDE families.
Including intervention samples in Kolmogorov-flow training roughly halves errors after changes in forcing wavenumber or amplitude at matched compute.
A few trajectories at new amplitudes substantially reduce extrapolation error; without physics pretraining, PhysDial matches or exceeds PDE foundation models on two turbulent flows.
The approach suggests simulators learn to use conditions only when training data make them necessary for prediction.

papers.abstract: We present the Autoregressive View Model (AVM), which generates a scene as a stream of views without constructing an explicit 3D representation. Through a unified in-context interface, AVM conditions on images or videos to generate short clips along a requested camera path. Visual context grounds reconstruction and interpolation, while a learned prior enables extrapolation into unseen regions. AVM retrieves relevant views from inputs and generated history to form a bounded active context. We fine-tune a pretrained bidirectional video diffusion transformer with flow matching in an N-in-1-out formulation. We then tune a causal model on its own rollouts to improve photorealism, reduce denoising steps, and limit long-horizon drift. We scale training to approximately 8M scenes and video clips. We evaluate generation capacity and scene persistence across benchmarks for camera control, text control, visual quality, dynamics, sparse and 4D reconstruction, and long-horizon consistency. The results demonstrate that AVM adapts to diverse input and output settings through one in-context interface.
authors: Jensen (Jinghao), Zhou, Samuel Rota Bulo, Denis Rozumny, Duncan Zauss, Peter Hedman, Nikhil Keetha, Philip Torr, Christian Rupprecht, Andrea Vedaldi, Peter Kontschieder
bullets: Uses visual context for reconstruction and interpolation, while a learned prior enables extrapolation into unseen regions.
Retrieves relevant input and generated views to maintain a bounded active context.
Fine-tunes a bidirectional video diffusion transformer with flow matching, then trains a causal model on its rollouts.
Evaluated across camera and text control, visual quality, dynamics, sparse and 4D reconstruction, and long-horizon consistency.
The abstract reports adaptation across diverse input/output settings through a unified in-context interface.

papers.abstract: Stereo vision is increasingly used for robotic manipulation, with a growing body of work incorporating it into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, the scarcity of large-scale, real-world stereo datasets remains a fundamental bottleneck for scaling such policies. Recent generative monocular-to-stereo methods target settings such as VR content and autonomous driving. No prior work produces realistic synthetic stereo data for robotic manipulation, where stereo supervision has come predominantly from simulation. We propose StereoEngine, which introduces two complementary methods to synthesize stereo data for robotic manipulation. In the first, we warp a monocular (left) video into the right view using estimated depth and inpaint the disoccluded regions with a video diffusion model, lifting monocular demonstrations into stereo pairs without training on real stereo. In the second, we render a stereo pair in simulation and jointly generate both photorealistic views, producing consistent left-right data without any real video as input. StereoEngine outperforms existing baselines in generated stereo quality, and using its synthetic data for policy mid-training or task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves downstream bimanual manipulation. Project website: https://stereoengine.github.io
bullets: Addresses the shortage of large-scale real-world stereo datasets for vision-language-action manipulation models.
Warps monocular left-view video into a right view using estimated depth and video-diffusion inpainting for disocclusions.
Alternatively, jointly renders photorealistic, left-right-consistent stereo views from simulation.
Produces higher-quality synthetic stereo data than existing baselines, according to the abstract.
Using the generated data for policy mid-training or task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves bimanual manipulation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Method Overview. StereoEngine-L applies when a ground-truth left video is available. The warping module (1) moves every left pixel to its position in the right view, giving a warped right video and a mask marking the pixels no left pixel could reach. A video diffusion model (2) fills the masked region from these and a language prompt ℓ, giving a right video (3) that pairs with the original left. StereoEngine-S applies when no real video exists. We render (1) the episode in simulation from two cameras, convert both renders to Canny edges, and (2) pass the edge videos to the model with two reference images and the instruction ℓ. The edge map defines the scene geometry, while the reference images supply the appearance of the real workspace such as background, lighting, and surface texture. Then (3) a video generation model generates the synthetic video. In both methods, the resulting stereo pairs can be used to train a downstream bimanual stereo-conditioned policy.

Fig. 4: Real-world rollouts. Each row shows a successful policy rollout by ExStereo [24] trained on StereoEngine data, from top to bottom: Stack Two Bowls, Lift Transparent Bottles, Close Door, Lift Two Bottles, and Container Plate. Both StereoEngine methods test Stack Two Bowls, while the other four tasks are tested on one of our methods. Columns show the progression of time (left to right).

Fig. 3: Warping Module. (1) the ground truth left view is abstracted into a grid of pixels, where A to N label the background and O1 to O4 label the object, and each pixel is given the disparity it must move by, d = 4 for the object and d = 1 for the background. (2) every pixel moves left by its own disparity, since the camera translates right. The object moves further and covers C,D,E, and the nearer pixel is kept, so only B survives. (3) the background G,H, I was hidden behind the object and never observed, so nothing can fill the gap it leaves and those columns become the mask. (4) the rest of the background shifts left by one, leaving the right border without any source. (5) the grid is mapped back to pixels to give the warped right view, correct where a pixel arrived and empty where the left camera never saw the surface.

Fig. 6: Comparison of RealSense and stereo. Top: an American football captured with a standard RGB camera. Bottom left: the 3D point cloud from an Intel RealSense D405 depth sensor where the red region shows geometric deformation of the ball’s surface. Bottom right: the point cloud recovered by FoundationStereo [25] from a stereo pair captured with a ZED Mini 2 where the same green region shows minimal deformation of the object.

Fig. 5: Synthetic episode generation. The top three rows show synthetic episodes generated by StereoEngine-S, one per task, from top to bottom: Stack Two Bowls, Lift Two Bottles, and Container Plate. Below the dashed line, the last row (Fold Clothes) shows a largescale data generation example from StereoEngine-L, where a real monocular demonstration is lifted into stereo. Within each row, adjacent columns form a left–right stereo pair, and successive pairs show the progression of time from left to right.
Fig. 7: Real-World Setup. Our real-world platform uses two AgileX PiPER arms. The pink dashed circle marks the ZED Mini 2 stereo camera that captures the stereo pairs.

Video Gen.: operates on videos instead of single images. No Stereo Pairs: requires no real stereo correspondences for training. Variable Baseline: synthesizes stereo videos with a controllable stereo baseline instead of a fixed one. Both Views: synthesizes both left and right views. Gen. Length: maximum number of frames generated in a single pass. ∗Extendable to arbitrary length via autoregression. †No public code available and generation length not reported in the paper.

TABLE III: Stereo generation quality for StereoEngine-L, on 50 heldout real stereo clips. These clips are different from the demonstrations used for training. Each method synthesizes a right view from the same groundtruth left video. CTC measures temporal consistency across generated frames. StereoEngine achieves the best score on every metric. Here, ↑ means higher is better, and ↓ means lower is better.

TABLE II: Real-world results. Success rate over 20 trials (higher is better). The Base Policy is the stereo-conditioned policy being trained (ExStereo [24] or StereoVLA [5]), and each column is a different training condition. In StereoEngine-L, each column is a different mid-training condition: No Mid. trains the policy directly with no stereo mid-training, and the remaining columns mid-train it on stereo data from SVG [15] and StereoCrafter [14] (baselines) or our StereoEngine (highlighted in green); all conditions share the same real fine-tuning data per task. In StereoEngine-S, no real demonstrations are used for training, so each column is a different source of task-specific training data: simulated point clouds versus our StereoEngine synthetic stereo. Across both, StereoEngine (Ours) gives the best performance.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models are orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8x slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8x B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.
authors: Gene Chou, Guandao Yang, Fujun Luan, Lars Mescheder, Wei Dong, Stephan Richter, Vladlen Koltun
bullets: Existing autoregressive video diffusion models are too slow for fluid interactive experiences.
Profiling shows VAE decoding and KV-cache updates contribute over half of end-to-end inference latency.
FastFrames replaces these components with lightweight alternatives in a family of fast models.
The 1.3B model achieves 36 ms per frame on a single B200 GPU while matching a much slower state-of-the-art model’s quality.
The 14B model achieves 45 ms per frame on an 8×B200 node with significantly better visual quality and realism, enabling real-time camera- and physics-conditioned generation.

Figure 5 Interactive generation and latency results. Left: example of interaction with LingBot’s official implementation vs. with FastFrames optimizations. Given a single keypress, FastFrames is 16× faster to respond. Right: generation latency of officially released implementations and our optimized implementations. We measure steady-state latency on NVIDIA B200 GPUs at 832×480 resolution with a full KV cache and include distributed optimizations such as Ulysses where officially supported. Times include diffusion sampling (four steps for LingBot and three for RealWonder), action conditioning, KV-cache updates, and pixel decoding. Our optimizations provide speedups of 3× to 22×. See the project website for the video demonstration.

A single linear projection (middle) cannot render sharp outputs, but is sufficient for recognizing the scene and suggests that pixel rendering does not require an expensive decoder.

Figure 4 Qualitative comparisons. We compare FastFrames-S with Causal Forcing++ at 1.3B parameters and FastFrames-L with Krea-Realtime at 14B. Each example shows frames at 0 and 5 seconds. FastFrames-S achieves comparable visual sharpness to Causal Forcing++, such as the details in the sculpture (first example) and leaves (second example), while being nearly 8× faster. FastFrames-L achieves comparable visual realism to Krea-Realtime, including composition of “paper origami dragon” (third), and legible text of “stay curious” (fourth) while being 10× faster. Only FastFrames meets an acceptable threshold (Deber et al., 2015) for seamless interactivity (≤ 50ms latency, equivalently ≥ 20 responses per second (RPS)) while matching or exceeding comparable baselines in visual quality.

papers.abstract: When a text-to-video diffusion model ignores part of a prompt, the usual first fix is to raise the classifier-free guidance scale. This paper is a measurement study of when that fix works. On Mochi, the same increase repairs failures on rare compositions ("a snowy beach") beyond what generating again does, does not repair negations ("a highway with no vehicles"), where it fixes fewer failures than generating again does, and changes nothing for events that must happen late in a clip ("a sandcastle that a wave washes flat"). Which of these happens can be known in advance, from the prompt and one inexpensive score. The score, which we call demand, measures how strongly the denoiser reacts to the part of the prompt that the failed video leaves out, and it is read from the first quarter of denoising, before any video exists. Our main finding is a condition: raising the scale is effective only when the prompt contains no negation and no event tied to a specific time, and when demand is sufficiently high, with recovery clearly higher above a fitted threshold than below it. Published corrections for the three failure types, used as fixed probes, behave as this account predicts. A short decision rule follows: before generating again, a user can tell whether the most common fix is worth trying, and what to use when it is not.
bullets: On Mochi, stronger guidance helps rare compositions such as “a snowy beach” more than regenerating.
It helps fewer negation failures, such as “a highway with no vehicles,” than generating again, and does not fix events that occur late in a clip.
A demand score, computed from the first quarter of denoising, measures the denoiser’s response to omitted prompt content before video generation finishes.
Guidance is effective when the prompt has no negation or time-specific event and demand exceeds a fitted threshold.
The study provides a decision rule for choosing between increasing guidance and generating again.

figures.caption: Figure 6. Recovery against demand.
