papers.abstract: Video world models should maintain a world that keeps evolving as the viewpoint changes. Yet when the camera turns away and returns, current models often freeze the unobserved scene, lose objects, or change their appearance, because content outside the view has no representation that keeps changing. We present PanoEvo, which uses a Panoramic Evolver to evolve the world state in the latent space of a panoramic video diffusion model, where every viewing direction is present at every time step, so the scene evolves whether or not it is observed. Existing panoramic video models are not trained to evolve a scene from a single image or the objects within it, so we build PanoEvo-Data, an event-centric dataset from real 360{\deg} videos, and train the Panoramic Evolver coarse-to-fine as an image-to-panoramic-video model. Since each view covers only a small part of the low-resolution panorama, directly projected views are blurry and often show low-quality details or structural errors. A Perspective Renderer, built on a perspective video diffusion model, reads this state via latent-space projection and direction-restricted cross-attention to render sharp, high-quality views. PanoEvo achieves the best overall score among 23 publicly evaluated models on WRBench and the highest total score on STEVO-Bench. Code, models, and data will be released.
authors: Longtao Jiang, Mingfei Han, Jianmin Bao, Tingjun Dai, Jinjie Wei, Zhiran Zhang, Xin Tao, Zhihui Li, Salman Khan, Xiaojun Chang
bullets: Addresses the failure of video world models to evolve off-screen content as viewpoints change.
Uses a Panoramic Evolver to update all viewing directions in latent space at every time step.
Introduces PanoEvo-Data, an event-centric dataset from real 360° videos, and trains the evolver coarse-to-fine from images to panoramic video.
Uses a Perspective Renderer with latent projection and direction-restricted cross-attention to generate detailed views from the panoramic state.
Reports the best overall score among 23 publicly evaluated models on WRBench and the highest total score on STEVO-Bench.

papers.abstract: Reference-to-video diffusion transformers pack the variational autoencoder (VAE) latents of all references and the generated tokens into one full-attention sequence, in which reference tokens make up about half. Because attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, these tokens take up an even larger share of the attention computation, yet most of them are static, smooth or irrelevant to the output. To accelerate reference-conditioned generation, we propose pruning and caching of reference tokens for video generation (PCRG), a training-free, plug-and-play method that uses two signals the model already computes to assign each reference token to one of three tiers, namely pruned, cached or kept. The first is a low-level redundancy r from VAE latents, since a token whose latent barely changes over time or across its neighbors adds little new content. The second is a high-level importance g from the vision-language-model (VLM) conditioner, where the attention that the prompt and any first or last frames pay to a token tells whether the output needs to read it. Tokens that are not redundant are kept, and redundant tokens are cached if important and pruned otherwise. Pruned tokens leave the sequence before the first step with all rotary position embedding positions unchanged. Cached tokens have their keys and values computed once and reused, and kept tokens are processed as usual. On MiniMax-H3, already distilled to 8 timesteps and quantized to int8, PCRG is 1.57x faster end to end on our V2V-Bench and 1.49x faster on the public VACE-Benchmark, while the quality of VBench drops by only 0.24% and 0.17%, respectively. PCRG shortens the sequence rather than changing how attention is computed or which steps are run, so it also stacks on step caching and sparse attention. On V2V-Bench it reaches 1.86x with TeaCache, 1.82x with Spark at nearly unchanged fidelity and 2.15x with Veda.
authors: Siyuan Wang, Haoran Li, Yi Yue, Tak L. Fung, Quan Chen
bullets: Targets the quadratic attention cost caused by reference tokens, which comprise roughly half of the sequence.

Achieves 1.57× and 1.49× end-to-end speedups on two benchmarks with only 0.24% and 0.17% VBench quality drops.
Combines with existing acceleration methods, reaching up to 2.15× speedup in the reported experiments.

papers.abstract: Amodal perception enables humans to perceive entire objects even when parts are occluded, a remarkable cognitive skill that artificial intelligence struggles to replicate. Recent diffusion-based methods have extended amodal completion from images to videos, yet they lack auxiliary priors to guide the reconstruction of heavily occluded content and to maintain temporal consistency over long sequences. We present REVEAL (REconstructing VidEo Amodal content via Language and flow guidance), a unified diffusion-based framework that integrates complementary motion and semantic priors for video amodal completion. A user-provided text query serves a dual role: it drives open-vocabulary video segmentation to obtain visible masks, and it provides semantic guidance for texture reconstruction. For amodal segmentation, we introduce optical flow guidance: by warping visible masks from previous frames to the current frame, the flow-warped mask propagates visible content into occluded regions and approximates the object's current shape, providing a strong shape prior even under simultaneous deformation and occlusion. For texture completion, text guidance constrains the reconstruction of occluded appearance while providing a stable semantic reference that helps maintain visual coherence throughout the reconstruction. We also contribute LAVAT, a new benchmark featuring long video sequences paired with text descriptions, enabling evaluation of text-guided video amodal completion under heavy occlusion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that REVEAL achieves state-of-the-art performance on existing benchmarks while maintaining high-quality temporal consistency over extended sequences. The project page is available at: https://uark-aicv.github.io/REVEAL/.
authors: Minh Tran, Winston Bounsavy, Ngan Le

Reports state-of-the-art performance on existing benchmarks with high temporal consistency over extended sequences.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art world models have been used to produce sequences of gameplay that accord with provided user-input actions. However, high quality, consistent gameplay generation often comes at the cost of inference speed, making real-time interactive play and ideation challenging. The substantial quantities of data used to train state-of-the-art models have also made custom training of these models appear impractical, limiting many of their potential uses in creative fields. In this work we demonstrate a major step towards efficient world models: achieving both fast high-quality inference, and improved data efficiency. This is done by replacing the next-token prediction paradigm with a two-stage discrete diffusion-based approach, introducing a lightweight refinement transformer which carries out iterative masked predictions. Building on an autoregressive world model capable of generating highly consistent and complex sequences over minutes (Kanervisto et al., 2025), we achieve substantial model speed-up (79x) with a modest quality trade-off. Additionally, we demonstrate that this model can be trained to reproduce high-quality, consistent gameplay using a dataset containing approximately one day (28 hours) of gameplay data. Our results demonstrate progress towards removing barriers to the use of world models in settings where real-time inference and data efficiency are essential.
authors: Raluca Stevenson, David Bignell, Jennifer C. White, Tabish Rashid, Emanuele Aiello, Mariya Hendriksen, Junha Hyung, Sadegh Aliakbarian, Abdelhak Lemkhenter, Marko Tot, Katja Hofmann, Sarah Parisot

papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. Unlike previous methods, where the denoising output leads to final pixels, DWD separates the two roles: the original denoising head continues to drive sampling, then the new DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step. We extend pretrained latent models with DWD efficiently by finetuning only the last few transformer blocks, training the DWD head with pixel quality losses while anchoring the denoising head to the pretrained model to preserve the sample trajectory. Across latent image and video generators, DWD removes the decoder and reduces inference cost while maintaining or even improving pixel quality. On Wan video generation, it visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by 23%. Remarkably, the same separation also improves pixel diffusion models that do not even use a decoder: a final-step DWD head produces substantially better texture detail in text-to-image generation, and improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models.
authors: Hansheng Chen, Shengqu Cai, Jan Ackermann, Rayhan Zirvi, Gordon Wetzstein, Xinchen Yan, Leonidas Guibas
bullets: Addresses the complexity and inference cost of decoders in latent diffusion models.

Works across image and video generators, reducing detail distortion and flickering; Wan’s warping error drops by 23%.
Also improves pixel diffusion models, raising ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43 and enhancing texture detail.

papers.abstract: The effectiveness of a video diffusion model's inference budget depends on where computation is spent along the denoising trajectory. Across eight equal-budget inference configurations, VBench total scores span 4.80 points, highlighting the importance of explicit allocation design. Our key insight is that guidance evaluations are not equally valuable across diffusion time: retaining the sampling updates while selectively reusing guidance can preserve generation quality with fewer denoiser evaluations. We introduce BATMoS (Budget Aware Temporal Mixture of Strategies), which routes between fresh classifier-free guidance and cached guidance using a single pretrained denoiser. A magnitude-based temporal rule assigns guidance reuse to low-magnitude blocks and reserves fresh guidance for the remaining blocks, with a single integer controlling the computation budget. The resulting schedule requires no additional router training or per-budget threshold search. Evaluated on CogVideoX-2B with 4,720 videos per configuration across all sixteen official VBench dimensions, BATMoS achieves the highest total score among the eight allocation policies and comes within 0.10 points of full classifier-free guidance using 20\% fewer branch evaluations. BATMoS also composes with feature reuse, reducing computation from 80 to 62 effective branch evaluations with a 0.11-point decrease in total score. These findings make temporal guidance allocation a practical mechanism for extracting more generation quality from a fixed inference budget.
authors: Zhixu Du, Kuo Yang, Jingwei Sun, Hai "Helen" Li, Yiran Chen
bullets: Inference quality varies substantially with how a fixed computation budget is allocated along the denoising trajectory.
BATMoS routes between fresh classifier-free guidance and cached guidance using a single pretrained denoiser.
A magnitude-based temporal rule reuses guidance in low-magnitude blocks and reserves fresh evaluations elsewhere, controlled by one integer budget parameter.
On CogVideoX-2B across all 16 VBench dimensions, it achieves the best score among eight allocation policies and comes within 0.10 points of full guidance with 20% fewer branch evaluations.
Combined with feature reuse, it reduces effective branch evaluations from 80 to 62 with a 0.11-point score decrease.

The vertical axis is logarithmic. The shaded region contains the blocks selected for guidance reuse at 𝐵 = 80. (b) Replacing one five-update block of fresh CFG with guidance reuse saves five branch evaluations. A prefix of the fixed magnitude ranking determines the schedule, with 𝐵 = 100 − 5𝑘 .

Fig. 3: Guidance allocation and feature reuse retain different quantities. (a) Full CFG refreshes the conditional– unconditional difference. A later guidance-reuse update combines that cached difference with a fresh conditional prediction. (b) Internal residual reuse operates inside two-branch CFG runs. Run boundaries refresh the stack, and one-branch guidance-reuse updates execute all blocks. The strip shows full-stack CFG (dark blue), guidance reuse (hatched red), and residual reuse (pale blue). Their update counts are 21, 20, and nine, yielding 62 effective NFE.

papers.abstract: Streaming video generation must sustain quality beyond the training horizon while handling self-generated history and growing cache costs. To address these challenges, we present MovieRoll, a base-to-distilled framework that connects streaming fine-tuning, long-rollout distillation, and long-horizon inference. We first establish a robust multi-step base through Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF), which jointly denoises chunks at progressive noise levels with bidirectional attention within each window and causal access to preceding history. To retain historical context efficiently, hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) exploits layer-wise attention patterns, retaining full history in shallow layers and sink--recent history in deeper layers. This reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality. Building on this base, cumulative long tuning with distribution matching distillation (CuLT-DMD) holds parameters fixed throughout each long self-rollout and averages local gradients before updating. Each update therefore combines supervision across temporal positions while retaining only one local computation graph, enabling efficient long-rollout training of a few-step generator. To extend generation beyond the training horizon, KV recomputation bounds context for both models, while guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) reduces guidance toward the clean endpoint to stabilize MovieRoll-Base. Complementing these modeling advances, FBCA attention and PS-VAE decoding support efficient training and streaming output. On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30s after training on videos of up to 15s, and MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among the compared methods across single- and multi-event evaluations up to 60s, combining sustained naturalness with active motion.
authors: Yunyang Ge, Weijie Kong, Ryan Xu, Yue Wu, Qi Tian, Jiangfeng Xiong, Bin Lin, Mingzhe Zheng, Shenghai Yuan, Zheyuan Liu, Jianwei Zhang, Li Yuan
bullets: Targets quality degradation beyond the training horizon, self-generated history, and increasing KV-cache costs.
WinTF builds a multi-step base using window-wise denoising with local bidirectional attention and causal access to prior history.
HieraKV reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality by adapting retained history across layers.
CuLT-DMD enables efficient long-rollout distillation by aggregating gradients across temporal positions while keeping one local computation graph.
On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30 seconds, while MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among compared methods through 60 seconds.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of MovieRoll. Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF) trains MovieRoll-Base through parallel window supervision conditioned on clean history and event prompts. After ODE initialization, Cumulative Long Tuning with Distribution Matching Distillation (CuLT-DMD) trains a few-step generator by averaging local gradients across long self-rollouts. Both models jointly denoise a rolling window, use hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) to retain history across layers, and rebuild the cache at a history threshold or prompt switch. Classifier-free guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) gradually reduces guidance during base-model denoising.

Figure 3 WinTF learns rolling generation through parallel supervision of windows with progressive noise levels. Phase offsets expose the model to both short prefill windows and full decoding windows. Within each window, later chunks receive higher noise levels. The attention mask combines bidirectional interactions within a noisy window with access to clean preceding history, while isolating noisy windows from one another. This allows multiple windows to be trained in parallel, each conditioned on its own event prompt and preceding clean history.

Figure 5 CuLT-DMD combines supervision across a long rollout in each generator update. The top panel shows local distillation supervision from teacher and critic predictions. LongLive-style training updates the generator from individual windows while carrying detached history forward. CuLT-DMD instead keeps parameters fixed throughout the rollout and averages the local gradients before updating. This incorporates supervision from multiple temporal positions while retaining one local computation graph at a time.

Figure 6 AnnealCFG reduces the late-denoising extrapolation produced by constant guidance throughout 30s generation. Across prefill and early, middle, and late decoding, the left plots show the additional latent-update magnitude induced by guidance. The right plots show its share in the final 20% of denoising steps. Annealing lowers both the late-step peaks and their contribution to the total update. Results aggregate 32 paired prompts, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals shown by bands and whiskers.

Figure 7 KV recomputation refreshes historical context for generation beyond the training horizon. Fullhistory caching expands the context as video length grows, while sliding-window caching retains dependencies on evicted chunks. At the history threshold, recomputation selects sink, intermediate, and recent chunks and causally re-encodes them into a fresh cache. This bounds the retained context and removes cached dependencies on discarded chunks before generation continues.

Figure 8 Flash Block-wise Causal Attention (FBCA) implements block-causal attention with efficient FlashAttention kernels. Each query block gathers its visible prefix, historical states, and current states into an independent attention sequence. KV unfolding and grouping organize these sequences within a per-call packing budget, and variable-length FlashAttention processes them before restoring the original block order. This preserves the required attention pattern while controlling the size of each packed buffer.

Figure 1 MovieRoll generates a minute-long video with continuous subject identity across six events. The sequence shows the same woman performing successive actions in one studio setting, with a new prompt every 10s. Each frame represents one event, and the text below summarizes its prompt.

Figure 4 Layer-dependent attention patterns motivate hierarchical history retention. In the WinTF-trained model, shallow layers distribute attention broadly across historical chunks, while deeper layers place relatively more attention on the sink and most recent chunks. The heatmap and lower entropy and coverage plots show this shift with depth. HieraKV follows these patterns by retaining full historical context in shallow layers and restricting deeper layers to the sink and most recent chunks.

Figure 9 The Parallel Streaming Variational Autoencoder (PS-VAE) supports continuous video decoding through temporal caching and spatial parallelism. The upper panel shows how cached decoder states carry temporal context across arriving latent chunks, allowing each chunk to be decoded as it becomes available. The lower panel distributes high-resolution decoding across GPUs through row partitioning and boundary exchange. Together, these designs support streaming output and reduce per-GPU decoding cost.

Figure 10 Qualitative comparison of 10s single-event video generation. Under the same prompt of a mermaid combing her hair on a seaside rock, MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled retain recognizable subjects and consistent surroundings as poses and waves change. Rows compare methods evaluated under the same prompt, and columns show successive temporal intervals within each 241-frame video.

Figure 11 Qualitative comparison of 30s single-event video generation. MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled preserve the facial features, clothing, and surroundings of a man eating at a bar as the action continues. Rows compare methods under the same prompt, and columns follow the 721-frame sequence, showing how subject and background consistency evolve during generation.

Figure 17 Memory and latency comparison across full-history and sink--recent attention allocations. The left plot shows slower cache-memory growth when fewer layers retain full history. At 18 cached chunks, the default HieraKV allocation of 6 global and 48 local layers reduces memory from 48.7 to 10.8 GiB and peak denoising-step latency from 33.8 to 15.8s relative to all-global attention. Measurements use MovieRoll-Base with CFG on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. Each timed denoising step includes both conditional and unconditional DiT evaluations. Timing excludes KV recomputation and VAE encoding/decoding.

Figure 16 Ablation of long-horizon extrapolation strategies. All three strategies use the same Stage 1 MovieRollBase checkpoint to extend generation from 10s training clips to 30s videos. Full-history and sliding-window caching produce increasingly washed-out backgrounds, whereas KV recomputation preserves clearer subject and street details through the end of the sequence.

Figure 12 Qualitative comparison of 60s single-event video generation. MovieRoll-Distilled preserves the diver and underwater environment with relatively stable colors as generation continues. Rows compare methods under the same diver-and-wreck prompt, and columns follow successive 10s intervals of the 1441-frame videos.

Figure 26 Examples of multi-event video generation with sequential prompts. The upper examples show threeevent, 30s videos from MovieRoll-Base, and the lower examples show six-event, 60s videos from MovieRoll-Distilled. Prompts change every 10s, with one frame representing each event. Both models retain recurring characters and settings as new interactions develop, such as a cat reacting to a robotic vacuum and a keeper responding to a seagull.

Figure 13 Qualitative comparison of 30s multi-event video generation. The sequence progresses from sketching a flower to observing a frog and raising a camera, with a prompt change every 10s. MovieRoll-Distilled depicts these action changes while retaining the botanist and rainforest setting. Each row shows one method, and each pair of columns corresponds to one event.

Figure 14 Qualitative comparison of 60s multi-event video generation. The sequence develops from paddling to successive interactions with an otter, including surfacing beside the kayak, handling a rock, and approaching the hull. MovieRoll-Distilled depicts this event progression while maintaining a consistent lake setting. Rows compare methods under the same six sequential prompts, and each column represents one 10s event.

Figure 27 Potential extensions of rolling-window video pretraining. (a) Smaller chunks allow finer noise progression and temporal advances at a fixed frame budget, while loss weighting or regularization could balance learning across noise levels. (b) Total-duration conditioning could guide overall pacing, while duration triggers locate active windows and shot transitions. Together with multi-shot training, these conditions could support coordinated shot sequences under one prompt.

Figure 24 Examples of 60s single-event videos generated by MovieRoll-Distilled. This first set of six examples includes miniature ships, an origami dragon, and underwater performances. MovieRoll-Distilled preserves subject appearance as waves, steam, and gestures evolve. Each two-row group follows one 1441-frame video from left to right and then top to bottom, with frame indices overlaid and its prompt below.

Figure 18 Ablation of HieraKV attention allocations. The comparison varies the allocation of 54 transformer blocks between full-history and sink–recent attention. With the default HieraKV allocation of 6 global and 48 local blocks, the rider and horse remain recognizable throughout the sequence. All-global attention progressively crops the subje ts, while all-local attention shifts toward a close rear view.

Figure 22 User preference comparison for multi-event video generation. MovieRoll-Distilled wins a majority of judgments against every evaluated baseline, with win rates from 62.3% to 81.9%. Each bar reports win, tie, and loss rates from the MovieRoll-Distilled perspective under the same prompt sequences, pooling judgments across 30s three-event and 60s six-event videos with ties included in the denominator.

Table 8 Shared architecture and history-cache configuration of the MovieRoll models. Both variants use an 8.3-billion-parameter backbone with text conditioning, a causal video VAE, and a five-chunk active window. The first six transformer blocks retain full history, while the remaining 48 retain the sink and most recent chunks, preserving broad historical context through a small subset of layers.

Table 2 Comparison of video decoding speed, memory use, and reconstruction quality. Single-GPU PSVAE outperforms the tested tiling methods in runtime and reconstruction PSNR. Spatial parallelism further reduces decoding time and per-GPU memory. With eight GPUs, PS-VAE achieves a 3.97× decoding speedup over its singleGPU version while preserving high numerical agreement. Measurements decode 1441 frames at 480× 864 on NVIDIA H20 GPUs in FP16.

Table 9 Inference settings of MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled. Distillation reduces sampling from 50 steps to 5 while preserving the shared rolling-generation pipeline. MovieRoll-Base uses guidance annealed from 4 to 1, whereas MovieRoll-Distilled operates without CFG. Both use the same chunk and window sizes and rebuild their KV caches at the same history threshold. Denoising passes are counted per output chunk, with the conditional and unconditional CFG branches contributing separately to the reported count.

Table 1 Efficiency comparison of block-causal attention implementations. The comparison evaluates fullhistory attention with three or five windows on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. FBCA achieves the lowest forward and backward runtimes across fixed and varying input shapes, with preparation taking less than 0.1s when shapes vary. In multiple-shape tests, it also reduces peak memory relative to FlexAttention, supporting efficient training across inputs with different spatial resolutions.

Table 10 Training stages and hyperparameters of MovieRoll. The two base-model stages introduce single-event and multi-event streaming generation. ODE initialization then transfers the base model to a few-step student, and CuLT-DMD trains it on self-generated rollouts. The columns summarize the data and optimization settings supporting this progression. The two distillation phases are denoted by P1 and P2, while G and F identify the generator and fake-score critic in the optimization settings for each phase.

Table 6 Single-GPU inference efficiency for 60s video generation. The table compares denoising and endto-end costs across methods at the listed resolutions for 1441-frame videos on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. Switching from FlashAttention-3 to SageAttention increases MovieRoll-Distilled end-to-end throughput from 1.52 to 2.04 FPS. Single-GPU throughput remains below the 24 FPS playback rate required for real-time generation.

Table 5 Quantitative ablations of training and inference designs. WinTF outperforms chunk-wise formulations, while the selected HieraKV allocation, KV recomputation, long-rollout CuLT-DMD, and AnnealCFG schedule achieve the highest total scores within their respective comparisons. Shaded rows identify these choices. Autoregressive formulations are evaluated at 241 and 721 frames, and the remaining comparisons use 721 frames. Higher ratings indicate better quality and less drift.

Table 14 Comparison ofGPT-5.2 andGemini-2.5-Proas video evaluators. Both evaluate the same 30s single-event videos and rank MovieRoll-Distilled first and MovieRoll-Base second. Method rankings agree closely, with Spearman correlation ρ = 0.930. We use Gemini-2.5-Pro because it provides greater score separation between methods, as shown by the statistical measures in the lower section.

Table 11 Rollout settings for the two CuLT-DMD training phases. Phase 1 uses single-event, 241-frame rollouts lasting 10s. Phase 2 extends training to two-event, 721-frame rollouts lasting 30s. Both phases average local gradients across each rollout, allowing one update to incorporate supervision from multiple temporal positions. Bounded score clips keep distillation supervision local as the generated sequence grows.

Table 15 Distribution of user-study judgments across baselines and video durations. The study collects 2616 preference judgments across single-event and multi-event comparisons. Each cell counts individual judgments for MovieRoll-Distilled versus the listed baseline at a given duration. Judgments are pooled across durations to calculate win, tie, and loss rates for each baseline, separately for single-event and multi-event generation. Each judgment contributes one vote, including ties.

Table 13 Conversion of HeliosBench quality and drift metrics to a common rating scale. The listed intervals map raw metric values to ratings from 1 to 10 for weighted aggregation. Higher quality scores and lower drift scores receive higher ratings, so higher converted ratings consistently indicate better performance.

Table 7 Inference scaling across GPU counts and attention backends. Increasing the GPU count improves MovieRoll-Distilled throughput with both backends, and SageAttention is faster at every tested count. On eight NVIDIA H20 GPUs, the best setting generates a 60s video in 152.2s, reaching 9.47 FPS. Real-time generation at 24 FPS remains a limitation even with eight GPUs. Videos contain 1441 frames at 480× 864.

Table 12 HeliosBench metrics, evaluators, and aggregation weights. Five full-video metrics cover aesthetics, dynamics, motion smoothness, semantic alignment, and naturalness. Four drift metrics measure changes between the beginning and end of a video. The aggregation weights give greater emphasis to semantic alignment and naturalness while retaining contributions from all four metrics of temporal drift.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient long video generation, but inference still incurs substantial computational costs from repeated denoising and KV cache operations. Existing acceleration methods reduce parts of this overhead, while historical KV reading and cache construction remain costly across video chunks. To address these challenges, we propose ScoutCache, a training-free framework that jointly optimizes denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction. We observe that shallow feature changes provide useful information for estimating clean latent updates, while historical KV dependence varies across Transformer layers and attention heads but remains relatively stable across video chunks. Based on these observations, we develop Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. We further introduce Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical reading budgets based on attention output perturbations, and Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to reduce cache construction costs by selecting informative spatial tokens while maintaining spatial coverage. Extensive experiments on Self-Forcing and LongLive using VBench and MovieGen demonstrate that ScoutCache achieves up to 2.28$\times$ and 1.86$\times$ speedups, respectively, while consistently improving generation quality without modifying pretrained model parameters.
authors: Hao Tan, Jinghui Qin, Xuming Hu
bullets: Targets the remaining inference bottlenecks in long-video generation: repeated denoising and KV-cache operations across video chunks.
Uses Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations.
Applies Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical KV-reading budgets across layers and attention heads.
Uses Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to select informative spatial tokens while preserving coverage.
Achieves up to 2.28× speedup on Self-Forcing and 1.86× on LongLive, with consistently improved quality and no pretrained-parameter changes.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in image and video generation have enabled high-fidelity synthesis at higher resolutions and longer durations, making the quadratic cost of dense self-attention a major bottleneck as visual token sequences grow. Sparse attention seeks to preserve generation quality at lower computational cost by retaining informative query-key interactions and omitting less consequential ones, with end-to-end gains depending on the cost of constructing sparse support and the efficiency with which the system maps the resulting workload to hardware. We survey sparse attention for visual generation through a 4+1+3 analytical framework that links algorithmic design to system implementation. The framework examines how static and dynamic methods use source information and the evidence derived from it to decide which interactions to retain and at what granularity, while accounting for the roles of reuse in reducing repeated computation and correction in compensating for omitted contributions. We relate these algorithmic choices to their implementation on hardware through the framework's three system dimensions of data organization, execution, and dataflow. We summarize common evaluation metrics and discuss open challenges and research directions, providing researchers and practitioners with a reference for the joint design of sparse attention algorithms and systems.
authors: Majun Zhang, Yuan Guo, Decheng Wu, Jiayang Xu, Changhao Pan, Fan Zhuo, Xiaoda Yang, Chenyuhao Wen, Zhou Zhao
bullets: Dense self-attention becomes a major bottleneck as image and video token sequences grow.
The proposed 4+1+3 framework analyzes static and dynamic sparsity, selection granularity, reuse, and correction for omitted interactions.
It links algorithmic choices to three system dimensions: data organization, execution, and dataflow.
The survey reviews evaluation metrics, implementation considerations, open challenges, and future research directions.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. The 4+1+3 framework for sparse attention. The source, evidence construction, granularity, and support specification determine which query–key pairs are retained. papers.abstract: Precipitation nowcasting involves two distinct scales of uncertainty: macroscopic storm evolution and fine-scale local convective variations. Current generative ensemble methods entangle both scales within independent random noise draws. This coupling causes two practical limitations: every ensemble member must execute the full sampling trajectory from scratch, so an N-member ensemble costs N times a single forecast; moreover, divergent trajectories spatially misalign heavy-rain echoes across members, causing standard pixel-wise averaging to blur critical high-intensity extremes. We present ForeSay, a generative nowcasting framework that decouples macroscopic evolution prediction from local stochastic detail generation. Given historical radar frames, a vision-language model first predicts a textual scenario of future storm dynamics to condition a Rectified Flow generator. Guided by this shared macroscopic prior, ensemble members share early trunk sampling steps to establish the storm trajectory and branch with fresh noise only in later steps to explore local convective details. Because members then differ mainly in local details, self-anchored support-consensus decoding replaces pixel averaging with discrete support voting to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores. Across six datasets, ForeSay achieves the best CSI at the highest precipitation thresholds, with relative improvements over the strongest baseline on each dataset ranging from over 10% to 84%. Our 8-member ensemble retains the forecasting skill and diversity of eight independently sampled runs while reducing computational cost from 8x to 5.2x that of a single forecast.
authors: Xudong Ling, Wenjie Luo, Chaorong Li, Tianxi Huang, Tao He, Guiduo Duan
bullets: Addresses the cost and blurring caused by independently sampled generative ensemble forecasts.
Uses a vision-language model to generate a textual storm-evolution scenario that conditions a Rectified Flow generator.
Shares early sampling steps across ensemble members, then branches with fresh noise for local convective details.
Uses support-consensus decoding instead of pixel averaging to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores.
Across six datasets, achieves the best high-threshold CSI, with reported relative gains of over 10%–84%; an 8-member ensemble costs 5.2× rather than 8× a single forecast.

papers.abstract: Directly aligning trajectory-distilled video generators slashes rollout costs and optimizes the deployed few-step model without teacher fine-tuning or re-distillation. However, conventional flow-matching preference objectives assume single-head local velocity supervision, mismatching the finite-interval, block-average transition interface of trajectory-distilled generators such as Parallel Decoding Distillation (PDD) and Parametric Trajectory Distillation (PTD). Naively supervising only the primary initial-subinterval velocity sub-head rather than the fused block-average velocity at block starts (DirectAlign) induces a severe training--inference mismatch that degrades quality below the unaligned baseline. We introduce BlockAlign, an interface-consistent preference optimization framework that constructs states at valid block boundaries, queries the fused block-level velocity predictor, and supervises span-normalized transition residuals-seamlessly supporting DPO-, NFT-, and rollout-style objectives while preserving the native few-step sampler. We further build a unified post-training pipeline integrating offline pairs, reward-free semi-online continuations, and online rollouts with hierarchical preference selection and objective-aware block scheduling. Experiments on multi-reference video generation across MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA and an in-house model RefVid-V4 show that BlockAlign consistently outperforms unaligned distilled models and DirectAlign in structural plausibility, reference consistency, and visual quality. Notably, our approach unlocks PDD's 5x few-step rollout speedup for 3x faster end-to-end online training, achieving statistically significant human preference gains over PDD baselines (54.0% vs. 33.3% wins/losses, or 61.8% non-tie win rate on RefVid-V4; 51.3% vs. 34.7%, or 59.7% non-tie win rate on MiniMax-H3) and up to an 82.7% win rate against DirectAlign.
authors: Jingyuan Zhu, Biaolong Chen, Yangyang Qin, Shengyang Shen, Yaohua Wang, Weiming Bai, Miao Lu, Aixi Zhang
bullets: Trajectory-distilled generators use finite-interval, block-average transitions, which conventional single-head preference objectives mismatch.
BlockAlign constructs valid block-boundary states, queries fused block-level velocities, and supervises span-normalized transition residuals.
The framework supports DPO-, NFT-, and rollout-style objectives while preserving the native few-step sampler.
A unified pipeline combines offline pairs, semi-online continuations, and online rollouts with hierarchical preference selection.

Across two multi-reference video-generation models, BlockAlign improves structural plausibility, reference consistency, and visual quality, with reported human preference gains over PDD and DirectAlign.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers rely on 3D full attention over tens of thousands of spatiotemporal tokens, and its quadratic cost dominates inference latency. Sparse attention reduces this cost, but existing methods face a dilemma: static methods apply predefined masks and cannot capture input-dependent attention, whereas dynamic methods reconstruct the sparse mask repeatedly, paying online to rediscover positional structure that is largely stable across inputs. To this end, we propose PoCoAttn, a training-free sparse attention framework that separates input-stable from input-dependent attention and resolves the former offline and the latter online. PoCoAttn features: (1) A relative-offset analysis of 3D query-key pairs, which shows that video attention decomposes into an input-stable positional prior that carries most of the attention mass and a small content-dependent residual. (2) A position-content collaborative sparse attention mechanism, which retrieves positional keys from offline-calibrated tables, selects content keys online with a head-adaptive ratio between the two sources, and compensates for the discarded keys to approximate full attention. (3) A step-adaptive budget allocation algorithm, which models how early-step sparse attention errors are amplified along the denoising trajectory and derives the optimal sparsity budget per step. Extensive experiments across four video diffusion models and three tasks show that PoCoAttn consistently achieves a better speed-fidelity Pareto frontier than state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, improving PSNR by 1.9 to 5.0 dB over baselines and delivering up to 4.1$\times$ attention and 2.0$\times$ denoising speedups over dense FlashAttention-3 attention.
authors: Jianwen Wu, Meiling Wang, Junkang Zhou, Yipeng Shen, Haoran You
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of 3D full attention over large spatiotemporal token sequences.
Separates mostly input-stable positional attention from a smaller input-dependent content residual.
Retrieves positional keys from offline-calibrated tables, selects content keys online, and compensates for discarded keys.
Allocates sparsity budgets across denoising steps based on error amplification, with head-adaptive position/content ratios.
Across four video diffusion models and three tasks, reports 1.9–5.0 dB PSNR gains over baselines and up to 4.1× attention and 2.0× denoising speedups versus dense FlashAttention-3.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PoCoAttn. (a) PoCoAttn decomposes attention into an input-stable positional part and an input-dependent content part. (b) At inference, each query tile looks up its positional key tiles in the positional table, selects content keys by pooled-query scores, and merges the discarded keys into virtual keys by weighted pooling; the per-head position–content ratio is solved offline. (c) The positional table is compiled offline from the per-head positional prior Ph(∆), obtained by averaging calibration attention over each relative offset ∆. (d) The step-wise budget ρs is solved offline by minimizing the local error et(ρt) weighted by its amplification A(t).

papers.abstract: A frozen diffusion generator may need to change several output properties while preserving others. We study when guidance faithfully realizes such a structured request and whether local inverse correction improves its direction. Our account links this benefit to the interaction between the request and the objective-specific remaining-sampler Jacobian: conditioning alone is insufficient. Spectral steering combines a request-specific cosine-gain predictor with damped inverse correction and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits. Scalar nulls and matched-movement controls test the predicted mechanism. Across 8,923 instances in a retrospectively identified local regime, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79, versus -0.11 for condition number. Experiments span images, audio, robotics, and control and planning, including complex character motion generation. On 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections improve unobserved-pixel PSNR over Adam by 3.25 dB at equal total derivative traversals. Together, the analysis and controls connect request-dependent geometry to directional gains and establish where these gains translate into downstream performance.
authors: Angelo Moroncelli, Alessandro Leanza, Loris Roveda
bullets: Studies when guidance changes desired properties while preserving others, emphasizing request-dependent local geometry.
Uses a cosine-gain predictor, damped inverse correction, and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits.
Across 8,923 local-regime instances, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79; condition number correlates at -0.11.
Across images, audio, robotics, and control/planning, including character motion generation, the method links geometry to downstream gains.
In 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections improve unobserved-pixel PSNR by 3.25 dB over Adam with equal derivative traversals.

papers.abstract: In cinematic storytelling, sound and visual transitions do not always coincide in lockstep: dialogue frequently bridges across cuts to reveal reactions or introduces new scenes via J- and L-cuts, while deliberate silences pace the scene. Existing audio-visual generative frameworks, however, lack explicit mechanisms to coordinate independent visual and acoustic timing over extended horizons. As narrative duration and shot complexity scale, these systems struggle to maintain long-range dialogue pacing, often hallucinating speech during intended silences or erroneously driving mouth movements on silent listeners. To enable fine-grained cinematic control, we present DECOUPAGE, a screenplay-driven framework for long-form, multi-shot, and multi-character joint audio-video generation. Rather than coupling modality boundaries by default, DECOUPAGE uncouples generation into independently bounded visual and acoustic tracks governed by persistent character identities. DECOUPAGE builds on a joint audio-video diffusion model with dual-schedule temporal cross-attention, incorporating a directorial Lip-sync mechanism that selectively decouples speech conditioning from visual facial dynamics during off-screen dialogue. On multi-shot conversational benchmarks, DECOUPAGE achieves precise control over shot transitions, audio timing, and visibility-aware lip synchronization, directing 15- to 60-second screenplay-driven audio-video generation with multimodal coherence.

Uses independently bounded visual and acoustic tracks while preserving persistent character identities across shots.

On multi-shot conversational benchmarks, controls shot transitions, audio timing, and off-screen dialogue for coherent 15–60-second generations.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in audio-driven avatar video generation have enabled increasingly realistic synthesis, yet achieving precise lip-audio synchronization, natural, human-like motion, and visual consistency over long sequences remains challenging. We present LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6, which builds on LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.5 to improve expressive naturalness and reduce error accumulation during extended generation, e.g., exaggerated lip movements and overly red, temporally unstable lip coloration, enhance the naturalness of facial expressions and coordinated head and body movements. These improvements are driven by a refined post-training pipeline that integrates reinforcement learning, improved classifier-free guidance strategies for DMD-based few-step distillation, long-video rollouts, and on-policy distillation. Together, these refinements improve expressive realism and enable the generation of videos exceeding 10 minutes while maintaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Arena evaluations show that LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 outperforms its predecessor and competing commercial audio-driven avatar models, demonstrating the effectiveness of the improved post-training pipeline.

papers.abstract: As text-to-image diffusion models see widespread deployment, removing unsafe or undesirable concepts without retraining has become a pressing need. Spectral methods are attractive because they are training-free and reversible, yet current variants apply the same output-value (OV) circuit intervention at every denoising step, assuming concept information is temporally uniform. This wastes intervention where concept energy is low while degrading image quality, an inefficiency that compounds across concept types. Through timestep-resolved spectral analysis, concept-specific energy is found to follow a consistent temporal hierarchy: content concepts decay fastest, object concepts are intermediate, and style concepts persist longest. This paper proposes Timestep-Adaptive Spectral Nullification (TASN), which adapts suppression strength and spectral components to the concept energy profile. Cross-attention at each timestep is decomposed into concept-aligned and concept-orthogonal components, and it is proved that when the orthogonal component is approximately stable, the collateral-minimizing schedule sets suppression proportional to concept energy. TASN implements this with a timestep-adaptive spectral subset tracking only active concept directions, strictly generalizing uniform Spectral Nullification (SN). On five red-teaming benchmarks, TASN lowers attack success rate below uniform SN while recovering the majority of its quality loss; ablations confirm gains arise from temporal targeting rather than reduced suppression, generalizing across concept categories and architectures.
authors: Chanaka Thushitha Bandara, Lakmali Nadeesha Kumari, Sen-Ching Samson Cheung
bullets: Uniform spectral interventions waste suppression when concept information is weak, harming image quality.

Ablations attribute the gains to temporal targeting, with generalization across concept categories and architectures.

papers.abstract: Video generation models have become increasingly capable of synthesizing realistic human motion, yet they often lose track of the very structure that makes the motion plausible. As generated human motion becomes more complex, videos can suffer from progressive body deformation and appearance drift across frames. Existing motion-controlled methods use explicit representations to stabilize generation, but typically rely on pre-defined motion sequences as references. This raises a fundamental question: if the base generator already produces a usable coarse motion, why replace it with an external one? ReMoVe answers this question by treating the coarse output as a motion hypothesis rather than a final result. ReMoVe recovers and refines the underlying motion, then renders the refined motion as 3D mesh and transfers facial appearance onto it, thereby improving motion accuracy and identity consistency. We further derive depth from the same 3D scene and camera trajectory to impose scene-level spatial consistency beyond the mesh. By jointly conditioning video generation models on mesh and depth, ReMoVe synthesizes high-quality motion videos with controllable camera trajectories and enhanced spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReMoVe improves human structural stability, appearance consistency, temporal coherence, and motion-following fidelity, while retaining the base generator's motion prior and offering accurate camera control.

papers.abstract: Distilling diffusion models into few-step student models substantially reduces sampling latency, but induces severe diversity collapse: samples generated from different random seeds show minimal variation. In this work, we investigate the root cause of this failure by probing the internal representations of student models relative to their teachers. We find that distilled students maintain total activation variance comparable to their teachers, but concentrate it into substantially fewer directions. This directional collapse is localized to an identifiable intermediate block at the initial denoising step. Consequently, diversity collapse stems from a misallocation of activation variance rather than an inherent loss of generative capacity. Guided by this finding, we propose ReDiverse to reinstate the missing variance directions. At training time, ReDiverse-FT fine-tunes a lightweight adapter that regresses student activations onto the teacher's, reviving the teacher's feature variance characteristic. At inference time, ReDiverse-TF introduces a training-free mechanism that steers activations along precomputed teacher principal directions. Across image and video distillation benchmarks, ReDiverse consistently restores sample diversity while preserving generation quality, further supported by the user study.
bullets: Distillation reduces sampling latency but causes severe variation collapse across random seeds.
Student models retain overall activation variance, but concentrate it in fewer directions than their teachers.
The collapse is localized to an intermediate block during the initial denoising step.
ReDiverse-FT uses a lightweight adapter trained to match teacher activations; ReDiverse-TF steers activations along teacher principal directions without training.
Across image and video benchmarks, both methods restore diversity while preserving generation quality, with additional support from a user study.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates diversity collapse in distilled diffusion models (image and video) and proposes a method to restore variance by probing activations, directly relevant to Video Diffusion.
papers.title: Restoring Diversity in Distilled Image and Video Generators by Probing Activations
papers.tldr: ReDiverse restores diversity in few-step distilled image and video generators by correcting directional activation collapse without sacrificing generation quality.

papers.abstract: Direct diffusion modeling of high-dimensional raw video data is challenging, and existing pixel-space methods often rely on specialized architectures. We introduce JVT (Just Video Transformer), a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer for pixel-space video diffusion, without a pretrained autoencoder, auxiliary detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections. We systematically examine video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization to identify design choices that balance generation quality and computational efficiency. The resulting JVT design achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings. The pixel-space formulation of JVT also naturally supports joint generation of pixel-aligned modalities. We demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity generation, which improves camera following relative to RGB-only baselines and yields explicit scene geometry without an additional reconstruction model at inference. These results highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video diffusion, and we hope our findings offer useful insights and practical guidance for future research.
authors: Jianjun Zhou, Hua Geng, Haoyu Guo
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of directly diffusing high-dimensional raw video pixels.
Studies video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization for quality–efficiency trade-offs.
Achieves quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in class-conditioned and unconditional generation.
Supports joint pixel-aligned modality generation, demonstrated with camera-conditioned RGB–disparity videos.
RGB–disparity generation improves camera following and provides explicit scene geometry without an inference-time reconstruction model.

papers.abstract: Direct image-to-video diffusion models entangle pixel synthesis with implicit latent motion, precluding persistent 3D mechanical equilibrium, mid-rollout intervention, and counterfactual force control. Conversely, single-pass programmatic 3D reconstruction from an uncalibrated photograph leaves monocular depth and support clearance underconstrained, causing reconstructed scenes to interpenetrate or collapse under gravity. We present TelePhysica, a closed-loop framework that reconstructs an executable, multi-regime physical world from a single photograph to drive stateful 3D interaction and trajectory-grounded video synthesis. A vision-language coding agent synthesizes separable visual meshes and declarative physical models within a two-stage verification loop that pairs pixel-aligned silhouette critique with a zero-force gravitational equilibrium preflight. The verified world compiles into a unified solver coupling rigid bodies, articulated chains, co-dimensional cloth shells, and 3D tetrahedral elastodynamics, whose simulated rollouts condition pretrained video diffusion models through pixel-aligned structural streams. On a 100-scene single-image benchmark, closed-loop execution raises equilibrium-verified world recovery from $0\%$ in single-pass synthesis to $81\%$. Controlled constitutive ablations show over an order-of-magnitude larger localized corner displacement and out-of-plane pleating in finite-element cloth than in matched rigid-plate proxies. Conditioning video diffusion on simulated trajectories increases dynamic motion-mask overlap by $2{\times}\text{--}5{\times}$ and preserves motion direction under counterfactual force reversals where direct image-to-video models fail.
authors: Ruiqi Shu, Xufeng Zhan, Yuanzhi Liang, Haibin Huang, Chi Zhang, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses image-to-video models’ lack of persistent 3D mechanics and single-pass reconstruction failures such as interpenetration or collapse.
Uses a vision-language coding agent with silhouette critique and zero-force gravitational preflight to build verified visual meshes and physical models.
Compiles scenes into a solver supporting rigid bodies, articulated chains, cloth shells, and tetrahedral elastodynamics.
On a 100-scene benchmark, equilibrium-verified recovery improves from 0% with single-pass synthesis to 81% with closed-loop execution.

Simulated trajectory conditioning improves dynamic motion-mask overlap by 2–5× and preserves motion direction under reversed forces; finite-element cloth exhibits stronger deformation than rigid proxies.

papers.abstract: Attention is essential for modeling spatio-temporal dependencies in video diffusion transformers, but its quadratic cost makes it a major inference bottleneck. Its high sparsity offers an opportunity to accelerate generation by focusing computation on important interactions. However, accuracy and execution favor different granularities: each query attends to its own key tokens, whereas GPU kernels work on tiles. We present Token2Tile, a training-free sparse attention operator that combines per-query scoring and a per-query residual with tile execution. An online low-rank space, computed directly from queries and keys to preserve attention logits, makes clustering, scoring, and residual approximation efficient. Token2Tile unites query-specific selections to allocate exact work across query clusters, then packs the selected keys into GPU tiles. On MiniMax-H3 and Wan2.1-14B, Token2Tile delivers 1.48-1.54x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention-3 with VBench scores within 0.5 points of dense. At comparable speeds on H3, it improves PSNR over SOL and SubBlock by 5.5-6.8 dB; on Wan, it exceeds SOL by 4.6-4.8 dB while running faster.
authors: Xuecheng Wu, Aichen Feng, Jinyan Chen, Qingjie Zhao, Julien Lai
bullets: Targets the quadratic inference cost of spatio-temporal attention in video diffusion transformers.
Uses per-query scoring and residual approximation in an online low-rank space derived from queries and keys.
Clusters query-specific selections and packs selected keys into GPU tiles for efficient execution.
Achieves 1.48–1.54× end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention-3, with VBench within 0.5 points of dense.
Outperforms SOL and SubBlock in PSNR at comparable or higher speeds on the evaluated models.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free sparse attention for video diffusion transformers, improves efficiency.

papers.abstract: We study how to repurpose video diffusion models (VDMs), pretrained on millions of videos, for dense 3D point tracking, where training data is scarce. Doing so is non-trivial, as it requires representing 3D tracks as video-like signals that may lie outside the natural-video distribution on which the VDM was trained. We thus systematically assess the effectiveness of two such video representations. The first, Residual 3D Tracking Video (RTV), encodes per-pixel 3D offsets relative to a query frame and allows recovery of 3D trajectories directly from the generated video. The second, Normalized Coordinate Map Video (NCMV), labels each pixel with a canonical coordinate invariant through time. This is closer to a natural video and easier for the VDM to learn, but requires additional post-processing with an off-the-shelf 2D tracker to recover 3D tracks. RTV tracks more accurately, while NCMV shows that a VDM can generate dense correspondence as a video. We instantiate both representations with LoRA adaptation of a frozen Wan backbone, conditioned on point maps from an off-the-shelf 3D reconstructor as a geometric scaffold. Trained with a single dynamic 3D tracking dataset, Track4D achieves competitive zero-shot tracking on four real and synthetic benchmarks. A regression readout that bypasses the video VAE and uses additional training data brings further improvement, demonstrating the potential of this direction for dense 3D tracking. We hope our analysis will inspire future work that leverages VDM priors for dense 3D tracking and 4D reconstruction. Project page: https://nirvanalan.github.io/projects/track4d
bullets: RTV encodes per-pixel 3D offsets and directly recovers trajectories, yielding more accurate tracks.
NCMV uses time-invariant canonical coordinates, making the representation more natural for video diffusion but requiring a 2D tracker for recovery.
Both representations use LoRA adaptation of a frozen Wan backbone, guided by point maps from an off-the-shelf 3D reconstructor.
Trained on one dynamic 3D tracking dataset, Track4D achieves competitive zero-shot performance across four real and synthetic benchmarks.
A regression readout that bypasses the video VAE and uses extra training data provides further improvement.

figures.caption: Figure 2: TRACK4D overview. (a) Generative readout. A frozen reconstructor supplies point maps P; the video VAE encodes them with video V into condition C. The LoRA-adapted video DiT denoises the RTV and NCMV latents, jointly by default, and the VAE decodes the videos. Hatched targets are noised in training and start from Gaussian noise at inference. Adding inverse-normalized RTV offsets to the query-frame point map gives 3D tracks; NCMV requires 2D tracking and lifting. (b) Regression readout. Point maps enter through a patch encoder, a private motion expert attends jointly with the video DiT, and a DPT head reads residuals without the output VAE (Section 3.4 and Figure 8). Flames denote trained modules, snowflakes frozen modules.

All methods receive the same VGGT-Ω point maps and draw the same 767 queries, the most-moving points of a dense grid, colored by image row. RTV and NCMV come from the joint Wan2.1-I2V-14B model (50 steps, no input-latent noise); NCMV tracks are read with CoTracker3, lifted with the same point maps, and frozen where NCMV support is lost (on camel, after the first frames). No ground truth or Sim(3) is used. More clips in Figures 9 and 10.

Left: input frames. Right: reconstructions from St4RTrack [19], TraceAnything [31], Any4D [23], and TRACK4D (ours). TRACK4D produces more temporally coherent trajectories with fewer outliers, particularly on articulated and deformable motion (e.g. moving mug, walking cows). All baselines are run from their official released checkpoints and inference scripts at the resolution recommended by the authors; sequences shown were selected to expose dynamic-object failure modes for the comparators. More DAVIS results appear in Figure 14.

A monocular video V and point maps P from an off-the-shelf reconstructor are encoded by the video VAE into the condition C; the VDM jointly generates the RTV ∆ and the NCMV M, and the decoded residuals are added to the query-frame point map. Figure 2 shows the current overview.

Figure 13: Effect of backbone size. Specifically, we show our model’s performance on four samples from PStudio [90], with sequence names on the left. For each sequence, we compare the results from TRACK4D-5B (in orange) and TRACK4D-14B (in green). Both RTV and NCMV are visualized. The Wan-14B-based TRACK4D shows better foreground-background factorization and sharper motion, suggesting benefits from stronger video diffusion models.
Figure 10: More DAVIS clips (continued). Same setup as Figures 6 and 9.

Figure 12: Ablation: absolute XYZ prediction vs. residual prediction. We visualize 3D tracking results at t = 0 and t = 24 on ADT [89] and PStudio [90] sequences. Left: predicting absolute 3D coordinates directly (w/o Residual Pred). Right: our residual formulation (Equation (4)). Absolute prediction produces noisy geometry with scattered outliers, whereas the residual formulation yields cleaner reconstructions with more coherent motion.

Figure 3: Prediction formulations (adapted from VDPM [22]). Each entry Pi(tj) (short for Pi(tj , π0), with the reference frame π0 fixed) gives the positions at time tj of the surface points observed in frame Ii. P (diagonal): geometry at each frame’s capture time. Q (column): timeinvariant prediction [22], referring every frame Ii back to the reference time t0. R (row): dense 3D tracking, propagating the query-frame point map P0 across all timestamps. TRACK4D encodes R explicitly as 3D offsets (RTV) and Q as normalized canonical colors (NCMV), from which R is recovered by 2D tracking.

Figure 9: More DAVIS clips, TrackCraft3R vs. the three TRACK4D readouts. Same setup as Figure 6. Because the view is fixed at frame 0, subjects that the camera follows leave the view in later frames (car-shadow, kite-surf, parkour). Over all 91 DAVIS clips, the median second difference of the projected tracks over consecutive frames, counting points inside the frame, is 6.5 px for TrackCraft3R and 1.8 px for TRACK4D-Reg (672-px-wide frames), and it is smaller for TRACK4D-Reg on 90 clips. This measures temporal smoothness, not accuracy.

Figure 14: More qualitative results. We show seven zero-shot inference results from DAVIS [70]. The first row shows RGB input, with eight frames sampled uniformly from a 49-frame clip, and the second and third rows show RTV and NCMV predictions. The query frame is the first frame shown in the first row. RTV encodes 3D offsets on the query-frame grid; NCMV encodes persistent coordinates on each video frame’s grid.

Figure 11: Failure case. TRACK4D predicts near-zero deformation in this video, where the camera moves with the object. Limited coverage of such camera-following-object trajectories in the training data is a plausible, but not conclusively established, cause (Appendix G.9).

papers.abstract: Recent video world models have witnessed the paradigm shift from single-agent to multi-agent involvements, which can reveal more complicated dynamics and cross-agent interaction in the real world. However, existing approaches commonly adopt implicit inter-agent communications via cross attention, which lack explicit geometry constraints and unified 3D state, thereby leading to poor multi-view consistency and struggling with recovering out-of-sight agents. In addition, most of them assume a static background, failing to represent uncontrolled background dynamics. To address these problems, we propose Artemis: a geometry-grounded multi-agent world model with explicit memory sharing. An explicit 3D world map is reconstructed from multi-agent observations to enforce a unified 3D state across agents, offering high cross-view consistency. Specifically, an action-guided geometric injection module is developed to simultaneously render decomposed foreground-background control maps, which are then injected into a diffusion transformer through a designed GeoAdapter block. Compared to previous methods assuming static-only background, our GeoAdapter can also distinguish uncontrolled non-agent dynamics, which are conditioned on their own multi-frame history positions to provide consistent motion cues. Keyframes selected from progressive video rollouts are used to progressively update the reconstructed 3D world maps. To effectively capture complex dynamic patterns, we curate a novel dataset sampled from the CARLA simulator called MA-CARLA. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method in terms of visual fidelity and cross-view consistency in the generated videos. In addition, our Artemis can support simultaneous multi-modal rollouts with both 2D video and 3D point map maintenance, scale to scenarios beyond two agents and multi-camera setting.
bullets: Addresses poor cross-view consistency, out-of-sight agent recovery, and static-background assumptions in prior multi-agent world models.
Reconstructs an explicit 3D world map from multi-agent observations to enforce a unified geometric state.
Uses an action-guided GeoAdapter to inject decomposed foreground–background control maps into a diffusion transformer.
Models uncontrolled background dynamics using their own multi-frame position histories, while keyframes progressively update the 3D map.
Introduces the MA-CARLA dataset; experiments report improved visual fidelity and cross-view consistency, with support for multi-modal 2D video/3D point-map rollouts and more than two agents.

papers.title: Artemis: Geometry-Grounded Multi-Agent Driving World Models with Shared 3D State and Progressive Memory Update

papers.abstract: Frontier video generation models work in a VAE latent space that compresses video in both space and time. This compression made training tractable, but now limits high-resolution, controllable, and interactive generation -- doubling resolution quadruples token count, conditions apply to groups of frames rather than individual ones, and each response must wait for the rest of its multi-frame block. We present PixVid, a simple yet effective method that lifts a pretrained latent video model to directly generate every frame in pixel space. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer and replaces the VAE decoder with a convolutional head that renders its outputs into pixels. We find that predicting clean video rather than velocity, together with a larger noise shift, is key to quality. Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, PixVid is competitive with the latent baseline within $\sim 1.3$M training clips. Working framewise in pixels, it generates at $2\times$ higher resolution with the same per-frame token count, keeps depth-conditioned video editing aligned under fast motion, and responds to each action at the next frame. Project page: https://chenshuo20.github.io/PixVid/
authors: Yanke Song, Shuo Chen, Chris Rockwell, Guande He, Nan Liu, Desai Xie, Tianpei Gu, Yong-Hyun Park, Aryan V S, Dennis Yuren Menn, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Xun Huang
bullets: Addresses latent compression limits on resolution, frame-level conditioning, and response latency.
Keeps the diffusion transformer while replacing the VAE decoder with a convolutional pixel-rendering head.
Finds clean-video prediction and a larger noise shift important for generation quality.
Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, it is competitive with the latent baseline using approximately 1.3M training clips.
Achieves 2× higher resolution at the same per-frame token count, preserves depth-conditioned editing under fast motion, and responds to actions on the next frame.

figures.caption: Figure 11. Detailer head architecture (patch size p=16). Top: the DiT’s pre-head tokens s, combined with the timestep embedding as SiLU(et + s), form a feature map on the token grid. A bottleneck convolution and L= log2 p=4 up blocks upsample it 2× per level to full resolution, and an output convolution predicts x̂0. Feature sizes are per frame, where D is the DiT width and Cℓ the width of up block ℓ. Bottom left: each up block is a 2× transposed convolution followed by a causal 3×3×3 convolution and SiLU. Bottom right: all convolutions are causal in time (kt=3): output frame t only reads frames t−2 to t, so in frame-by-frame generation the head keeps the previous two frames as a streaming cache.

Figure 2. Lifting a pretrained latent video DiT to pixel space. Top: the pretrained latent model. A linear pixel-latent alignment, fitted offline, is fused with the pretrained patch embedding to obtain a pixel patch embedding. Bottom: PixVid. A timestep calibration rescales noisy pixel input to the signal-to-noise ratio the pretrained DiT was trained on. The DiT is initialized from the latent model, and a convolutional detailer head replaces the linear head and VAE decoder to predict the clean video directly.

Figure 15. High-Resolution Video Generation. Left: text-to-video samples generated by our pixel model at a resolution of 1664× 960. Right: native-resolution crops of the boxed regions. Figure 6. Control-to-screen latency. Control inputs, e.g. turn right (→), turn left (←), and look down (↓), arrive over time (top row). Colors indicate which control each generated frame reflects. Latent model: controls are reflected in the next block. With block size N this means a wait of up to N − 1 frames. We use N = 4 for this visualization. Pixel model (ours): generates one frame per control, so controls are reflected with zero wait, making it better suited for real-time interactive generation.
Figure 5. Depth-conditioned Editing. Our pixel model enables precise video editing under high motion, while the temporally compressed latent model morphs and blurs fast-moving objects.

A new up block L+1 is prepended to the detailer head and initialized as nearest neighbor upsampling. With token count unchanged, we train at 2× resolution at the same DiT cost.

papers.selection_reason: Lifts latent video diffusion to pixel space for higher resolution and controllability; fits video generation research.
papers.title: Back to Pixels: Lifting Latent Video Diffusion into Pixel Space
papers.tldr: PixVid lifts a pretrained latent video diffusion model into pixel space to enable higher-resolution, framewise, and more interactive video generation.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models are able to generate samples with high-quality appearance and textural qualities. However, content produced by these methods is known to exhibit significant physical errors. This is because, in a classical video generation setting, all physical reasoning must take place simultaneously and exclusively within the diffusion process.We propose to resolve these issues by redistributing the task of physical reasoning onto a language model-backed keyframe generation module, which allows for explicit reasoning in language, and fine-grained control over the appearance of the video at important moments in the video. We then condition a video generation model with these keyframes, reducing the role of the diffusion model to the simpler task of interpolating between physically-correct intermediate states, rather than inferring an entire sequence with diffusion. Results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Physics-IQ Verified benchmark and PhyGenBench.
authors: Felix O'Mahony, Daniel Olmeda Reino, Roberto Cipolla, Ayush Tewari
bullets: Video diffusion models often generate visually strong videos with substantial physical inconsistencies.
A language model-backed module explicitly reasons about and generates physically meaningful keyframes.
A video generator is conditioned on these keyframes, simplifying diffusion to interpolation between intermediate states.
The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on Physics-IQ Verified and PhyGenBench.
The approach focuses on improving physical reasoning through explicit keyframe planning.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Conditioning model detail. Keyframes are inserted into the typical conditioning stack of blank frames at locations designated in Equation 3. This is then passed to the VAE, and is subsequently treated as normal conditioning in the Wan pipeline. The conditioning is concatenated with a mask indicating which keyframes are filled, and with the latent noise before being passed to the transformer. The mask and latent conditioning is appended before each denoising step.

Fig. 9. Left: Conditioning Wan2.2-5B on 𝑁 equally spaced ground truth keyframes, for 𝑁 between 1 and 6, raises the Physics-IQ Verified score from 27.7 to 67.4. Right: Editing the final keyframe with the same image edit model used in our pipeline yields a new video, here with the inner petals recoloured.

Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed method. We design a keyframe module which reasons about the physical evolution of a given scene and produces keyframes with timestamps and an expanded caption. These are then used as the conditioning signal for Wan2.2, resulting in videos with more accurate physical plausibility.

Fig. 6. Physics-IQ Verified score against cost per video for the image-to-video models of Table 1, with costs as listed on the Physics-IQ Verified leaderboard [Anates Labs 2026] on 8 October 2026. Costs follow the leaderboard’s normalization, which scales generation cost to 24 fps and 1280-pixel-wide output and then adds any language-model cost; for K2V this is the leaderboard’s Wan2.2 generation cost plus our planning cost from Table 4. The dashed line traces the cost score frontier, and vertical bars show the standard deviations of Table 1.

Fig. 7. Left: Compared to vanilla Wan2.2, the quality of our generations (measured by mean squared error above physical variance) does not rise over the 5 seconds of a video. Beneath, keyframe density shows that our approach distributes keyframes relatively evenly throughout videos on Physics-IQ Verified, with spikes at 0s and 5s, as these keyframes are required for each video. Right: The time taken to produce keyframes shows that the language model spends compute efficiently, spending more time on scenes which require more careful planning and less time on simpler scenes.

Fig. 3. Keyframe module detail. A VLM planning agent orchestrates a recursive loop producing keyframes. The first frame is passed to an image editor with an instruction from the VLM to produce the appearance of the frame later in time. The VLM reviews this frame and, if deemed correct, the frame is added to a stack of keyframes. The VLM repeats this process, now passing the top image to the image editor to add to the keyframe stack. Once all keyframes are produced, the model finishes, returning an expanded caption describing the motion of objects in the video with the keyframe stack.

Fig. 5. Qualitative results from our approach. The top row shows an example from Physics-IQ Verified and the bottom row an example from PhyGenBench. These results highlight the diverse placement of keyframes in different videos, and the physical quality of the resulting generated videos.
