papers.abstract: Video generation models synthesize realistic motion, but can they respond correctly to changes in initial geometry? We introduce GeoFlip, a video generation benchmark centered on physical outcome flips induced by geometry. With shared physical settings and textual prompts held fixed, GeoFlip applies controlled interventions to support extent, object placement, and mechanism configuration, constructing paired scenes with contrasting reference events, such as remaining stable versus falling or tipping. These pairs test whether models translate geometric differences in the first frame into correct physical evolution. The benchmark comprises 482 scene pairs and 964 reference videos across six physical categories, with reference outcomes established through procedural scene construction, physics simulation, and numerical validation and verification of physical events. We evaluate 16 models for image to video generation along three dimensions: event correctness, structural integrity, and similarity to reference videos. We examine evaluation consistency with independent vision language judges. On the 442 conditions shared by all models, the highest event correctness averaged across tasks is 27.98%, revealing substantial limitations in physical generation conditioned on geometry. Model strengths vary across physical mechanisms, and the three evaluation dimensions capture distinct capabilities. Typical failures include ignoring geometric changes, generating incorrect object motion, bending rigid objects, and introducing additional components. Rank correlations between judges reach 0.906 for event correctness and 0.929 for structural integrity. By combining controlled geometric interventions, verifiable physical references, and multidimensional evaluation, GeoFlip assesses progress from visual realism toward physical consistency conditioned on geometry.

papers.abstract: Few-step flow models generate samples through a handful of large denoising transitions. Applying GRPO to such models requires introducing stochasticity into the denoising transitions, and when a single transition spans a wide range of noise levels, the choice of the resulting stochastic policy becomes a major factor in optimization. Recent constructions constrain the policy to preserve the target flow coefficients, but this constraint admits a family of policies and offers no criterion for choosing among them. We introduce Geo-FSRL (Geometry-Optimized Few-Step Reinforcement Learning), built on a selection principle: at a fixed conditioning state and timestep pair, choose the admissible policy that minimizes the conditional KL divergence induced by any given nonzero velocity-output update. Within a coefficient-preserving family of isotropic Gaussian transitions, this criterion reduces to minimizing a single scalar geometry factor that determines the conditional KL for every velocity-output update. The same factor governs velocity-space Fisher information and conditional transition log-likelihood-ratio variance. We derive the unique closed-form optimizer within this family, shared across all nonzero update magnitudes and directions, with transition coefficients determined by both the source and target noise levels. Because the minimized geometry factor still varies across timesteps, we further adopt gradient-scale matching from prior work and derive closed-form policy-gradient and KL weights that normalize explicit score scales and reference-KL curvature. Geo-FSRL trains on the original few-step schedule and retains the deterministic solver at inference. Our method achieves higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS on both image generation and video generation models under the 4-step setting. Code is available at https://github.com/ModelTC/LightX2V/tree/main/lightx2v_rl

This criterion reduces to a scalar geometry factor that also controls velocity-space Fisher information and transition log-likelihood-ratio variance.
The method derives a unique closed-form transition optimizer and timestep-dependent policy-gradient and KL weights through gradient-scale matching.
Experiments report higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS on both image and video generation models in the 4-step setting; inference retains the deterministic solver.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have become the leading paradigm in generative modeling, yet many applications require sampling from distributions that are not those of any single pretrained model, but are instead defined through combinations of several models, possibly tilted toward high values of a downstream reward. Naively combining the scores of the models yields incorrect samples, while existing corrections are restricted to specific families of targets. In this work, we introduce the generalized Feynman-Kac correctors (GFKC), a principled framework for sampling from an arbitrary target function of several pretrained diffusion models. We show that the geometric interpolation between an arbitrary initial function and the target function of the models satisfies a Feynman--Kac partial differential equation, and derive its potential in closed form. To evaluate this potential during generation, we further generalize the log-probability ODE to track the density of each model along trajectories driven by a different velocity field. The resulting algorithm operates entirely in the log domain, incorporates reward-based steering at no additional conceptual cost, and corrects the generation on the fly, without retraining or fine-tuning the models. We validate the method on analytic Gaussian models, where it closely matches the ground-truth targets, and on diffusion models trained on MNIST, where it samples from non-trivial combinations of the models and enables effective steering.
bullets: Naively combining diffusion-model scores produces incorrect samples, and prior corrections support only limited target families.

papers.abstract: Compositional motion transfer requires a model to extract motions from multiple reference videos, and apply each motion to a user-specified object in one target scene. Existing methods normally struggle to reliably assign different reference motions to the correct target objects, thus a motion intended for one object may affect another. Meanwhile, some motion-specific tuning approaches are still facing another issue: they must run a new optimization whenever the reference video changes, making repeated transfers inefficient. To address these limitations, we propose RART, a framework that unifies object-wise motion extraction, target-region anchoring, and frame-aligned injection into a frozen video Diffusion Transformer for multi-object motion transfer. For each reference motion, RART extracts temporally ordered features from the masked reference video, and then conditions them on the target first-frame mask to form mask-anchored motion tokens. Frame-aligned motion cross-attention allows each generated frame to read only the motion tokens at the corresponding time slots, composing all object motions in one denoising process. During training, a motion-attention routing loss encourages each target region to attend to its corresponding motion tokens and reduces interference between objects. Therefore, RART can handle novel reference-target combinations without per-video optimization. Experiments show that RART achieves accurate motion preservation, efficient inference, and strong compositional generalization.
authors: Yuze Li, Fuchen Long, Xinlong Sun, Cheng Yan, Xinyu Zhang, Xi Chen

papers.abstract: Embodied world models should not only imagine plausible futures, but also perceive the geometric, semantic, and motion structure of the evolving world. We present GenSight, a unified embodied world model that brings future video generation and dense perception into a single pretrained video diffusion transformer. GenSight uses a unified spatiotemporal representation for video, depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow. Built on a shared DiT backbone, GenSight uses lightweight task modulation to predict all modalities within the same architecture. All tasks are jointly optimized within a unified velocity prediction space. At inference, GenSight supports two complementary modes: multi-step future video generation with aligned dense predictions and single-step dense perception from an observed video. By unifying modality representation, model architecture, and prediction space, GenSight avoids separate modality-specific pipelines and couples appearance, geometry, semantics, and motion in a shared representation. It promotes cross-modal consistency and allows dense perception to benefit from the spatiotemporal priors learned through video generation. Trained on embodied manipulation data spanning multiple robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, GenSight demonstrates strong performance in both video generation and dense 4D perception, highlighting the effectiveness of unifying seeing and imagining for embodied world modeling.
authors: Haitang Feng, Zhuoman Liu, Zhennan Wang, Sheng Wang, Juelin Li, Chengzhi Zhao, Hexiang Wei, Lin Shao

Trained on embodied manipulation data across robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, it shows strong performance in generation and dense 4D perception.

papers.abstract: Edited endpoint images make the target of an image-to-video transition explicit and can improve transition completion, but also preserve context in the source image's layout. Full-frame endpoint conditioning turns this preserved context into requirements on the video's final state, potentially inducing temporal artifacts. We measure discontinuity with Hard-Cut (HC), late background reversal with Background Motion Reversal (BMR), and motion suppression with Dynamic Degree (DD). These artifacts appear across five video models spanning training-free and learned endpoint conditioning, in model-specific forms. We study Partial, a selective conditioning scheme that constrains only an edit-relevant region estimated from image-editor attention and leaves the remaining terminal content to the video model. Across three backbones on TC-Bench-I2V, Partial reduces temporal artifacts relative to full-frame conditioning, with no significant difference in Transition Completion Ratio (TCR); on Wan2.2-Turbo, uniformly weakening conditioning does not reproduce these reductions. A donor-context intervention keeps full-frame conditioning and replaces only the context outside the edit-relevant region with the final frame of a Partial video. It lowers HC and BMR on HunyuanVideo-1.5 and lowers BMR while restoring DD on Wan2.2-Turbo, with no significant difference in TCR, so constraint extent alone does not account for these artifacts. Together, these findings suggest that edited endpoints should serve as partial future goals, although edit relevance does not guarantee future validity. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/wannagetacat/Edited-Endpoints-I2V.
authors: Sihyun Kim, Sanghyun Jo, Kyungsu Kim

papers.abstract: Topology-agnostic motion generation aims to synthesize motions for diverse characters with arbitrary skeletons. Unlike conventional motion generation, which assumes a fixed skeletal template, this setting must handle diverse joint configurations and inconsistent joint semantics across characters. Existing methods address this challenge through dense full-joint modeling, which incurs substantial computational cost and hinders learning transferable motion patterns across diverse skeletal topologies. We present ETA-Motion, a topology-agnostic motion generation framework based on sparse joint learning. Instead of learning motion from all joints, our method uses a compact subset of joints to reduce redundancy and trains the motion generator on the resulting sparse skeleton. To facilitate correspondence across diverse topologies, we introduce semantic joint embeddings that combine textual and visual cues, together with topology-aware training objectives for preserving skeletal structure. Although ETA-Motion is trained only on sparse skeletal observations, it supports full-skeleton motion generation during inference. Experimental results demonstrate that ETA-Motion outperforms existing topology-agnostic baselines while significantly improving efficiency and generalization to unseen motions and unseen topologies.

papers.abstract: Current datasets for text-to-video generation are largely limited to short clips depicting a single event or coarse-grained captions. As a result, they provide limited supervision for modeling long-take temporal dependencies, often leading to temporally inconsistent generations when describing multiple events. In this paper, we introduce MEV, a multi-event video dataset designed for long-take video generation. MEV provides high-quality real-world videos where subjects can perform a sequence of distinct, non-overlapping events, featuring precise temporal boundaries and fine-grained procedural annotations. This event-centric discretization reduces confounding factors and enables models to support temporally localized conditioning and build long-take videos from atomic event units. Furthermore, we introduce a comprehensive annotation pipeline that segments videos into temporally grounded events, and generates structured captions at both the global level and the event level. In addition, under an event-centric evaluation protocol, we conduct multi-event generation experiments by fine-tuning on MEV with temporally grounded event conditioning, leading to improved long-take event transitions and more coherent content. We believe this work provides a publicly available resource for multi-event fine-tuning and event-centric evaluation, together with practical insights into learning from temporally structured video-text data.

papers.abstract: We address the task of long-video, camera-controlled generation from a single image. The dominant autoregressive paradigm suffers from two key limitations: (1) error accumulation over time, as distant frames are conditioned on previously generated outputs rather than ground truth, leading to drift; and (2) ambiguity in how to incorporate camera control. Standard solutions to both--such as self-forcing and conditioning on explicit 6-DOF poses--either incur significant computational overhead or produce drifting scene geometries over time. We propose a simple and lightweight framework that combines autoregressive generation (WanAR) with hierarchical long-context denoising (FixAR). To enforce scene geometry remains consistent with input cameras, we draw from feed-forward novel-view synthesis and reformulate video generation as a warping-and-inpainting problem. To mitigate drift, we introduce a hierarchical denoising strategy in which different stages condition on different temporal histories. Specifically, we first generate frames conditioned on the immediate past, and then refine them using a second denoiser conditioned on a temporally subsampled long-range history to enforce global consistency. This fine-to-coarse scheme enables each generated frame to effectively condition on the full temporal context without incurring a prohibitive cost. Experiments on RealEstate10k and DL3DV demonstrate that WanAR+FixAR outperforms prior methods for camera-controlled long-video generation, producing results that are both temporally stable and consistent with input camera trajectories.
authors: Kaihua Chen, Yiming Gong, Deva Ramanan, Tarasha Khurana
bullets: Targets error accumulation and ambiguous camera-control conditioning in long autoregressive video generation.
Recasts generation as a camera-guided warping-and-inpainting problem to preserve scene geometry.
Uses immediate temporal history for initial generation and subsampled long-range history for refinement.
Evaluated on RealEstate10k and DL3DV, where it outperforms prior methods in temporal stability and camera-trajectory consistency.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of WanAR, FixAR, and InterpolatAR. We build upon WAN Team et al. (2025), a video diffusion model, and adapt it for camera-controlled autoregressive video generation in static 3D scenes. All three stages share the same Wan2.1 backbone weights, with a different stage-specific LoRA checkpoint loaded for each stage. At each rollout, we estimate depth using MoGe-2 Wang et al. (2025c) on the input frame (or the last generated frame from the previous rollout), and warp it into future camera poses to provide geometry-aware conditioning for WanAR (top). While WanAR can generate plausible long videos autoregressively, visual drift and artifacts gradually accumulate over multiple rollouts. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a hierarchical denoising framework with a second-stage denoiser, FixAR (middle), which refines temporally subsampled keyframes generated across different rollouts using a broader temporal context. Finally, since FixAR only operates on sparse keyframes, we apply InterpolatAR to synthesize intermediate frames between adjacent refined keyframes (bottom). The entire three-stage pipeline can itself be rolled out autoregressively to further extend the video. This hierarchical fine-to-coarse formulation enables both accurate camera control and temporally stable long-horizon video generation.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on RealEstate10k and DL3DV. We show qualitative results on two test scene from RealEstate10k (top two examples) and DL3DV (bottom two examples) across a range of video generation, and novel-view synthesis baselines. We see that proposed WanAR + FixAR combination of models “renders” the scene using scale-consistent camera poses (as compared to ray encoding in DFoT or Plucker conditioning in LingBot), and show that hierarchical denoising mitigates drift over time which some autoregressive baselines like VMem struggle with. We also note that TrajectoryCrafter, a method designed for novel-view synthesis (in short sequences) is also surprisingly strong at the task of camera-controlled minute-long video generation.

Figure 1: In this work, we consider the problem of camera-controlled video generation. Existing approaches condition on cameras represented as ray encodings or Plucker coordinates, but these learn poses up to a global scale factor. We draw from literature in feed-forward novel-view synthesis that warp given views into future poses and reformulate video generation as video inpainting (left). While this allows for precise camera control, minute-long autoregressive video generation in this setup still suffers from drift and error accumulation over time. We propose a hierarchical denoising scheme (right) that looks at multiple rollouts from the inpainting stage and corrects for long horizon artifacts.

Figure 6: We identify a key limitation of existing camera-conditioned methods. When explicit 6- DOF poses are used as conditioning—e.g., via Plücker coordinates or ray maps Song et al. (2025); Team et al. (2026b)—it is difficult to enforce a consistent scale between the scene and the camera trajectory. As a result, generated videos may exhibit visual inconsistencies (top), reflecting scenes rendered under an arbitrary pose scale. Importantly, standard camera-control metrics Xiao et al. (2025) perform a scale alignment with ground-truth camera poses prior to evaluation. Consequently, even when predicted camera trajectories are incorrect up to a global scale factor, they can still achieve low error (bottom), masking this failure mode. Current methods evaluating performance with the PSNR metric circumvent this issue, as they overfit to the pose distribution in a particular datasets, which indicates their limited generalization to other scene or camera trajectories. In our approach, we mitigate this issue by aligning MoGE depth predictions to ground-truth depth for each rollout, and by adopting a warping-and-inpainting formulation for long-video generation. We also adopt novel-view synthesis protocols for evaluation, and instead benchmark methods for camera-control with the masked PSNR (mPSNR) metric.

Figure 5: Top-k evaluation. We note that generative methods for camera-controlled video generation can produce multi-modal outputs for unseen regions of the scene as camera pans in new direction. We conduct such an evaluation for our method. Our finding is that the performance of our final predictions improves with respect to the ground-truth as more samples are drawn from WanAR (thereby covering the generation of multiple plausible 3D scenes in the future).
Figure 4: Qualitative analysis of hierarchical denoising. WanAR exhibits drift over long rollouts, while FixAR mitigates the drift and cleans up accumulated artifacts.

Table 5: Computational cost comparison with baselines. Runtime and peak GPU memory are measured on 280-frame RealEstate10K videos using a single 80GB H100 GPU. We also report our method at 480× 832× 49 for a resolution-matched comparison.

Table 2: Comparison to state-of-the-art on DL3DV Ling et al. (2024). We compare our method with prior art on the DL3DV dataset which has more challenging camera motion, like sudden translation changes, and 360◦ camera pan. Despite this, our method outperforms baselines by a considerable margin. Once again, mPSNR demonstrates better camera control with our warp-and-inpaint strategy for long video generation.

Table 1: Comparison to state-of-the-art on RealEstate10K Zhou et al. (2018). We compare our hierarchical diffusion strategy to state-of-the-art approaches for long video generation and novelview synthesis of static scenes. Our first finding is that a combination of WanAR + FixAR beats all prior art on RealEstate10K, which we attribute to better camera control in WanAR, and better drift mitigation from FixAR. One surprising finding is that novel-view synthesis approaches like TrajectoryCrafter in fact perform better at this task than many long video generation works. With mPSNR, we show better retention of visible regions particularly driven by precise camera control.

Table 7: Comparison of different geometry estimation methods. We initialize WanAR using the first-frame depth estimated by each method and report performance after one rollout. Results are similar across estimators, indicating limited sensitivity to the choice of depth estimator.

Table 6: Ablation on FixAR keyframe interval and sequence length. We compare 49-frame and 25-frame FixAR variants under different keyframe intervals. The 49-frame model remains stable across its training range, while larger intervals degrade the performance of the 25-frame model.
Table 4: Comparison of different conditioning strategies. The Plucker baseline adds a convolutional adapter to the Wan2.1-14B backbone, and is finetuned on Re10K using the same setup.
Table 3: Quantitative analysis of hierarchical denoising. FixAR improves generation realism and leads to consistent gains across evaluation metrics.

papers.abstract: Simulation-to-reality translation must bridge the appearance gap between synthetic and real domains while preserving structural and semantic consistency. Conditioning-based methods achieve spatial alignment but introduce computationally expensive control modules. Paired-data methods achieve realism but rely on complex synthesis pipelines, often altering scene geometry and semantics. Training-free editing methods avoid both constraints but lack a learned appearance prior, limiting their perceptual quality. Recently proposed phase-preserving diffusion presents a promising alternative, but Fourier-domain formulations are constrained by global spectral coupling. This coupling induces spatial artifacts such as ringing and boundary leakage, thereby degrading structural and semantic consistency. We introduce Wavelet Phase Diffusion, which addresses this through two components. First, we operate in the Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Packet Transform domain, whose localized wavelet packets enable spatially adaptive phase injection without global spectral interference. Second, Low-Frequency Randomization (LFR) replaces the low-frequency packet, decoupling the model from the synthetic illumination prior and enabling in-distribution real-world appearance. Both components train on unpaired open-domain data, and introduce negligible inference overhead. The spatial locality further enables instance-level translation, where individual objects or regions are translated to photorealistic appearance independently while the surrounding scene remains untranslated. On vKITTI $\to$ KITTI image translation, $\psi$-PD outperforms prior methods in realism and semantic consistency while maintaining competitive structural alignment. For CARLA video translation, $\psi$-PD approaches the realism of paired-data methods while reducing VLM planner ADE and FDE by $5.4\%$ and $5.1\%$, respectively.
authors: Kaiwen Wang, Frank Bieder, Yinzhe Shen, Carlos Fernandez, Jan-Hendrik Pauls, Omer Sahin Tas
bullets: Uses localized phase injection in the Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Packet Transform to avoid Fourier-domain ringing and boundary leakage.
Applies Low-Frequency Randomization to remove dependence on synthetic illumination and produce in-distribution real-world appearance.
Trains on unpaired open-domain data with negligible inference overhead.
Supports instance-level translation, allowing selected objects or regions to be translated independently of the surrounding scene.
On vKITTI→KITTI and CARLA translation, it improves realism and semantic consistency, and reduces planner ADE/FDE by 5.4%/5.1%.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of ψ-PD. Source and noise latents are decomposed by DT-CWPT into a low-frequency packet and multiple highfrequency packets. Source phase (green) is injected per packet under the cutoff map F while the low-frequency packet is randomized (LFR), and the inverse transform yields the structured noise ϵ̂.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on vKITTI→ KITTI. Competing methods either hallucinate structure or distort lane/vehicle semantics; ψ-PD preserves both while achieving realistic appearance. See Sec. 5.4 for per-method analysis.

Figure 5. Qualitative comparison on CARLA video translation. Baselines either retain CARLA’s synthetic look or trade realism for altered semantics (weather, traffic lights, lanes); ψ-PD matches Ditto’s realism while keeping semantics intact. See Sec. 5.4.

Figure 7. Zero-shot instance-level video translation. The task requires only the character’s mirror reflection (highlighted in green in the first input frame) to appear photorealistic while the surrounding comic-style scene remains untranslated. Ditto translates the entire frame indiscriminately and cannot isolate the edit to the reflection region; ψ-PD confines the translation to the target region via a per-pixel map.
Figure 8. Ablation: Pareto frontiers (realism vs. consistency).
Figure 2. Fourier- vs. Wavelet-domain low-pass filtering. Fourier exhibits non-local ringing near edges, while DT-CWPT preserves local geometry and edge structure more faithfully.
Figure 6. VLM planning on translated CARLA frames. Predicted waypoints (red) vs. ground-truth (green).

Table 2. Quantitative evaluation on video translation (CARLA). Relative changes w.r.t. the input are reported in %. Bold indicates best, underlined second best. FlowEdit is an image-only method and is not applicable to video. sKID is reported ×102.

Table 1. Quantitative evaluations for image translation (vKITTI→ KITTI). Bold indicates best, underlined second best. VACE and Ditto are video-native and thus not evaluated here. KID is reported ×102.

papers.abstract: Video stylization typically transforms entire scenes, while local artistic editing requires precise region--style association, spatial control, and temporal consistency. We introduce LociArt, a unified paradigm for free-style local video stylization that explicitly specifies where to stylize and what style to apply while preserving non-target content. At its core, GRNStyle builds on Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) and introduces a polar style-aware mask that embeds style identities as equal-norm directions within selected regions. Complementary representation--geometry conditioning combines encoded mask features with raw-mask spatial support, integrating spatiotemporal context with geometric control. To provide paired supervision, we develop an automated pipeline combining global stylization, video object removal, matting, and compositing, and construct the LociArt-100K Dataset with 100K local stylization pairs. We further establish the LociArt Benchmark, comprising 80 source videos and 84 target masks covering 168 foreground/background stylization cases, with a Style Prototype Similarity (SPS) evaluation scheme for regional style quality and complementary measures of non-target preservation and temporal consistency. Experiments show that GRNStyle outperforms existing methods in regional style quality and spatial control while maintaining strong temporal consistency. Qualitative examples further illustrate joint stylization of multiple regions with the same or different learned styles, despite training only on single-region, single-style pairs. Together, these components provide a unified foundation for learning and evaluating controllable local video stylization. Project page: https://higherhu.github.io/lociart/.
authors: Yuxuan Chen, Feng Xie, Jiagao Hu, Fuhao Li, Zepeng Wang, Fei Wang, Daiguo Zhou
bullets: Addresses precise region–style association, spatial control, and temporal consistency in local video editing.
GRNStyle uses polar style-aware masks and representation–geometry conditioning to combine style identity with explicit spatial support.

Experiments report stronger regional style quality and spatial control than existing methods, with strong temporal consistency and multi-region stylization capabilities.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models can reach useful sample quality before copying training examples, but fast optimization can compress this generalization window by accelerating sample-specific fitting. We investigate this effect through update geometry and propose Quality-Gated De-whitening (QGD), a controller that retains a fast polar-update prefix and progressively restores fixed-gain momentum. Our random-feature analysis separates covariance-controlled, curvature-equalized and amplitude-controlled memorization clocks. Under aligned spectral assumptions, it establishes a finite-exposure condition under which a fixed-gain tail recovers a delay proportional to dataset size. QGD implements this principle with a confirmed quality gate, a bounded decay envelope and causal copy feedback. Immediate switching is the conservative limit; gradual control balances delayed copying against continued quality improvement. We pair QGD with Copy-Budgeted Selection (CBS), which applies simultaneous binomial calibration to a frozen checkpoint family, followed by a fresh evaluation of the released checkpoint. On 2,000-image CIFAR-10 subsets, QGD preserves the polar baseline's quality-arrival time while expanding its useful interval by 8.32x and reducing common-checkpoint copying by 75.9%. With identical calibration and independent quality evaluation, QGD achieves FID 75.56 versus 79.37 for SGD with the same selector. Exposure-matched controls, independent detector audits and transfer to flow matching and dance generation support adaptive exposure control as a practical way to improve the quality-copying tradeoff.
bullets: Fast optimization can shorten the interval between useful generation and copying training examples.
Quality-Gated De-whitening (QGD) transitions from polar updates to fixed-gain momentum using quality and copy feedback.
Theory identifies memorization clocks and a finite-exposure condition supporting delays that scale with dataset size.
On 2,000-image CIFAR-10 subsets, QGD expands the useful interval 8.32× and reduces common-checkpoint copying by 75.9%.
Copy-Budgeted Selection calibrates checkpoint choice while using a fresh evaluation of the released model; results also transfer to flow matching and dance generation.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Quality-Gated De-whitening (QGD) to control memorization in diffusion models, improving the quality-copying tradeoff, which is a significant technical contribution to video generation.
papers.title: Controlling Polar Exposure to Delay Memorization in Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: QGD adaptively controls optimization exposure in diffusion models to delay memorization while preserving sample-quality progress.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in restoring high-quality images in a zero-shot manner. Unfortunately, extending this success to video restoration is challenging due to the substantial computational resources required to pre-train video diffusion models. A rising trend seeks to address video restoration by utilizing a pre-trained image diffusion model, initiating restoration from either frame-wise independent or identical Gaussian noise. Yet, these approaches often fall short, as such simple noise initiations fail to capture and utilize the inherent temporal correlations within degraded video frames. In this work, we propose taming noise initialization for zero-shot video restoration, which preserves the intrinsic temporal correlations by generating initial noises directly using DDIM inversion on the corrupted video frames themselves. Building on this, we introduce an adaptive noise blending strategy that suppresses degradation patterns encoded during DDIM inversion while gradually steering the noise toward a Gaussian distribution. To further emphasize temporal consistency, we propose measurement-guided trajectory attention to better align features across frames. Extensive experiments on multiple video restoration tasks demonstrate that our method outperforms existing zero-shot approaches, consistently achieving superior results on the DAVIS, REDS4, and Set8 datasets.
authors: Chong Wang, Zixuan Fu, Hao Cheng, Siyuan Yang, Alex C. Kot, Bihan Wen
bullets: Problem: Frame-independent or identical Gaussian initialization fails to capture temporal correlations in degraded videos, while training video diffusion models is costly.
Method: Generate initial noise from corrupted frames via DDIM inversion to preserve temporal structure.
Adaptive noise blending suppresses inverted degradation patterns while progressively moving noise toward a Gaussian distribution.
Measurement-guided trajectory attention further aligns features across video frames.
Experiments across multiple restoration tasks on DAVIS, REDS4, and Set8 show consistent improvements over existing zero-shot approaches.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Subsequently, an adaptive noise blending strategy is employed to mitigate the degradation pattern in the inversion noise XT , while directing the noise toward a Gaussian distribution. After that, the temporal correlation is further exploited by measurement-guided trajectory attention during the sampling process.

papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based video restoration with temporally coherent noise initialization is transferable to video diffusion and generation interests.
papers.title: Taming Noise Initialization for Zero-shot Video Restoration with Image Diffusion Priors
papers.tldr: A zero-shot video restoration method improves temporal consistency by initializing image-diffusion restoration with degradation-aware, adaptively refined noise rather than simple Gaussian noise.

papers.abstract: Distribution-matching distillation enables high-quality image generation in only a few denoising steps. However, distilled student models often map different initial noise samples to similar outputs under the same prompt. To locate where diversity is lost, we compare the teacher and student along the sampling trajectory. The largest measured reduction in the response to different initial noises occurs during the first, high-noise step. When we replace the first step with the teacher's corresponding trajectory and leave the final three student steps unchanged, most of the output diversity returns. This suggests that the first step is a key point for restoring diversity. Motivated by this finding, we introduce \emph{ReSeed}, a post-distillation method that adds a seed-response bias adapter only to the first student step and aligns its velocity with the teacher's first-interval secant velocity. All student weights and later denoising steps remain unchanged. We evaluate ReSeed on three text-to-image models (SD3-Medium, SD3.5-Medium, and FLUX.1-dev) and one text-to-video model (Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B). For a distilled 4-step FLUX.1-dev model, \emph{ReSeed} requires only $0.00196\%$ additional trainable parameters relative to the base model and is trained on 8,000 prompt--noise pairs, while keeping the distilled student fully frozen and requiring no target images, perceptual losses, or adversarial losses. It improves DINO diversity by $48.3\%$ while maintaining competitive visual quality. These results show that substantial diversity can be recovered through a lightweight, data-efficient tuning of only the first denoising step, without finetuning the full student model.
authors: Wenwu Tang, Dong Wang, Yun Cheng, Olga Saukh
bullets: Diversity is lost primarily during the first, high-noise denoising step.
Replacing that step with the teacher’s trajectory recovers most output diversity while leaving later student steps unchanged.
ReSeed adds a first-step seed-response bias adapter aligned with the teacher’s first-interval velocity; the student remains otherwise frozen.
Evaluated across three text-to-image and one text-to-video model, it improves DINO diversity by 48.3% for a distilled 4-step FLUX.1-dev model while preserving competitive visual quality.
The method uses 0.00196% additional trainable parameters and 8,000 prompt–noise pairs, without target images, perceptual losses, or adversarial losses.

papers.title: A First-Step Bias Restores Lost Diversity in Diffusion Model Distillation

papers.abstract: Interactive world generation requires models to follow successive commands while preserving relevant history and action consequences. We present Hy-Nomas, a video world model with an 8B diffusion backbone that supports free-form text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple interaction turns. It generates variable-length segments conditioned on current inputs and cached history. Our central design aligns structured video captions with action-aware causal attention: descriptive context remains accessible across segments, while action instructions are restricted to their intended temporal windows. A vision-language Prompt Enhancer (PE) translates user requests and multimodal interaction histories into structured conditions for the next segment. A multi-stage curriculum progressively introduces causal generation, text interaction, camera control, and training on model-generated histories, followed by diffusion distillation. In human evaluation, Hy-Nomas shows superior performance over existing world models. We release model weights, code and benchmarks, together with a lightweight adaptation workflow, to support reproducible research on interactive world generation.
authors: Qiaoling Chen, Jiaxiang Cheng, Xueqing Deng, Tiankai Hang, Ji Hou, Jiaqi Li, Yifan Liu, Tao Lu, Junshu Tang, Yu Tang, Yao Teng, Yu Tian, Heng Wang, Weizhi Wang, Xiyao Wang, Xilun Wu, Mingyu Yang, Yangbin Yu, Rui Zhao, Longjun Cao, Linghao Chen, Haoyi Duan, Jiaming Han, Mingji Han, Enhua Jiang, Shunkai Li, Yanzhe Liang, Qinwei Ma, Cong Wang, Lei Wang, Bing Wu, Ke Xing, Ray Ying, Zhentao Yu, Key Zhang, Yuan Zhou, Zhengguang Zhou, Kai Zou
bullets: Supports successive text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple interaction turns.
Generates variable-length video segments conditioned on current inputs and cached interaction history.
Uses action-aware causal attention to preserve descriptive context while limiting actions to their intended time windows.
A vision-language Prompt Enhancer converts user requests and multimodal histories into structured next-segment conditions.
Human evaluations report better performance than existing world models; weights, code, benchmarks, and an adaptation workflow are released.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Overview of the model architecture. A structured multi-segment prompt, a video clip, and a camera trajectory are encoded into text, video, and camera tokens, respectively. Text and video tokens are processed by N = 54 dual-stream MMDiT blocks. Within each block, segmentwise causal attention with 3D RoPE allows tokens to attend to the current and preceding segments, while diffusion timestep embeddings modulate both streams. The two streams pass through separate MLPs, and camera cross-attention further conditions the video stream on camera tokens. During autoregressive generation, keys and values associated with both text and video tokens are stored in the KV cache as context for subsequent segments. The 3D VAE decoder maps denoised video latents to RGB frames. Purple, blue, and green denote the text, video, and camera streams, respectively.

Figure 10: Overview of Hy-Nomas-Bench. Top: Model outputs for an example case from Bench-3 (interleaved text–camera control). Bottom: (a) World settings span diverse scenes, visual styles, subjects, and viewpoints. (b) 280 cases cover multi-turn text interaction, camera navigation, interleaved control, and spatial memory. (c) Unified control maps instructions to text, binary key states [T, 8] (W/A/S/D and four arrow keys), or per-frame 4 × 4 camera-to-world matrices [T, 4, 4], where T is the frame count. Generation continues across turns without world resets. (d) Three annotators evaluate prompt following, physical plausibility, camera control, and memory consistency through pairwise comparisons. Results are summarized by win/tie/loss rates and net win rate (win minus loss, in percentage points).

Figure 2: Data pipeline. Raw videos are split, transcoded, and filtered by basic video properties and visual quality. Hierarchical clustering supports within-cluster deduplication, and a VLM assigns labels to each video from a predefined taxonomy. Video tagging adds captions and, for selected clips, camera-trajectory annotations. Across each training stage, adaptive sampling adjusts the training distribution in response to weaknesses identified from evaluations of earlier stages.

Figure 1: Interactive world generation with Hy-Nomas. Free-form text instructions and continuous camera control can be interleaved across successive interaction turns. At each turn, a vision-language Prompt Enhancer converts the user request and observed world history into a structured text prompt and a duration for the next video segment. Conditioned on these inputs and cached context, Hy-Nomas autoregressively generates the next segment, allowing the world to unfold through continued interaction.

Figure 6: Comparison of segment-wise and action-aware causal attention. (a) Tokens attend to all video and text tokens in the current and preceding segments. (b) Action-aware masking further restricts access to action-specific text tokens. Colors indicate query-to-key modality pairs; gray cells are masked. head denotes the environment description for the current segment, and a0, . . . , an denote actions within that segment.

Figure 3: Structured video captioning. The VLM annotates segments sequentially, maintains subject identities, interleaves scene and camera descriptions chronologically, and records subject actions separately with timestamps. A final text-only turn reviews, translates, and validates the annotations to produce aligned English and Chinese captions. During training, camera-motion sentences and their tags are removed when camera trajectories are available and retained otherwise.

Figure 4: Structured caption format. Video-level fields define perspective, style, and shared subject profiles. Segment descriptions interleave scene information and camera-tagged motion chronologically, excluding main-subject references. The first segment provides a full description; later segments describe changes. Subject actions and their visible outcomes are recorded separately in action-tagged entries using subject tokens. Action intervals are non-overlapping and remain within segment boundaries.

Figure 7: Segment Forcing with streaming backward. Each current segment receives a flowmatching loss; a one-step low-noise estimation supplies cached context for later segments. Streaming backward retains only one segment’s computation graph at a time, accumulating gradients for a single optimizer step after the full sequence. The cache update of the final segment is skipped.

LoRA-SFT denotes the distilled model with the trained LoRA weights merged into it.

Figure 9: Prompt Enhancer (PE) workflow. PE generates an initial dense caption in the first turn. In subsequent turns, users can choose text prompts or camera control, and PE combines the selected input with the full interaction history to generate a dense caption that AR-DiT uses to produce the next video segment. Each turn’s dialogue and generated video are appended to the history.

papers.abstract: Recent advancements in text-guided 3D editing, particularly with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), have shown promise but still lag behind the flexibility of 2D editing tools. Existing methods face a critical trade-off between preserving multi-view consistency and allowing structural modifications. Image-based editors can also struggle to apply the intended edit to objects viewed from unusual angles. To address these limitations, we introduce VidEdit3D, a framework that reformulates 3D scene editing as a trajectory-based video editing task. By drawing a parallel between camera movement in static 3D scenes and temporal dynamics in video, we leverage the robust spatiotemporal priors of pre-trained Video Diffusion Models (VDMs) to encourage semantic and structural coherence across views. Specifically, we propose Trajectory-Guided Rendering (TGR) to select informative keyframes and construct smooth video clips aligned with VDM input requirements. To propagate edits from an anchor view to these clips, we develop Flow-Aligned Video Editing (FAVE), a training-free framework incorporating an Editing Consistency Guidance (ECG) mechanism. ECG contrasts source and edited image conditions at a shared latent state, using scheduled source-image amplification to strengthen adherence to the edited reference while maintaining original scene context. Finally, we introduce Region-Selective 3DGS Refinement (RS-GS) to strictly confine geometric and appearance updates to target primitives, reducing background attribute leakage. Experiments demonstrate stronger instruction alignment and better multi-view consistency than the baselines.
authors: Yanming Yang, Chenxi Song, Tong Zhao, Juntao Xu, Wenhao Rao, Yiwen Chen, Yiwei Wang, Chi Zhang
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between structural editability and multi-view consistency in existing 3D and image-based editors.
Uses Trajectory-Guided Rendering to select keyframes and create smooth camera-aligned video clips.
Applies Flow-Aligned Video Editing with Editing Consistency Guidance to propagate an anchor-view edit across views.
Uses Region-Selective 3DGS Refinement to limit geometry and appearance changes to target regions and reduce background leakage.
Experiments show stronger instruction alignment and improved multi-view consistency than baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of VidEdit3D. We reformulate 3D scene editing as a trajectory-based video editing task. The pipeline consists of three key stages: (1) TGR: We organize selected views into smooth video clips. (2) FAVE: Given a user-edited anchor frame, we propagate the edit across the clip using a pretrained VDM. This module incorporates ECG for semantic alignment and a self-attention-based mask for background preservation. (3) RS-GS: We lift the 2D edits back to 3D via inverse rendering to confine updates to the target Gaussians.

papers.abstract: Generating videos of a specific subject from a few reference images remains challenging when the camera reveals surfaces that are not visible in the input. Early subject-to-video (S2V) methods condition on a single reference image and must therefore infer the subject's unseen appearance and geometry as the viewpoint changes. To address this limitation, recent methods extend S2V to multiple reference views, providing more information about the subject from different viewpoints. However, they do not explicitly specify the 3D structure that connects these observations. In addition, existing training data do not guarantee that viewpoint changes preserve the same underlying 3D subject. We present OmniShowcase, built on two components: (i) a fully automated data synthesis pipeline that produces training videos along diverse camera trajectories, with viewpoint variation driven by underlying subject geometry, even spanning full 360-degree orbits; and (ii) a geometry-conditioning method that provides the video model with a turntable of surface-normal maps reconstructed from the reference views without requiring temporal alignment with the generated frames. We construct Showcase-4K, a corpus of 3D-asset-based videos covering twelve camera motions across 88 trajectory configurations with reconstruction-derived surface-normal conditioning, and ShowcaseBench, a held-out evaluation set with the source meshes and camera parameters used to render each video. Experiments show state-of-the-art subject identity and 3D consistency while maintaining competitive video quality and motion. Project page: justin4ai.github.io/OmniShowcase
authors: Junyeong Ahn, Geonwoo Kim, Kinam Kim, Gihwi Kim, Hoonjin Jung, Hyojin Jang, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Addresses unseen subject surfaces and inconsistent 3D structure during viewpoint changes.
Uses an automated pipeline to synthesize videos with geometry-driven camera motion, including full 360° orbits.
Conditions generation on surface-normal maps reconstructed from reference views without requiring temporal alignment.
Introduces Showcase-4K for training and ShowcaseBench for evaluation with known meshes and camera parameters.
Reports state-of-the-art subject identity and 3D consistency with competitive video quality and motion.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of OmniShowcase. From N=4 reference views, we reconstruct 3D geometry and render a surface-normal turntable. The reference images and normal condition are injected into the reference pathway of a LoRA-tuned image-to-video diffusion transformer. The model uses appearance information from the reference views and 3D structure from the normal condition to generate the target video without per-subject optimization.

Figure 2: Automated 3D-consistent data synthesis pipeline. From a curated 3D asset (Deitke et al., 2023), Blender renders the target orbit and four reference views. (a) The target is composited into a prompt-driven scene by video inpainting (Jiang et al., 2025); (b) the four views are reconstructed in 3D (Li et al., 2026) and rendered as the surface-normal turntable used as the condition. Every stage runs without human intervention.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of training data. Uni3C (Cao et al., 2025) is an image-to-video model, so every surface the camera path uncovers is generated. Ours renders the subject from a 3D asset and generates only the background.

Figure 10: 3D reconstruction from generated video. The subject is segmented out of each method’s generated orbit and lifted to a coloured point cloud, the same reconstruction evaluated by GT-CD, shown here from four viewpoints so the geometric differences are visible directly. Baselines recover a thin shell of the surfaces their orbit actually sweeps, while ours closes the volume.

Figure 7: Additional qualitative comparison. Four further subjects under diverse camera trajectories, with the same method ordering as Figure 5. Each block pairs the four reference views and the prompt, whose +[tag] suffix names the trajectory (Appendix G.2), with generated frames from every method.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison with baselines. 3DB denotes 3DreamBooth. Given a teapot and a jar of peach gummies, we compare OmniShowcase against four baselines. Red boxes mark where identity or 3D structure breaks down.
Figure 6: Conditioning ablation. Given a biplane and a bulldozer, we compare the three conditioning variants against ours. Marked regions highlight where identity or 3D structure breaks down.
Figure 8: Trajectory and scene control. One subject driven by several camera configurations, including arc, zoom-in and truck, with the background also varied by the prompt for each trajectory.

Figure 9: Trajectory control in a fixed scene. The same subject and background under different camera configurations, from full orbits to an arc and a zoom-out, where only the camera trajectory changes between rows. Inference only.

Figure 13: Failure cases. Left two. Prompt adherence and the commanded rotation both hold, but the surroundings render with flat shading and little material detail, so the clip reads as slightly synthetic. Right two. Both receive four reference views of a subject caught in four different poses. The upper one is prompted in the usual static style and settles into an averaged pose that matches none of the references, while the lower one is asked to follow the motion in step with the orbit and tangles in 3D at the transitions between poses.

papers.abstract: Few-step distillation is essential for deploying modern video diffusion models. Among existing approaches, Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) has emerged as a highly promising paradigm by achieving strong output-space fidelity without adversarial training, while remaining flexible across various student architectures. We observe, however, that DMD fundamentally relies on an output-space objective, lacking explicit regularization on the model's internal representations. As the distillation step count aggressively shrinks, this output-only supervision becomes insufficient, causing the distilled student to degrade in both fine-grained spatial structures and coherent temporal dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce Self Flow Forcing (SF$^2$), which incorporates a predictive representation loss into the DMD framework without altering its output objective. By providing the student and an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) teacher with heterogeneous noise levels, we establish an information asymmetry. This formulation forces the student to predict the teacher's internal representations from a more corrupted input, effectively integrating self-supervised representation alignment into distribution matching. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SF$^2$ effectively mitigates temporal flickering and consistently improves both spatial fidelity and motion quality. Furthermore, the proposed mechanism is architecture-agnostic - seamlessly supporting both bidirectional and causal models - and requires no external feature extractors, introducing minimal computational overhead.
authors: Junyi Chen, Haiyu Zhang, Zhoujie Fu, Tengfei Wang, Chunchao Guo
bullets: DMD’s output-only supervision can fail at very low step counts, harming fine spatial detail and coherent motion.
SF² adds a predictive representation loss while preserving DMD’s original output objective.
A student receives a more corrupted input than its EMA teacher and predicts the teacher’s internal representations.
Experiments report less temporal flickering and consistent gains in spatial fidelity and motion quality.
The method is architecture-agnostic across bidirectional and causal models and needs no external feature extractor.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SF2. From the student’s denoising trajectory, the cleanest prediction drives the standard DMD loss LDMD, while two intermediate states (xt, xs) with t > s feed the SF2 branch: a spatial mask mixes them into an asymmetric, highly corrupted input for the student, while the EMA teacher sees only the cleaner xs. Hidden states from asymmetric layers are aligned via learnable projectors with a stop-gradient cosine loss Lrep. The teacher is updated by EMA and requires no external pre-trained features.

Figure 6: Quantitative evaluation on interactive video generation. We evaluate the adherence of the generated video to the input camera and action conditions. Compared to the WorldPlay baseline, SF2 achieves notably higher translation, rotation, and action accuracy across training steps, demonstrating that a stronger internal representation leads to more precise state transitions in interactive environments.

Figure 7: Qualitative camera trajectory alignment. Reconstructed 3D point clouds and camera trajectories from the generated videos. The trajectory produced by SF2 (blue) tightly tracks the input condition (green), whereas the WorldPlay baseline (red) exhibits severe drift. This visualizes how the stronger internal representation of SF2 enforces strict adherence to complex control signals.

Figure 2: Qualitative comparison on causal few-step T2V generation. Top row: multi-step bidirectional Wan2.1 teacher. Rows 2–5: few-step distilled causal students (CausVid, Self-Forcing, Causal-Forcing, SF2). The four panels expose four facets of representation-level coherence that the rep loss is designed to compress into the student: articulated-motion plausibility (top-left), event irreversibility (top-right), object persistence (bottom-left), and scene-structural stability (bottomright). SF2 satisfies all four, whereas baselines fail in distinct ways on each.

papers.abstract: Most action-conditioned video world models remain limited to a single player, while existing multiplayer models support only small, fixed groups of agents. We introduce FlockWorld, an artificial-life environment built on Reynolds's Boids algorithm for studying population-scale multi-agent video world models. Specifically, FlockWorld renders synchronized egocentric crops, assigns distinct colors to preserve camera-agent identity across views, exposes rule-derived accelerations as actions, and lets the number of camera agents be configured independently of the size of the surrounding population. We further introduce FlockDiT, an action-conditioned latent diffusion transformer trained with flow matching on FlockWorld data to jointly generate synchronized egocentric videos for multiple agents. Our results suggest that joint generation benefits agent detection at density-matched settings and that diffusion forcing improves rollout fidelity. Together, FlockWorld and FlockDiT provide a controlled testbed for multi-agent video generation.
authors: Meryem Koksal, Yunzhe Wang, Volkan Ustun
bullets: Addresses the limitation of existing action-conditioned video world models, which typically support one agent or small fixed groups.
Builds an environment from Reynolds’s Boids algorithm with synchronized egocentric views, color-based agent identities, and configurable camera-agent and population sizes.
Introduces FlockDiT, an action-conditioned latent diffusion transformer trained with flow matching for joint multi-agent video generation.
The abstract reports improved agent detection in density-matched settings and better rollout fidelity with diffusion forcing.
Provides a controlled testbed rather than a claim of broad real-world performance; its scope is artificial-life simulation.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in image editing have enabled fine-grained and highly controllable visual modifications. However, achieving similar levels of controllability in video editing remains an open challenge, particularly for precise local edits, dynamic temporal effects, and consistent lighting across frames.In this paper, we propose EditDistill, a framework that distills image-level visual transformations from edits to guide video editing.Specifically, given a source video and an edit prompt, we first generate an edited version of the initial video frame using an off-the-shelf image editing model. We then distill the visual transformation of this original-edited image pair into a compact representation termed an edit descriptor.This descriptor is injected into a video diffusion model through our lightweight fusion module, which steers the denoising process toward the desired edit. To align the video trajectory with the demonstrated image edit while preserving motion and layout, we train with edit-descriptor alignment and DINO structural consistency losses, and derive an equivalent inference-time guidance formulation under flow matching.Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves strong performance on standard benchmarks and produces high-quality video editing results across diverse scenarios. For more details and videos, please refer to the anonymous webpage: https://yu-shaonian.github.io/EditDistill-Web/.
authors: Guojun Lei, Hong Li, Hongbing Yang, Lixue Gong, Chi Wang, Zheng Dong
bullets: Addresses the challenge of precise local edits, dynamic effects, and consistent lighting in videos.
Generates an edited first frame, then distills the source–edited image transformation into an edit descriptor.
Injects the descriptor into a video diffusion model through a lightweight fusion module to steer denoising.
Uses edit-descriptor alignment and DINO structural consistency losses to preserve motion and layout.
Reports strong benchmark performance and high-quality results across diverse video-editing scenarios.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of EDITDISTILL. Stage I encodes the transformation between an image pair (Is, Ie) into the edit descriptor d. Stage II keeps the Wan2.1-I2V-14B video diffusion frozen and trains the inject modules to inject d into selected transformer blocks by lightweight feature fusion modules steering the diffusion denoising toward the desired edit to produce a temporally coherent video V e from the video V s.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison. EDITDISTILL performs both local and global edits while keeping the main subject, background, and motion stable. In contrast, other methods may miss the desired edit, unintentionally change nearby regions, or produce unstable results across frames.

Figure 7: Stage I edit descriptor model. The Delta VAE encoder extracts a stochastic descriptor from the source and edited VAE latents by combining shared features, their explicit feature difference, and a multi-scale encoder. The Delta VAE decoder receives only the source latent and descriptor, and reconstructs the edited latent through descriptor-conditioned residual blocks with self- and cross-attention.

Figure 4: Descriptor attention. Cross-attention maps show that local edits concentrate on the regions that need to change, while global edits such as relighting or stylization produce broader but still structured responses. The descriptor behaves as a transformation operator rather than a fixed mask or copied target image.
Figure 6: Relighting comparison. The distilled descriptor captures a global lighting transformation and guides coherent relighting across frames while preserving scene geometry and motion.
Figure 8: Frame-wise descriptor attention. The same edit descriptor re-localizes to the relevant moving regions across different video frames.

Figure 2: EDITDISTILL encodes the visual transformation between image editing pair into a compact edit descriptor, and combines the edit descriptor alignment constraint with the DINO structural similarity loss to distill the image editing capability into the denoising trajectory of video editing.
Figure 9: Qualitative ablation. Removing individual branches or alignment losses weakens either edit fidelity or temporal preservation, matching the quantitative trends in Section 5.3.
Figure 10: More results in traffic environments.
Figure 11: Additional video editing results.

For evaluation metrics, CLIP-E and CLIP-T measure edit fidelity; DINO-sim measures preservation of unedited regions; Temp. and Warp measure temporal coherence; FVD measures perceptual video quality. Best results are in bold and second best results are underlined.

papers.abstract: While interactive video world models require autoregressive generation, directly adapting pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into autoregressive ones with teacher forcing can disrupt their visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality. In this paper, we introduce Mix Forcing, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (MoBA) attention. Mix Forcing jointly trains a video diffusion model with both teacher forcing and bidirectional training, yielding a strong causal initialization for few-step post-training. In self-attention, Mix Forcing leverages teacher forcing to learn causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while using bidirectional attention to preserve pretrained visual priors. To support online text interaction, Mix Forcing further adopts a chunk-wise cross-attention design that conditions each video chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, without exposing future instructions to the current chunk. Following causal pre-training on a 14B image-to-video model, we apply consistency and distribution matching distillation to obtain a four-step autoregressive generator. Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks, including WBench and SANA-WM-Bench, show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control. Notably, our model supports high-fidelity long-horizon generation without quality degradation even over one-hour rollouts. Project page is here: https://zelingao98.github.io/mixforcing
authors: Zelin Gao, Hao Ouyang, Jiapeng Zhu, Qiuyu Wang, Jingye Chen, Zichen Liu, Xing Zhu, Yujun Shen, Yinghao Xu
bullets: Addresses the degradation of visual priors when adapting bidirectional video diffusion models to causal, autoregressive generation.
Introduces MoBA attention, jointly combining teacher-forced causal prediction with bidirectional training for causal initialization.
Uses chunk-wise cross-attention to condition video on shared environment context and local instructions without revealing future prompts.
Applies consistency and distribution-matching distillation to produce a four-step autoregressive generator.
Reports state-of-the-art visual quality, event following, and camera control, with high-fidelity rollouts lasting up to one hour on reported benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Pipeline of our interactive video world model. Given an initial image and an environment prompt pe, an interactive world is simulated by our four-step causal video model. Based on the KV-cached history context and user inputs, including the camera pose ei and the local prompt pi, each latent chunk is generated autoregressively and decoded into a video clip by the VAE decoder.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparisons with state-of-the-art methods. (a) Camera-controlled roaming: our model preserves structure and fine details during viewpoint changes, whereas other methods suffer from blurring or distortion. (b) Online prompt interaction: our model follows each event prompt with a consistent scene, whereas other methods respond with delays or break scene consistency.

Figure 1: Long-horizon interactive video rollout with camera control and memory. Top: a single one-hour autoregressive rollout generated by our model trained with Mix Forcing, following successive prompt updates under keyboard camera control. Bottom: a memory case, where the camera looks away and later returns, and previously observed regions (A: waterfall; B: red foliage) remain consistent when revisited.
Figure 4: Pairwise user study on InBench. Each bar compares our model with one baseline and shows the percentages of judgments preferring ours, rating a tie, and preferring the baseline.

Figure 3: MoBA attention block. For selfattention (left), each noisy TF chunk attends only to itself and its clean history, while the appended BID noisy latents attend only to one another bidirectionally. For cross-attention (right), TF chunks attend to the shared environment prompt pe and their corresponding local prompt pi, while BID chunks attend to the global prompt pg .

IQ0–2 and IQ8–10 denote imaging quality over the first and last 2 seconds. The best results are in bold, and the top three are highlighted from dark to light blue.

papers.tldr: Mix Forcing converts bidirectional video diffusion models into efficient autoregressive world models while preserving visual quality and enabling long-horizon interactive generation.

papers.abstract: Video world models are expected to generate videos that accurately follow specified camera trajectories while maintaining consistent 3D structures. However, existing models are predominantly trained on densely sampled videos with small inter-frame camera motions. When applied to sparse, large step trajectories, they often produce frozen frames, inaccurate camera motion, and severe geometric drift. We attribute this degradation to a mismatch between the gradual viewpoint transitions seen during training and the large viewpoint changes required at inference time. To address this problem, we propose Dense Trajectory Teacher Distillation (DTTD), a post-training framework that transfers a model's generation capability from dense trajectories to large camera motions. Given a sparse trajectory, DTTD interpolates additional camera poses to construct a dense trajectory covering the same path. The frozen base model then generates reliable teacher videos along this familiar dense trajectory, and pose aligned teacher observations are used to evaluate candidate videos generated under the original sparse trajectory. In this way, the model serves as its own generation teacher, requiring neither additional video data nor a stronger external video generator. We further combine dense teacher supervision with geometry aware rewards that assess cross frame consistency and camera trajectory following, and use the resulting preferences for offline preference optimization. To stably expand the model's motion range, we introduce a cumulative curriculum that progressively incorporates larger motion steps while retaining simpler trajectories to reduce capability forgetting.
authors: Shuofeng Sun, Linqing Zhao, Haibin Yan
bullets: Existing models often fail on sparse, large-step camera trajectories, producing frozen frames, inaccurate motion, and geometric drift.
DTTD interpolates sparse camera paths into dense trajectories that the frozen base model can reliably generate.
Pose-aligned dense teacher videos supervise candidate outputs generated on the original sparse trajectory, without extra data or an external teacher.
Geometry-aware rewards measure cross-frame consistency and trajectory following for offline preference optimization.
A cumulative curriculum progressively increases motion difficulty while retaining simpler trajectories to limit capability forgetting.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Pipeline of DTTD. We construct camera trajectories with different motion magnitudes through interpolation, and design dense trajectory evaluation and geometric evaluation to improve the model’s performance when faced with large-motion trajectories.

Figure 1: Generation video examples. When the camera trajectory is sparse and the motion magnitude is large, the model may produce static frames, geometric collapse, camera-following failure, and other issues. Furthermore, we can see that by densifying the trajectory and reducing the motion magnitude, the model’s output quality can be substantially improved, which demonstrates the rationality of our dense trajectory evaluation. After alignment with our method, the model’s geometric consistency, following capability, and visual quality are effectively improved when faced with largemotion trajectories.

Figure 3: Visualization of generation videos.

papers.abstract: Controlling the camera relative to a moving subject in an existing video is challenging: behaviors such as maintaining a frontal view require the camera to adapt to the subject's changing position and orientation, making the desired trajectory difficult to specify in advance. Existing camera-controlled video-to-video methods typically rely on explicit trajectories or reference motions, which do not directly express these dynamic camera--subject relationships. We introduce semantic camera motion control, a novel video-to-video task in which a reference video and a target motion label specify the desired subject-relative camera behavior without an explicit target trajectory. Our method, SemCam, learns to realize this behavior while preserving source content. It combines shared-basis low-rank adaptation with motion-conditioned modulation, while a background-consistency loss encourages fidelity in regions visible in both reference and target videos. We construct 661 paired videos covering eight semantic camera behaviors and evaluate on a separate 109-scene benchmark using subject-relative motion metrics, appearance measures, and a user study. SemCam achieves a semantic-motion success rate of 68.6%, compared with 45.3% for Vista4D, the strongest evaluated baseline, while maintaining comparable subject identity preservation.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of specifying camera motion around subjects whose position and orientation change over time.
Uses a reference video plus a target motion label to express behaviors such as maintaining a frontal view.
Combines shared-basis low-rank adaptation, motion-conditioned modulation, and a background-consistency loss.
Evaluated on 661 paired videos and a separate 109-scene benchmark covering eight semantic camera behaviors.
Outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline on semantic-motion success while maintaining comparable subject identity preservation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: SemCam method overview. Reference-video tokens are concatenated with noisy target-video tokens zt and processed by the DiT. The motion label m selects a motion-specific LoRA factor Ak, paired with a shared basis B, and a learned embedding em that predicts modulation residuals (∆γm,∆βm,∆gm). These residuals are added to the timestep-dependent modulation parameters. Fire icons indicate trainable components; the pretrained backbone remains frozen.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison with camera-control baselines. Four examples compare SemCam (highlighted in blue) with Vista4D [LLS∗26], TrajectoryCrafter [YHXS25], ReCamMaster [BXF∗25], and CamCloneMaster [LSB∗25]. Each example is labeled by the requested camera behavior; rows show the input and method outputs, and columns show four frames sampled over time.

Figure 4: Semantic camera control across diverse scenes. Each cell shows three frames from the input video (top, blue) and SemCam’s output (bottom) for the labeled camera behavior. Outputs are generated independently from each input video and motion label. Examples span people, animals, vehicles, and stylized subjects; all clips are included in the supplementary videos.

Figure 5: User study comparing our method against Vista4D [LLS∗26] (top) and CamCloneMaster [LSB∗25] (bottom), conducted with 55 participants. Each horizontal bar shows the fraction of responses preferring our method

Figure 6: Ablation study. Two semantic camera motions (columns; two frames per clip) for the full model and each ablation of Tab. 3. Our full model both executes the requested camera motion control and preserves the scene.

Middle: Side rotation (top) and follow (bottom). Right: The corresponding combinations, showing upward camera movement combined with rotation (top) or subject-following (bottom).

papers.abstract: Continuous visual world simulation requires coupling evolving scene geometry with temporally persistent appearance. We present UniWorld, a unified framework that integrates depth trajectories and reference appearance within a shared video generation model. The central design maintains visual and geometric histories on a common timeline. Noise-aligned overlapping continuation places generated history at the prescribed sampling noise level and commits only newly generated latents. Rolling depth latent state preserves the corresponding geometric controls, incrementally reads newly available geometry, and keeps the conditioning fixed within each sampling window. Together, these mechanisms ensure exact preservation of latent history while bounding the active depth state by the window size. We evaluate continuous generation, paired history interventions, and long-horizon behavior across diverse scene categories. The same generator supports estimated, native, and on-demand simulator depth, while cached and incremental execution paths produce bitwise-identical outputs. Appearance changes and geometric control branches operate through the same interface without modifying committed history. The measured steady-state DiT execution path achieves real-time generation throughput, demonstrating the efficiency of UniWorld for continuous visual world simulation.
authors: Xin Zhang, Yabo Chen, Shuaiwei Wang, Zixuan Duan, Haibin Huang, Feng Xu, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coupling temporally persistent visual appearance with changing scene geometry.
Uses noise-aligned overlapping continuation to preserve generated latent history while committing only new content.
Maintains rolling depth latents and fixed per-window conditioning to control geometry with bounded active state.
Supports estimated, native, and on-demand simulator depth, with cached and incremental execution producing identical outputs.
