papers.abstract: Generating multiple videos of a dynamic scene from a single reference video requires synthesizing both observed and unobserved content consistently across viewpoints. Existing camera-control methods for video diffusion typically rely on architectural mechanisms, including camera embeddings, cross-view attention, and geometric conditioning. Although effective for static scene content, these approaches often struggle with the fine-grained, dynamic geometry that must remain coherent across views and over time. We synchronize the diffusion process itself by sampling the Gaussian noise prior in a canonical 3D space derived from the source video and rasterizing it into target cameras, rather than sampling independently in each 2D image plane. Our method, SyncVid, lifts a monocular video into a canonical 4D representation, associates noise with scene geometry and unseen space, and rasterizes the resulting structured noise into arbitrary views. Because rendering can introduce local correlations, we further propose a cross-view-consistent whitening procedure that decorrelates neighboring pixels while preserving correspondence across views. The structured noise serves as the diffusion prior for a LoRA-adapted pretrained video diffusion model, requiring no architectural modifications. By enforcing spatiotemporal and cross-view coherence at the source of stochasticity, SyncVid generates synchronized videos and improves both perceptual quality and cross-view consistency in our experiments. Project page: https://qualcomm-ai-research.github.io/SyncVid-Webpage.
authors: Farhad G. Zanjani, Animesh Karnewar, Fatih Porikli, Amirhossein Habibian
bullets: Addresses the challenge of generating temporally and cross-view coherent videos from a single reference video, especially for dynamic geometry.
Lifts the source video into a canonical 4D representation and rasterizes geometry-aware noise into target camera views.
Introduces cross-view-consistent whitening to reduce local correlations while preserving correspondence across views.
Uses the structured noise as the prior for a LoRA-adapted pretrained video diffusion model without architectural modifications.
Experiments report improved perceptual quality and cross-view consistency, though the abstract provides no quantitative results.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SyncVid. Given a source video, SyncVid (1) lifts the observations into a canonical 4D point representation; (2) samples a Gaussian noise vector for each 3D primitive in the scene; and (3), after specifying novel camera trajectories, rasterizes and whitens the shared 3D noise into the corresponding views. These synchronized priors guide video diffusion to produce temporally and cross-view consistent videos from multiple cameras.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on a Multi-ViewBench example with an Arc-right trajectory.

Figure 2: View-consistent whitening Noise vectors z𝑖 are attached to 3D primitives and the cubemap; rasterization therefore provides cross-view correspondence, while overlapping footprints induce local correlation. We reduce this correlation with a per-pixel orthonormal transformation Q𝑝 derived from the rasterized canonical anchor position X𝑝 using random Fourier features and reduced QR (dashed box). Because Q𝑝 depends on X𝑝 rather than screen coordinates, pixels observing the same surface point share the transformation across views and over time. The resulting noise pattern (right) is approximately i.i.d. Gaussian within each frame while remaining cross-view synchronized.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models have learned rich 3D/4D priors, making them promising for scene generation and video re-rendering. However, their use in spatial tasks is limited by imprecise camera control, spatial and temporal inconsistencies, and entangled camera motion with scene dynamics. Existing approaches, such as task-specific fine-tuning and post-process warping, often introduce visual artifacts, generalize poorly, or incur high computational costs. We propose WorldForge V2 to achieve accurate camera control while preserving the generative capabilities of pretrained video models. We first develop a training-free guidance framework using warped references to iteratively refine generation along a target camera path. Optical-flow analysis identifies motion-related latent channels for selective guidance, helping separate motion control from appearance. A dual-path strategy further compares guided and unguided predictions to correct artifacts from imperfect references. Together, these components guide viewpoint changes while preserving scene appearance and object motion. To reduce refinement costs, v-cache approximates the correction using the preceding denoising prediction, avoiding an additional model evaluation. We further extend motion localization from latent channels to network blocks and introduce Trajectory LoRA, which concentrates adaptation on blocks most responsive to trajectory guidance. A two-stage training strategy teaches these adapters to denoise the states encountered during guided generation, using limited supervision effectively. This enables reliable camera control with very little training data, with a single training scene already supporting generalization to unseen scenes. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations across multiple datasets show that our method achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and trajectory accuracy in camera-controlled video generation.
authors: Chenxi Song, Yanming Yang, Tong Zhao, Ruibo Li, Joey Tianyi Zhou, Chi Zhang
bullets: Addresses imprecise camera control, temporal/spatial inconsistencies, and entanglement between camera motion and scene dynamics.
Uses warped-reference guidance, optical-flow-based motion localization, and dual-path prediction to refine generation along target camera paths.
Introduces v-cache to reduce refinement cost and Trajectory LoRA to adapt only trajectory-responsive network blocks.
A two-stage training strategy enables reliable control with limited supervision; one training scene can generalize to unseen scenes.
Experiments across multiple datasets report state-of-the-art camera trajectory accuracy and generation quality.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of WorldForge V2. Given a single image or video frame and a target camera trajectory, the scene geometry is reconstructed and rendered into trajectory-aligned warped frames. WorldForge V2 first performs training-free trajectory guidance in the predicted clean latent space using IRR, FLF, and DSG. Building on this framework, we further introduce an efficient route that directly fuses trajectory information in the noisy latent space with V-Cache, together with a trajectory-sensitive lightweight LoRA scheme for camera trajectory control using only limited training data. The resulting video follows the specified camera path while preserving the generative capability of the pretrained video diffusion model.

Fig. 5. Qualitative comparison of camera-controlled scene generation. Our LongCat and H3 models recover coherent object shapes and material detail from incomplete warped references, including thin structures and partially revealed objects. Compared with the baselines, they produce fewer rendering remnants and more continuous geometry, preserving scene appearance as the camera reveals new content.

Fig. 3. Qualitative comparison for 3D novel-view synthesis and 4D trajectory-controlled re-rendering. For single-image 3D generation (left), our method produces more coherent geometry and plausible newly revealed content. For dynamic re-rendering (right), it preserves human appearance and object motion while reducing floating structures and flattened faces. The training-free guidance yields more realistic results in both static and dynamic scenes.

Fig. 9. Qualitative comparison of Trajectory LoRA training strategies. For LongCat (a) and H3 (b), two examples per backbone place the input and warped reference beside No LoRA, Standard FM, and the full method. The full strategy reduces fragmented geometry and residual rendering artifacts, producing more continuous surfaces and finer scene detail than No LoRA and Standard FM. Red boxes and enlarged crops compare corresponding regions.

Fig. 6. Qualitative transfer of Trajectory LoRA across camera-control methods. Without additional fine-tuning, the same trained LongCat adapter improves surface continuity and object detail in WAH [18] and GWF [16], demonstrating transferable trajectory control.

Fig. 4. Noise-state consistency under different reference-insertion strategies. Direct Insertion leaves gaps in the inferred-noise mean and log-variance between visible and model-generated regions, accompanied by noisy patches and broken structure. IRR reduces these gaps, and V-Cache approximates its correction while retaining continuous surfaces and clear geometric detail.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents can now build small playable games in minutes, but the results usually look like programmer art: gray blockouts, colored geometric primitives, and flat semantic blobs. We present AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns such footage into high-quality visuals with characters, motion detail, and effects. Throughout, it keeps the layout, camera, and every entity's position and timing intact. Our AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres that agents build, such as tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, and crowd runners. AnyGameRenderer takes plain video as its game-state input, with no complex representations such as engine G-buffers, per-object class labels, or low-poly proxies. Gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes all work as input. It also preserves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, and entities appear and disappear on the right frame. We implement AnyGameRenderer by LoRA fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 ref2va, a 33B reference-video-conditioned video generation model. Training uses $\sim$10k paired clips from three sources: (i) multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games exported from GEAR, an AI game-creation tool; (ii) two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine, with programmatically controlled crowds, count changes, and entity scales; and (iii) real gameplay recordings, with pairs reconstructed via 3D-box detection. To evaluate the entity correspondence, we propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, scored against ground-truth boxes. Compared with the base model, AnyGameRenderer better preserves entity correspondence: temporal match rises from 50.9\% to 62.9\%, missed count changes fall from 34.7\% to 21.3\%, and fewer entities are hallucinated or left unrendered.
authors: Ruicong Liu, Liangyang Ouyang, Fengbo Lan, Zhixiang Wang, Kaipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses programmer-art visuals produced by AI-built games.
Uses video-to-video generation from plain footage, without G-buffers, object labels, or 3D proxies.
LoRA-fine-tunes a reference-video-conditioned video model on paired game-rendering clips and gameplay recordings.
Introduces an entity-level benchmark with 59 held-out cases and 753 entities.
Improves temporal entity matching from 50.9% to 62.9% and reduces missed count changes from 34.7% to 21.3% versus the base model.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of AnyGameRenderer. (a) Paired data from three sources. GEAR games use multi-stream rendering, which pairs each game render with several aligned crude streams such as blockouts and semantic maps. Unreal Engine scenes use two-stream rendering, which pairs a full render with blockouts. Real gameplay recordings are converted into blockouts by detecting 3D bounding boxes. (b) One training sample: the crude clip is the input video <Video 1>, the target’s first frame serves as an optional anchor, and a six-segment caption defines which real entity each crude shape represents and what must be preserved. (c) Text, <Video 1>, anchor, and noisy target tokens form one sequence for the frozen MiniMax-H3 DiT. Only the LoRA adapters on self-attention and feed-forward layers are trained, and the model renders the input gameplay in the prompted style.

The zero-shot model leaves crude shapes unrendered (rows 1–4), drops the input viewpoint for out-of-domain styles (rows 5–6: a top-down blockout becomes a frontal anime scene or a first-person voxel scene), and adds captionnamed characters although the input has only two blocks (row 7). AnyGameRenderer fixes all three. For rows 5–6, the “GT” column is the original in-domain render and serves only as a layout reference.

This allows style switching and skips modeling, texturing and animation.

papers.abstract: Cinematic video generation requires both temporal inference from limited inputs (i.e., sparse rather than frame-by-frame guidance) and factor-aware control of character, scene, action, and camera. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer useful priors for both capabilities, but their representations are not automatically actionable for video generation: a Video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) may bypass them through native conditioning pathways, and using them does not ensure either factor-aware control or generation-compatible temporal prediction. We propose Factor-Aware Predictive Learning (FAPL), which establishes effective MLLM latent use as a shared prerequisite and then targets the two capabilities with complementary learning signals. First, latent-only generator grounding trains the DiT with a frozen MLLM and connector, strengthening the DiT's use of MLLM latents for generation. Second, for factor-aware control, paired videos specify a target-factor change and non-target preservation, and factor-span replacement trains the DiT to realize this relationship in its output. Third, for temporal inference, text-only and text-plus-complete-video observations share a video target, and the trained DiT is then frozen while the MLLM and connector are optimized through it. This final stage trains limited-input representations for generation while retaining complete-observation reconstruction as a complementary training mode. Extensive experiments demonstrate our consistently better performance on three cinematic video generation tasks (i.e., sparse-to-video, factor-aware editing, and multi-shot generation) over baselines and validate FAPL's contributions to MLLM feature use, temporal control, and factor coordination.
authors: Songlin Yang, Zhe Wang, Xiaotong Zhao, Xi Wang, Ran Zhang, Shuai Li, Taiyi Wu, Songlian Li, Eric Liu, Alan Zhao, Anyi Rao
bullets: Addresses the gap between useful MLLM representations and their reliable use by video diffusion transformers.
Uses latent-only generator grounding to make the DiT depend on frozen MLLM latents.
Learns factor-aware editing through paired videos with target-factor changes and non-target preservation.
Trains temporal inference from text or incomplete video by optimizing the MLLM and connector through a frozen DiT.
Reports consistently better performance than baselines across sparse-to-video, factor-aware editing, and multi-shot generation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of Factor-Aware Predictive Learning (FAPL). Stage I freezes the MLLM and its original connector and trains the DiT using MLLM latents. Stage II retains this configuration and swaps factor-specific output spans between paired examples to supervise factor-aware changes. Stage III freezes the trained DiT and jointly updates the MLLM and connector through video reconstruction, and text-only and text-plus-complete-video inputs share the same generation target.

Figure 2: MLLM latents are easily bypassed in existing MLLM–DiT models. (i) Under MLLMonly conditioning, Omni-Video 2 (1.3B DiT) produces noise, while Omni-Video 2 (14B DiT) and UniVideo produce artifacts and depict one person’s successive actions as two people acting differently. MLLM latents alone therefore fail to provide reliable generation guidance in these examples. (ii) Under conflicting conditions, VAE references dominate the output.

Figure 4: Under limited inputs, baseline models fail to predict temporal visual details. With only text and no visual references, we compare UniVideo with FAPL (Ours), highlighting representative baseline limitations across four cinematic factors. (i) Character. Long hair is generated as short hair, failing appearance details specified only by text. (ii) Scene. The background is not preserved and incorrect content appears. (iii) Action. The requested sequence, e.g., gesturing outward with the left hand and extended fingers, is missing. (iv) Camera. UniVideo ignores the instruction and keeps the camera static, while Ours orbits around the character. FAPL better realizes promptspecified appearance, scene, and motion from text alone.

Figure 5: FAPL improves factor-aware control. For each factor, we modify only the corresponding description in the structured prompt and generate twice, comparing UniVideo with FAPL (Ours). UniVideo does not confine the change to the requested factor and alters unrelated content, whereas Ours modifies the selected factor while preserving the others. This indicates that factor-level latent augmentation enables selective control.

Figure 1: Cinematic video generation requires inference from limited inputs and factor-aware control. (i) The man turns toward the box, places his right hand on top, and steadies the bundle with his left hand. Text-only conditioning misses this sequence, while observing the complete video enables the same model to reproduce it. (ii) Keeping the descriptions of all other factors fixed and replacing only the character-related prompt, the non-character factors change as well. These cases illustrate failures in temporal inference and factor control, with editing providing a probe of what the generator changes and preserves.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based audio-visual generation methods typically perform joint denoising of audio and video latents throughout the entire sampling trajectory, repeatedly executing modality-specific denoising branches and cross-modal attention at every timestep. However, we observe that such uniform joint computation is not always necessary. The key is a modality-asymmetric recoverability: audio-side drift introduced by mid-stage caching can be substantially reduced by only a few terminal joint denoising steps, whereas video-side degradation caused by caching leads to persistent loss of motion and temporal details. This asymmetry suggests that inference acceleration should selectively cache recoverable audio-side computation while preserving full video refinement. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{Convergence-Adaptive Audio-Visual Cache (CAVC)}, a training-free modality-asymmetric caching framework. CAVC adopts a sandwich-structured computation allocation: after detecting that audio denoiser outputs enter a cache-tolerant regime, it caches and reuses the audio denoiser output to bypass audio denoising and cross-modal attention in the middle stage, while the video branch continues independent spatio-temporal refinement; a few joint steps are then restored at the end to reduce accumulated cross-modal drift and improve synchronization. Experiments across multiple public benchmarks demonstrate that CAVC achieves 1.10--1.35x wall-clock acceleration, improves several visual dynamics and temporal statistics, and maintains competitive audio fidelity and audio-visual alignment.
authors: Lifan Jiang, Yibo Zhao, Senlin cheng, Bolei Xu, Xiaobo Li, Can Ye, Dehai Zhao, Deng Cai, Boxi Wu
bullets: Addresses unnecessary joint audio-video denoising and cross-modal attention at every sampling step.
Uses a training-free, convergence-adaptive cache with sandwich-structured computation allocation.
Caches audio denoiser outputs in a cache-tolerant middle regime while video undergoes full spatio-temporal refinement.
Restores a few terminal joint denoising steps to reduce cross-modal drift and improve synchronization.

Across public benchmarks, achieves 1.10–1.35× wall-clock acceleration while maintaining competitive audio fidelity and audio-visual alignment and improving several visual dynamics and temporal statistics.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the CAVC framework. The denoising trajectory (t = T → 0) is dynamically partitioned based on modality convergence. (1A) Full AV Warm-up: During early high-noise stages, audio/video branches and AV cross-attention fully execute to establish semantic binding. (Trigger τ): An online monitor tracks audio prediction changes; once stabilized, the audio cache activates. (1B) Cached Continuation: Cached audio predictions are reused. Bypassing the expensive audio branch and AV attention frees the video branch for independent spatio-temporal refinement without being over-constrained by static audio. (2) Final Joint Refinement: Full joint computation is terminally restored for a few steps to reduce accumulated cross-modal drift and refine audio-visual synchronization before decoding.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison of audio-visual joint generation. Given the text prompt “a cat playing with a ball in the yard”, the generic Cache-DiT and TeaCache baselines exhibit visible artifacts and weaker prompt following. For this 121-frame 1K example, their cache-state estimation and update operations also introduce net overhead (see Table 1). In contrast, CAVC achieves a 1.15× inference speedup while preserving stronger visual quality, spatio-temporal consistency, and dynamics.

Figure 5. Empirical trigger curves over the forward execution index k for threshold values 0.30, 0.50, and 0.80. Solid lines show the mean instantaneous audio cache residual (top) and video-only residual (bottom), shaded regions show dispersion, and vertical dashed lines mark the corresponding mean trigger indices kτ . The reported CAVC configuration uses θ = 0.30 and W = 3.

Figure 1. A: CAVC generates high-fidelity video frames synchronized with complex audio waveforms. B: On General-80, training-free CAVC achieves a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off across generation quality, cross-modal alignment, and measured wall-clock inference speed. C: CAVC exploits modality-asymmetric recoverability: mid-stage audio-side drift induced by caching can be substantially reduced by a short terminal joint refinement, whereas video-side degradation is difficult to recover. CAVC preserves full video refinement while bypassing recoverable audio-side computation in the middle stage.

Figure 3. Empirical approximation residuals over the forward execution index k. Top: The instantaneous audio cache residual grows after cache triggering (dashed lines) but stays within a stable empirical range; a tighter threshold T (θ in text; e.g., 0.3) delays the trigger and lowers the observed residual ceiling. Bottom: The video-only residual stabilizes and decays, suggesting that the dominant cross-modal dependencies are established during Phase A warm-up.

(d) Hyperparameter analysis on threshold (θ ) and window size (W ). The configuration θ = 0.30,W = 3 is selected as the default setting, balancing acceleration and recoverability. papers.abstract: Recent advances in text-to-video generation have substantially improved visual fidelity, yet existing models still struggle to understand the physical evolution implicit in user prompts, making it difficult to generate videos with continuous physical state evolution. Here, we propose PhyEvolve, a multi-agent framework that enhances natural-language prompts through structured state-evolution planning. PhyEvolve consists of three agents: a Director, a Physical Evolver, and a Composer. Given a user prompt and an optional first frame, the Director grounds the scene and disentangles physical events from observation changes. The Physical Evolver uses scene evidence to identify physical mechanisms then constructs causally linked state transitions that unfold throughout the video, whether visible or not. The Composer utilizes these transitions to enhance the original prompts. Without retraining or model modification, PhyEvolve works directly with existing generators through prompt replacement. Extensive experiments on four major benchmarks show that PhyEvolve achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming the cutting-edge prior agentic baseline by 7.9 percentage points on average. These results demonstrate that explicit causal state-evolution planning improves physical consistency and state continuity in generated videos through natural-language prompt enhancement.
authors: Yang-Hao Zhou, Lixing Tan, Zhiqi Li, Guang Yang, Xiao Yang
bullets: Addresses poor modeling of continuous physical evolution in text-to-video generation.
Uses three agents: Director, Physical Evolver, and Composer.

Evaluated on four benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results and a 7.9-point average gain over a prior agentic baseline.

papers.abstract: Adding control to video generation often requires training, which demands additional computational resources, data, or architectural changes. We propose a training-free approach that utilizes pretrained video diffusion models to control object layout and motion using coarse layouts. Our method operates in two passes: first, it steers spatiotemporal placement through prompt-guided cross-attention to produce a coarse visual guide; second, this guide conditions the same model to generate a high-quality, layoutconsistent video. The approach enables coordinated motion with strong temporal consistency, supporting diverse trajectories and object interactions without additional training. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently outperforms prior work in overlap and trajectory accuracy, as well as visual quality across static, dynamic, and multi-object scene settings.
authors: Asaf Joseph, Moshe Mandel, Ohad Fried
bullets: Addresses the computational and architectural costs of training-based video-generation control.
Uses prompt-guided cross-attention to create a coarse spatiotemporal visual guide.
Conditions the same pretrained model on this guide to generate layout-consistent videos.
Supports diverse trajectories, coordinated motion, and multi-object interactions without additional training.
Experiments report improved overlap, trajectory accuracy, and visual quality across static and dynamic scenes.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our training-free layout-guided video synthesis pipeline. Given a text prompt and spatiotemporal layout constraints, we first perform Layout Generation, where the latents of a frozen text-to-video diffusion model are optimized using a cross-attention-based layout loss. This latent refinement process aligns token-specific attention with the target layout and produces a coarse spatiotemporal guiding video in latent space. Next, after the guide is optionally spatially and/or temporally upsampled, we render the final video: the guiding video is injected at an early timestep into the video diffusion pipeline. This second stage refines appearance and details while preserving the imposed layout and motion, yielding the final high-quality video.

Fig. 4. Outputs of Text-to-Video (T2V) and our method (Ours) across different backbone models (LTX-2, WAN 2.2), together with the corresponding attention maps extracted from an intermediate timestep. Attempting to control layout via textual prompt (underlined) fails, whereas controlling the attention map results in a video that corresponds to the desired layouts (orange/blue bounding boxes).

Trailblazer (TB) and FreeTraj (FT) introduce bicycle artifacts, and Peekaboo (Peek.) shows weaker alignment. Right: multiple-object layout; empty frames indicate unsupported methods. Remaining methods fail to maintain spatial and temporal consistency: the explosion occurs prematurely, and the person does not follow the left-to-right trajectory specified by the blue box.

Fig. 8. Additional applications of our method. Left: video editing, where the input video is transformed according to the text prompt. Right: stylization, where only selected semantic elements retain color while the rest of the scene remains monochrome.

The guide fails to capture the interaction between the boy and the scarf: the hands remain static instead of grasping and moving the scarf, resulting in motion that lacks coordination between the objects.

Fig. 5. Comparison of different learning rates during optimization. In each section, guide (top) and refined (bottom) videos are shown. The left column (low learning rate) produces guide videos with weaker adherence to the intended layout (indicated by orange squares). In contrast, the right column (high learning rate) achieves stronger layout adherence, but at the cost of reduced visual quality.

papers.abstract: This paper addresses the problem of creating immersive volumetric videos from sparse and low-resolution capture resources. Conventional dense multi-view reconstruction methods can produce high-quality volumetric videos, but their reliance on costly capture setups makes them impractical in real-world scenarios. Recent approaches use generative models to relax capture requirements, but still suffer from limited resolution and 4D inconsistency. To overcome these constraints, we propose RealMe, a unified framework built around a high-resolution video diffusion model that enhances limited captures into high-resolution (2K), 4D-consistent videos for volumetric video reconstruction. Specifically, RealMe constructs auxiliary data from capture videos and encodes them into latents along with layout-aware positional embeddings. The video diffusion model adapts factorized spatio-temporal attention to the multi-view capture layout, denoises these latents across viewpoints and time, and decodes them into enhanced videos to refine the 4D representation. This adaptation helps the model capture temporal dynamics and multi-view relationships, leading to more 4D-consistent generation. To reduce the data gap between generated videos and real captures, we apply a latent frequency loss that provides frequency-domain supervision in latent space. Extensive experiments on the public DNA-Rendering benchmark and our self-captured RealVV dataset demonstrate that RealMe is able to create immersive volumetric videos and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity and 4D consistency.
authors: Chenxu Zhou, Zhiyuan Yu, Yudong Jin, Yinji Shentu, Yu Zhang, Jiaming Sun, Xiaowei Zhou
bullets: Targets costly dense multi-view capture requirements and the limited resolution and 4D consistency of prior generative methods.

Uses latent frequency-domain supervision to reduce the gap between generated videos and real captures.
Experiments on DNA-Rendering and the self-captured RealVV dataset show improved visual fidelity and 4D consistency over existing methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our framework. These auxiliary videos are fed into a high-resolution video diffusion model to produce enhanced videos, which are then used together with the input captures to optimize the 4DGS representation for volumetric video reconstruction. The detailed model architecture is illustrated in Fig. 3.

Fig. 3. Model architecture.Weuse a ControlNet [Zhang et al. 2023] branch to inject control signals from condition latents and text features. DiT blocks use these signals with layout-aware positional embeddings to denoise noisy latents via factorized spatio-temporal attention.

The examples cover both short-focus and long-focus views. RealMe better preserves scene backgrounds, human appearance, and view-dependent details.

Fig. 8. Additional qualitative comparisons for novel view synthesis on DNA-Rendering. papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk, yet producing plausible continuations does not guarantee that they capture how scenes evolve. Under teacher forcing, strong temporal redundancy may allow local visual continuity to serve as a shortcut for current-chunk denoising, reducing the pressure to model visual evolution. We introduce Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), an auxiliary objective jointly optimized with teacher-forced denoising that predicts temporally separated chunks without access to the intervening visual context. Drawing supervision directly from training videos, FCP requires no additional pretrained visual encoder and leaves autoregressive inference unchanged. Our method achieves superior physical plausibility over standard teacher-forced autoregressive training with a lower overall training compute budget, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of future-chunk supervision for modeling visual evolution. Intriguingly, our visualizations suggest that FCP fosters a more structured representation space, which may be valuable for building autoregressive world models.
authors: Ruopeng Gao, Yukun Huang, Jiarui Hu, Shuai Wang, Wenbo Hu, Ying Shan, Limin Wang
bullets: Teacher forcing can exploit temporal redundancy, favoring local continuity over genuine modeling of visual evolution.
FCP adds an auxiliary future-chunk prediction objective alongside teacher-forced denoising.
The method uses training videos directly, requires no pretrained visual encoder, and does not alter inference.
It improves physical plausibility while using less overall training compute than standard teacher-forced training.
Visualizations suggest FCP produces a more structured representation space, potentially benefiting autoregressive world models.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based video generation models (VGMs) can produce visually plausible videos, yet their camera ego-motion often drifts over long horizons. Camera ego-motion determines how the viewpoint changes between frames and is essential for maintaining consistent geometry and trajectories. To address this problem, we propose CausalAlign, a causal alignment framework with two components. First, we diagnose how precise ego motion is represented, used, and retained within VGMs using linear probes and causal interventions, revealing a rise-and-fall pattern during denoising. Second, we strengthen ego-motion state in VGM by aligning the representations at the identified layers to a 3D foundation model through delta-token space. This space encodes the changes between consecutive frames, allowing the alignment to focus on ego-motion dynamics rather than static scene content. With Wan2.2 fine-tuned on DL3DV and RealEstate10K, CausalAlign can largely improve motion accuracy, geometric consistency, and temporal smoothness, while preserving visual quality. For example, it improves geometric consistency by more than 20% relative to the base model. Moreover, with the fine-tuned VGM, CausalAlign improves the success rate of world action models (WAMs) by 10 points on mobile manipulation tasks of RoboCasa365 benchmark. Overall, CausalAlign improves ego-motion consistency in diffusion-based VGMs and yields noticeable gains in embodied models.
authors: Kai Zhu, Yintianrun Zhang, Shuwei Jiang, Ruolin Zuo, Yixin Chen, Duomin Wang, Miao Liu, Yin Li, Daquan Zhou, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: Targets ego-motion drift, which harms geometric and trajectory consistency in generated videos.
Uses linear probes and causal interventions to locate where ego-motion is represented, used, and retained during denoising.
Aligns representations at identified layers in delta-token space, emphasizing frame-to-frame motion changes over static scene content.
Fine-tuned on DL3DV and RealEstate10K with Wan2.2, it improves motion accuracy, geometric consistency, and temporal smoothness while preserving visual quality.
The improved video model also raises world action model success rates on RoboCasa365 mobile-manipulation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CausalAlign. Left: Existing approaches rely on external 3D caches that may propagate errors, optimize output-level preferences without directly supervising ego-motion states, or align 3D features at randomly selected layers. Middle: Our CausalAlign first identifies the targeted layers through causal diagnosis and then strengthens ego-motion states through delta-token alignment. Right: CausalAlign consistently improves camera ego-motion consistency in video generation and largely boosts downstream mobile manipulation performance.

Figure 3: Ego-motion diagnosis and retention. We compare base model Wan2.2 and our method CausalAlign through probe decodability and causal intervention effects across layers (sub-figure (a) & (b): results are averaged over timesteps) and across denoising timesteps (sub-figure (c) & (d): results are averaged over layers). Dashed vertical lines represent the selected alignment locations and shading shows the 10th–90th percentiles over the averaged dimension. Our method CausalAlign can raise both signals from rise-and-fall to rise-and-maintain pattern, indicating improved ego-motion retention.

Figure 2: Three stages of CausalAlign training. CausalAlign transfers ego-motion knowledge from a 3D teacher to the VGM through three-stage training. In Stage 1, consecutive features from a streaming 3D foundation model are encoded into a teacher delta-token space that captures inter-frame geometric transitions. In Stage 2, a projector maps VGM DiT features into the same delta-token space and is frozen after training, using a small subset of the training split. In Stage 3, with full training split, LoRA adapters are optimized only at the identified VGM layers using delta tokens, while the projector remains frozen.

Figure 5: Additional evidence for geometric state forgetting. (a) Linear and MLP probes both show a rise-and-fall pattern in ego-motion decodability. (b) Motion-only interventions produce substantially larger causal effects than norm-matched content-only controls. (c) Geometry commitment K(s) rises early and remains high, while the decodability D(s) and motion-specific causal effect C(s) reused from (a) and (b), respectively, decline during late denoising. Both probes and causal effects decline at later stages, while geometry commitment remains high, supporting the existence of geometric state forgetting.

Figure 6: Successful mobile manipulation rollouts. We visualize two policy rollouts on RoboCasa365, showing a robot placing a bowl into a refrigerator and moving a bread basket to a counter. Both examples demonstrate successful execution of mobile manipulation tasks.

Table 1: Camera ego-motion consistency. We evaluate videos generated from the DL3DV and RealEstate10K evaluation splits with the same estimators and generation settings. Methods without camera control receive the first frame and text prompt; methods that require control also receive camera trajectories and 3D caches. Bold indicates the best result for each metric. CausalAlign improves all seven metrics over Wan2.2 and leads on six of seven metrics.

Table 4: Delta-token ablations. We compare (a) semantic regions with matched-width PCA projections of equally supervised unpartitioned encoders and (b) 128D delta tokens with original 8192D/4096D LingBotMap features. Best values within each panel are bold. Delta tokens lead all six metrics in both panels.

Table 11: Effects of adapter updates and weight averaging. We evaluate different update configurations and weight averaging strategies on the 5B backbone, reporting improvements over the original model. Scaling the update at layer 22 to 0.25 achieves the highest mean gain of 0.769% among the compared configurations.

Table 3: Transfer to world action models. We report success rates (%) on the three RoboCasa365 Target100 task groups. Bold marks the best value in each column, including ties. CausalAlign improves Fast-WAM across all three groups, increasing average success from 43.5% to 54.2% and Atomic-Seen success by 19.0 percentage points.

Table 10: Effects of auxiliary motion objectives. We compare supervision using relative poses, motion dynamics, and their combination on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B under identical training settings. Relative pose supervision achieves the largest trajectory gain of 3.525%, while combining both objectives provides better geometric and temporal preservation.

Table 9: Effects of alignment placement and temporal modulation. We compare LoRA updates at different layer groups and strategies for temporal modulation on Wan2.2-14B, reporting composite gains with 95% confidence intervals. The layers selected by causal diagnosis achieve the largest gain of 3.109%, while the temporal modulation comparisons have confidence intervals that include zero.

Table 12: Effects of training objectives and configurations. We compare different objectives for motion, geometry, and appearance under various training configurations on the 5B backbone. Relative pose alignment at step 72 achieves the highest mean gain of 0.982% among the compared configurations.

Table 13: Training and evaluation settings for Fast-WAM. We summarize the training configuration and evaluation protocol for mobile manipulation on RoboCasa365 Target100. The protocol evaluates the policy on 18 Atomic-Seen tasks with 50 rollouts per task, providing the settings used to assess downstream performance.

Table 2: Visual quality preservation. We evaluate Wan2.2 and CausalAlign using VBench-I2V (quality, I2V score, and smoothness) together with FVD, CLIP, SSIM, and LPIPS. Bold indicates the best result for each metric, including ties. CausalAlign preserves visual quality comparable to Wan2.2.

Table 7: Camera trajectory accuracy under explicit conditioning. We compare CausalAlign with the native Wan2.2 camera control model and FantasyWorld using identical camera trajectories, initial frames, and text prompts. CausalAlign achieves the best results on six of seven metrics, while FantasyWorld has the lowest relative translation error.

Table 6: Ego-motion consistency in text-to-video generation. We evaluate Wan2.2-14B-T2V and CausalAlign using the same text prompts and geometric estimators. CausalAlign improves all seven metrics across motion magnitude, geometric consistency, and temporal dynamics.

Table 5: Visual quality in text-to-video generation. We compare Wan2.2-14B-T2V and CausalAlign using VBench and complementary visual metrics. CausalAlign improves quality, semantic score, FVD, and LPIPS while preserving smoothness, with slightly lower CLIP and SSIM scores.

Table 8: Specialization of delta-token regions. We evaluate the ego-motion, geometry, and visual regions using probes with a common dimension of 24 on 256 scenes across three seeds. Each region performs best on its corresponding task, demonstrating the effectiveness of semantic partitioning.

papers.abstract: Understanding and modeling light transport in human-centric scenes is a longstanding challenge. While recent progress in diffusion models has boosted research in relighting, precise illumination control still lags, primarily due to the scarcity of diverse, high-quality, precisely labeled video relighting datasets. Existing end-to-end relighting approaches model light transport implicitly through neural networks, which substantially complicates controllability. In contrast, some works resort to path-traced irradiance cues as an explicit blueprint for light transport. However, such constructed irradiance cues are prone to artifacts and hinder generative quality when directly used as control signals. With the key observation that noise corruption removes high-frequency artifacts and preserves low-frequency light transport, we introduce an asynchronous joint-modeling paradigm that facilitates fine-grained illumination control. During two-stage training, we force the model to jointly denoise RGB and ground-truth irradiance frames with separate timesteps scheduling. A domain matching strategy is applied to the second stage to bridge the domain gap between irradiance cues and ground-truth irradiance maps. At inference time, we introduce an asynchronous hijacked generation pipeline that facilitates flexible illumination control. For training data, we develop a multi-illumination high-quality synthetic video dataset with paired irradiance maps using a powerful game engine. Trained exclusively on this dataset, our model exhibits robust generalization to real- world scenarios and outperforms prior approaches in both lighting fidelity and generative quality. The code and dataset will be publicly released.
authors: Henglei Lv, Bailin Deng, Xiaoqiang Liu, Yichen Wang, Haoxian Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Lin Gao
bullets: Addresses limited high-quality, precisely labeled video-relighting data and poor controllability in implicit light-transport models.
Jointly denoises RGB and ground-truth irradiance frames using separate timestep schedules across two training stages.
Uses domain matching to reduce the gap between constructed irradiance cues and ground-truth irradiance maps.
Introduces an asynchronous inference pipeline for flexible illumination control.
Trains on a synthetic multi-illumination video dataset and reportedly generalizes to real scenes, improving lighting fidelity and generative quality over prior methods.

papers.abstract: Full 3D attention is costly in video Diffusion Transformers. Block-sparse attention reduces this cost by computing only selected attention blocks. However, existing methods either overlook the potential to optimize sparsity allocation or rely on heuristic rules or local metrics to guide it. In this work, we observe that sparsifying attention in different layers and at different denoising steps affects final-video fidelity to substantially different degrees. Yet the identities of the most sensitive layer-step pairs remain nearly unchanged across inputs. Building on these findings, we propose Allocating Layer-step Latency by Output Tests (ALLOT), a training-free sparsity allocation method. Treating each layer-step pair as a cell, ALLOT estimates each cell's contribution to final-video error through (i) cell probing and (ii) trajectory calibration, then jointly optimizes cell densities under a measured-latency budget. It preserves existing selection strategies and kernels, replacing only the allocation component. At equal or shorter wall-clock time, ALLOT outperforms every compared allocation strategy with XAttention, with an 11.8 dB PSNR gain on HunyuanVideo. Extensive experiments across four additional published pipelines on Wan2.1, Wan2.2, and HunyuanVideo show that ALLOT outperforms or ties the default in all nine settings.
authors: Tianze Xia, Xiaoling Zhou, Ruya Lan, Yiqiao Liao, Chengru Song, Shiming Xiang
bullets: Full 3D attention is expensive, and different layer–step pairs have unequal effects on final-video fidelity.
ALLOT estimates each pair’s error contribution using cell probing and trajectory calibration.
It jointly optimizes sparsity densities under a measured-latency budget while retaining existing block-selection strategies and kernels.

Across five video diffusion pipelines and nine settings, ALLOT outperforms or matches the default allocation; with XAttention, it achieves an 11.8 dB PSNR gain on HunyuanVideo at equal or lower runtime.

papers.abstract: The scarcity of high-quality annotated visual data remains a critical bottleneck for autonomous-driving perception. Simulators provide training data at scale, but the limited realism of synthetic videos compromises perception performance in real-world applications. To address this limitation, we propose NeuralSRender, a sim-to-real video translation framework that enhances the photorealism of synthetic videos while maintaining geometric consistency with the source scenes. Built on a pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT), NeuralSRender uses a lightweight projector to inject geometric and material priors from G-buffers, and LoRA enables parameter-efficient adaptation. The model is trained in two stages: it first learns G-buffer conditioning from synthetic videos with accurate G-buffers, then adapts to real-world appearance using real videos with estimated G-buffers. During the second stage, an additional LoRA module is trained while the projector and first-stage LoRA remain frozen to reduce interference from estimation noise. NeuralSRender introduces only 1.45\% parameter overhead and can be trained on consumer-grade GPUs with 24 GB of memory. To support training and evaluation, we introduce GenReal, a large-scale driving video dataset comprising synthetic and real-world videos with corresponding G-buffers. Experiments demonstrate improved photorealism with competitive geometric consistency. Training perception models on our translated videos instead of raw simulator renders improves detection $\mathrm{AP}_{50}$ on nuImages from 35.1 to 40.6 and segmentation mIoU on Cityscapes from 32.4 to 40.8. Our code, data, and model weights are available at: https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/NeuralSRender.
authors: Yipeng Lu, Youqi Liao, Zhenyu Wang, Yuning Peng, Zhen Dong
bullets: Targets the realism gap between simulator-generated videos and real-world autonomous-driving imagery.
Injects geometric and material priors through a lightweight G-buffer projector and adapts a pretrained video DiT with LoRA.
Uses two-stage training: synthetic G-buffer conditioning followed by real-world appearance adaptation with an additional LoRA module.
Introduces GenReal, a driving-video dataset containing synthetic and real videos with corresponding G-buffers.
Translated videos improve nuImages detection AP50 from 35.1 to 40.6 and Cityscapes segmentation mIoU from 32.4 to 40.8; geometric consistency remains competitive.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of NeuralSRender. In Stage I, the G-buffer projector and LoRA modules are trained on synthetic videos with accurate G-buffers. In Stage II, the model is adapted to real-world videos using estimated G-buffers. In Stage II, the projector is frozen to protect the conditioning mechanism learned from synthetic data, while only the LoRA modules are optimized.

Fig. 1. Photorealistic sim-to-real synthesis with the proposed NeuralSRender. Our approach leverages video generation priors to synthesize photorealistic driving videos from G-buffers, reducing reliance on high-fidelity textures and materials while enabling text-guided changes in weather and time of day.

Fig. 4. Qualitative comparison of control signals and training strategies. Depth and edge controls produce overly smooth results with semantic, texture, color, and lighting errors. Basecolor control provides richer appearance cues but may flatten geometric structures. Two-Stage w/o Freeze degrades learned lighting and shadow patterns, while Single-Stage training may distort geometry and road markings. Our full model best preserves geometry, markings, textures, lighting, and shadows.

Fig. 3. Qualitative results on the synthetic test sets (GenReal-City and GenReal-CARLA). Unlike baselines that retain artificial simulator aesthetics, our approach leverages the explicit geometry and physical priors of G-buffers, alongside text prompts, to achieve photorealistic sim-to-real synthesis while maintaining structural integrity.

papers.abstract: Reward guidance methods sample an exponential tilt of a base density using a diffusion model trained with only samples from the base distribution. Existing methods use what we call external guidance: additive terms in the drift or multiplicative terms on the transition probabilities. We propose internal guidance which leaves the output of the base denoiser unmodified and instead changes the point at which it is evaluated. For discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube $\{-1,1\}^{d}$, the denoiser of any linearly tilted density is exactly the base denoiser evaluated at a shifted and rescaled input. In practice the base denoiser is a neural network trained on noised samples of the base distribution. The required evaluation points for sampling the tilted density would be out-of-distribution for basic noising of the base distribution. We modify the training algorithm with random diagonal rescalings of the data, so that the denoiser network learns both in- and out-of-distribution evaluations of the denoiser relative to the base distribution. A single denoiser network samples binary reward tilts, class labels, and infilling with no fine-tuning and no external guidance term.
bullets: Addresses reward-guided sampling from exponential tilts using only a diffusion model trained on base-distribution samples.
Exploits an exact identity: for discrete hypercube data, the denoiser of a linearly tilted density equals the base denoiser at a shifted and rescaled input.
Trains the denoiser with random diagonal data rescalings so it supports the required out-of-distribution evaluation points.
A single network handles binary reward tilts, class-conditional sampling, and infilling without fine-tuning or external guidance terms.

papers.abstract: Game engines and coding agents can specify the layout, motion, and camera of a scene, yet turning such coarse structure into realistic video requires a renderer that follows the structure and completes the appearance it leaves open. Existing renderers are tied to the representation of one engine, need tens of denoising steps or a costly distillation of their own, and learn from conditions that are not aligned with their target videos. We present SolarRenderer, a structure-conditioned video renderer that adapts a frozen MiniMax-H3 33B backbone with two lightweight LoRAs. Structural videos enter the native reference pathway of the backbone at the positions of the frames they describe, without a type identifier and described only in plain text, so that a single control LoRA follows arbitrary structural representations. Starting from a pretrained four-step LoRA, structure-guided distribution matching renders in four steps, 12.3 times faster than 50-step sampling, while preserving the learned control. A block-causal variant extends the same design to streaming and renders 768p video in real time. To train the model, we build a frame-aligned corpus of 136K clips from game engines, simulators, and YouTube videos. Experiments on an in-distribution test set and a generalization benchmark of 16 structural representations show that SolarRenderer achieves state-of-the-art results across both, and generalizes to 11 unseen representations, including pose skeletons, drawings, and point clouds.
authors: Guian Fang, Shengju Qian, Dongyue Lu, Junchao Huang, Lutao Jiang, Xin Wang, Yiren Song, Li Jiang, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Addresses renderers that are engine-specific, slow, and trained with misaligned conditions.
Adapts a frozen MiniMax-H3 33B backbone using two lightweight LoRAs and a shared native reference pathway for arbitrary structural inputs.
Uses structure-guided distribution matching to render in four steps, reported as 12.3× faster than 50-step sampling.
A block-causal variant supports real-time 768p video streaming.
Trained on 136K frame-aligned clips; achieves state-of-the-art results on in-distribution and generalization benchmarks, including 11 unseen representations.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon video generation requires retaining an ever-expanding history, but conditioning on its growing token sequence is costly. Existing methods restrict or compress historical context, potentially losing information needed for future generation. This work proposes ReCam, which groups local spatiotemporal blocks of historical latents into vectors and projects them directly into the high-dimensional hidden space of a Diffusion Transformer. The model learns to use the resulting memory tokens through native self-attention, reducing token count while retaining block-level access to the full history. To mitigate temporal drift during autoregressive rollout, we further introduce dual-pointer denoising with separate noise schedules for recent context and target frames. Among the evaluated methods, ReCam achieves the highest VBench-Long overall score of 80.1 and competitive static-scene revisitation performance on R2M-Bench. It also leads on all four consistency metrics for off-screen subject reappearance, including clothing consistency of 4.09 versus 3.03 for the best baseline.
authors: Yukuo Ma, Cong Liu, Junke Wang, Junqi Liu, Haibin Huang, Zuxuan Wu, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses the cost and information loss of conditioning on growing video histories.
Groups local spatiotemporal latent blocks into vectors and projects them into a Diffusion Transformer’s hidden space.
Uses native self-attention for block-level access to the full history with fewer tokens.
Introduces separate noise schedules for recent context and target frames to improve autoregressive stability.
Achieves the top reported VBench-Long score (80.1) and leads all four off-screen subject reappearance consistency metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of ReCam. Historical latents are grouped into local spatiotemporal blocks and projected into memory tokens by a lightweight MLP. The first frame remains a clean visual anchor. Native self-attention connects the historical memory and current chunk, while text cross-attention is applied only to the current chunk.

Figure 1 A coarse read on fine-grained history. We compare our method with other representative methods. Keyframe-based approaches, such as CaM [Yu et al., 2025], typically employ an external rule-based selector to retrieve a subset of frames as memory. In contrast, compression-based methods [Zhang et al., 2025] encode history into a compact representation through a separate reconstruction stage. Different from these approaches, ReCam allows the video model itself to learn how to represent history and how to retrieve it via its native attention mechanism.

papers.abstract: Egocentric action transfer aims to decouple the semantic action from egocentric observations and reproduce them in new visual contexts, enabling scalable world simulation, embodied policy learning, and robotic data generation. Existing approaches to transferring actions rely on condition-guided video generation, which converts the observation video into explicit geometric controls (e.g., hand poses or meshes) to drive synthesis. However, these methods introduce geometric estimation errors, making it difficult to preserve physically plausible interactions when transferred to new scenes. Alternatively, motion transfer methods directly extract motion patterns from the observation video, yet motion-level features alone cannot encode rich contact dynamics, frequently leading to severe hand structural collapse and implausible contact layout. To address both limitations, we present EgoACT, a test-time framework for egocentric action transfer that operates directly on the denoising process of video diffusion models without requiring additional geometric estimators. EgoACT uses Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring to stabilize reference-consistent hand-object structure in the early denoising stage, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration to refine reliable local correspondences in the mid-to-late denoising stages. Together, these two components preserve transferable action semantics while improving temporal coherence and interaction realism. We further establish EgoActionBench, a benchmark for evaluating action preservation, visual quality, and hand-object plausibility across diverse egocentric manipulation scenarios. Experiments show that EgoACT generates more coherent and physically plausible interaction videos than strong baselines.
authors: Yue Ma, Pengjie Song, Xinyu Wang, Yi He, Zeqian Long, Fangneng Zhan, Kaichen Zhou, Hongyu Liu, Hongfa Wang, Peihao Li, Haoyang Huang, Nan Duan, Qifeng Chen
bullets: Existing condition-guided methods suffer from geometric estimation errors, while motion-only transfer often loses contact dynamics and causes hand collapse.
EgoACT is a test-time framework that operates directly during video-diffusion denoising.
Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring stabilizes hand–object structure early in denoising.
Sparse Correspondence Calibration refines reliable local correspondences in later denoising stages.
EgoActionBench evaluates action preservation, visual quality, and hand–object plausibility; experiments report more coherent and physically plausible videos than strong baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the proposed framework. Given an egocentric manipulation video, our framework uses a reference branch and an optimized generation branch for test-time action transfer. We apply Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring (VSA) in the early denoising steps to preserve hand-object structure, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration (SCC) in the mid-to-late steps to refine local correspondences and improve interaction realism.

Figure 6. The overview of EgoActionBench. EgoActionBench contains 350 reference manipulation videos and 1,400 target prompts, covering indoor/outdoor scenes, single-/two-hand interactions, and diverse manipulation categories. The benchmark evaluates whether generated videos preserve the reference action semantics while adapting to new visual contexts.

Figure 5. Gallery of proposed method. EgoACT can transfer a wide range of egocentric manipulation videos, covering diverse interaction categories, object types, and motion patterns. The generated videos preserve plausible hand-object structure, contact dynamics, and temporal coherence while adapting the reference action to new visual contexts.

Figure 16. More Comparison with Baseline. Our method consistently produces more coherent action transfer and more plausible handobject interactions than baselines, which often suffer from structural collapse, temporal inconsistency, or physically unrealistic interactions.

Figure 14. Failure case. Our method may struggle with actions involving very fast hand or object motion, which can lead to motion blur, temporal aliasing, or loss of hand-object correspondence. This limitation is primarily due to the base video diffusion model, which was not specifically trained to handle rapid egocentric dynamics and tends to produce temporally smoothed outputs when the inter-frame displacement is large.
Figure 8. Qualitative comparison. Compare with previous methods, our method preserves stable hand-object layout and object response.
Figure 10. More visual results.

Figure 4. Illustration of the proposed SCC. (a) Direct transfer injects the reference action without correction, which may lead to errors in weak hand-object interactions. (b) Applying correction throughout the whole denoising process over-constrains early generation, making it difficult to decouple transferable action from source observation. (c) Our SCC performs sparse correspondence calibration only in the mid-to-late denoising stages, where the action layout has been established and local interaction details can be refined, improving temporal consistency and hand-object realism.
Figure 11. More visual results.
Figure 12. More visual results.
Figure 13. More details about EgoActionBench. EgoActionBench covers diverse egocentric manipulation scenarios and is annotated by scene type, and object category.

Figure 7. User Study. B1–B5 denote VACE, Mask2IV, CosHand, InterDyn, and DiTFlow, respectively. Our method is consistently preferred by human evaluators, achieving the highest excellent/good ratio across all evaluated aspects.

Figure 2. Motivation. Motion transfer suffers from hand structural collapse and lacks physical interaction. Condition-guided generation preserves hand shape but produces physically implausible contact. Our method maintains both hand structure and realistic interaction.
Figure 9. Visual ablation. VSA suppresses structural collapse, while SCC improves local correspondence.

Figure 15. Attention Visualization. We visualize the crossframe attention maps before and after enabling VSA during the early denoising stage. Without VSA, attention is dispersed across irrelevant regions, failing to capture coherent hand-object structure. With VSA enabled, the attention concentrates on interactionrelevant areas such as hand, object, and contact regions, indicating that the generation trajectory is better aligned with the reference structural layout. This confirms that VSA effectively anchors the hand-object skeleton through velocity-guided alignment, resulting in more structurally consistent attention patterns.

papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models have recently achieved remarkable progress in Real-world Image Super-Resolution (Real-SR). However, existing methods consistently exhibit a persistent seesaw effect: enhancing perceptual realism compromises structural fidelity. This effect, we argue, is not intrinsic to diffusion models, but largely stems from the architectural constraints of prevailing two-stage frameworks. To address this challenge, we propose PixelSR, a novel single-stage Pixel Diffusion Transformer for Real-SR that operates directly in pixel space. Specifically, PixelSR consists of two core designs: Pixel-space Conditional Diffusion and Orthogonal Flow Decoupling. The former establishes an effective pixel-space restoration framework by integrating spatially aligned LR conditioning, visual semantic guidance, and lightweight texture refinement, thereby bypassing VAE compression and enabling end-to-end optimization directly in RGB space. Complementarily, the latter decomposes the asymmetric flow target into a low-rank semantic component and a noise-free orthogonal texture component. By routing these components to specialized branches, it achieves decoupled optimization with reduced mutual interference. Benefiting from these designs, our PixelSR restores perceptually realistic details while faithfully preserving structural content. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that PixelSR not only achieves competitive performance, but also effectively mitigates the fidelity--realism seesaw effect.
authors: Xiang Lv, Kai Zhao, Qiang Wang, Qiao Mo, Chao Zhou, Mingwen Shao
bullets: Targets the realism–fidelity trade-off attributed to architectural limitations in two-stage diffusion frameworks.
Uses pixel-space conditional diffusion with aligned low-resolution conditioning, semantic guidance, and lightweight texture refinement.
Introduces Orthogonal Flow Decoupling to separate low-rank semantic and orthogonal texture components into specialized branches.
Avoids VAE compression and enables end-to-end optimization directly in RGB space.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks show competitive performance and mitigation of the fidelity–realism seesaw effect.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed PixelSR framework. PixelSR comprises Pixel-space Conditional Diffusion (PCD) and Orthogonal Flow Decoupling (OFD). Left: PCD performs end-toend RGB-space restoration using spatially aligned LR conditioning, visual semantic guidance, and lightweight pixel-level texture refinement. Right: OFD factorizes the asymmetric velocity target into a projected low-rank component and a deterministic orthogonal residual, which empirically exhibit semantic- and texture-dominant characteristics, respectively. Their predictions are assigned to specialized DiT and PiT branches and recombined into the full velocity for flow matching, enabling task-aligned optimization with reduced interference.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on challenging real-world examples. PixelSR better preserves the text layout and feather structure while recovering fine-grained details consistent with the HR references, whereas several competing methods exhibit distorted characters, irregular textures, or over-smoothed results. Best viewed zoomed in.

Figure 5: Ablation of PixelSR components on RealSR. The bars and green curve report PSNR and MANIQA, respectively. Pixel-space x0-prediction provides a substantially stronger baseline than pixel-space v-prediction, while the successive PCD and OFD designs further improve fidelity and perceptual quality.

Figure 6: Frequency analysis of OFD branch specialization. Restoration results (top) and corresponding power spectra (bottom) under increasing orthogonal scale α. Larger α progressively strengthens fine textures and mid-to-high-frequency responses, while α = 1 denotes the default OFD output. All spectra share the same color scale.

Figure 10: Qualitative comparison on challenging real-world examples. PixelSR better preserves the original text layout and character structures while recovering fine-grained image details, whereas several competing methods exhibit distorted characters, irregular textures, or over-smoothed results. Best viewed zoomed in.

Figure 11: Qualitative comparison on challenging real-world examples. PixelSR better preserves high-frequency textures and fine structural details, whereas competing methods often produce oversmoothed surfaces, irregular patterns, or artificial artifacts. Best viewed zoomed in.

Figure 3: Visualization of orthogonal target factorization. With the Procrustes-aligned projector, the projected component mainly retains global content and coarse structures, while its orthogonal complement emphasizes edges, text patterns, and high-frequency textures.

Figure 9: t-SNE visualization of semantic and texture features. We sample 300 images from each of five ImageNet categories and visualize features from the two PixelSR branches. Semantic features form compact category-aware clusters, while texture features are more dispersed due to diverse local details, supporting the effectiveness of our OFD.

Figure 7: Representative image matrix of UGCSR benchmark. The benchmark covers ten semantic categories: humans, animals, text-rich images, natural scenes, urban scenes, indoor scenes, plants, food, tools, and everyday objects. Two representative degraded images are shown for each category.

Table 2: Ablation of pixel-space flow formulations on LSDIR. All variants use the same PCD network and parameter count. OFD improves over monolithic uA-prediction through explicit factorization and branch assignment.
Table 3: Implementation details of PixelSR.

Table 4: No-reference quality comparison of LR and HR images across real-world paired SR benchmarks. Results are reported as mean ± standard deviation. The best results among LR and HR images are highlighted in bold and underlined, respectively.
