papers.abstract: Rapid advances in diffusion models have raised concerns about privacy, harmful content, and copyright violations. Concept erasure methods aim to address these risks by removing undesirable concepts from pretrained models without full retraining. However, existing approaches often degrade non-target generation quality through heuristic strength scaling (e.g., classifier-free guidance or negative prompt scaling), leading to uncontrolled and excessive semantic drift. To address this, we propose Push-Pull Attentional Anchoring (PPAA), a mechanism in the cross-attention space that displaces target representations while anchoring the scale of erasure via bounded cosine-similarity constraints. By using a relative similarity ratio instead of an absolute difference, our adaptive threshold represents a meaningful percentage of semantic retention, facilitating a single value to be applied uniformly across layers. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple concept categories, including celebrities, artistic styles, nudity, and intellectual property. Our method achieves favorable trade-offs against prior approaches on Stable Diffusion v1.4 and demonstrates its applicability to modern architectures such as FLUX.
authors: Nattanat Chatthee, Tagon Sompong, Ekapol Chuangsuwanich, Supasorn Suwajanakorn
bullets: Addresses semantic drift caused by heuristic erasure-strength scaling in existing concept-erasure methods.
Operates in cross-attention space, displacing target representations while constraining their cosine similarity.
Uses a bounded relative similarity ratio to express semantic retention and apply one adaptive threshold across layers.
Evaluated on celebrities, artistic styles, nudity, and intellectual property concepts.
Reports favorable trade-offs on Stable Diffusion v1.4 and applicability to FLUX.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: Concept erasure and preservation results on FLUX. (a) Qualitative comparison on representative identity, style, and character concepts. Our method erases target concepts, such as Barack Obama, Van Gogh, and Mickey Mouse, while preserving non-target concepts, such as Will Smith, Picasso, and Donald Duck. ESD causes substantial semantic shifts in non-target concepts, whereas UCE fails to semantically erase Mickey Mouse. (b) Quantitative results. Accuracy measures target-concept detection after erasure, and CMMD measures preservation relative to the original FLUX model; lower is better for both metrics. These results demonstrate the applicability of our objective to FLUX while maintaining a favorable erasure–preservation trade-off.

Fig. 2: Erasure–Preservation score across concept categories. We compare our method with existing concept erasure approaches across four categories: Celebrity, IP Entity, Artistic Style, and Nudity. The vertical axis measures erasure effectiveness using the Unlearning Score or classifier accuracy for detecting the target concept, where lower values indicate stronger erasure. The horizontal axis measures preservation effectiveness using CMMD (×1000), where lower values indicate better preservation of non-target concepts. Each point denotes a hyperparameter setting; baselines vary their erasure-strength parameter when available, whereas our method varies only mpush. In particular, it achieves the Pareto frontier in the erasure–preservation trade-off for Celebrity, Artistic Style, and IP Entity erasure. For Nudity, our method achieves results comparable to DUO, while maintaining stronger erasure–preservation trade-offs across the other categories.

Fig. 8: Training-Free Trajectory Probing Results. We evaluate robustness to trajectory-based attacks using the prompt “a photo of a naked person” on nudityerased models. Base shows images generated without applying the attack procedure. Attacked (Best) denotes the image most aligned with the attack concept according to the CLIP score among all generated samples during the probing trajectory. The remaining rows show randomly sampled images obtained from the attack method. Although our method is not explicitly trained with robustness-oriented objectives (e.g., DUO and STEREO), its behavior under this attack appears competitive to that of existing methods such as MACE, UCE, SUMA, and ESD.

Fig. 10: Concept erasure and preservation results on the Z-Image model. We show that our method can be applied to Z-Image, a recent text-to-image model based on a Scalable Single-Stream Multimodal Diffusion Transformer, achieving effective concept erasure while preserving the quality of non-target generations.

Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison of erasure methods. Our method erases the target concepts (e.g., Rihanna identity and Picasso style) while preserving the non-target concepts (e.g., Margot Robbie identity and Claude Monet style). Compared with existing approaches, our method achieves a favorable erasure–preservation trade-off.

Fig. 6: Ablation Study on Design Choices. Ours denotes the full method, which uses cosine distance in Lpush, Lpull, and Lpreserve, together with the relative-margin formulation and preservation losses (Lpreserve, Ldenoise). Each variant removes one component: the relative-margin formulation, the cosine-distance formulation (replaced with L2 distance), or the preservation losses. Each point corresponds to a different push margin. The x-axis measures same-domain preservation (CMMD ×1000, lower is better) and the y-axis measures unlearning score (detection accuracy, lower is better). The full method consistently achieves the best erasure–preservation trade-off, while removing any component degrades performance, indicating that each component contributes to the overall improvement.

Fig. 15: Additional Qualitative Comparison on Intellectual Property Entity Erasure. Prompts corresponding to the target concepts are shown in red, while prompts corresponding to the non-target concepts are shown in blue. Images in the same row are generated using the same random seed across all methods for fair visual comparison.

Fig. 16: Additional Qualitative Comparison on Intellectual Property Entity Erasure. Prompts corresponding to the target concepts are shown in red, while prompts corresponding to the non-target concepts are shown in blue. Images in the same row are generated using the same random seed across all methods for fair visual comparison.

Fig. 7: Erasure–Preservation Trade-off Across Concept Categories. We compare our method with existing concept erasure approaches across four categories: Celebrity, IP Entity, Artistic Style, and Nudity. For Celebrity and Artistic, we provide both same-domain and generic-domain preservation scores. Our method consistently performs well across categories. In particular, it achieves the Pareto frontier in the erasure–preservation trade-off for Celebrity, Artistic Style, and IP Entity erasure. For Nudity, our method performs comparably to DUO. However, DUO performs poorly in the other categories.

Fig. 12: Additional Qualitative Comparison on Celebrity Erasure. Prompts corresponding to the target concepts are shown in red, while prompts corresponding to the non-target concepts are shown in blue. Images in the same row are generated using the same random seed across all methods for fair visual comparison.

Fig. 11: Additional Qualitative Comparison on Celebrity Erasure. Prompts corresponding to the target concepts are shown in red, while prompts corresponding to the non-target concepts are shown in blue and are randomly sampled. Images in the same row are generated using the same random seed across all methods for fair visual comparison.

Fig. 5: Controllable semantic deviation induced by semantic push. As mpush decreases from 0.80 to 0.20, the generated images progressively move away from the erased target concepts while retaining coherent visual content. Examples include artistic style, celebrity identity, and IP entity erasure, illustrating the controllable semantic separation induced by Lpush.
Fig. 13: Additional Qualitative Comparison on Artistic Style Erasure.
Fig. 14: Additional Qualitative Comparison on Artistic Style Erasure.

Fig. 9: Exploratory token selection for semantic push. We compare three tokenselection variants for Lpush: applying it to both the concept-relevant token(s) and the EOS token, only to the EOS token, and only to the concept-relevant token(s). The concept-token-only variant localizes the semantic change more strongly to conceptspecific information, indicating a promising refinement for reducing unintended changes to non-target attributes such as pose and background.

Table 1: Success rate of recovering the erased nudity concept via UnlearnDiff [40]. Comparison of Pre-Attack Success Rate (Pre-ASR), Attack Success Rate (ASR), and average attack time. Lower Pre-ASR and ASR indicate stronger erasure robustness, while higher Avg Time (mins) indicates greater resistance to the attack. Although our method is not explicitly optimized for robustness, it remains competitive among methods without robustness-focused objectives (MACE, UCE, AC, and ESD).

Table 2: Robustness against CCE attacks [27] and preservation under nudity erasure. Lower ASR indicates stronger robustness against CCE attacks, and lower CMMD indicates better preservation. Our method achieves a favorable robustness– preservation trade-off. In contrast, DUO and STEREO suppress CCE recovery more strongly but significantly compromise preservation, whereas UCE and ESD provide weaker trade-offs under this protocol.

Table 4: Same-domain preservation concepts used in evaluation. For Celebrity and Artistic Style Erasure, we randomly sample 50 celebrities and 50 artistic styles from the list provided by [24]. These concepts measure preservation performance within the same semantic domain as the erased concept.

Table 3: Statistics of the pull-loss denominator sim(W0pe,W0pg) on SD1.4 across evaluated concepts. papers.abstract: Diffusion-based video matting has recently emerged as a leading approach, leveraging video diffusion priors from internet-scale pretraining to achieve strong zero-shot generalization from limited synthetic data. However, the heavy compute of these diffusion backbones limits inference to a short chunk of just 6 to 24 frames, so even ordinary videos span multiple chunks. Because each chunk is matted independently from coarse mask guidance, existing methods fail to maintain consistency across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency. We address this with a mask-guided diffusion-matting framework built on two ideas. The RGB and mask conditioning are represented as separate token streams that interact through full spatio-temporal self-attention, letting the model adaptively combine fine RGB texture with coarse mask layout rather than committing to a fixed channel-wise fusion. On top of this, we propose a novel pair of learnable embeddings, the preserve token and the refine token, that act as a per-frame conditioning interface and enable a sliding-window inference scheme in which already-generated mattes are propagated across chunk boundaries for local temporal consistency, complemented by a globally shared reference anchor at every chunk to prevent error accumulation in long sequences without any additional training. Across standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild long footage, our framework outperforms prior diffusion-based methods in both fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, and uniquely maintains consistency across chunk boundaries on long videos.
authors: Sangbeom Lim, Seoung Wug Oh, Heeji Yoon, Seungryong Kim, Joon-Young Lee
bullets: Addresses flickering edges and discontinuous transparency caused by independently processing short video chunks.
Uses separate RGB and mask token streams with full spatio-temporal attention for adaptive conditioning.
Introduces learnable preserve and refine tokens to propagate previous mattes during sliding-window inference.
Adds a shared reference anchor to maintain global consistency and limit error accumulation without extra training.
Outperforms prior diffusion-based methods in fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, including on long in-the-wild videos.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the VideoMaMa++ training and inference. (Top) During training, RGB frames are paired with either a binary mask or the ground-truth alpha matte as guide input, encoded into separate token streams by a frozen VAE encoder E , and tagged with a refine token (R) or preserve token (P). The DiT processes both modes jointly within a single clip, supervised against the ground-truth matte. (Bottom) At inference, long videos are processed in a sliding-window manner. Each chunk receives the refine token on its non-overlapping frames and the preserve token on its overlap frames, which carry the previous chunk’s predicted matte. A globally selected reference anchor frame is additionally supplied as preserve input to every chunk, providing a stable anchor that prevents error accumulation across the sequence.

Figure 3: Long-video temporal consistency. Qualitative comparison between VideoMaMa++ and other methods. The comparison methods exhibits visible flickering at chunk boundaries or struggles to capture fine-grained details, while VideoMaMa++ produces smooth transitions across chunks while still capturing fine-grained details that emerge in later chunks.

Figure 6: Annotation noise in AM-2K [25]. The ground-truth alpha mattes in AM-2K often miss fine-grained internal details, that VideoMaMa++ correctly recovers. Because MAD averages pixelwise error over the entire image, these missing details penalize accurate predictions and inflate the reported error. MAD-T, computed only within the transition region, isolates the matting quality that actually matters and avoids the bias introduced by such annotation gaps.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can produce unsafe content, while output filtering intervenes only after synthesis. We investigate whether native generation signals enable early detection of unsafe and adversarial inputs. We find that classifier-free guidance exposes strong safety signals in conditional responses, accessible through compact statistics and linear readouts. Based on this finding, we propose Conditional Semantic Trajectory Interception (CSTI), which aggregates activation contrasts between conditional and unconditional responses at early checkpoints for calibrated risk detection. CSTI fits concept-specific detectors using canonical concept and safe examples, without attack samples, intermediate image decoding, or generator modification. Across five generators, four adversarial attack collections, and two general NSFW datasets, CSTI achieves the strongest overall performance among six baselines at a matched 5% FPR. Early interception reduces generation latency by over 60% on intercepted paths. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of native conditional responses for early safety interception.
authors: Yanchun Li, Yujin Wu, Gangkai Shen, Ming Yang, Li Zeng, Xianlong Wang, Hangtao Zhang, Shujuan Tian
bullets: Addresses the limitation of output filtering, which acts only after unsafe content is synthesized.
Uses contrasts between conditional and unconditional responses at early diffusion checkpoints with compact statistics and linear readouts.
Trains concept-specific detectors from canonical concept and safe examples, without attack samples.
Across five generators, four attack collections, and two NSFW datasets, it had the strongest overall performance among six baselines at 5% FPR.
Intercepting unsafe generations early reduced latency by over 60% on intercepted paths.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of CSTI. (a) Native CFG provides paired conditional and unconditional activations at the same generation state. Their difference forms a conditional contrast. (b) Compact channel statistics at early checkpoints form a multi-checkpoint representation, illustrated here using updates 5, 10, and 15. (c) A lightweight concept head is fitted from canonical risk and safe examples, while an independent safe set calibrates the interception threshold. In this example, CSTI decides once at update 15.

Figure 3. Early safety readability across layers, sampling stages, and classifiers. (a) Layer-wise TPR at a matched 5% FPR across five generators and two risk concepts. (b) TPR of individual checkpoints and their joint representation at a matched 5% FPR. (c) Mean empirical FPR under the standard safe calibration protocol, with each variant fitted and calibrated independently rather than matched to 5% FPR. (d) TPR comparison of classifier families using the same early representation at a matched 5% FPR. Results are aggregated across generators and prompt collections as appropriate.

Figure 1. From late checking to early interception. (a) Crafted prompts can induce unsafe generations. (b) Post-generation safety checks incur the full generation cost. (c) In this example, CSTI reads early CFG activations at steps 5, 10, and 15, intercepting risky inputs while allowing accepted requests to continue unchanged. Intermediate images are shown only for illustration.

Table 2. Main comparison of unsafe-input detection at a matched 5% FPR. We report TPR (%, ↑) on unsafe inputs across five text-toimage generators, six nudity collections, and two violence collections. Macro averages collections within each concept and then weights the two concepts equally. Bold and underlined values indicate the best and second-best results, respectively.

Table 4. False-positive comparison on OVERT. We report FPR (%, ↓) on 1,600 near-concept samples. papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos but remain computationally expensive. Sparse attention and temporal caching reduce computation within and across denoising steps, respectively, offering a natural composition. However, predictions produced with sparse attention become sources for temporal reuse, coupling their errors along the sampling trajectory. We observe that improving the accuracy of these sources recovers fidelity without changing the reuse schedule, and that sparsification errors remain directionally aligned across nearby steps, suggesting that correction information can be shared rather than recomputed. These observations motivate RECAP, a training-free method that couples sparse attention with hierarchical caching through reciprocal correction, adaptively coordinated by online error feedback. Cached dense refinement corrects omitted interactions in current sparse estimates, while fresh sparse statistics track input changes and regulate the aging correction. The resulting predictions then renew the sources for whole-step prediction reuse, allowing prediction history to advance between dense refreshes. We evaluate RECAP on multiple video diffusion models against sparse-attention methods, caching methods, and their direct compositions. On HunyuanVideo at 720p 5-second generation, RECAP achieves a 3.05x speedup and outperforms all tested direct compositions in both fidelity and inference speed.
authors: Tiange Xu, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of diffusion transformers for high-quality video generation.
Uses training-free reciprocal correction: cached dense refinement fixes sparse-attention omissions, while fresh sparse statistics monitor input changes.
Employs online error feedback to coordinate sparse attention, hierarchical caching, and correction aging without changing the reuse schedule.
Evaluated across multiple video diffusion models against sparse-attention, caching, and direct-composition baselines.
On HunyuanVideo at 720p for 5-second videos, reports a 3.05× speedup and better fidelity and speed than tested direct compositions.

papers.abstract: RGBA video generation is essential for creating compositable visual assets in filmmaking, game development, and digital content production. However, generating high-quality RGB appearance alongside temporally coherent transparency remains a significant challenge. Existing text-to-RGBA video methods often entangle RGB and alpha distributions and offer limited control over the precise appearance of a target asset. In addition, incorporating image conditioning typically suffers from the emergence-disappearance effects, which fail existing first-frame or first-and-last-frame conditions due to their fully transparent boundary frames. To address these issues, we present Wan-Alpha++, a unified framework that brings controllable RGBA video generation to both text- and image-to-video diffusion backbones through a shared RGBA latent space, extending our conference version Wan-Alpha from the text-conditioned setting to image-conditioned generation with an interior reference frame. Our method first learns shiftable RGB-alpha distributions while preserving the pretrained RGB prior. Specifically, we introduce a transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion objective to produce distinguishable RGBA latent representations, and a transparency-guided mean sampler that shifts the noise distribution to improve transparency generation and enable spatial controllability. Building upon this RGBA generation prior, we introduce temporal phase reparameterization for image-conditioned effect generation. By cyclically transforming a zero-positive-zero alpha pattern into a positive-zero-positive pattern, it relocates visible content to both temporal boundaries, facilitating effective appearance conditioning with limited RGBA data.
authors: Haotian Dong, Xin Wang, Wenjing Wang, Chen Li, Jing Lyu, Yan Tina Luximon, Ping Li, Wanchao Su, Ke Xu, Di Lin
bullets: Targets entangled RGB–alpha generation and weak image-conditioning behavior at transparent video boundaries.
Uses a shared RGBA latent space across text-to-video and image-to-video diffusion backbones.
Introduces transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion and a transparency-guided mean sampler for improved and spatially controllable transparency.
Applies temporal phase reparameterization to convert zero-positive-zero alpha patterns into boundary-visible positive-zero-positive patterns for image conditioning.
Extends Wan-Alpha from text-conditioned generation to image-conditioned transparent effects using an interior reference frame.

papers.abstract: Despite achieving high visual fidelity, video models still suffer from physical hallucinations, limiting their reliability as world simulators. Existing methods leverage model-internal or external signals to improve physical plausibility, but their roles and limitations require a unified explanation. We propose a two-dimensional physical-hallucination risk framework that defines low-density sampling risk and high-density drifting risk. The first risk captures generations assigned low likelihood by the video model, for example, a ball suddenly teleporting despite the model favoring continuous motion, while the second risk captures physical inconsistencies in high-likelihood generations, for example, a ball bouncing progressively higher without additional energy. Our analysis explains how model-internal signals steer sampling toward higher-density regions of the learned distribution to address low-density sampling risk. However, higher model likelihood does not guarantee physical plausibility, motivating external guidance to address high-density drifting risk. Based on this framework, we develop Hallucination-Aware Sampler (HA-Sampler), which applies external physical guidance within latent refinement to generate physically plausible videos, and HA-Scorer, which derives a likelihood-based signal from the generator itself for evaluating generated videos using continuous normalizing flow (CNF), with coarse ODE integration and finite-difference divergence estimates. Experiments on Physics-IQ and VideoPhy benchmarks support our theoretical analysis and demonstrate that our methods outperform the compared sampling and scoring SOTA baselines.
authors: Chenyan Zheng, Fan Wu, Ruibo Li, Jiaxing Li, Minghao Yang, Bang Zhang, Guosheng Lin
bullets: Defines low-density sampling risk as unlikely events and high-density drifting risk as physically inconsistent but likely generations.
Explains that model-internal likelihood signals can reduce low-density errors but cannot ensure physical plausibility.
Introduces HA-Sampler, which applies external physical guidance during latent refinement.
Introduces HA-Scorer, a generator-based likelihood signal using continuous normalizing flows for video evaluation.
Experiments on Physics-IQ and VideoPhy support the analysis and report better performance than compared SOTA baselines.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models primarily rely on general-purpose ODE-based numerical methods for training-free accelerated sampling, but performance degrades with coarse time discretization. In this paper, we propose optimal linear leaps (LEAP), a specialized method grounded in theoretical and empirical investigations of sampling trajectory geometry. Built upon low-dimensionality and cross-trajectory consistency, LEAP formulates a supervised least-squares optimization problem within the local trajectory subspace, achieving a precise approximation of future states without model evaluations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LEAP outperforms previous methods across diverse modalities, including text-to-image (Stable Diffusion 3.5, FLUX.1-dev) and image-to-3D (TRELLIS.2) generation. Furthermore, LEAP can be seamlessly integrated into existing solver-based methods, offering a plug-and-play enhancement for modern diffusion models. Code is available at https://github.com/zju-pi/LEAP.
authors: Haowei Zheng, Zhenyu Zhou, Jiawei Chen, Can Wang, Defang Chen
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by coarse time discretization in accelerated diffusion sampling.

Approximates future sampling states without additional model evaluations.
Works across text-to-image and image-to-3D generation, including Stable Diffusion 3.5, FLUX.1-dev, and TRELLIS.2.
Can be integrated as a plug-and-play enhancement with existing solver-based methods.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot diffusion image compression based on reverse channel coding achieves high perceptual quality at low bitrates without retraining, yet its bitstream remains vulnerable to bit flips. Prior work has shown that a joint combinatorial representation can amplify a single bit flip into substitutions of multiple atoms and that indexing each atom independently confines this error propagation. However, independent indexing reduces the number of atoms that fit within the bit budget and gives the decoder no indication of which atoms are corrupted. To address these issues, we propose BitFlat, a training-free error-localizing bitstream framework with two components. Blockwise Locality Alignment (BLA) decomposes the globally coupled atom selection at each diffusion step into independent selection units, each describing one signed atom from a dedicated codebook with a fixed-width field, so that any bit error affects only the unit in which it occurs. Reliability-Aware Diffusion Control (RADC) uses the bits saved by BLA to impose structured valid-codeword constraints within each field and converts the decoding state of each field into a binary reliability gate, which turns detected corrupted atoms into erasures at known positions and excludes them from noise synthesis. BitFlat requires neither target residuals nor additional network forward passes and leaves the diffusion model unchanged. Experiments on Kodak, DIV2K, and CLIC2020 show that BitFlat outperforms conventional, learned, and diffusion-based codecs at bit error rates from $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-2}$ and, even with $26.7\%$ fewer bits, surpasses Robust Turbo-DDCM.
authors: Xinfeng Deng, Li Zhou, Haitao Chen, Shengjie Wu, Lingjin Kong, Nan Li, Haitao Zhao, Dongtang Ma

Reliability-Aware Diffusion Control detects invalid fields, gates corrupted atoms, and excludes them from noise synthesis.
Training-free: requires no target residuals, extra network forward passes, or diffusion-model changes.
Outperforms conventional, learned, and diffusion codecs across tested bit-error rates, and surpasses Robust Turbo-DDCM with 26.7% fewer bits.

papers.abstract: Video generation models produce visually compelling motion but systematically fail on fluid phenomena, including smoke, fire, and explosion debris, where outputs lack coherent vortical structure and collapse to bland dynamics that violate the physics of real fluids. Classical solvers achieve high physical fidelity but require detailed 3D scenes and carefully tuned parameters, making them impractical for in-the-wild imagery and video generation. We address this gap by injecting a data-driven fluid prior into a pre-trained video model, trained on a mixture of high-fidelity Houdini simulation data with paired velocity-field ground truth and curated in-the-wild fluid video data for appearance diversity. The core of our approach is a dual stream architecture that predicts per-frame velocity fields alongside RGB, supervised by simulation ground truth. This auxiliary signal regularizes generation toward physically consistent motion and exposes an interpretable physical quantity that we further leverage as a reward for velocity-aware direct preference optimization. Our model produces substantially more realistic fluid dynamics sequences than strong video baselines and optimization-based methods. Project page: https://y-zheng18.github.io/FluidGen/

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate streaming video of arbitrary length by conditioning each new chunk of frames on those already generated. However, they suffer from exposure bias, where a model trained on clean context must continue from its own imperfect outputs, and errors compound until quality collapses within seconds (drift). Existing methods either require cluster-scale base retraining, apply training-free inference corrections with inconsistent results, or train frozen-base correctors for sampling and cache errors. We instead find that drift is largely deterministic and therefore learnable, as holding the noisy state fixed while varying only the history reveals a counterfactual velocity gap that is ~95% systematic across noise seeds. Based on this observation, we introduce Clean Forcing, which trains a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector on the frozen base model to regress this gap, with a closed-loop stage that adds DAgger-style aggregation and a drift-contraction objective to expose the corrector to its own rollouts. Because the clean histories can be the base model's own single-shot generations, training needs no real videos, and the merged corrector adds no inference cost. In 50 s text-to-video generation, Clean Forcing reduces {\Delta}-drift from +11.3 to +1.65 without real video and to -0.16 with 40 real clips, improving on the best published result of +3.57 with over 150x less data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Clean Forcing outperforms prior methods in aesthetic quality and data efficiency with reduced drift for long-horizon video generation.
authors: Wenqing Wang, Joonghyuk Shin, Jonathan Tremblay, Chan Hee Song, Yun Fu
bullets: Addresses exposure bias and compounding errors that cause streaming video quality to collapse over time.
Learns a counterfactual velocity gap shown to be largely deterministic across noise seeds.
Trains a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector using closed-loop, DAgger-style rollout aggregation and drift-contraction training.
Requires no real videos when using the frozen base model’s own single-shot generations, and adds no inference cost after merging.
In 50-second generation, reduces Δ-drift from +11.3 to +1.65 without real video and to −0.16 with 40 real clips, outperforming prior reported results with far less data.

papers.title: Clean Forcing: Drift-Resistant Autoregressive Video Diffusion with a Frozen Base

papers.abstract: Language-guided video generation often captures scene content while missing the requested motion. We present ViMoLa (Video Motion Language), which predicts a motion prior from language and injects it into a frozen image-to-video backbone. A spatial vector-quantized autoencoder compresses dense trajectories into 64 tokens from a 512-entry codebook; a 28M-parameter transformer predicts the tokens from text; and zero-gated cross-attention adapters condition every frozen Wan~2.2 DiT block through forward hooks. Trained on 462K videos from Something-Something~v2 and Kinetics-400, ViMoLa raises directional accuracy from 0.287 to 0.442 (chance 0.250), with similar measured generative quality. Across-prompt shuffled codes achieve 0.283, supporting the importance of prompt-matched token content. A low-rank adapter reaches 0.428 at 1.45% additional forward-pass FLOPs, and reusing the tokenizer and language model with newly trained CogVideoX adapters raises accuracy from 0.301 to 0.398. Control remains imperfect: oracle codes reach 0.531, compound-motion gains are smaller, and the adapter does not explicitly preserve token-to-patch assignments.
bullets: Targets the common failure of videos to follow requested motion despite matching scene content.
Compresses dense trajectories into 64 discrete tokens and predicts them from language with a 28M-parameter transformer.
Uses zero-gated cross-attention adapters to condition frozen Wan 2.2 DiT blocks; a low-rank variant adds 1.45% forward-pass FLOPs.
Raises directional accuracy from 0.287 to 0.442, with similar measured generative quality; shuffled motion codes provide little benefit.
Control remains imperfect: oracle codes reach 0.531, compound motions improve less, and token-to-patch assignments are not explicitly preserved.

papers.abstract: Existing motion transfer methods excel at exact, rigid motion replication from reference videos to target scenes, whereas they often fail to account for the compatibility between the transferred motion and the target scene environment in accordance with physical laws. In this work, we propose MotionShift, a novel motion transfer framework that achieves high-fidelity motion transfer while ensuring physical compatibility with the target scene. In particular, we design a planner--evaluator iterative motion adaptation mechanism, in which a Large Language Model (LLM) acts as the planner to generate motion trajectories by leveraging its strong semantic reasoning capabilities, while a Vision-Language Model (VLM) serves as the evaluator to rectify the motion based on its superior visual perception and scene understanding. Through this planner--evaluator synergistic reasoning process, the motion is adapted to the target scene in a training-free manner. The adapted motion is then used as a generative condition for an image-to-video (I2V) model to render videos in the target scene. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MotionShift achieves high-fidelity and physically compatible motion transfer across diverse and complex scenes. Moreover, we show that MotionShift can be readily integrated into existing trajectory-conditioned I2V models, endowing them with realistic motion transfer capabilities.
authors: Yanchen Liu, Junyao Gao, Yanan Sun, Wensheng Chen, Guangming Lu, Wenjie Pei
bullets: Addresses the lack of physical and environmental compatibility in existing reference-video motion transfer methods.
Uses an LLM planner to generate motion trajectories and a VLM evaluator to visually assess and rectify them.
Iteratively adapts motion to the target scene without additional training.
Feeds the adapted motion as conditioning to an image-to-video model for target-scene rendering.
Experiments report realistic, physically compatible transfer across diverse complex scenes and integration with existing trajectory-conditioned I2V models.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of MotionShift. Given a reference video and a target image, we first initialize a motion trajectory for the target scene. Then, through planner–evaluator iterative adaptation, we refine the trajectory to produce an environment-compatible trajectory and a corresponding motion prompt. Finally, these are progressively rendered into the output video: a motion generation model converts the trajectory into a semantic mask sequence, and an appearance rendering model synthesizes the final video from the masks and target image.

Fig. 5. Visual comparison with baseline methods. MotionShift exhibits superior motion consistency and environmental adaptability, accurately capturing perspective variations, realistic reflections, and synchronized hand movements compared to baseline approaches.

Fig. 4. Illustration of Planner–Evaluator Iterative Adaptation. At the beginning of each iteration, we leverage the semantic reasoning capability of the planner (LLM) to infer object–environment interactions and perform detailed motion planning along the given trajectory, producing a corrected motion trajectory. We then construct a pseudo video based on the target image and the corrected trajectory, and feed it to the evaluator (VLM) to assess visual consistency and physical plausibility, which then outputs revision suggestions. These suggestions are then appended to the planner’s instruction prompt, and we iteratively refine the motion trajectory until the evaluator detects no major issues.
Fig. 9. Visual results of Go-with-the-Flow using the initial trajectory vs. the environment-compatible trajectory produced by MotionShift as a plugin.
Fig. 3. Illustration of environment-compatible motion transfer, where identical reference motions adapt naturally to different scenes, yielding contextually consistent behaviors.
Fig. 7. Ablation on planner–evaluator adaptation. We compare variants by disabling adaptation, removing the evaluator, or replacing the planner.

papers.title: MotionShift: Environment-Compatible Motion Transfer via Planner-Evaluator Synergistic Adaptation
papers.tldr: MotionShift enables high-fidelity motion transfer that adapts to target-scene constraints through training-free planner–evaluator reasoning.

papers.abstract: Synthesizing a monocular video from a new camera trajectory requires preserving the observed scene geometry and motion while completing regions that become newly visible. Feed-forward 4D reconstructors recover the structure of the observed scene, whereas video diffusion models provide a generative prior for completing unseen content. We introduce Holo4D, a video reshooting framework that uses reconstructed 3D trajectories as a holistic source-view 4D scaffold. We project these trajectories into the requested views and encode their geometry and source appearance to guide a pretrained video diffusion model. Together with the source video and target cameras, the scaffold grounds generation in reconstructed observations while leaving unsupported regions to the generative prior. Experiments demonstrate the value of trajectory-based conditioning for camera control and novel-view synthesis. The framework accommodates different 4D reconstructors without retraining the video generator, allowing it to benefit from future advances in source reconstruction. More details can be found in our project page.
authors: Yushi Lan, Zeren Jiang, Koichi Namekata, Xingang Pan, Chuanxia Zheng, Andrea Vedaldi
bullets: Addresses monocular video synthesis along new camera trajectories with newly visible content.
Builds a holistic 4D scaffold from reconstructed 3D scene trajectories and motion.
Projects scaffold geometry and source appearance into target views to condition a pretrained video diffusion model.
Uses source video and target cameras to ground generation in observations while delegating unsupported regions to the generative prior.
Experiments show trajectory-based conditioning improves camera control and novel-view synthesis; the generator requires no retraining for different reconstructors.

figures.caption: Figure 2: HOLO4D overview. Top (4D scaffold): a 4D reconstructor R recovers persistent 3D trajectories, paired with sampled source colors, which are projected into the target cameras and encoded into track features T. Bottom (video diffusion): source and noisy target latents are concatenated along width; each DiT block concatenates T with its hidden features along channels (null on the source half) and adds camera features C encoded from Plücker rays. Flames and snowflakes mark trained and frozen modules (Appendix B). Trajectory panels show a subset of the dense tracks; the top-right overlay is for visualization only. The output is obtained by iterative denoising; Figure 11 details the DiT block.

Static and dynamic source pixels were rendered into a hybrid target-view RGB-D cache (projected RGB, depth, and visibility), which conditioned the video diffusion model together with Plücker rays and projected 3D tracks. This version removes the rendered RGB-D branch and keeps the track branch (Figure 2).

Figure 2: HOLO4D pipeline. An off-the-shelf 4D reconstructor estimates source geometry and 3D tracks from the input video. We split source pixels into static and dynamic regions using track motion. Static regions are fused from camera-coverage keyframes, dynamic regions use time-synchronized per-frame reprojection, and valid masks indicate observed target-view support. The resulting hybrid RGB-D condition is injected together with target-camera Plücker rays and 3D tracking tokens, and the VDM synthesizes the target-view RGB video.

papers.abstract: Camera-conditioned video diffusion models often suffer from inaccurate camera control and geometric inconsisten- cies because camera constraints and estimated geometry are only weakly enforced during denoising. Existing reme- dies often require costly geometry-aware fine-tuning or ad- ditional 3D supervision. We introduce GeoART, a training- free self-refinement framework that improves camera con- trollability through geometry-aware test-time scaling. At selected denoising steps, GeoART generates multiple can- didates within the Predict-and-Perturb cycle and eval- uates them using a geometry prior, without directly modify- ing the denoising trajectory. A confidence gate suppresses unreliable geometric evidence, while rank-calibrated prob- abilistic selection combines score magnitude and relative rank to choose the next refinement state. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in camera controlla- bility, multi-view consistency, and visual quality over exist- ing sampling and self-refinement methods, without training or modifying the pretrained video diffusion model
bullets: Addresses weak enforcement of camera constraints and estimated geometry during denoising.
Generates and evaluates multiple candidates at selected denoising steps within a Predict-and-Perturb cycle.
Uses a confidence gate to suppress unreliable geometry signals.
Applies rank-calibrated probabilistic selection to combine score magnitude and relative rank.
Reported experiments show consistent gains in camera controllability, multi-view consistency, and visual quality without modifying or retraining the pretrained model.

papers.abstract: Novel view synthesis under trajectory changes is essential for autonomous driving simulation, yet existing methods struggle to generate consistent videos when extrapolating to unseen viewpoints such as lane shifts. Reconstruction-based approaches maintain geometric consistency but degrade in visual quality under large viewpoint changes, while reconstruct-then-restore methods often produce visually plausible frames yet suffer from geometric and temporal inconsistencies. We present GeoV2V, a geometry-grounded video-to-video diffusion framework that synthesizes temporally coherent driving videos along novel trajectories by integrating LiDAR and depth-derived geometric priors with full-video conditioning in the Wan 2.1 backbone. A key challenge in learning cross-lane transformations is the lack of synchronized multi-trajectory supervision in real-world datasets. To address this, we also introduce Para4D, a synthetic dataset capturing synchronized multi-lane driving videos within dynamic scenes, which provides explicit supervision for lane-shift generation and serves as a strong training prior for geometry-consistent view synthesis. Experiments on Waymo, nuScenes, and Para4D demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in visual quality, geometric consistency, and robustness to complex lighting dynamics under large trajectory shifts. Project page: https://xiyuche.github.io/GeoV2V/
authors: Yuchen Xi, Yuhan Guo, Chenwei Hou, Zixu Liu, Jin Fang, Jason Liu, Ruigang Yang
bullets: Targets novel-view synthesis for autonomous-driving simulation under large trajectory changes.
Uses LiDAR- and depth-derived geometric priors with full-video conditioning in the Wan 2.1 video diffusion backbone.
Introduces Para4D, a synthetic dataset with synchronized multi-lane driving videos for explicit lane-shift supervision.
Evaluations on Waymo, nuScenes, and Para4D show strong visual quality, geometric consistency, and robustness to complex lighting dynamics.
Scope: the method addresses trajectory extrapolation, especially cross-lane transformations, where real-world synchronized supervision is limited.

papers.abstract: Video generation models synthesize visual sequences from text and image inputs. Extending video generation to long animations requires actions, dialogue, camera coverage, and narrative developments to remain coordinated across scenes. Executable scene programs make these decisions available for inspection. Constructing an entire story before observing its execution can leave later scenes dependent on unrealized events. We present SpriteStage, a progressive scene programming framework that builds animation through iterative enactment and engine reorchestration. Iterative enactment generates each scene from an accepted world checkpoint and narrative snapshot, executes it on a shared spatial stage, and uses runtime and visual feedback to revise the relevant actions or story beats. The accepted outcome becomes the starting state for the next scene. Engine reorchestration maps the resulting draft to production assets and engine capabilities while retaining its events, geometry, and timing. Inspection of the assembled sequence and frozen replay carry the accepted performance into the final video. Three complete animations, ranging from approximately 9.9 to 14.3 minutes, demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in producing extended narratives through scene programming and engine execution.
authors: Zhaoqi Wang, Zijian Zhang, Jiamou Liu
bullets: Targets the coordination of actions, dialogue, camera coverage, and narrative developments across long animations.
Builds each scene from an accepted world checkpoint and narrative snapshot, then uses runtime and visual feedback for revision.
Reorchestrates scene drafts onto production assets and engine capabilities while preserving events, geometry, and timing.
Uses sequence inspection and frozen replay to transfer accepted performances into the final video.
Demonstrated through three complete animations lasting approximately 9.9–14.3 minutes.

papers.tldr: SpriteStage generates long-form animations by progressively scripting, executing, inspecting, and revising scenes while carrying accepted world states forward.

papers.abstract: Unified audio-video creation requires a single model capable of text-conditioned joint synthesis, bidirectional cross-modal generation, and instruction-guided editing across both modalities. Existing methods rely heavily on paired corpora, which are scarce for joint generation and even rarer for editing. Consequently, they are spent learning single-branch generative and editing capabilities that abundant unimodal data could readily teach, rather than on the cross-modal coupling. Furthermore, prevailing systems apply a single shared noise schedule to both modalities, neglecting two critical limitations. First, due to the significant discrepancy in information density, video requires prolonged high noise to organize spatial and motion structure, whereas the sparser audio signal can settle earlier during the synthesis process, the dynamics a uniform schedule might compromise. Second, lockstep denoising leaves asymmetric workflows, such as conditioning on one modality to synthesize or edit another, untrained. We present UniAVC, which addresses both obstacles. It first trains each branch on unimodal dataset to full generative and editing competence, and subsequently dedicates paired data to exploit cross-modal correspondence. Modality-decoupled schedulers meanwhile warp the noise schedule independently from a shared timestep, while subtasks with one clean modality directly supervise asymmetric configurations. These settings respectively enable intent-aware editing, which preserves one modality intact while enlisting it to constrain the other, and post-inference self-refinement, which regenerates only an unsatisfactory branch against an accepted one. UniAVC thus spans multiple creation tasks from a single set of weights without task-specific adapters.
authors: Kien T. Pham, Yuhao Liu, Chong Hou Choi, Zhenqi He, Yanghao Wang, Chenyang Lei, Rui Liu, Qifeng Chen, Long Chen
bullets: Addresses scarce paired audio-video data by first training audio and video branches on abundant unimodal data, then using paired data for cross-modal learning.
Uses independently warped noise schedules so video can denoise longer while audio settles earlier.
Trains asymmetric workflows where one clean modality guides synthesis or editing of the other.
Supports intent-aware editing that preserves one modality while modifying the other.
Enables post-inference self-refinement by regenerating only an unsatisfactory modality, without task-specific adapters.

(b) Each branch first attains full generative and editing competence on unimodal data in parallel; both branches are subsequently frozen, and the paired corpus is used solely to train the cross-modal bridges.

papers.abstract: Simulation-to-real driving video diffusion models can translate photorealistic scenes, but they typically represent pedestrians and cyclists, vulnerable road users (VRUs), as generic object classes. This is insufficient for vulnerable road users whose safety-relevant appearance depends on articulated pose and identity. We present BodyBridge and Grounded Body Layers (GBL), a simulator-derived, pixel-aligned representation that combines scene geometry, canonical per-pixel body correspondence, and exact VRU masks. GBL provides explicit articulation to the video diffusion model, emphasizes VRU regions during control-branch post-training, and supports additive composition with scene-geometry control at inference. It also enables per-joint evaluation of generated VRUs and a failure taxonomy for identity errors. On CARLA-to-real translation, BodyBridge improves near-range PCK@0.5 by 22% over the released depth-conditioned baseline. Replacing normal-map body control with canonical correspondence reduces body flips by 18%, while composition reduces near-range facing flips by 27%. These results show that explicit body grounding complements scene-level control and improves pose-faithful VRU generation. All code, data, and model checkpoints will be made publicly available to support reproducible, pedestrian-aware autonomous driving research.
bullets: Addresses the limits of generic VRU representations, whose articulated pose and identity are safety-relevant.
Introduces Grounded Body Layers (GBL): simulator-derived, pixel-aligned body correspondence, scene geometry, and exact VRU masks.
Uses VRU-focused control-branch post-training and additive composition with scene-geometry control at inference.
On CARLA-to-real translation, improves near-range PCK@0.5 by 22% over a released depth-conditioned baseline.
Canonical correspondence and composition reduce body flips by 18% and near-range facing flips by 27%, respectively.

papers.abstract: Sign language production (SLP) aims to synthesize expressive signing motion from written text. Modeling signing motion presents two key temporal challenges. First, fine-grained hand articulations demand higher temporal resolution than relatively slower body movements. Second, signing events unfold over variable durations, calling for adaptive temporal scheduling during generation. To address these challenges, we first introduce a Multi-Rate Vector Quantizer (MRVQ), an articulation-decoupled motion tokenizer that represents the body and both hands as separate discrete streams at distinct temporal resolutions. Building on this representation, we propose BLANC (BLock-wise Adaptive diffusioN with Articulatory Clock), a gloss-free SLP framework that generates variable-duration motion blocks causally while denoising tokens in parallel within each block. At its core, a Latent Articulatory Clock (LAC) learns temporal structure from multi-scale motion-derived partitions to predict block durations and sequence termination during generation. We further introduce inference-time body-conditioned hand refinement to improve coordination across articulators. Extensive experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily demonstrate that BLANC achieves state-of-the-art performance in sign language production.
authors: Youngmin Kim, Seoyeong Hwang, Sujung Hong, Seong Jae Hwang
bullets: Addresses the need for fine-grained hand timing and variable-duration signing events.
Uses a Multi-Rate Vector Quantizer to encode the body and both hands as separate streams at distinct temporal resolutions.
Generates variable-length motion blocks causally while denoising tokens in parallel within each block.
A Latent Articulatory Clock predicts block durations and when generation should terminate.
Body-conditioned hand refinement improves coordination; experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily report state-of-the-art performance.

papers.abstract: Pixel-space diffusion models have recently re-emerged as a compelling alternative to latent diffusion, avoiding the lossy latent bottleneck and separately trained autoencoder. JiT shows that a vanilla diffusion transformer can generate directly in pixel space by replacing the commonly used velocity prediction ($\boldsymbol{u}$-prediction) with clean image prediction ($\boldsymbol{x_0}$-prediction). In this work, we revisit this choice and introduce MFlow, an adaptive parameterization that learns to interpolate between $\boldsymbol{x_0}$- and $\boldsymbol{u}$-prediction across principal directions of the data, learned end-to-end with diffusion training. We find that the preferred parameterization varies systematically with the data representation and model capacity -- notably, increasing model capacity shifts preference toward velocity prediction. We evaluate MFlow across ImageNet, UCF-101 video, and large-scale text-to-image generation, demonstrating competitive or improved generative performance across diverse settings. In addition, we find that vanilla pixel diffusion transformers, irrespective of parameterization, retain a persistent high-frequency deficit relative to real images. To address this, we introduce ConvRefiner, a lightweight convolutional module trained post-hoc with an adversarial loss while keeping the diffusion backbone frozen. With only a small amount of additional training, ConvRefiner restores the high-frequency statistics of generated images while preserving FID. Project webpage: https://soumik-kanad.github.io/mflow-diffusion/.
authors: Soumik Mukhopadhyay, Long Mai, Abhinav Shrivastava, Aniruddha Mahapatra
bullets: Pixel diffusion avoids the lossy latent bottleneck and separately trained autoencoder, but its prediction parameterization strongly affects performance.
MFlow learns the preferred interpolation between x₀- and u-prediction across data principal directions during diffusion training.
The preferred parameterization depends on data representation and model capacity; larger models favor velocity prediction more strongly.
Experiments on ImageNet, UCF-101 video, and large-scale text-to-image generation show competitive or improved generative performance across settings.
Pixel diffusion transformers exhibit a persistent high-frequency deficit; post-hoc ConvRefiner addresses it with lightweight adversarial training while freezing the backbone and preserving FID.

We reshape the first 64 eigenvectors of the 16 × 16 × 3 patch-PCA basis into RGB patches; the value λ denotes the variance of each direction. The leading ordering interleaves patch-global or very low-frequency modes with spatially varying modes. In particular, PC0 is dominated by low-frequency patch-level tone, PC1 is an approximately uniform chromatic mode, PC2–PC3 encode spatial gradients, and PC4 returns to an approximately uniform chromatic mode. Eigenvector signs are arbitrary, so the interpretation is based on spatial structure rather than the displayed color polarity.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models (VDMs) trained on internet-scale data encode a rich prior on appearance, motion, and physics that is difficult to replicate with explicit 3D rendering and costly 3D data capture. We introduce Video Diffusion Avatars (VDAs), a method that creates photo-realistic, multi-view consistent avatars from a single image by fine-tuning a VDM for precise control over camera viewpoint, facial expression, and upper-body pose. Departing from 3D morphable models (3DMMs), VDAs use a learned expression space that lifts the expressiveness ceiling of 3DMMs, e.g., for the tongue and mouth interior. However, learned expression codes exhibit heavy viewpoint bias, as our DISTRACT benchmark reveals. We show that this bias can be removed through disentanglement, enabling their use as driving signals for multi-view consistent avatars. Camera and upper-body pose are controlled jointly via proxy-mesh renderings, giving independent control over expression, pose, and viewpoint. A camera-triplet training strategy makes the approach efficient: our models train for 34 hours on a single A100 using only public multi-view data. VDAs outperform state-of-the-art single-image 3D avatars on novel-view reenactment, reducing face LPIPS by 29% and improving perceptual quality (JOD) by 66% on BecomingLit. A static 3DGS reconstruction probe further confirms that our generations are the most multi-view consistent. Built on a video prior, VDAs produce effects beyond the reach of explicit renderers, including physically plausible hair dynamics, shadows, reflections, and refractions.
authors: Simon Giebenhain, Tobias Kirschstein, Liam Schoneveld, Davide Davoli, Zhe Chen, Matthias Nie{\ss}ner
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of reproducing video diffusion models’ rich appearance, motion, and physics priors with explicit 3D methods.
Fine-tunes a video diffusion model using disentangled learned expression codes and proxy-mesh renderings for independent control.
Uses a camera-triplet training strategy and public multi-view data to improve efficiency.
Outperforms prior single-image 3D avatars on novel-view reenactment, with lower face LPIPS and higher perceptual quality on BecomingLit.
Produces effects difficult for explicit renderers, including plausible hair dynamics, shadows, reflections, and refractions.

papers.abstract: On AWS Trainium2, every component of a diffusion model runs as a program compiled ahead of time for fixed shapes, while pipelines differ across models, prompt lengths across requests, and caching decisions across denoising steps. We present Difflet, a serving engine in which five model pipelines share one compilation backend, joint attention is split across cores by attention head, and a host controller decides at each denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse its earlier output. A small probe program computes the caching signal on the device and returns one number per step, and a resident model process keeps every program loaded across requests. Across five image and video model families, fused attention accelerates denoiser steps by 1.2-4.3x over the same framework using PyTorch/XLA attention, and at 32.8k visual tokens it is the only attention that compiles. On four of the five models, resident serving is 1.5-3.4x faster than standalone runs that reload weights from a warm file cache for each generation.
authors: Bin Ma, Min Yu, Vijay Kodamalla, Jialin Liu, Dong Li
bullets: Addresses fixed-shape compilation constraints across varying pipelines, prompt lengths, and denoising-time caching decisions.
Uses one compilation backend for five pipelines, splits joint attention across cores by head, and fuses attention computation.
A host controller selectively reuses denoiser outputs, guided by a device-side probe that produces one caching signal per step.
Fused attention is 1.2–4.3× faster than PyTorch/XLA attention and is the only attention variant compiling at 32.8k visual tokens.
Resident serving is 1.5–3.4× faster than reloading weights for each generation on four of five models.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have become a common backbone for high-quality text-to-image and text-to-video generation, but repeated dense self-attention remains a major inference bottleneck as token sequences grow and the same operator is invoked across many denoising steps. Our study suggests that dense attention in pretrained DiTs contains reusable layer/head-specific high-mass structure that can be identified from a small offline calibration set and reused across future generations. This leads to Sink-Sparse Hybrid Attention, a train-free attention replacement that reuses static sink masks and supplements them with a lightweight pooled-KV branch, while leaving model weights and sampling schedules unchanged. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, the method attains 1.54$\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining generation quality. On Z-Image-Turbo, it attains 1.57$\times$ end-to-end speedup with competitive GenEval2 performance. These results indicate that reusable importance-aware sparse support can provide an effective train-free acceleration path for both T2V and T2I DiTs.
authors: Bingxin Xing, Yu Zhang, Jiatong Ding, Lei Lu, Ping Wang
bullets: Targets the inference cost of repeated dense self-attention in DiTs with long token sequences and many denoising steps.
Uses small offline calibration to identify reusable, layer/head-specific high-mass attention structure.
Combines static sink masks with a lightweight pooled-KV branch as a train-free attention replacement.
Achieves 1.54× end-to-end speedup on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B while maintaining generation quality.
Achieves 1.57× end-to-end speedup on Z-Image-Turbo with competitive GenEval2 performance; scope covers T2V and T2I DiTs.

papers.title: Sink-Sparse Hybrid Attention for Efficient Inference in T2I/T2V Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: Sink-Sparse Hybrid Attention accelerates pretrained text-to-image and text-to-video diffusion Transformers by reusing calibrated sparse attention structure without retraining or changing sampling schedules.

papers.abstract: Large-scale diffusion models are commonly trained with a constant learning rate (LR) and exponential moving average (EMA), despite the strong performance of LR decay and Schedule-Free optimization in training large language models. We study whether EMA is uniquely suited to diffusion training, or whether stronger alternatives have been underexplored. Our theory shows that averaging a constant-step trajectory has an inherent optimization limitation, whereas LR decay and Schedule-Free optimization admit vanishing stationarity guarantees under standard nonconvex assumptions. Empirically, LR decay and EMA provide complementary benefits: combining decay with EMA further improves the standard baseline at most tested starting points, although the gain remains sensitive to when decay begins. Schedule-Free avoids this timing requirement and consistently outperforms EMA with a constant LR across training stages, achieving both lower fixed-evaluation objectives and better generation quality. Our analysis further shows that all three strategies substantially reduce parameter variability, yet stronger stabilization is not always better: EMA with a constant LR retains comparatively higher parameter variability, while aggressive decay combined with EMA achieves the lowest checkpoint variability but also weakens continued optimization. Schedule-Free substantially reduces parameter variability while preserving more late-stage progress, providing a better balance between parameter stability and continued optimization. Finally, the benefits of Schedule-Free extend beyond pretraining to ReFL and generator-side DMD, demonstrating its transferability across distinct diffusion optimization settings. Overall, our results suggest that large diffusion models need more than parameter averaging alone: effective optimization requires balancing variance reduction with continued optimization.
authors: Chuyu Hu, Huanran Chen, Shitong Shao, Yinpeng Dong
bullets: Constant-step EMA has theoretical optimization limits, while learning-rate decay and Schedule-Free optimization support vanishing stationarity guarantees under standard nonconvex assumptions.
Learning-rate decay and EMA are complementary, but decay’s benefit depends sensitively on when it begins.
Schedule-Free consistently outperforms constant-LR EMA across training stages in both fixed-evaluation objectives and generation quality, without requiring decay timing.
Aggressive decay with EMA minimizes checkpoint variability but can hinder continued optimization; Schedule-Free reduces variability while preserving late-stage progress.
Schedule-Free also transfers to ReFL and generator-side DMD, suggesting applicability beyond diffusion pretraining.

papers.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a standard component of conditional diffusion models, and guided generation performance has become the \textit{de facto} measure of state-of-the-art models. Recent work on latent diffusion models seeks to learn latent spaces that are easier to model with diffusion. However, under CFG, generation additionally depends on how conditions are arranged in the latent space. We study this arrangement under discrete class conditions, termed \emph{class geometry}, and investigate what class geometry allows a latent space to work well with CFG. Under a Gaussian class model, we show that shifting variance from intra- to inter-class at fixed total variance makes classes more distinguishable under noise, and derive a noisy posterior objective whose per-sample descent direction is proportional to the oracle CFG correction. Based on the analysis, we propose Prototype Regularization (PR), a lightweight surrogate for the intractable noisy posterior objective, which applies a cosine prototype classifier to spatially pooled latents. With a controlled training budget (20 epochs for VAE, 80 epochs for DiT), adding PR to an LDM baseline reduces guided gFID on ImageNet from 3.31 to 2.28, surpassing a DINOv3-aligned VA-VAE (2.44) with negligible overhead. We further demonstrate that PR generalizes to pseudo-labels derived from clustering, continuous text-embedding conditions, and video latents. Together, our findings highlight class geometry as a critical factor in guided generation and take a first step toward CFG-compatible representation learning. Our project page is available at: https://maps-research.github.io/cfg-geometry/.
authors: Haoming Liu, Junhao Zhu, Shaoyi Zheng, Yuanhe Guo, Jinnuo Liu, Shenji Wan, Hongyi Wen
bullets: Motivation: CFG performance depends not only on diffusion modeling but also on how conditions are arranged in latent space.
Analysis: Under a Gaussian class model, increasing inter-class variance relative to intra-class variance improves class distinguishability under noise.
Method: Prototype Regularization (PR) approximates a noisy-posterior objective using a cosine prototype classifier over spatially pooled latents.
Result: Adding PR reduces ImageNet guided gFID from 3.31 to 2.28 with negligible overhead under the stated training budget.
Scope: PR also works with clustering-based pseudo-labels, continuous text embeddings, and video latents.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Noisy marginals of zt at several t ∈ (0, 1) for toy Gaussian mixtures with fixed total variance but different allocations between inter-class and intra-class variance. Background colors mark the Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) decision regions argmaxc qc(zt), with opacity proportional to the confidence maxc qc(zt). With larger inter-class variance, classes become separable at smaller t, i.e., at noisier levels, and the confident MAP regions align more closely with the true class supports.

Figure 5: Oracle velocity fields on toy Gaussian mixtures with fixed total variance. From top to bottom, the fraction of variance allocated to class means increases. For each space, we show the conditional velocity v⋆c (conditioned on the red class), the unconditional velocity v⋆u, and the correction g⋆c = v⋆c − v⋆u at t ∈ {0.2, 0.5, 0.8}. Gray contours mark the 95% density region of zt, and dots mark the class means of zt. With clearer class geometry, the conditional and correction velocities point more consistently toward the target class mean, and the correction vanishes where the posterior concentrates on the target class. Zoom in for the best view. Better view with colors.

Figure 2: (a) Energy decomposition of per-channel normalized latents into global mean ∥µ∥2, interclass variance Ec∥µc−µ∥2, and intra-class variance E∥z−µc∥2. (b) Average target-class posterior E[qc(zt)] on noised validation latents (solid) and CFG sampling trajectories (dotted), where qc(zt) is computed analytically from the empirical distribution of ImageNet training latents under Gaussian forward corruption. (c) gFID (10K samples) versus guidance scale ω; diamonds mark the minima of the displayed curves (ω⋆). PR allocates more energy to inter-class variance, makes the target class identifiable earlier and more confidently, and reaches a lower best gFID at a larger ω⋆.

Figure 1: Simulations under the Gaussian class model with K = 1000 classes and latent dimensions d = 8192 (Eq. 4). (a) Oracle CFG correction strength along time t (t = 1 is clean), for varying inter-class variance fraction α. The correction vanishes once the target-class posterior concentrates. (b) Monte Carlo average of the analytic target-class posterior under forward corruption. Larger α yields earlier posterior concentration. (c) Posterior losses (normalized by logK) versus α, on cleanonly and uniform-time corrupted latents. Both posterior losses are non-increasing in α.

Figure 3: UMAP visualization of full and spatially pooled latents from LDM, VA-VAE, and PR (ours). We encode 50K validation images and plot latents from 50 selected classes, colored by class label. Latents are normalized per dimension before UMAP. PR produces noticeably tighter and better separated class clusters. Zoom in for the best view. Better view with colors.

Table 6: Training and evaluation configurations for ImageNet experiments. Full-budget experiments use 8 GPUs; reduced-budget ablations use 2 GPUs. Both budgets use the same architectures and evaluation protocol, with experiment-specific CFG search ranges listed below.

All alignment to CLIP-L adopts its text embeddings. CLIP denotes mean cosine similarity of CLIP embeddings calculated from text captions and generated images. All cluster labels use K = 1000. The best results are in bold.

Table 2: Center transplantation on LDM latents (z′ = z − µLDM c + µRef c ). Rescaled LDM centers match the inter-class energy of full PR centers. Random centers match the pooled PR energy. Spatially constant centers are broadcast over the spatial grid. ω⋆ denotes the best CFG scale.
Table 3: PR with different label set pairings for stage-1 regularization and stage-2 conditioning. We report guided gFID / unguided gFID below. The best result per-column is in bold.

Table 8: Ablation on prototype shape (reduced compute budget). All variants use the default PR setting (cosine prototype classifier on clean-only latents) and differ only in the output shape of spatial average pooling applied before the classifier, where 16×16 corresponds to no pooling. Overall, prototypes with lower resolutions perform best: 1×1 prototypes (i.e., global average pooling) achieve the best rFID and gFID without CFG, and 2×2 prototypes achieve the best gFID with CFG, while further increasing prototype resolution consistently degrades generation quality. This suggests that reducing the spatial resolution of prototypes benefits generation, likely because it avoids imposing class-level layout constraints on the latent space.

Table 10: Ablation on DINO pseudo-label granularity (reduced compute budget). This group of experiments uses a separate hyper-parameter setup, so the results are comparable within this table but not with other tables. Reconstruction is largely insensitive to the choice of targets. Unguided gFID degrades as K increases, while guided gFID remains comparable across K except for overly fine clusters. The nested variant (i.e., partitioning each of the 64 clusters into 16 sub-clusters) achieves the best generation among unsupervised targets (best unguided gFID and guided gFID close to GT labels), showing the feasibility of hierarchical PR.

Table 9: Ablation on the temperature of PR (reduced compute budget). τ scales the cosinesimilarity logits of the prototype classifier, where a smaller τ yields a sharper softmax. The default τ = 0.1 was fixed prior to this ablation and is used throughout the main text. All PR variants improve over LDM both with and without CFG, and the differences among τ values are small compared with the gain from adding PR, indicating that τ = 0.1 is a reasonable default. Adjusting τ (e.g., τ = 0.3 here) may bring further improvements, though the best value is likely setting-dependent.

Table 11: Composability of PR and VA-VAE. This group of experiments uses the same separate hyper-parameter setup as Tab. 10, so the results are comparable with that table but not with the others. We apply PR on top of VA-VAE, which aligns to DINOv3-L features. Combining the two yields better generation both with and without CFG, at the cost of mildly degraded reconstruction, indicating that PR is complementary to external feature alignment for generation.

Table 4: Generalization to video latents on UCF-101 (Soomro et al., 2012) using LeanVAE16 (Cheng & Yuan, 2025) and Latte-XL/2 (Ma et al., 2025). Official denotes the VAE and LatteXL/2 checkpoints provided by LeanVAE, used without further training. We report FVD and action classification accuracy with and without CFG. The best results are in bold.

Table 1: Results of class-conditional generation on ImageNet. All quality metrics are evaluated with 50K samples. Purity measures the fraction of each latent’s k = 10 nearest neighbors that share its class, averaged over 50K normalized validation latents. Best results are highlighted in bold.

Table 7: Ablation on the classifier type in PR (reduced compute budget). We vary the classifier head (cosine vs. linear) and the latent on which PR is applied (clean latents only vs. noisy latents at uniformly sampled timesteps). The cosine head on clean-only latents achieves the best rFID and gFID, both with and without CFG. Applying PR on uniform-time noisy latents over-regularizes the latent space: the top PCA component degenerates into a near-constant channel that fails to capture spatial variations (i.e., over-smoothed latents). The linear head, optimized with additional weight decay, collapses to a trivial solution that arbitrarily inflates the latent norm to enlarge the logits.

papers.tldr: The paper shows that shaping latent class geometry improves classifier-free guidance (CFG) and proposes a lightweight prototype regularizer to make representations more CFG-compatible.

papers.abstract: Creative intent in video editing can be expressed through text instructions (e.g., "remove the people"), image references (e.g., subject appearance), video references (e.g., camera movement), or a combination of the above. We introduce OmniXRef, a unified framework for multimodal multi-reference video editing that allows users to combine variable numbers of text, image, and video references to control diverse attributes of a source video. We first devise a unified input design with a reference-bank interface and introduce $R^2$-RoPE to support generalization to more references. Then our model, OmniXRef-Model, uses a single-stream diffusion transformer to jointly process the source video and multimodal context from an MLLM in an interleaved sequence. To address the scarcity of training data for video-reference editing, we construct OmniXRef-Data using synthesis pipelines for different editing tasks and combinations of references. We use curriculum learning to progressively increase task complexity and resolution. To support systematic evaluation of video as a control modality, we introduce OmniXRef-Bench, a benchmark for video-reference attribute transfer across Camera, Motion, Content, Style, and Visual Effects (VFX). Comprehensive evaluations show that our OmniXRef-Model outperforms task-specific baselines and commercial models.
authors: Xiaoyan Cong, Tianyu Wang, Hyeonho Jeong, Zhifei Zhang, Yuqian Zhou, Yijun Li, Shaoteng Liu, Zhe Lin, Srinath Sridhar, Soo Ye Kim
bullets: Addresses the challenge of controlling video edits with variable combinations and numbers of multimodal references.
Uses a reference-bank interface, R²-RoPE for reference scalability, and a single-stream diffusion transformer with MLLM-derived context.
Builds synthetic OmniXRef-Data and applies curriculum learning to handle limited video-reference editing data and increasing task complexity.
Introduces OmniXRef-Bench for evaluating video-reference attribute transfer across camera, motion, content, style, and VFX.
Reports better performance than task-specific baselines and commercial models in comprehensive evaluations.
