papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation let users create high-quality videos from natural language descriptions, yet obtaining results that match user intent remains time-consuming: individual generations are computationally expensive, and underspecified prompts force repeated cycles of generation, inspection, and revision. Existing video prompt optimization methods improve generation through automatic rewriting, but cannot supply the ideas and preferences that were not in the initial description. We propose ProactGen, a video generation framework that learns proactive clarification, eliciting user intent through questions grounded in generated video drafts. Specifically, we train a vision-language model as a questioning policy with reinforcement learning: observing the initial prompt and a video draft, it learns to ask the questions most valuable to downstream generation, rewarded by the alignment between the final generated video and a target reference. We further find that effective questioning does not require drafts of final-output quality, and exploit this property by generating drafts with fewer denoising steps, keeping the added cost of clarification low. Experiments show that ProactGen improves target alignment over direct generation by at least 1.8x the gain of the strongest baselines. Moreover, a single round of ProactGen already exceeds the alignment that the strongest baseline reaches after four refinement rounds, in 29% of its time.
authors: Zhixiao Wang, Yang Chen, Yifan Xu, Chenbin Li, Yue Chang, Kai Long, Fengming Dong, Limin Wang
bullets: Addresses underspecified prompts that otherwise require costly generate–inspect–revise cycles.
Uses a vision-language model trained with reinforcement learning to ask questions based on the initial prompt and a video draft.
Questions are optimized for their value to downstream generation, using final-video alignment to a target reference as the reward.
Low-cost drafts with fewer denoising steps keep clarification overhead small.
A single round outperforms the strongest baseline’s four-round refinement alignment in 29% of the time, and achieves at least 1.8× its alignment gain over direct generation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ProactGen. The questioning policy asks scoped questions conditioned on the initial prompt and a low-cost video draft; a simulated user answers from the reference video; the answers are merged into a refined prompt from which the final video is generated at full budget. During training, the alignment between the final video and the reference is the reward for updating the questioning policy; all other components are frozen.
Figure 3: Per-sample time versus target alignment (InstanceCap, DS-DTW). The horizontal axis is linear up to 50 s and logarithmic beyond.

Figure 1: A user’s initial prompt often omits preferences the user already has in mind (here, the hand gesture, the boy’s posture, the table’s material, and the framing). (a) Automatic prompt optimization rewrites the prompt from the prompt alone, so missing preferences can only be guessed. (b) Uncertainty-based clarification asks the user, but derives its questions from the prompt text without knowing what the generator will actually produce. (c) ProactGen first observes what the generator produces for the prompt through a low-cost draft, asks the user targeted questions grounded in it, and learns what to ask from the alignment of the final video.

Figure 4: Qualitative examples. Each row shows the reference video, the initial prompt, the draft, three question–answer pairs, and the final video, with the refined prompt below and answers highlighted. papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have increased the demand for reliable watermarking for copyright protection, yet the robustness of video watermarks against removal attacks remains underexplored. Most watermark-removal methods originate from the image domain: signal optimization injects imperceptible pixel-domain perturbations, whereas generative resynthesis produces a visually similar instance through diffusion synthesis. When extended to videos, the former introduces temporally varying noise that causes visible flickering, while the latter regenerates fine-grained structures inconsistently across frames, leading to structural motion inconsistency. To evaluate video watermark robustness, we propose PoseRegen, a pose-consistent reconstruction framework that removes watermarks while preserving the original content and motion. PoseRegen first applies a temporally shared viewpoint transformation to disrupt watermark-bearing spatial patterns and then jointly reconstructs the transformed sequence with a pose-conditioned video model. A frozen video DiT processes the complete sequence with its reference-video latent, and full-sequence Flow Matching supervision keeps identity and background consistent across frames. To further preserve motion structure, we introduce a lightweight Pose-Conditioned Motion Consistency Adapter that adapts the frozen backbone to temporally ordered pose guidance and constrains body-part trajectories throughout reconstruction. Experiments on eleven video watermarking schemes show that PoseRegen reduces the average bit accuracy to 0.505, near random guessing, while outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.34% on motion-related VBench metrics. These results reveal a practical vulnerability of current video watermarks and highlight the need to evaluate robustness jointly with temporal and motion quality.
authors: Yifan Liao, Zhen Sun, Zhicong Huang, Jiaming He, Zongmin Zhang, Xi Ai, Cheng Hong, Xinhu Zheng, Xinlei He
bullets: Existing image-based removal methods cause video flicker or inconsistent structure when applied frame by frame or through resynthesis.
PoseRegen uses a temporally shared viewpoint transformation followed by pose-conditioned, full-sequence reconstruction.
A frozen video DiT with Flow Matching preserves reference content, while a motion adapter constrains pose and body-part trajectories.
Across 11 watermarking schemes, watermark bit accuracy falls to 0.505—near random guessing—and motion-related VBench scores improve by 9.34% over the strongest baseline.
The work emphasizes evaluating watermark robustness together with temporal and motion quality.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have steadily demonstrated outstanding performance in high-fidelity, controllable generation across diverse scenarios, following the "pretraining-finetuning" paradigm established in LLMs. Despite these advances, conventional DMs still face critical limitations in sophisticated reasoning, autonomous exploration of generation pathways, and adaptability to complex, human-aligned objectives. Inspired by RLHF's success in LLMs, RL has recently emerged as a pivotal post-training mechanism to iteratively refine DMs through reward-driven trajectory optimization. This paper presents the first comprehensive review of RL-driven DMs and an empirical analysis of how RL reshapes the diffusion process towards experience-centric, goal-directed generation. We propose a novel technical panorama elucidating RL's multifaceted roles in diffusion-based language, multimodal, robotic, and scientific models, with a granular focus on diffusion trajectory optimization and reward engineering. Through extensive experiments on multiple task-specific benchmarks, we systematically evaluate representative methods to intuitively highlight the advantages of different RL post-training strategies. Furthermore, we reveal and dissect three crucial bottlenecks that currently hinder the real-world deployment of RL-driven DMs: reward design fragility, exploration-exploitation trade-off in high-dimensional generation spaces, and training instability under sparse rewards. Based on these perspectives, we provide a principled roadmap for the integration of RL into DMs and outline promising future research directions for robust, interpretable RL-diffusion systems. We also construct a public repository to continuously track the latest developments in this rapidly evolving field: https://github.com/MAIR-Lab-HUST/Awesome-RL-for-Diffusion-Models.
authors: Zhiyuan Ma, Jiabao Wei, Tianyu Wang, Hanqing Wang, Jiadong Pan, Haowen Xu, Liangliang Zhao, Ruixun Liu, Yuhan Wang, Yuwei Zhang, Liang Feng, Junhao Xiao, Kaiyan Zhang, Xuekai Zhu, Daizong Liu, Biqing Qi, Yihao Liu, Ganqu Cui, Ning Ding, Linfeng Zhang, Jianjun Li, Kun He, Xiang Bai, Bowen Zhou
bullets: Identifies limitations of conventional diffusion models in reasoning, autonomous exploration, and complex human-aligned objectives.
Presents a technical panorama of RL’s roles in diffusion models, emphasizing trajectory optimization and reward engineering.
Evaluates representative RL post-training strategies across multiple task-specific benchmarks.
Highlights three deployment bottlenecks: fragile reward design, exploration–exploitation challenges, and instability under sparse rewards.
Proposes a roadmap for robust, interpretable RL-driven diffusion systems and provides a public resource repository.

papers.selection_reason: Reviews RL-driven post-training for diffusion models, including multimodal and generation settings directly relevant to diffusion-based video generation.
papers.title: Reinforcement Learning-driven Diffusion Models: Language, Vision, and Beyond
papers.tldr: This paper reviews and empirically analyzes how reinforcement learning post-training makes diffusion models more goal-directed, adaptable, and aligned across language, vision, robotics, and scientific applications.

papers.abstract: Training-free object removal commonly redirects self-attention away from the target region, but on few-step distilled diffusion models this often leaves object-shaped residuals. We identify a temporal mismatch: a structured prediction forms inside the mask at the first forward, and the short trajectory offers few later chances to revise it, while attention rerouting acts mainly in later steps. Across four distilled backbones, magnitude-matched single-forward interventions show that background-directed state correction affects the final result more than attention rerouting. We therefore propose ReState, which corrects the masked clean prediction toward background evidence retrieved from the input using a noise-level-aware weight that vanishes at the final forward. ReState retains object-excluding attention as a complementary constraint and adds no denoiser evaluations. Across two paired benchmarks and two few-step backbones, ReState achieves the best masked PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among training-free methods, improving PSNR by 3.17 dB on average over the strongest baseline. On OBER-Test, it also outperforms the 50-step attention-forcing reference on all three metrics at 6.7x lower latency. The same configuration transfers to two additional distilled backbones without retuning. Project page: https://tdrlee.github.io/ReState
authors: Donghwan Lee, Sanghyun Jo, Sihyun Kim, Ziseok Lee, Kyungsu Kim
bullets: Few-step diffusion models can preserve object-shaped artifacts because structured errors arise early, while attention rerouting acts mostly later.
ReState applies noise-level-aware state correction using background evidence from the input, with the correction fading at the final forward.
It retains object-excluding attention as a complementary constraint and requires no additional denoiser evaluations.
Across two paired benchmarks and two few-step backbones, it reports the best masked PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among training-free methods, with a 3.17 dB average PSNR gain over the strongest baseline.
On OBER-Test, it surpasses a 50-step attention-forcing reference at 6.7× lower latency and transfers to two additional distilled backbones without retuning.

papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation enables rectified-flow models with diffusion-transformer architectures to combine task-specific capabilities within a single student. However, matching model outputs does not guarantee that their internal representations are aligned, and it remains unclear where and when additional feature supervision is most useful. We analyze the teacher-student feature mismatch across Transformer blocks and denoising timesteps, and find that the mismatch is concentrated in deeper Transformer blocks during early denoising and persists after OPD distillation, indicating ineffective distillation. Motivated by this observation, we introduce FocusOPD, which augments the base OPD objective with token-wise directional feature alignment restricted to deep layers and early denoising steps. Across two rectified-flow backbones and multiple OPD objectives, FocusOPD improves capability transfer in compositional generation, text rendering, and preference-based evaluation. On the primary benchmark, it improves over DiffusionOPD from 0.953 to 0.967 on GenEval, from 23.797 to 23.944 on PickScore, and from 6.052 to 6.199 on LAION-Aesthetic. Ablations show that selective deep and early supervision is more effective and efficient than alignment over the full network and trajectory.
authors: Xinrui Lin, Shumin Wang, Suqi Song, Fan Li, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: Feature mismatches concentrate in deep Transformer blocks during early denoising and remain after conventional OPD.
The method adds token-wise directional feature alignment only in these deep layers and early timesteps.
Evaluated across two rectified-flow backbones and multiple OPD objectives for compositional generation, text rendering, and preference evaluation.
On the primary benchmark, GenEval rises from 0.953 to 0.967, PickScore from 23.797 to 23.944, and LAION-Aesthetic from 6.052 to 6.199.
Ablations indicate selective supervision is more effective and efficient than aligning the full network and denoising trajectory.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses distillation for diffusion models, a core technique in video generation. The focus on feature alignment in deep layers and early denoising steps offers insights into improving the efficiency and quality of diffusion-based video generation.
papers.title: FocusOPD: Structure-Guided On-Policy Distillation for Diffusion Models

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) dominate video generation but suffer from high inference cost due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Sparse attention mitigates this by skipping unnecessary computation in the attention matrix, but existing methods apply a fixed sparsity ratio throughout denoising and struggle to accurately determine which computations to skip. To address these limitations, we analyze attention dynamics through attention entropy and mean attention distance, and find that attention becomes increasingly concentrated across denoising steps. We further observe that blocks selected early continue to capture a large fraction of the total attention weight at later steps. These findings suggest two acceleration opportunities: the sparsity ratio should grow as denoising progresses, and earlier search results can be reused to reduce the search space. Based on these findings, we propose Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search (GSRS), a training-free framework that retains more computation early and progressively reduces it later, while restricting subsequent searches to an early candidate set to reduce search overhead. GSRS adopts Top-p selection for adaptive sparsity control, supported by a precise evaluation scheme that computes exact attention weights within the FlashAttention computation at negligible overhead. Experiments on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1 validate that GSRS achieves 1.55$\times$--2.21$\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality comparable to full attention.
authors: Yun Dai, Yuyun Chen, Jiarui Wen, Huiping Zhuang, Cen Chen, Ziqian Zeng
bullets: Video DiTs are slowed by quadratic self-attention, while fixed-sparsity methods poorly reflect changing attention patterns during denoising.
Attention becomes increasingly concentrated over denoising steps, and early-selected blocks retain much of the later attention weight.
GSRS is training-free: it keeps more computation early, reduces it progressively, and restricts later searches to an early candidate set.
Top-p selection provides adaptive sparsity, with exact attention-weight evaluation integrated into FlashAttention at negligible overhead.
Validated on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1, GSRS delivers 1.55×–2.21× speedup while maintaining quality comparable to full attention.

papers.title: Sparse Attention for Video Generation Acceleration via Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search

papers.abstract: Real-time mobile volumetric video enables immersive free-viewpoint experiences, but delivering high-quality 3D content under constrained bandwidth and computation remains challenging. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) systems, such as V$^3$, enable efficient mobile streaming by encoding time-varying Gaussian attributes with commodity video codecs and hardware decoding. However, existing pipelines treat all Gaussians as frame-varying signals, which is poorly suited to full-scene content where large portions remain temporally stable. Our empirical study shows that frame-wise adaptation and video coding of all Gaussians cause quality degradation in complex full-scene content, particularly in temporally stable regions. To address this issue, we propose ResStreamGS, a residual-sensitive dual-stream framework that processes Gaussians according to their temporal behavior. ResStreamGS identifies residual-sensitive primitives through lightweight probe adaptation and reuses stable Gaussians within each Group of Pictures (GOP). Stable Gaussians are transmitted once per GOP, while only residual-sensitive Gaussians remain in the frame-wise hardware-decodable video stream. Experiments on complex full-scene volumetric videos show that ResStreamGS improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51--8.35~dB over a controlled V$^3$-style all-Gaussians baseline, reduces amortized payload by up to 56.5%, and achieves 30.883~FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G platform.
authors: Haoran Liu, Di Wu, Wang Luo, Hengyuan Na, Miao Hu, Guocong Quan
bullets: Targets quality degradation and bandwidth/computation inefficiency when all Gaussians are treated as frame-varying.

On complex full-scene videos, improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51–8.35 dB and reduces amortized payload by up to 56.5% versus a controlled V$^3$-style baseline.
Reaches 30.883 FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G platform.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video models often generate the visual concepts requested in natural language prompts but fail to satisfy their intended ordering, timing, and persistence requirements. We propose representing these requirements as specifications in a formal Temporal Logic, and introduce Temporal Specification Guidance (TSG), a training-free inference-time framework that turns temporal specifications into executable objectives for guiding video generation during sampling. TSG scores traces of visual concept evidence using differentiable quantitative semantics and uses the score's gradients to construct a specification-guided denoising direction. We instantiate this framework with video-text attention traces, efficient differentiable scores for Metric Temporal Logic, and gradient-derived attention biases. This instantiation requires neither an external concept classifier nor backpropagation through the video transformer. Its attention-steered forward pass yields a denoising direction that augments classifier-free guidance (CFG). On a benchmark of 220 prompts spanning 11 categories of temporal constraints, including ordered object entry and state transitions, this instantiation improves specification satisfaction accuracy over CFG by 9.5-20 percentage points across five models, with minimal memory overhead. These results demonstrate the potential of temporal specifications and differentiable satisfaction objectives as a flexible interface for controlling video generation.
authors: Avishree Khare, Hideki Okamoto, Bardh Hoxha, Georgios Fainekos, Rajeev Alur
bullets: Targets failures in event ordering, timing, and persistence despite correct visual concepts.

Evaluated on 220 prompts across 11 temporal-constraint categories and five models, improving satisfaction accuracy by 9.5–20 percentage points over CFG.
Requires no external concept classifier or backpropagation through the video transformer, with minimal memory overhead.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal generation covers discrete, continuous, and hybrid paradigms. Discrete approaches with single-codebook visual tokenizers align naturally with text modeling but have limited representational capacity. Continuous and hybrid approaches retain richer visual representations, but they model text and images in heterogeneous spaces with different training objectives, potentially introducing optimization conflicts between modalities with misaligned representation spaces. These choices expose a central question: how to efficiently model high-capacity visual representations alongside textual content in a shared optimization space within a single backbone. We present Intern Lumina U2, to our knowledge the first diffusion language model to represent multi-codebook visual tokens in a fully discrete space. Each visual position is represented by a group of codes from complementary codebooks, increasing its representational capacity while preserving compatibility with discrete text modeling. At the input, the embeddings are concatenated at each position; at the output, a lightweight multi-codebook autoregressive head predicts the codes within each position sequentially, while the diffusion backbone processes all positions in parallel. Built on the unified 4D representation of AToken, Intern Lumina U2 supports image, video, and 3D inputs within a single backbone and achieves leading performance among unified models in visual understanding, image generation, and image editing. We further build a full-stack training, inference, and evaluation system on both Ascend and NVIDIA platforms to verify the cross-platform effectiveness of our model. We also improve the inference efficiency through a stability-aware sampling strategy, which combines confidence-plateau-guided unmasking approach with drift-triggered cache refreshing mechanisms, accelerating image generation by 4.45x.
authors: Qian Yu, Zongyang Qiu, Juncheng Yan, Hongliang Li, Qi Qin, Keqi Wang, Siqi Luo, Junkui Ju, Yapeng Mi, Tiantian Lu, Tian Liu, Pengyu Xie, Chenhao Ji, Minghui Zhang, Yiang Zhao, Siyu Yan, Haiying Xu, Yanbo Wang, Jianghan Shen, Yuandong Pu, Jiayi Lei, Borui Zhang, Jinxin Shi, Bo Zhang, Yuhang Zang, Shenglong Ye, Lixin Gu, Hongjie Zhang, Linghan Liu, Xinyuan Chen, Yuewen Cao, Lihe Zhang, Xiaohong Liu, Junjun He, Qiangwei Liu, Qi Zhang, Yu Cheng, Tianfan Xue, Hui Xiong, Chang Xu, Yu Qiao, Yihao Liu, Bin Fu

Represents each visual position with complementary code groups, concatenating their embeddings and predicting codes sequentially with a lightweight head while denoising positions in parallel.
Built on AToken’s unified 4D representation to support image, video, and 3D inputs.

papers.abstract: Sampling from continuous flow-based generators such as flow matching models requires numerical ODE or SDE integration, making inference cost depend on the number of function evaluations (NFEs). In practice, the sampling budget is inherited from prior work or selected through expensive FID-versus-NFE sweeps, using FID to assess image-generation quality, requiring sample generation and evaluation at multiple budgets. This makes sampling-budget selection dependent on repeated empirical evaluation. We therefore ask a complementary question to solver design and timestep allocation: for a fixed pretrained model and solver, what numerical resolution is sufficient? We introduce FLOWBUDGET, a training-free estimator of solver-relative sampling complexity. Using simulation-free interpolation probes of the learned dynamics, FLOWBUDGET normalizes the leading one-step discretization error by the motion, estimates its coefficient from interpolation probes, and maps a numerical tolerance to a step budget using the solver order. We derive estimators for numerical solvers in flow~matching sampling, namely Euler and Heun for ODE sampling and additive-noise Euler--Maruyama for SDE sampling, and connect the ODE coefficients to terminal integration error. Experiments on SiT, FlowDCN and Rectified Flow models, spanning flow-model architectures and formulations, test whether FLOWBUDGET can estimate the NFE budget without generating samples at multiple budgets or performing an FID-versus-NFE sweep. The code is available at https://github.com/Yasaman-dt/FlowBudget
authors: Zahra Dehghani, Pablo Piantanida, Mohammadhadi Shateri
bullets: Addresses the costly, empirical selection of numerical resolution for pretrained flow-based generators.
Uses training-free, simulation-free interpolation probes of learned dynamics to estimate normalized one-step discretization error.
Derives budget estimators for Euler and Heun ODE solvers and additive-noise Euler–Maruyama SDE sampling.
Maps a target numerical tolerance to an NFE budget using solver order and relates ODE estimates to terminal integration error.
Evaluated across SiT, FlowDCN, and Rectified Flow models and formulations.

papers.abstract: Representation-alignment methods effectively accelerate the diffusion transformer training. REPA, for example, uses a pretrained vision encoder to supervise an intermediate layer through an MLP projection head which is discarded after training. It aims to import semantics from the vision encoder to the diffusion backbone. While this objective is achieved at early layers by back-propagating the alignment loss, there is no guarantee that later layers, supervised by the velocity prediction loss alone, can well access such semantics. We propose a simple solution, representation conditioning (RECON), to improve semantics in later layers. During training, we feed the pretrained vision encoder tokens into later layers; during inference, because we no longer have the clean image, we reuse the MLP head (as a proxy to the vision encoder) and project its output tokens to the later layers. Our method adds no parameters and leads to much faster convergence: RECON is $63\times$ faster than SiT and $25\times$ faster than REPA. Code is available at https://github.com/saeidrazavi/RECON
authors: Saeed Razavi, Xingjian Leng, Liang Zheng
bullets: REPA aligns early diffusion layers with a pretrained vision encoder, but later layers may not access those semantics effectively.
RECON feeds vision-encoder tokens into later layers during training.
At inference, it reuses the discarded MLP projection head as a proxy for the vision encoder to generate conditioning tokens.
The method adds no parameters and reports convergence 63× faster than SiT and 25× faster than REPA.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.abstract: Interactive video generation commonly relies on small bidirectional chunks to reduce response latency. Yet our preliminary experiments show that larger chunks improve video quality and better utilize GPU parallelism, allowing more latents to be sampled with only a modest increase in sampling time. Motivated by these observations, we propose Speculative Sampling, a strategy that combines the modeling power of large bidirectional windows with the low-latency interaction of small ones. It expands the modeling window by appending noise latents as padding and caches the resulting predictions for reuse when the condition remains unchanged. Predictions are delivered incrementally, while the uncommitted future remains replaceable. Our latency analysis shows that this removes the waiting-time lower bound imposed by chunk boundaries, shifting the optimization focus from reducing chunk size to accelerating per-chunk sampling. Bidirectional window size thus becomes a decision variable for jointly optimizing visual quality and sampling time, rather than a necessary constraint on low-latency interaction. This opens a path to serving large bidirectional models in interactive streaming systems without complex streaming post-training.
authors: Yubo Huang, Yuxuan Zhang, Jiaming Liu, Sirui Zhao, Enhong Chen
bullets: Interactive video systems use small bidirectional chunks for responsiveness, but larger chunks can improve quality and GPU utilization.
The method expands the modeling window with noise padding and reuses cached predictions when conditions remain unchanged.
Video predictions are delivered incrementally while uncommitted future content remains replaceable.
The approach removes the waiting-time lower bound caused by chunk boundaries, shifting focus to faster per-chunk sampling.
It supports serving large bidirectional models for interactive streaming without complex streaming-specific post-training.

papers.abstract: We present KinoGen, a framework that synthesizes customizable humanoid loco-manipulation references through kinematically grounded video generation. KinoGen conditions a pretrained video generator on calibrated renders of the target robot and object in a simulated task instance and recovers the reference by fitting the same models to the generated two-view video, so that the reference lies in the robot configuration space by construction without a human body proxy or retargeting. Body, hand, and object priors initialize the reconstruction, and direct optimization against cross-view evidence refines it. Since an edited keyframe is simply another rendered state, a user can prescribe a goal object pose, regenerate the video around the edited keyframe, and obtain a reference that satisfies the pose exactly. Across eight loco-manipulation tasks, KinoGen yields lower penetration and foot skating than video-based baselines and preserves over 90% of annotated contacts, and its customized references satisfy every prescribed target with substantially less penetration than direct interpolation. Tracking policies trained on the synthesized references are deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. Project webpage: https://kinogen-humanoid.github.io/.
authors: Qi Wu, Lulu Zhao, Sanghyun Hahn, Rishi Yennu, Emmy Yang, Dingqi Zhang, Tao Pang, Jiuguang Wang, Kuan Fang
bullets: Conditions a pretrained video generator on simulated renders of the target robot, object, and task.
Reconstructs robot and object motion by fitting the same models to generated video, avoiding human-body proxies and retargeting.
Supports exact goal-pose customization by editing a keyframe and regenerating the surrounding video.
Across eight tasks, reduces penetration and foot skating versus video-based baselines while preserving over 90% of annotated contacts.
References satisfy prescribed object poses and support deployment of tracking policies on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive generation underlies real-time, causal video synthesis and is the backbone of video world models. Today's dominant approach distills a bidirectional diffusion model into a causal few-step student, but existing pipelines make this conversion prohibitively expensive, requiring offline Probability Flow ODE} (PF-ODE) trajectories that cost tens of thousands of GPU-hours and terabytes of storage. We show it can be made dramatically more efficient. Pushing this efficiency to its extreme, we reduce trajectory supervision to a single sample, the strictest setting possible, and find that it causes severe quality collapse. We trace this to the teacher's trajectory geometry: the high-noise regime, governing semantic layout and motion, and the low-noise regime, governing fine texture exhibit fundamentally different curvature and optimization behavior, so a single monolithic student cannot jointly fit both, causing severe representation interference. Motivated by this, we propose Glance Forcing, a lightweight distillation framework that decouples the denoising trajectory into two complementary slow and fast experts, each guided by a tailored, stage-specific objective, while keeping the pretrained teacher entirely frozen. This decoupling further reveals a general mechanism underlying few-step distillation: PF-ODE distillation mainly straightens the few-step trajectory geometry, while the subsequent distribution-matching stage independently governs distributional quality. Using only one PF-ODE trajectory, Glance Forcing already surpasses the fully-trained state-of-the-art baseline, raising the VBench Total score from 84.04 to 84.22 while cutting trajectory-collection cost from thousands of GPU-hours to about one A100-GPU-hour, with markedly larger gains in dynamic degree, VisionReward, and instruction-following, and consistent preference from human raters over strong baselines.
authors: Zhuobai Dong, Junchao Yi, Hu Jian Guo, Linjie Li, Rui Zhao, Alex Jinpeng Wang
bullets: Existing causal distillation pipelines require tens of thousands of GPU-hours and terabytes of PF-ODE trajectory data.
The authors attribute single-sample quality collapse to different optimization geometry in high-noise semantic/motion and low-noise texture regimes.
Glance Forcing uses two frozen-teacher-guided slow and fast experts with stage-specific objectives to decouple these regimes.
With one PF-ODE trajectory, it raises VBench Total from 84.04 to 84.22 and reduces trajectory collection to about one A100-GPU-hour.
It also reports gains in dynamic degree, VisionReward, instruction following, and human preference over strong baselines.

Expert-specific objectives further enhance temporal consistency and spatial fidelity.

papers.abstract: Pairwise preference feedback has become a widely adopted supervision signal for reinforcement learning in video generation models, as pairwise comparisons provide a more reliable alternative than pointwise scalar ratings for evaluating the quality of generated videos. Specifically, we define a preference graph for each GRPO group under a pairwise evaluator, where nodes represent sampled rollouts and edges encode pairwise preferences. Auditing 6,976 on-policy comparison graphs, we find that cyclic preferences are prevalent and persist throughout training. Naive pairwise reward aggregation based on average win rates discards the underlying comparison structures and treats each rollout independently, which may introduce unreliable advantage estimates for certain rollouts and consequently affect reinforcement learning optimization. Therefore, we propose the \emph{Reliability-Anchored Preference Walk} (\ours{}), a graph-aware advantage aggregation method that strengthens the global preference signal from win rates with reliable relational evidence from cyclic preference graphs through a reliability-guided preference walk. Under matched evaluator, comparison protocol, group size, prompt schedule, and query budget, \ours{} requires no additional evaluator queries beyond the observed comparisons within each rollout group and improves over Pairwise-GRPO across controlled comparisons, transfer settings, and blind human evaluations.
authors: Xinrui Lin, Fan Li, Shumin Wang, Dehong Kong, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: Pairwise preferences for video rollouts often form cycles, which persist during training.
Win-rate aggregation ignores relational structure and can yield unreliable rollout advantages.
Reliability-Anchored Preference Walk combines global win rates with reliability-guided evidence from preference graphs.
It uses only comparisons already observed within each rollout group.
The method improves over Pairwise-GRPO in controlled, transfer, and blind human evaluations, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RAP-Walk. Top: methods share the Pairwise-GRPO pipeline and differ only in advantage construction. Bottom: (a) same-prompt videos exhibit quality trade-offs; (b) pointwise rewards are normalized independently; (c) v1, v2, and v3 form a directed cycle yet have identical row-wise win rates, so win-rate aggregation assigns them identical advantages; (d) RAP-Walk uses reliable edges and multi-hop paths to correct the win-rate anchor.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison across eight prompts. Each prompt shows four frames from videos generated by Pretrained, Pairwise GRPO, and RAP-Walk. Pretrained denotes the original Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B model without LoRA post-training. All methods use matched prompts and initial noise.

Figure 2: Five-node illustration of cyclic preference propagation. (a) A cyclic preference graph with reliability-aware propagation. papers.abstract: We present Kandinsky S2V 1.0, an open family of speech-to-video models for controllable audio-driven human animation, comprising Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite (2B parameters) and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro (21B parameters). From a single reference image, a speech waveform, and a text prompt, the models generate long-form 25 FPS video in which lip motion, expression, pose, and gesture follow the speech. The architecture draws text and audio conditioning from one Qwen2.5-Omni model and adds a reference-aware three-scale visual memory. Training starts from the Kandinsky 5.0 Video foundation models [1] and combines mixed reference-memory layouts with an area-adaptive face loss. The training corpus contains 1.17M single-speaker clips selected by active-speaker detection, with captions generated directly in English and Russian. A side-by-side human evaluation against the strongest open-source baseline and two proprietary commercial models shows that Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro performs comparably to or better than these models on average and is also preferred for lip synchronization. On common speech to video benchmarks, Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro rank among the top performing models according to mean rank over five reported metrics. Beyond the base models, we provide {\pi}-Flow distilled variants of both Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro. The distilled Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro model generates video in 16 sampling steps without classifier-free guidance, achieving a 5.4 times end-to-end speedup over the base model, while matching or exceeding it on nearly all reported benchmark metrics. To accelerate open research and deployment in speech-to-video generation, we release the code, model checkpoints, and diffusers integration under the MIT license.
authors: Nikolay Semenov, Artem Riabinin, Sergey Bassenko, Anna Averchenkova, Julia Agafonova, Anastasia Aliaskina, Kirill Kozlov, Lev Novitskiy, Nikita Samsonov, Nikolai Gerasimenko, Denis Dimitrov

Pro performs comparably to or better than evaluated open and proprietary models, with preferred lip synchronization; both rank highly on common benchmarks.
π-Flow distillation enables the Pro model to generate in 16 steps without classifier-free guidance, delivering a reported 5.4× end-to-end speedup while largely preserving quality.

papers.abstract: Memory for long-horizon video generation must satisfy two competing requirements: it must remain bounded so generation can continue indefinitely, while still recovering what was observed at a place when the camera returns, regardless of how long ago it was seen. Reconstruction-based memories provide spatial recall by caching and reprojecting explicit geometry, but require growing storage and depend on estimated 3D structure. Recurrent memories keep a constant-size state, but retention is governed by temporal recurrence, causing old observations to fade with time. We introduce SMART, a slot memory addressed by region tokens, which combines bounded storage with spatially addressed recall. SMART stores content in a constant-size slot recurrence whose writes are addressed by the observing camera and whose reads are queried by the rendering camera, without constructing an explicit 3D representation or maintaining a growing cache. Consequently, recall is conditioned on inter-view geometry rather than on recency. Each read additionally provides a confidence estimate that conditions a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, allowing it to selectively trust retrieved content while relying on its generative prior elsewhere. On long trajectories in Memory Maze and Minecraft, SMART maintains high-fidelity recall far beyond its training horizon while using constant memory and per-step cost.
authors: Eren Cetin, Julius Erbach, Vukasin Bozic, Hyojun Go, Zixiang Zhao, Nikolai Kalischek, Federico Tombari, Konrad Schindler, Dominik Narnhofer
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between bounded memory and recalling observations when the camera revisits a location.
Uses a constant-size slot recurrence with writes keyed by the observing camera and reads queried by the rendering camera.
Avoids explicit 3D reconstruction and growing caches by conditioning recall on inter-view geometry.
Provides confidence estimates to a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, which balances retrieved content with its generative prior.
On Memory Maze and Minecraft trajectories, maintains high-fidelity recall beyond the training horizon with constant memory and per-step cost.

papers.abstract: Dense cardiac dynamics are essential for assessing cardiac function, yet in practice clinicians often observe only extremely sparse measurements. However, recovering full dynamics from such sparsity is a highly ill-posed problem due to the lack of temporal cues. While auxiliary time-series signals like ECG provide physiological guidance, effectively exploiting them is challenging due to the cross-modal representation gap and phase misalignment. In this work, we present CardioFAD, a Focus--Align--Diffuse paradigm that reformulates sparse cardiac dynamic synthesis as a recoverability--alignability anchor discovery problem. Our core insight is that resolving extreme temporal ambiguity requires a compact set of anchor states that are both sufficient to recover the visual trajectory and reliable for ECG--visual alignment. We therefore learn motion-salient keyframes under two complementary principles: trajectory sufficiency, which preserves trajectory-critical intra-modal motion content, and anchor alignment, which promotes consistent inter-modal correspondence at these anchors. We implement the Focus and Align modules optimized by the two aspects. Diffuse then performs two-stage generation by first synthesizing keyframes and subsequently interpolating the remaining frames. Extensive experiments on cardiac MRI and echocardiography videos demonstrate superior visual quality, temporal coherence, and improved functional consistency under the extreme one-shot regime.
authors: Junkai Liu, Haofan Wu, Nay Aung, Joao A. C. Lima, Steffen E. Petersen, Le Zhang
bullets: Addresses the severe temporal ambiguity of cardiac dynamic synthesis from extremely sparse observations.
Learns motion-salient keyframes that are both trajectory-sufficient and aligned with ECG signals.
Uses a Focus–Align–Diffuse pipeline: identify keyframes, align visual and physiological information, then generate keyframes and interpolate remaining frames.
Experiments on cardiac MRI and echocardiography show improved visual quality, temporal coherence, and functional consistency in the one-shot setting.

papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanism behind why diffusion models memorize their training data remains an open question in generative modeling. In this paper, we examine this question from two perspectives: (a) the model-level perspective concerning the onset of memorization in a model during training, and (b) the sample-level perspective concerning the proclivity of an individual sample to be memorized by a given model. We show that the so-called input loss curvature, or the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of the diffusion model's training loss, is an effective metric for quantifying both perspectives on memorization. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that input curvatures averaged across training and validation samples can identify when a model is likely to start regurgitating its training data when tracked over training time. However, this metric is not sufficient for measuring an individual sample's likelihood of being memorized. To address this perspective, we introduce a counterfactual definition of memorization in diffusion models, extending the analogous notion from supervised learning proposed by [Feldman, 2019]. We prove that this counterfactual memorization is controlled by the input curvature of the leave-one-out model, thus establishing a direct theoretical link between a sample's local loss landscape and its generation likelihood. We validate our derived bounds through several empirical experiments and show that input-dependent curvature provides a proxy for memorization.
authors: Shashank Sule, Xinyue Yu, Boonam Shin, Yuxuan Liu, Abolfazl Hashemi, Hayden Schaeffer
bullets: Memorization is studied both as a training-time model behavior and as an individual sample property.

Curvature alone does not adequately measure whether a specific sample will be memorized.
The paper defines counterfactual memorization for diffusion models and proves it is controlled by input curvature of a leave-one-out model.
Experiments validate the theoretical bounds and support input-dependent curvature as a memorization proxy.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates memorization in diffusion models using loss curvature, providing a theoretical and empirical framework for understanding generative model behavior.
papers.title: Loss Curvature as a Sampling-Free Proxy for Memorization in Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: Input loss curvature, measured via the diffusion-loss Hessian, is a sampling-free proxy for detecting model-level memorization and estimating sample-level memorization under a counterfactual definition.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models generate visually compelling short-term sequences but often struggle to preserve scene geometry and object structure over time. In this paper, we first demonstrate that current video attention cannot identify reliable correspondences across frames, with responses dispersed across multiple regions even after recognizable scene structure has emerged. We argue that reliable cross-frame associations are essential for information exchange as scene structure forms in video generation. Thus, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (GAD), which transfers correspondences from a frozen geometry model's attention to video attention. Extracted from clean videos, these correspondences link the same static surface or moving object across frames. Since structure formation begins in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise, we apply attention distillation at a student layer selected according to the noise timestep. After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding locations. Experiments across all three video backbones demonstrate improved long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency, with geometric gains across generation lengths. On Wan2.2 5B, GAD improves cross-frame matching accuracy by at least 30% over the Wan baseline on both long-range benchmarks. Notably, GAD achieves these gains without additional inference modules, offering a promising approach to efficient and consistent video-based world simulation. Project page: https://fantasy-amap.github.io/GAD/.
authors: Junfeng Ni, Ziyu Zhu, Fan Jiang, Yu Liu, Chiyu Wang, Jiawei Zhang, Zhaoxu Sun, Mu Xu, Siyuan Huang, Yixin Chen
bullets: Video diffusion models often lose scene geometry and object structure over time because their attention produces dispersed cross-frame correspondences.
GAD transfers attention correspondences from a frozen geometry model trained on clean videos to video attention.
Distillation targets a noise-timestep-dependent student layer, reflecting how structure forms from deeper to shallower layers during generation.
Across three video backbones, GAD improves long-range scene and dynamic temporal consistency across generation lengths.
On Wan2.2 5B, it improves cross-frame matching accuracy by at least 30% over the baseline on both long-range benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Few-step distillation reduces the sampling cost of diffusion and flow models, but existing approaches often require auxiliary score models or specialized architectures. We show that simple on-policy velocity regression already provides a strong foundation for 4-NFE generation. To represent teacher velocity variation within each coarse transition, we introduce Pivot, a training-only residual proxy that separates local corrections from the student's interval-mean prediction. We further repel the student from weaker teacher predictions, providing a lightweight mechanism for avoiding undesirable modes. The resulting framework, Simplified Matching Distillation (SMD), remains entirely regression-based, requires neither online score estimation nor adversarial training, and leaves the deployed generator unchanged. We evaluate SMD on image generation and editing, 3D generation, video synthesis, and joint audio--video generation, scaling to 33 billion parameters. At 4-NFE, SMD outperforms strong few-step baselines and surpasses multi-step teachers on several benchmarks. It also supports cross-model, multi-teacher, and causal-video distillation.
authors: Jiawei Zhang, Ziyu Wan, Nanye Ma, Long Zhao, Dong Chen, Hongyu Liu, Qifeng Chen, Dongdong Chen
bullets: Uses on-policy velocity regression as the foundation for few-step distillation.
Introduces Pivot, a training-only residual proxy that captures teacher velocity variation within coarse transitions.
Repels the student from weaker teacher predictions to reduce undesirable modes.
Evaluated across image, 3D, video, and joint audio–video generation, including models up to 33B parameters.
Supports cross-model, multi-teacher, and causal-video distillation; reports outperforming strong few-step baselines and surpassing multi-step teachers on several benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models have emerged as a foundation for long-horizon world rollout. However, when extended far beyond their training windows, these models suffer from progressive drift: visual quality deteriorates, motion becomes inconsistent, and object identity gradually collapses as generated frames are recursively reused as context. We study a supervision-horizon gap: short-horizon distillation leaves later rollout states without direct supervision. We show that matching short-window marginals need not determine long-horizon behavior, while longer on-policy trajectories expose delayed failures to training. This motivates temporal manifold matching at scale for long-horizon world models. Building on this insight, we introduce LongForcing, a distillation approach that scales teacher supervision to long student self-rollouts. LongForcing preserves the short-horizon teacher-forcing and causal ODE-distillation stages, while replacing the realscore teacher in the final distribution-matching stage with an extended-horizon bidirectional teacher. The long-horizon teacher supervises extended student self-rollouts using the standard distribution-matching formulation, without modifying the student architecture or increasing inference cost. We evaluate LongForcing on text-to-video generation and interactive action-conditioned world models, achieving a VBench Quality score of 85.52 and improving WorldRoamBench 60s action score by 23.9 points in first-person ablations. Qualitative stress tests further sample interactive rollouts up to 24 hours, far beyond the training horizon. These results suggest that scaling supervision along the temporal axis is a practical step toward long-horizon world models. The project website and code are at https://github.com/Fantasy-AMAP/LongForcing.
authors: Ziyu Zhu, Zhaoxu Sun, Fan Jiang, Mengchao Wang, Junfeng Ni, Ting-Bing Xu, Zhicheng Liu, Mu Xu
bullets: Targets progressive visual degradation, motion inconsistency, and object-identity collapse beyond the training horizon.
Identifies a supervision-horizon gap: short-window distillation does not constrain delayed rollout failures.
Extends temporal manifold matching by replacing the final-stage realscore teacher with an extended-horizon bidirectional teacher.
Preserves the student architecture and inference cost while supervising long self-rollouts.
Reports a VBench Quality score of 85.52, a 23.9-point improvement on the WorldRoamBench 60s action score in first-person ablations, and qualitative rollouts up to 24 hours.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc linearization is an attractive way to accelerate pretrained Video Diffusion Transformers (Video DiTs), yet existing methods largely treat the quality loss induced by attention replacement as a recovery problem. We show that a more fundamental bottleneck lies upstream: \emph{initialization}. Random initialization discards pretrained knowledge, whereas manual weight reuse transfers it through rigid and incomplete source--target correspondences. We introduce \textbf{LinMorph}, which recasts Video DiT linearization as a learnable softmax-to-linear weight transformation problem. Instead of copying predefined counterparts, LinMorph learns a cross-parameter morphism that lets each target Gated DeltaNet (GDN) parameter draw jointly from pretrained query, key, value, and output projections, including for parameters with no direct softmax counterpart. A single morphism is shared across layers and learned through local teacher alignment, while producing layer-specific initializations from their respective pretrained weights. The resulting weights are then materialized as independent GDN modules for progressive distillation and joint recovery.Since the morphism operates in weight space rather than token space, it can be learned on short, low-resolution clips and directly reused at larger video scales. Across pretrained Video DiTs, LinMorph enables markedly faster recovery and better final generation quality than random initialization and heuristic weight reuse. Results show that efficient linearization depends not only on how a converted model is recovered, but critically on how pretrained knowledge is transferred before recovery. Project page: https://lonelyling.github.io/LinMorph.
authors: Lingyi Long, Congyue Zhao, Xiaoou Li, Yanmin Qian, Tao Huang
bullets: Identifies initialization—not only post-conversion recovery—as a key bottleneck in Video DiT linearization.

Allows each GDN parameter to combine information from pretrained query, key, value, and output projections, including unmatched parameters.
Uses local teacher alignment on short, low-resolution clips, then applies layer-specific transformed weights for progressive distillation and recovery.
Reports faster recovery and better final generation quality across pretrained Video DiTs than random or heuristic initialization.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for unified text-vision synthesis, surpassing traditional U-Net architectures in generative tasks. One key innovation lies in its Multimodal Self-Attention (MM-SA) interaction, where image and text tokens are concatenated and processed via self-attention. However, this mechanism poses significant challenges for editing, rendering conventional U-Net-based attention manipulation methods ineffective. To address this limitation, we propose QK-Edit, a training-free framework that exploits the unique attention dynamics of MM-DiTs for precise text-guided image and video editing. By introducing a novel query-key manipulation strategy, our method isolates and adjusts critical attention components to achieve an optimal balance between prompt fidelity and structural consistency. This enables seamless edits across various tasks, including object addition, object removal, object replacement, changing background, changing material, changing color, and style transformation. Notably, it can be easily implemented with feature replacement in inference. QK-Edit demonstrates superior editing performance on state-of-the-art models, such as FLUX and HunyuanVideo, effectively bridging the gap between generative power and editable flexibility in MM-DiTs, and paving the way for scalable multimodal content creation.
authors: Tiancheng Shen, Zilong Huang, Xiangtai Li, Zhijie Lin, Jiyang Liu, Yitong Wang, Jiashi Feng, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Jun Hao Liew
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of applying conventional U-Net attention-editing methods to MM-DiTs with concatenated image-text tokens.
Manipulates query-key interactions to balance prompt fidelity with preservation of the original structure.
Supports object addition, removal, replacement, background and material changes, color edits, and style transformations.
Implemented through feature replacement during inference, without additional training.
Demonstrates effective editing on MM-DiT models including FLUX and HunyuanVideo.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity surgical video generation is increasingly important for surgical education, simulation, and downstream AI training, as conventional simulation pipelines are limited by cost, realism, and scenario diversity. Adapting generic text-to-video diffusion models to surgical procedures remains difficult, however, due to complex anatomical structures, intricate tool-tissue interactions, the inherently hierarchical nature of surgical workflows, and the scarcity of curated training data outside a few well-studied procedures. We propose a surgical video generation framework that combines hierarchical procedural annotation with curriculum transfer learning. Surgical procedures are decomposed into three levels (phase, task, and action) and a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model is progressively adapted from coarse to fine-grained surgical context, supported by a dynamic sampling strategy that handles variable-resolution and variable-length surgical clips. We instantiate the framework on Bilateral Axillo-Breast Approach robotic thyroidectomy, a procedure for which no curated benchmark currently exists. Relative to the preceding task-level model, the final action-level model reduces FVD by 20.1% and FID by 15.7%, and a matched-budget ablation indicates that these gains arise from the curriculum design rather than from additional training. A user study with six clinicians rates visual realism highly while highlighting remaining gaps in anatomical accuracy and clinical reliability. The proposed framework offers a step toward AI-driven surgical simulation in procedures where curated data are scarce.
authors: Youngbin Kong, Seungho Lee, Jae Kyung Shin, Jong-hyuk Ahn, Hyoun-Joong Kong, Kyu Eun Lee
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of generating surgical videos with complex anatomy, tool–tissue interactions, hierarchical workflows, and scarce curated data.
Decomposes procedures into phase, task, and action levels, then progressively transfers these contexts into a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model.
Uses dynamic sampling to accommodate surgical clips with varying resolutions and lengths.

On Bilateral Axillo-Breast Approach robotic thyroidectomy data, the action-level model improves FVD and FID over the task-level model; matched-budget ablation attributes gains to the curriculum design.
Six clinicians rated visual realism highly but identified remaining limitations in anatomical accuracy and clinical reliability.

papers.abstract: Recent video super-resolution (VSR) models achieve efficient one-step generation through diffusion distillation. However, high-resolution inference remains costly, and distilled models are difficult to align with human preferences. These challenges call for improvements in both model architecture and training strategy. We present \textbf{FlashVSR+} to address both limitations. On the architecture side, we introduce hybrid attention based on the strong locality observed in pretrained VSR models, while retaining sparse global interaction for long-range consistency. It achieves up to $2\times$ DiT speedup and 45\% lower peak memory, enabling spatially untiled 4K VSR on a single 24GB RTX 4090. On the training side, we propose Reward-Yield Distribution Matching Distillation (Ry-DMD) for preference-aligned one-step generation. Ry-DMD uses reward-weighted teacher rollouts to incorporate black-box rewards into distribution matching, without backpropagating through the reward model. We further show that Ry-DMD generalizes beyond VSR to T2I generation. Together, FlashVSR+ delivers stronger restoration quality and substantially improves high-resolution efficiency, with consistent gains in user preference. We release our code, models, and training data at \href{https://www.flashvsr.tech}{\textcolor{FlashBlue}{\textbf{www.flashvsr.tech}}}.
authors: Ruchang Yao, Shi Guo, Junhao Zhuang, Mingde Yao, Xin Cai, Jiahao Zhan, Bin Fu, Xinyuan Chen, Yu Qiao, Tianfan Xue
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of high-resolution VSR and the difficulty of aligning distilled models with human preferences.
Uses hybrid attention that emphasizes local interactions while preserving sparse global context for long-range consistency.
Introduces Reward-Yield Distribution Matching Distillation (Ry-DMD), which uses reward-weighted teacher rollouts without backpropagating through the reward model.
Reports up to 2× DiT speedup and 45% lower peak memory, enabling untiled 4K VSR on a single 24GB RTX 4090.
Achieves stronger restoration quality and consistent user-preference gains; Ry-DMD also generalizes to text-to-image generation.

papers.abstract: Model providers can support image protection, but open-weight deployment introduces practical constraints. We propose four requirements: protection effectiveness, clean fidelity, compatibility, and tamper resistance. We incorporate long-horizon attack simulations to strengthen resistance to protection removal. Experiments with a single protection tool show improved resistance to re-alignment at a cost to clean fidelity, motivating further research toward practical model-side protection.
authors: Jihye Kang, Jiwon Park, Namhyuk Ahn
bullets: Open-weight deployment creates constraints beyond user-side image defenses.
Protection should balance effectiveness, clean fidelity, compatibility, and tamper resistance.
Long-horizon attack simulations are used to improve resistance to protection removal and re-alignment.
Experiments with one protection tool show stronger re-alignment resistance but reduced clean fidelity.
Further research is needed for practical model-side protection.

Columns (a) and (b) are indistinguishable by design: over the 100 evaluation images the mean distortion between them is 45.1 dB PSNR, 0.990 SSIM and 0.010 LPIPS. The target in (d) is never published. With it the edit is still far from that clean-image edit at t = 20, although the pattern is no longer crisp. The simulated attacks used in tamper-resistance training are drawn from a pool of thirty-six configurations, one per epoch in the listed order, so a twenty-epoch run sees encoder-scope attacks first and decoder-tail attacks after.

Table 5: What each group of the tamper-resistance objective contributes. All models are trained for twenty epochs and evaluated under the same attack; ablations remove the epoch-long refresh or a loss component from Equation 2. Protection is measured by LPIPS between the edit of a protected image and the edit of its clean counterpart, reported before the attack and after twenty epochs of it. Fidelity is measured by the PSNR of an unprotected reconstruction against the original autoencoder’s, measured before the attack. Removal denotes the first attack epoch at which protection LPIPS falls to or below the unaligned reference of 0.225; > 20 indicates that the threshold was not reached within the first 20 attack epochs. The last two ablations illustrate that a delayed removal epoch can coincide with substantial loss of clean fidelity.

Table 4: Additional protection and clean-fidelity metrics for the models in Table 1. Protection is reported in LPIPS and SSIM between the edit of a protected image and the edit of its clean counterpart, so larger LPIPS and smaller SSIM both mean stronger protection. Table 1: Protection effectiveness, clean fidelity, and tamper resistance. Protection is measured by LPIPS before attack and after 20 epochs of encoder re-alignment. Fidelity is pre-attack reconstruction PSNR relative to the original autoencoder. Removal denotes the first attack epoch at which protection LPIPS falls to or below the unaligned reference of 0.225; > 20 means the threshold was not reached.

Table 3: How well each way of guessing the attacker’s position actually predicts it. Tamper-resistance training evaluates its objective at some approximation of where the attacker will be, and the two candidates are K differentiable inner steps from the current weights, or the offset reached by running the attack for one full epoch. Each row reports the cosine between that approximation’s parameter displacement and the displacement a real re-alignment attack has reached after t epochs, together with the ratio of their lengths at t=10. A cosine near zero means the approximation points somewhere else; a small norm ratio means it points the right way but has barely moved. The two blocks differ only in which objective the approximation descends; the ground truth is the same re-alignment attack in both.

Table 6: The trade-off along one run of tamper-resistance training, sampled every five epochs. The first row is the aligned checkpoint the run starts from, so reading down the table shows what each further five epochs of training buys and costs. papers.abstract: Video world models must generate physically plausible futures, not just realistic frames. Existing approaches typically use semantic, physical, or predictive information to guide the visual generation stream, leaving a fundamental question: where inside the generator should predictions of scene evolution live? Standard video tokens jointly encode appearance and dynamics, but provide no distinct state for learning and reading predictive dynamics. We answer this question with the Physical Registry: temporally grounded registry slots inside a video DiT that are initialized from an observation-conditioned forecast, co-evolve with video tokens, and receive future-representation supervision, making predictive dynamics an explicit, readable state of the generator. In a controlled comparison of predictive-state interfaces on Physics-IQ Verified, Physical Registry improves vanilla fine-tuning by 9.9/8.7 points on I2V/V2V, the largest gain among the interfaces we compare. Across all Cosmos and WAN backbones, Physical Registry improves Physics-IQ Verified scores. With only 0.45% additional parameters, it enables Cosmos 3 Nano 16B to surpass the published I2V score of Cosmos 3 Super 64B (43.56 vs. 42.7). On WorldModelBench, it also improves physical adherence and the total score for all four evaluated backbones. Because the registry becomes candidate-specific while remaining readable, the Physical Registry Selector (PRS) ranks emerging futures by how far their intermediate registry readouts depart from the shared forecast before full denoising is complete. Across four backbones, this selection improves I2V scores by 5.6-15.9% without completed-video external scoring. Together, these results support a broader principle: dynamics prediction should live as an explicit model state that co-evolves with the video representation. papers.abstract: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models have emerged as powerful generative priors across domains ranging from molecular design to high-resolution image synthesis. However, standard diffusion sampling is inherently biased toward high-likelihood regions, often limiting the diversity of outputs. In many domains, a single, high-likelihood sample is insufficient. Instead, diverse portfolios of high-performing solutions are required, motivating methods that uncover a model's full expressive range. Here we show that integrating Quality-Diversity (QD) optimisation with diffusion models enables the discovery of diverse, high-performing outputs. We first propose Quality-Diversity Diffusion, a framework that adapts QD to diffusion models by directly optimising the model's latent noise and conditioning embeddings and leveraging embedding models to quantify diversity. Second, we introduce a novel h-space Spectral Mutation operator, which guides search along directions of maximal semantic sensitivity by analysing principal singular vectors of the model's input-to-activation Jacobian. We evaluate our combined approach, Spectral-Guided Quality-Diversity Diffusion, on text-to-image generation. Against 12 baselines, our method consistently achieves the lowest FID score, demonstrating an excellent balance of image quality and diversity.
authors: Hannah Janmohamed, Joao Correia, Penousal Machado, Antoine Cully
bullets: Standard diffusion sampling favors high-likelihood regions, limiting output diversity when portfolios of strong solutions are needed.
Quality-Diversity Diffusion optimizes latent noise and conditioning embeddings while using embedding models to measure diversity.
The h-space Spectral Mutation operator searches along semantically sensitive directions identified from principal singular vectors of input-to-activation Jacobians.
On text-to-image generation, the combined method achieved the lowest FID among 12 baselines, indicating a strong quality–diversity balance.

papers.abstract: Explicit point correspondence is attractive for adapting video generators: it describes how visible surfaces move, but can overwrite the appearance prior learned by a large pretrained model. We study this tension in a 5.01B-parameter text-to-video diffusion transformer. ACROSSVAM2.0 combines a confidence-weighted track-and-visibility head, zero-initialized residual feedback, and asymmetric PCGrad that removes only the auxiliary component opposing the primary flow-matching gradient on shared LoRA parameters. The design preserves the generator exactly at initialization and protects its primary update during adaptation. In a four-way ablation trained for 1,000 steps with three independent seeds, the full method lowers KLT forward-backward cycle error in all three seeds relative to a matched flow-only continuation (mean seed-level difference -0.00711, SD 0.00505), while robust sharpness remains positive in all three. An expanded 24-prompt evaluation (216 videos) yields 9.7% lower aggregate CoTracker3 cycle error than the matched control and near-matched performance on six VBench dimensions; however, the seed-level tracking effect is heterogeneous and I3D-FVD regresses from 0.1824 to 0.2022. These results support a bounded claim: conflict-aware adaptation improves correspondence consistency without broad perceptual degradation, but does not uniformly improve video quality. We release equations, pseudocode, matched outputs, source tables, and artifact provenance.
bullets: Addresses the tension between explicit surface-motion supervision and preserving a pretrained video generator’s appearance prior.
Combines confidence-weighted track/visibility prediction, zero-initialized residual feedback, and asymmetric PCGrad on shared LoRA parameters.
Preserves the generator exactly at initialization and protects the primary flow-matching update during adaptation.
Improves aggregate CoTracker3 cycle error by 9.7% versus a matched control, with near-matched performance across six VBench dimensions.
Tracking improvements are heterogeneous across seeds, and I3D-FVD regresses from 0.1824 to 0.2022; video quality is not uniformly improved.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion enable novel-view video synthesis from a single input video, supporting world modeling, embodied intelligence, and robotic simulation. However, existing methods process camera trajectories independently, lacking the cross-trajectory consistency needed for coherent, navigable 4D worlds. We introduce Demiurge, an autoregressive video rerendering pipeline built on a dynamic 4D point-cloud memory cache. It promotes cross-trajectory consistency through four components: (1) an appearance video diffusion model that synthesizes photorealistic novel-view videos conditioned on the 4D memory; (2) a memory-consistent video depth completion model that aligns known-region depths with cached geometry and completes missing regions, mitigating scale ambiguity and discontinuities during memory updates; (3) memory-aware dual-stream warping that provides high-fidelity visual guidance and occlusion cues for novel-view synthesis; and (4) geometry-aware video refinement that enhances perceptual quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and three key capabilities: coherent spatiotemporal lattice construction over dense multi-view trajectories; large-parallax video rerendering under challenging camera motions, including 180-degree rotations with no input-view overlap; and geometry-faithful outputs that can be directly optimized into high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts. Project page: https://hanxinzhu-lab.github.io/demiurge_project_page/.
authors: Hanxin Zhu, Jianqi Ma, Cong Wang, Zhihao Hu, Junyao Gao, Tianyu He, Junyan Lin, Jiayin Xiao, Jiateng Shou, Sen Liang, Weidong Zhang, Zhibo Chen, Jun Zhang
bullets: Addresses cross-trajectory inconsistency in existing novel-view video synthesis methods.
Combines appearance diffusion, memory-consistent depth completion, dual-stream warping, and geometry-aware refinement.
Supports coherent spatiotemporal reconstruction across dense multi-view camera trajectories.
Handles large-parallax motion, including 180° rotations without input-view overlap.
Produces geometry-faithful videos that can be optimized into high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts.

papers.abstract: Training-free sparse attention is a practical route to efficient video diffusion transformer inference, yet existing methods typically fix the competition domain at each query row for every attention head. Prior work primarily addresses how to estimate token-level importance within this fixed domain; whether the domain itself should adapt to head heterogeneity remains under-specified. We introduce EG-Sparse, a training-free framework that routes low-entropy heads to a grouped cross-head pool while retaining per-row local selection for high-entropy heads, using only scores already materialized by the sparse pipeline. A controlled diagnostic fixes the ranking score and varies only the competition rule: grouped cross-head selection reduces low-entropy-head reconstruction error by 9.8%, whereas forcing high-entropy heads into an all-head global pool increases it by 7.9%. Across four configurations, EG-Sparse achieves higher video quality while reducing attention density and GPU denoising latency compared with strong training-free sparse-attention baselines. Mechanism ablations further show that selective domain adaptation outperforms uniform, random, and fixed domain-assignment policies. These results support competition-domain adaptation as a distinct design axis within centroid-guided training-free sparse attention.
authors: Tiantian Liu, Meng Wan, Zhiqiang Liang, Jue Wang, Ningming Nie, Yangang Wang
bullets: Existing methods use a fixed competition domain for every attention head, despite head heterogeneity.
EG-Sparse routes low-entropy heads to grouped cross-head selection while keeping high-entropy heads on per-row local selection.
A controlled diagnostic found grouped selection reduced low-entropy-head reconstruction error by 9.8%, while global pooling increased high-entropy-head error by 7.9%.
Across four configurations, the method improved video quality while lowering attention density and GPU denoising latency versus strong training-free baselines.
Ablations favored selective domain adaptation over uniform, random, and fixed assignment policies.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of EG-Sparse. A fixed row-wise domain constrains low-entropy heads because the budget cannot flow across rows to where it is most needed, whereas indiscriminate all-head global competition penalizes high-entropy heads. EG-Sparse resolves both: entropy routes low-entropy heads to a grouped cross-head pool, retains per-row local selection for the remaining heads, and merges both masks for execution by the sparse attention kernel.

This heterogeneity motivates head-adaptive competition domains.

papers.abstract: Can autoregressive video diffusion be accelerated further when only four denoising steps remain? Existing feature caching approaches struggle in this regime, as large feature changes between denoising timesteps undermine both direct reuse and lightweight predictors. We observe that features across video chunks remain strongly correlated at matching denoising timesteps, offering a complementary source of guidance. Building on this insight, we introduce TGuide, a framework that accelerates autoregressive video diffusion through a lightweight Anchor-Transport-Correct (ATC) predictor guided by historical sampling trajectories. Our ATC combines two complementary references: the current chunk's preceding-step features preserve its spatial structure, while the previous chunk's same-timestep features provide information at the target denoising stage. By integrating these references through spatial retrieval and adaptive correction, ATC improves velocity prediction accuracy despite the large gaps between denoising steps. To mitigate error accumulation across both denoising steps and video chunks, we train the predictor on its own autoregressive rollouts, allowing it to adapt to states shaped by its own earlier predictions. An optional confidence-aware scheduler further adjusts the quality-efficiency trade-off. Experiments on Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, and HY-WorldPlay show that TGuide preserves generation quality while achieving denoising speedups of up to $1.89\times$ over the original 4-step generators. On Self Forcing, TGuide generalizes from 81-frame training videos to 333-frame generation, approximately four times the training length, while exceeding the original model's VBench score.
authors: Zhuo Chen, Bin Zou, Fanyue Wei, Lixin Duan, Angela Yao, Wen Li
bullets: Addresses feature-caching failures caused by large changes between the few remaining denoising steps.

Applies spatial retrieval and adaptive correction to improve velocity prediction across large denoising gaps.
Trains on its own autoregressive rollouts to reduce error accumulation across denoising steps and video chunks.
Evaluated on Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, and HY-WorldPlay; on Self Forcing, it generates 333-frame videos from 81-frame training videos while exceeding the original model’s VBench score.
